forks.description: Personal AI Infrastructure for upgrading humans.
forks.summary:
# Technical Briefing: Personal_AI_Infrastructure

## The Problem
This repository represents four self-contained projects—Releases, Packs, Tools, and Bundles—rather than a unified codebase. At 1,548 files with 2137 functions and 622 classes across TypeScript, Vue, and Shell, the structure reflects a portfolio of AI-enabled tools rather than a single product. For a technical client, the challenge is navigating this fragmented architecture to identify where value can be extracted or risk managed.

## What This Does
The repository organizes around four domains: **Releases** (955 files, 187 code files) distributes versioned AI skill packages; **Packs** (541 files, 156 code files) contains modular skill implementations including browser automation, agent frameworks, and observability; **Tools** (10 files, 4 code files) provides CLI and hook-system utilities; and **Bundles** (5 files, 1 code file) offers opinionated installations. Recurring techniques across projects include browser-skill patterns (iframeClick/iframeFill in `Packs/pai-browser-skill/src/skills/Browser/index.ts`), hook-system orchestration (`Packs/pai-hook-system/src/hooks/lib/IdealState.ts`), and agent factory logic (`Packs/pai-agents-skill/src/skills/Agents/Tools/AgentFactory.ts`). The code touches databases (7 functions), files (11 functions), models (5 functions via replicate.run/anthropic), and outbound networks (3 functions).

## How It Is Wired
Execution originates at `main` in `Bundles/Official/install.ts:548`, which reaches 399 functions and is itself called from 1 place. The most connected entry point is `fetch` at `Packs/pai-observability-server/src/Observability/apps/server/src/index.ts:52`, called from 54 places. Traced paths show two shortest routes to external effects: `iframeClick -> click -> sessionCommand -> fetch -> createTheme -> getThemes` [db via `db.prepare`], and `main -> generateWithFlux` [model via `replicate.run`]. The internal call graph contains 1,534 resolved edges between self-contained modules; no circular dependencies exist across the 438 analyzed code files. Hub modules with high fan-in include `Packs/pai-observability-server/src/Observability/apps/client/src/types` (Ca: 10, Ce: 0) and `Packs/pai-hook-system/src/hooks/lib/paths` (Ca: 9, Ce: 0). Files with the widest blast radius include `Packs/pai-browser-skill/src/skills/Browser/index.ts` (46 functions, called from 4 files) and `Bundles/Official/install.ts` (calls into 64 functions).

## How To Use It
**Setup:** No Dockerfile or single build command exists across the four projects. Each project requires its own package management—the `package.json` files in `Packs/pai-agents-skill/src/skills/Agents/Tools/`, `Packs/pai-browser-skill/src/skills/Browser/`, and `Packs/pai-observability-server/src/Observability/apps/client/` imply pnpm or npm install steps. No lockfile is committed; verify dependency reproducibility before production use.

**Configuration:** Environment variables are defined in `.env.example` at the root. The observability server requires database setup referenced in its `package.json` and `vite.config.ts` configs. Browser-skill packs reference Claude Code API tokens in `.github/workflows/claude.yml`.

**Running it:** To invoke the primary entry point, execute the `main` function from `Bundles/Official/install.ts`. For pack development, use the individual pack directories' build scripts. For observability, start the server from `Packs/pai-observability-server/src/Observability/apps/server/src/index.ts`.

## Real-World Use
A practical scenario: an organization wants to deploy browser-automation capabilities across user workstations. The `Packs/pai-browser-skill/src/skills/Browser/Tools/BrowserSession.ts` defines `saveState`, `cleanup`, and `checkIdleTimeout` functions callable from 34 other files. A developer can instantiate a `BrowserSession`, invoke `launch` to open a page, use `iframeFill` at line 474 to populate form fields, then `sessionCommand` to persist state. The path reaches `fetch` (called from 54 places) to interact with external services, and writes to the ideal state store via `appendStateUpdate` in `Packs/pai-hook-system/src/hooks/lib/IdealState.ts`. Database changes propagate through `readIdealState` → `appendStateUpdate` → persistence in the hook system's YAML-backed store.

## Code Health & Issues
Static analysis of 438 code files identified 80 findings across 4 kinds:

- **Duplicated code blocks** — 28,287 repeated 6-line blocks across 384 files, including `.claude/statusline-command.sh`, `Packs/pai-statusline/src/statusline-command.sh`, and `Packs/pai-agents-skill/src/skills/Agents/Tools/AgentFactory.ts`. Fix: extract shared helpers; DRY the repeated logic.
- **High branching density** — 33 files with dense decision points, notably `Packs/pai-hook-system/src/skills/CORE/Tools/TranscriptParser.ts` (89 branch points over 235 lines) and `Packs/pai-observability-server/src/Observability/apps/client/src/components/AgentSwimLane.vue`. Fix: decompose decision-heavy logic; consider table/strategy dispatch.
- **Oversized files** — 13 files exceeding 600 lines, including `Packs/pai-observability-server/src/Observability/apps/client/src/components/AgentSwimLane.vue` (607 lines). Fix: split into cohesive units by responsibility.
- **Deep nesting** — 14 files with max indentation depth of 7, including `Packs/pai-art-skill/src/skills/Art/Tools/Generate.ts` and `Packs/pai-observability-server/src/Observability/apps/client/src/utils/chartRenderer.ts`. Fix: flatten with early returns/guard clauses.

SDLC observations: no lockfile exists beside the `Packs/pai-agents-skill/src/skills/Agents/Tools/package.json` manifest; GitHub Actions workflows lack test invocation steps; 16 manifests have no Dependabot/ Renovate configuration; a 7.6MB `ul-circuit-embossed-v5.png` in `Releases/v2.3/.claude/skills/CORE/USER/TERMINAL/` is not LFS-tracked; the test suite covers 2 files against 395 source files (ratio 0.005); and secrets (`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`) are stored in `.github/workflows/claude.yml` with fork-triggerable workflows.

## The Bottom Line
This is a portfolio-grade collection of four loosely coupled AI infrastructure projects rather than a single product. The browser-skill and hook-system patterns are the most reusable technical assets, and the code health audit reveals significant SDLC gaps: unpinned GitHub Actions, missing lockfile, minimal test coverage, and committed secrets in fork-triggerable workflows. Teams seeking modular AI skill packs with browser automation capabilities can extract value here, but should expect to establish their own CI/CD, dependency management, and secret-handling practices. The repository is best suited for organizations wanting to assemble custom AI tooling from proven primitives, not those needing an out-of-the-box integrated system.

forks.name: feathr
forks.description: Feathr – A scalable, unified data and AI engineering platform for enterprise
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Data‑science teams need a reproducible way to define, materialize, and serve feature pipelines at scale while keeping the same logic across batch, streaming, and online inference. Maintaining separate codebases for transformation, registry, and UI quickly becomes a coordination nightmare and introduces hidden drift between development and production.

## What This Does  
Feathr is a modular platform that bundles the core feature‑store engine (`feathr-impl`), configuration helpers (`feathr-config`), a Python‑centric client library (`feathr_project`), a React UI (`ui`), and three registry back‑ends (`registry/*`). The Python client (`feathr_project/feathrcli/cli.py`) lets users declare feature transformations in pure Python, registers them via the registry services (`registry/purview-registry/main.py`, `registry/sql-registry/main.py`), and materializes results on Spark clusters (`feathr-compute`). The UI (`ui/src/components/...`) provides a visual catalog and lineage view. All components are packaged as Docker images (`FeathrSandbox.Dockerfile`, `FeathrRegistry.Dockerfile`) and orchestrated through Gradle builds (`feathr-impl/build.gradle`, etc.).

## How It Is Wired  
* **Entry point** – `feathr_project/feathrcli/cli.py` parses the CLI, loads `feathr_project/feathr/client.py`, and builds a `FeatureRegistry` object.  
* **Client → Registry** – `client.py` imports `feathr_project/feathr/registry/_feature_registry_purview.py` (the largest file, 1,222 LOC) or the SQL variant, which contact the respective service via HTTP/REST.  
* **Registry → Compute** – Registry services (`registry/*/main.py`) forward materialization requests to the compute layer (`feathr-compute/src/main/scala/...`) which launches Spark jobs using `feathr_project/feathr/spark_provider/_databricks_submission.py`.  
* **Compute → Data** – Spark jobs read raw sources (e.g., Hive, Azure Blob) and write feature tables back to the same storage, leveraging the `pandas`‑based utilities in `feathr_project/feathr/utils/`.  
* **UI ↔ Registry** – The React UI (`ui/src/components/FlowGraph/...`) calls the registry REST endpoints to list features and display lineage. The most‑connected UI module is `ui/src/components/FlowGraph/interface` (4 inbound imports, 0 outbound).  
* **Dependency graph** – 222 internal modules, 66 import edges, no cycles. The hub `feathr_project/feathr/__init__` imports 20 other modules but is not imported itself, indicating a low‑risk, low‑coupling entry point.  
* **Build & Deploy** – Gradle compiles the Scala/Java core (`feathr-impl`, `feathr-config`, `feathr-data-models`). The UI is built with npm (`package.json` implied by the presence of `npm` as the package manager). Dockerfiles produce self‑contained images; the sandbox image is the recommended quick‑start.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/feathr.git
cd feathr

# Build core libraries (requires Java 11+ and Gradle)
./gradlew build            # compiles all *.gradle projects

# Build the UI (requires Node 16+)
cd ui && npm ci && npm run build && cd ..

# Build the sandbox container (includes UI, client, compute)
docker build -f FeathrSandbox.Dockerfile -t feathr-sandbox:latest .

# Run the sandbox (ports: UI 80, Jupyter 8888, Interpret 7080)
docker run -it --rm -p 8888:8888 -p 8081:80 -p 7080:7080 \
  -e GRANT_SUDO=yes feathr-sandbox:latest
```

*Configuration* – The sandbox expects environment files under `registry/access_control/.env` and `ui/.env`. Those files are currently committed and must be removed (see health section). Production deployments replace them with secure secret stores (Azure Key Vault, etc.).

*Running a feature pipeline* – After the container is up, use the CLI inside the sandbox:

```bash
python -m feathrcli register -f examples/feature_definition.py
python -m feathrcli materialize -f my_feature_anchor
```

The CLI invokes `feathr_project/feathr/client.py`, which talks to the registry service and triggers a Spark job via the compute module.

## Real‑World Use  
A data‑science team can define a time‑window aggregation in `my_feature_anchor.py`, register it with `feathrcli register`, and then schedule nightly materializations through Azure Data Factory. The UI shows the feature lineage, allowing model owners to audit point‑in‑time joins before training. Because the same Python definition drives both offline materialization and online serving, drift is eliminated.

## Code Health & Issues  

**Measured static‑analysis findings (97 total)**  
- **High – Deep nesting** (46 instances, e.g., `feathr_project/feathr/definition/feature.py`) – flatten with early returns.  
- **High – Duplicated blocks** (1570 lines across 217 files) – extract shared helpers.  
- **High – Oversized files** (3 files > 1 k LOC) – split into focused modules.  
- **Medium – Broad exception handling** (8 files) – catch specific exceptions.  
- **Medium – File opened without context manager** (2 files) – use `with open(...)`.  

**Code‑health audit (12 findings)**  
- **High** – Pin GitHub Actions to commit SHAs (`.github/workflows/*`).  
- **High** – Add a lockfile beside `feathr_project/pyproject.toml`.  
- **High** – Remove committed `.env` files (`registry/access_control/.env`, `ui/.env*`) and rotate credentials.  
- **High** – CI does not run the test suite; add a test step to the existing workflows.  
- **Medium** – Declare least‑privilege `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions.  
- **Medium** – Enable Dependabot or Renovate for dependency updates.  
- **Medium** – Pin Docker base images by digest (`registry/purview-registry/Dockerfile`).  
- **Medium** – Add a dependency‑vulnerability scan to PR checks.  
- **Medium** – Expand the README (currently 236 bytes).  
- **Medium** – Set `persist-credentials: false` on the checkout step of the PyPI publish workflow.  

No critical findings were reported, but the presence of committed secrets and missing CI test execution are immediate blockers for production use.

## The Bottom Line  
Feathr delivers a complete, enterprise‑grade feature‑store stack with clear separation of concerns across compute, registry, client, and UI. The codebase is functional but suffers from maintainability issues (deep nesting, duplicated logic) and several security‑related hygiene problems that must be remedied before adopting it in a regulated environment. Teams comfortable managing multi‑language builds (Java/Scala, Python, TypeScript) and Docker deployments can extract immediate value, provided they address the high‑severity health findings.

forks.name: MirageKit
forks.description: Peer to Peer screen sharing framework from macOS to iPadOS, visionOS, and macOS
forks.summary:
## The Problem

Streaming a macOS screen to another Apple device normally means either Apple's own AirPlay (which is locked down and not embeddable) or a third-party service that routes traffic through a relay server. MirageKit solves the embeddable, peer-to-peer problem: a macOS host captures windows or a virtual display, encodes HEVC, and pushes frames over UDP directly to a client on iPadOS, visionOS, or macOS — no server in the path.

## What This Does

MirageKit is a Swift Package that ships both sides of the stream. The host side (`Sources/MirageKit/Public/Host/`) captures via ScreenCaptureKit, encodes with `HEVCEncoder.swift`, and advertises over Bonjour (`BonjourAdvertiser.swift`). The client side (`Sources/MirageKit/Public/Client/`) discovers hosts, decodes with `HEVCDecoder.swift`, and renders through `MetalRenderer.swift` inside SwiftUI views (`MirageStreamView.swift`, `MirageStreamContentView.swift`).

Input is forwarded back: `MirageHostInputController.swift` and the `Public/Input/` types (`MirageMouseEvent.swift`, `MirageKeyEvent.swift`) carry mouse, keyboard, and gesture events from client to host. The framework also handles virtual displays (`CGVirtualDisplayBridge.swift`), remote unlock (`UnlockManager.swift`), and menu-bar passthrough (`MenuBarMonitor.swift`).

## How It Is Wired

The static import graph resolved 0 internal modules and 0 import edges across 76 files, so the module wiring has not been mapped for this repository yet — the flow below is traced from the README and file structure, not from a resolved call graph.

Execution starts at `MirageHostService.start()` (`Sources/MirageKit/Public/Host/MirageHostService.swift`). From there the host advertises `_mirage._tcp` via Bonjour, accepts TCP control connections, and streams video over UDP with clients registering stream IDs. The client entry point is `MirageClientService.connect(to:)` (`Sources/MirageKit/Public/Client/MirageClientService.swift`). The network boundary is crossed in `HybridTransport.swift` and `ConnectionManager.swift` (TCP control + UDP video); the capture boundary in `WindowCaptureEngine.swift` (ScreenCaptureKit); the display boundary in `CGVirtualDisplayBridge.swift` (virtual display creation).

`MirageHostService.swift` is the widest blast radius — it is split across nine `+` extension files (`+AppStreaming`, `+DesktopStreaming`, `+Input`, `+VirtualDisplay`, etc.), and `StreamContext.swift` at 1,299 lines carries the session state everything else touches. A change in either ripples across most of the host.

## How To Use It

Add it as an SPM dependency, per the README:

```swift
.package(url: "https://github.com/EthanLipnik/MirageKit.git", from: "0.0.1"),
```

Requirements from the README: macOS 26+ for host streaming, iOS 26+ / visionOS 26+ for clients, Swift 6.2+. Host setup is `try await hostService.start()` with a `MirageHostDelegate`; client setup is `try await clientService.connect(to: host)` then `requestWindowList()`. No environment variables or config files are documented — configuration lives in Swift code (`MirageStreamingSettings.swift`, `MirageAppPreferences.swift`). The README notes this is active development with possible breaking changes.

## Real-World Use

A Mac app that shares a specific window to an iPad: the host creates a `MirageHostService`, the client discovers it via Bonjour, requests the window list, and renders the decoded `CVPixelBuffer` in a `MirageStreamView`. Input events from the client's SwiftUI view route back through `MirageHostInputController` to the captured app.

## Code Health & Issues

From static analysis (not opinion), 66 findings across 76 Swift files: 11 high, 50 medium, 5 low.

- **High** — Deep nesting (25 occurrences): max indentation depth 8 in `WindowCaptureEngine.swift`, `StreamContext.swift`, `MirageClientService.swift`. Fix with early returns/guard clauses.
- **High** — Duplicated code: 35 repeated 6-line blocks across 15 files, including `StreamController.swift` and `MirageStreamContentView.swift`. Extract shared helpers.
- **High** — Oversized files (7): `StreamContext.swift` at 1,299 lines; `MirageClientService.swift` and `MirageStreamView.swift` also flagged. Split by responsibility.
- **Medium** — High branching density (27): `CursorMonitor.swift` has 29 branch points over 66 lines. Consider strategy dispatch.
- **High** — No CI: 76 source files, no workflow builds or tests anything. Add a build+test workflow on push and pull_request.
- **Medium** — Tests: 1 test file against 76 source files (ratio 0.013). The suite cannot cover this codebase; add tests to the highest fan-in modules first.

## The Bottom Line

The architecture is sound — clean separation of capture, encode, transport, and render, with a sensible public API. The risk is engineering discipline: no CI, nearly no tests, and several files too large to hold in one head. Use it if you need embeddable Apple-to-Apple P2P streaming and can absorb the maintenance cost of a pre-1.0 framework.

forks.name: spectre
forks.description: GPU-accelerated Factors analysis library and Backtester
forks.summary:
## The Problem

Factor research and backtesting in Python traditionally run on CPU. The `zipline.pipeline` engine takes seconds to evaluate a single factor on a few thousand assets. This repo attacks that bottleneck with GPU-accelerated factor computation, claiming 30–70x speedups over `zipline` in its own benchmarks.

## What This Does

`spectre` is a GPU-accelerated factors library and backtester built on PyTorch. The `spectre/factors/` package provides a factor engine (`engine.py`), factor primitives (`basic.py`, `statistical.py`, `technical.py`), and filter/label classes. The `spectre/data/` package handles data ingestion from CSV, Arrow, Yahoo, Quandl, and IEX sources. The `spectre/trading/` package covers the backtest side: portfolio, position, blotter, events, and stop models.

The README positions it as compatible with `alphalens` and `pyfolio`, and the codebase is pure Python over PyTorch tensors, so it integrates with deep learning models directly.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts at `run` in `spectre/factors/engine.py:410`, which reaches 174 functions — the largest reach of any entry point in the repo. The engine calls into `compute`, which fans out to `agg` (21 call sites), `nanmean` (17), `nansum` (10), and `unmasked_sum` (9). The `FactorEngine` class is called from 22 places, and `CsvDirLoader` from 25.

The dependency hub is `spectre/factors/factor.py`: 140 functions, 44 classes, imported by 25 files. It defines the operator overrides (`__add__`, `__mul__`, etc.) that make factor expressions composable. Its blast radius is the widest in the repo — change it and most of the factor system moves.

The cost of that centrality is visible in the module graph: `factor.py`, `engine.py`, `basic.py`, and `trading/__init__.py` all sit inside circular import cycles (16 modules total). Anyone modifying these files must track mutually-reachable imports, which makes refactoring slow and error-prone.

File-by-file map:

- `spectre/factors/factor.py` — factor expression base, operator overloading, the hub
- `spectre/parallel/algorithmic.py` — tensor operations, split/revert/padding, 58 functions
- `spectre/factors/filter.py` — filter and selection primitives
- `spectre/trading/blotter.py` — trade recording and metrics, 64 functions
- `spectre/factors/engine.py` — the run orchestration, data loading, caching
- `spectre/data/arrow.py` — the only file that both reads/writes files and makes an outbound network call (ingest)

## How To Use It

Setup requires Python 3.7+, PyTorch 1.3+, and Pandas 1.0+. The README documents:

```bash
pip install --no-deps git+git://github.com/Heerozh/spectre.git
conda install pytorch torchvision torchaudio cudatoolkit=11.0 -c pytorch
conda install pyarrow pandas tqdm plotly requests bs4 lxml
```

The quick-start path: ingest data with `YahooDownloader.ingest()`, load it via `ArrowLoader`, build a `FactorEngine`, add factors, call `engine.run(start, end)`. The full example is in `examples/dual_ema_on_apple.py` and `examples/smart_beta.py`. Configuration lives in `spectre/config.py`.

## Real-World Use

A typical workflow: download 5 years of S&P 500 data, load it into an `ArrowLoader`, attach a momentum factor (`EMA` shift/sum per the README's Barra example), run the engine over a date range, and feed the resulting factor values into `alphalens` for analysis. The same `FactorEngine` can move to CUDA with `engine.to_cuda()` for large universes.

## Code Health & Issues

Static analysis (not opinion) found 53 issues: 33 high, 20 medium.

- **High — deep nesting (31 occurrences):** `spectre/factors/factor.py`, `spectre/data/dataloader.py`, `spectre/factors/engine.py` reach indentation depth 11. Control flow is hard to follow; fix with guard clauses and extracted inner blocks.
- **High — import cycles (16 modules):** `factor.py`, `engine.py`, `basic.py` participate in circular imports. Breaking these requires extracting shared types or deferring imports.
- **High — oversized files (3):** `factor.py` at 909 lines, plus `blotter.py` and `test_factor.py`. Changes ripple widely.
- **Medium — file opened without context manager (2):** `spectre/data/quandl.py`, `setup.py` — potential handle leaks.
- **Medium — duplicated code:** 11 repeated 6-line blocks across 6 files including both examples and `spectre/data/csv.py`.

SDLC gaps: no CI/CD pipeline exists, so nothing runs the build or tests on merge. Dependencies are pinned in `requirements.txt` without a lockfile, so builds are not reproducible. Tests exist (59 files) but are not gated by automation.

## The Bottom Line

The factor engine is genuinely fast and the API is clean for expression-style factor construction. The trade-off is code quality: circular imports and deep nesting make `factor.py` and `engine.py` expensive to modify safely. Use it if you need GPU factor throughput and can tolerate a codebase that needs careful refactoring before substantial changes.

forks.name: nautilus_trader
forks.description: A high-performance algorithmic trading platform and event-driven backtester
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Quantitative traders need a single code‑base that can back‑test strategies on historic market data **and** run them live without rewriting logic. Existing stacks force separate back‑tester and execution engines, leading to drift between simulation and production results.

## What This Does  
`nautilus_trader` delivers a Rust‑centric, event‑driven engine with a Python front‑end. Core trading logic lives in the `crates/` workspace (≈1 560 Rust source files) while the `python/` package supplies a thin, idiomatic API for strategy authors.  

Key entry points are in `crates/adapters/architect_ax`:
* `crates/adapters/architect_ax/bin/http_public.rs` – `main` starts the HTTP server that exposes the public API.  
* `crates/adapters/architect_ax/src/data.rs` – `start` boots the internal data pipelines.  

Adapters for major venues (Binance, Bybit, BitMEX, etc.) live under `crates/adapters/…` and implement SBE codecs (e.g. `exchange_info_response_codec.rs`) that marshal binary messages to Rust structs.

## How It Is Wired  

1. **Process start** – `main` in `http_public.rs` (line 32) is the only top‑level entry point. It creates an `AxEnvironment` via `from_env`, which reads secrets (`Secrets::from_env()`) – the sole outbound **cryptographic** operation.  

2. **Environment bootstrap** – `from_env` pulls configuration from `.env.example` (API keys, URLs). The environment is then passed to the HTTP client (`crates/adapters/architect_ax/src/http/client.rs`), which owns the only network‑calling code (e.g., `base_url`, `cancel_all_requests`).  

3. **Message flow** – Incoming HTTP requests are dispatched to handlers in `crates/adapters/architect_ax/src/websocket/…`. The most‑used functions across the codebase are:
   * `from_str` – 259 call sites  
   * `get_buf`, `get_buf_mut`, `set_limit` – each >200 call sites (used by every SBE codec)  

   These buffer utilities form a **hub**: any change to their signature ripples through >600 functions, so they carry the widest blast radius.  

4. **Adapter codecs** – The Binance SBE codecs (e.g., `exchange_info_response_codec.rs`, `new_order_full_response_codec.rs`) each define `wrap`, `encoded_length`, `get_buf_mut`, etc. They are called from 5–36 other files and collectively account for >1 200 function definitions.  

5. **External effects** – Apart from the initial secret load, the only outbound calls are:
   * HTTP client requests (network)  
   * File reads/writes (e.g., loading test JSON via `load_test_json`) – 2 functions  
   * Cryptographic secret handling – 7 functions  

   No database access is visible in the static graph; persistence is likely delegated to external services not compiled into the repo.

6. **Cycle / hub analysis** – The call graph shows dense inter‑connections around the buffer utilities and SBE codec wrappers, but no obvious cycles. The concentration around `from_str` and buffer helpers suggests any refactor there will require extensive test coverage.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/nautilus_trader
cd nautilus_trader

# Build the Rust workspace (requires Rust 1.92)
cargo build --release

# Optional: run the Docker environment (DockerfileUbuntu + compose)
docker compose -f .docker/docker-compose.yml up --build

# Set required env vars (copy template)
cp .env.example .env
# edit .env with API keys, URLs, etc.

# Start the HTTP server (the documented entry point)
cargo run --bin http_public --manifest-path crates/adapters/architect_ax/Cargo.toml
```

The Python package can be installed from the `python/` directory with `pip install .` after the Rust wheels are built (see `github/actions/publish-wheels` workflow for the exact build steps).

## Real‑World Use  
A quant writes a strategy in Python, imports `nautilus_trader`, and registers callbacks with the HTTP API. The same code can be executed against a historical data feed by pointing the `AxEnvironment` to a file‑based data source, then switched to live trading by swapping the environment to use the Binance adapter. No code changes are required between back‑test and live runs.

## Code Health & Issues  

- **Medium – Enable Dependabot** – 38 manifests lack an automated update bot (`.github/dependabot.yml` missing).  
- **Medium – Dependency vulnerability gate** – No scan in CI; add `dependency-review-action` or `osv-scanner`.  
- **Medium – Large test assets** – `tests/integration_tests/adapters/betfair/resources/responses/betting_list_market_catalogue.json` (41 MB) should be moved to Git LFS or external storage.  
- **Low – Workflow timeouts** – `.github/workflows/build-docs.yml` and three others lack `timeout-minutes`, risking stalled runs.

All other hygiene checks (tests, CI, Dockerfile, license, lockfile) are present.

## The Bottom Line  
`nautilus_trader` offers a solid, high‑performance Rust engine with a Python façade, suitable for teams that need tight parity between simulation and production. The codebase is well‑structured but hinges on a few core utilities (`from_str`, buffer helpers) that are hot spots for change. Addressing the medium‑severity health items (dependency automation, large binaries) will improve maintainability for production deployments. Ideal for quant teams comfortable with Rust‑Python interop and looking for an open‑source, event‑driven trading stack.

forks.name: maptoposter
forks.description: Transform your favorite cities into beautiful, minimalist designs. MapToPoster lets you create and export visually striking map posters with code.
forks.summary:
## The Problem
Generating a stylized map poster normally means GIS tooling, a design editor, or a paid API. This repo collapses that into one CLI command: give it a city, a country, and a theme, and it renders a minimalist PNG poster locally.

## What This Does
The entire program is a single script, `create_map_poster.py`, containing 11 functions. It resolves a city's coordinates, loads a visual theme from `themes/*.json` (17 themes), and renders a poster to `posters/` with a timestamped filename. Three Roboto font files in `fonts/` handle typography.

Themes are pure JSON data — color palettes, edge styling, and per-feature rules — so adding a theme requires no code changes. The README documents 20+ example invocations across cities and themes.

## How It Is Wired
Execution starts at the CLI in `create_map_poster.py`. `create_poster` is the hub: it calls `create_gradient_fade` (twice), `get_edge_colors_by_type`, and `get_edge_widths_by_type`, and the pipeline resolves coordinates through `get_coordinates`. `load_theme` reads the JSON theme, `load_fonts` loads the font faces, and `generate_output_filename` names the output PNG. Two functions touch the filesystem.

`get_available_themes` is the most reused helper, called from 2 places including `list_themes`. The module graph is a single node with zero import edges and no cycles, so the blast radius is contained: change `create_poster` and you affect the whole render path; everything else is leaf code. A theme lookup or font change touches nothing downstream.

## How To Use It
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
python create_map_poster.py -c "New York" -C "USA" -t noir -d 12000
python create_map_poster.py --list-themes
```

Configuration is theme JSON only — no environment variables or API keys are required. The `-d` flag sets radius in meters (4000–6000 for dense centers, 15000–20000 for full metros). Output lands in `posters/` as a dated PNG.

## Real-World Use
A print shop or design studio can script poster generation for client cities: loop over a city list, pick a theme per city, and batch-render. The `--list-themes` flag plus the JSON theme files make it easy to preview and extend the palette without touching the render code.

## Code Health & Issues
Static analysis found 1 finding (0 high, 1 medium):

- **Medium/Resilience** — Broad exception handling in `create_map_poster.py`: bare `except` swallows errors indiscriminately. Fix: catch specific exceptions; re-raise or log the rest.
- **Medium/Supply chain** — No Dependabot or Renovate configured for `requirements.txt`; advisories go unpatched until a manual audit.
- **Medium/Repo hygiene** — Large binaries committed: `posters/tokyo_japanese_ink_20260108_165830.png` is 15.9MB, with 12 blobs over 5MB total. Move to Git LFS or object storage to avoid paying for them on every clone and CI checkout.

SDLC gaps: no test files, no CI pipeline, and `requirements.txt` has no lockfile, so builds are not reproducible.

## The Bottom Line
A clean, single-purpose tool with a well-separated theme system — adding a theme is trivial and the CLI is well documented. The gaps are operational: no tests, no CI, no dependency pinning, and multi-megabyte PNGs bloating the repo. Fine for generating posters; not something to build infrastructure on without hardening first.

forks.name: personalized-recommender-course
forks.description: 👕 Open-source course on architecting, building and deploying a real-time personalized recommender for H&M fashion articles.
forks.summary:
Here's a concise, professional technical briefing for the `personalized-recommender-course` repository, written in the style of a senior AI engineer consultant report.

---

## The Problem

This repository delivers a hands-on course for building a real-time personalized recommender for H&M fashion articles. It spans feature engineering, two-tower neural network training, MLOps via Hopsworks, KServe deployment, and a Streamlit web interface. While the scope is broad and the educational value is clear, the codebase shows several structural and quality concerns that would need addressing before it could safely power a production system.

## What This Does

The repository implements a 5-module FTI (Feature/Training/Inference) architecture using Hopsworks Feature Store, two-tower embedding models, and vector-based real-time inference. Core workflows are concentrated in `recsys/training/two_tower.py` (23 functions, 8 types), `recsys/inference/llm_ranking_predictor.py` (6 functions, 2 classes), and `recsys/ui/recommenders.py` (9 functions). Data flows through `recsys/features/` for preprocessing, `recsys/hopsworks_integration/` for store interaction, and `recsys/ui/` for the Streamlit frontend. The system reads H&M raw data, computes features, trains user/item embeddings, registers models, and serves recommendations via a KServe-backed online pipeline.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts at `streamlit_app.py:103` (`main`), which reaches 37 downstream functions. The internal call graph shows 137 resolved call edges. Key entry points and their callers:

- `get_feature_store` – called from 4 places; participates in a circular import with `recsys/hopsworks_integration/feature_store.py`
- `predict` – called from 4 places; invoked via `llm_recommendations -> should_show_item x3`
- `sample` – called from 3 places; feeds `compute_ranking_dataset`
- `should_show_item` – called from 3 places; called by `llm_recommendations x3` and `customer_recommendations x2`
- `df_to_ds` – called from 2 places; used by `get_train_val_split`
- `get_model` – called from 2 places; feeds `deploy -> get_model x2`
- `track` – called from 2 places; invoked by `display_item x2` and `display_llm_item x2`

The most connected module is `recsys/config` (Ca=10, Ce=0, instability=0), followed by `recsys/ui/recommenders` (instability=0.8) and `streamlit_app` (instability=1, Ce=5). Two circular import cycles exist involving `recsys/hopsworks_integration/__init__.py` and `recsys/hopsworks_integration/feature_store.py`, which increases cognitive load when tracing dependencies.

The traced exit from the process goes through `main -> customer_recommendations -> predict [model via self.llm.invoke]`, indicating the LLM-powered ranker makes an outbound model call. File I/O and network calls are limited but present: `recsys/ui/utils.py` opens files without a context manager, and several functions make network calls to Hopsworks.

## How To Use It

**Setup**: This is a Python project. Install with `pip install -e .` or `uv pip install -e .` from the root, as `pyproject.toml` is present. No Dockerfile exists; local Python 3.x is the intended runtime.

**Configuration**: Environment variables and secrets are expected in `.env.example`. The `.github/workflows/ml_pipelines.yaml` workflow references secrets and has no `permissions` declaration and no `timeout-minutes`. The code-health audit confirms secret-shaped paths are present in `assets/github_actions_secrets.png`.

**Running it**: Start the Streamlit demo with `streamlit run streamlit_app.py`. The live demo is hosted at https://decodingml-hands-on-personalized-recommender.streamlit.app/ but runs in 0-cost mode, scaling to 0 instances during idle periods and requiring 1–2 minutes to warm on first interaction.

## Real-World Use

This codebase is suited for learning, prototyping, and coursework. A practical scenario: a data science team clones the repo, populates the Hopsworks feature store with H&M interaction data, trains the two-tower model via the notebooks, and iterates on the LLM ranking logic in `recsys/hopsworks_integration/llm_ranking_serving.py`. The Streamlit app provides a quick UI for testing recommendations per user. Because no test suite exists, changes to feature engineering or model logic carry regression risk.

## Code Health & Issues

The measured code health audit (5 findings, 0 critical) identifies:

forks.name: x-algorithm
forks.description: Algorithm powering the For You feed on X
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
The “For You” feed must merge two very different content sources—posts from accounts a user follows (Thunder) and globally retrieved posts (Phoenix)—and rank them in real‑time. Maintaining low latency while applying a heavy transformer model and many hydration/filter steps creates a high‑maintenance codebase that is hard to reason about and test.

## What This Does  
The repository is a portfolio of four self‑contained services:

* **home‑mixer** – orchestration layer that hydrates queries, runs candidate sources, applies filters and scorers, then returns a ranked list. Core files: `home-mixer/main.rs`, `home-mixer/lib.rs`, `home-mixer/candidate_hydrators/*`, `home-mixer/filters/*`, `home-mixer/scorers/*`.  
* **thunder** – provides in‑network posts and low‑level storage. Entry points: `thunder/main.rs` and `thunder/lib.rs`; key logic in `thunder/posts/post_store.rs` and `thunder/kafka/tweet_events_listener_v2.rs`.  
* **candidate‑pipeline** – a reusable pipeline that can be invoked by either home‑mixer or external services. Entry point: `candidate-pipeline/candidate_pipeline.rs` (function `execute`). Handles request IDs, source selection, hydration, filtering, scoring and post‑selection.  
* **phoenix** – Python wrapper around the Grok‑based transformer model used for scoring. Declared in `phoenix/pyproject.toml`; runtime code lives in `phoenix/grok.py` and related modules.

All four share a common data model (candidate structs, filters, scorers) defined across the Rust crates.

## How It Is Wired  

1. **Start** – `home-mixer/main.rs` (line 30) launches the service and calls the orchestration function chain (≈19 functions).  
2. **Query Hydration** – `home-mixer/query_hydrators/user_action_seq_query_hydrator.rs` builds a `PureCoreData` struct (via `home-mixer/candidate_pipeline/candidate_features.rs`).  
3. **Candidate Sources** –  
   * In‑network: `thunder/posts/post_store.rs` (`new`, `insert_posts`, `mark_as_deleted`).  
   * Out‑of‑network: `phoenix/run_retrieval.rs` (calls the Grok model in `phoenix/grok.py`).  
4. **Pipeline Execution** – `candidate-pipeline/candidate_pipeline.rs`’s `execute` function (line 53) is the central hub; it reaches 34 distinct functions, invoking:  
   * `hydrate` → `fetch_vf_results` (candidate‑pipeline/hydrator.rs)  
   * `filter` → `filter` (candidate‑pipeline/filter.rs) – called from 10 places overall  
   * `score` → `apply` (home‑mixer/scorers/phoenix_scorer.rs) – 19 calls from `compute_weighted_score`  
   * `select` → `selector` (candidate‑pipeline/selector.rs)  
   * `post_selection_hydrators` and `post_selection_filters` (home‑mixer) for final trimming.  
5. **Scoring** – `home-mixer/scorers/phoenix_scorer.rs` invokes the Python model via a FFI bridge (not shown in the static graph) and produces engagement probabilities.  
6. **Response** – `home-mixer/server.rs` serializes the ranked list back to the client.

**Blast‑radius hotspots** – `filter`, `request_id`, and `hydrate` appear in the highest fan‑in lists (10, 5, 2 callers respectively). Changing their signatures or side‑effects will ripple through many modules. The import graph shows no circular dependencies, but the call graph contains deep nesting (max depth 8) in files such as `thunder/kafka/tweet_events_listener_v2.rs` and `candidate-pipeline/candidate_pipeline.rs`, increasing cognitive load for modifications.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/x-algorithm
cd x-algorithm

# Build all Rust crates
cargo build --workspace

# Run unit tests (only 2 currently)
cargo test --workspace

# Install the Python scoring component (optional, needed for Phoenix scoring)
cd phoenix
pip install -e .
```

*No Dockerfile or Makefile is present; the build relies on Cargo for Rust and pip/uv for Python.*  
Configuration files are not shipped in the repo; the service expects runtime environment variables for database connections, Kafka endpoints, and model paths (these are referenced in `thunder/kafka/*` and `phoenix/run_ranker.rs`). Without them the binaries will panic on start.

## Real‑World Use  
A production feed request hits the home‑mixer HTTP server (`home-mixer/server.rs`). The server hydrates the user context, calls `candidate-pipeline::execute`, which pulls recent tweets from Thunder, retrieves candidates from Phoenix, runs the transformer scoring, applies deduplication and relevance filters, then returns the top‑K list to the client. The entire path is bounded to a few hundred milliseconds on typical hardware.

## Code Health & Issues  

- **High – Add CI** – No workflow files; 72 source files are never built automatically.  
- **Medium – Enable Dependabot** – Only `phoenix/pyproject.toml` is present; no lockfile or bot config.  
- **Medium – Expand Test Suite** – 2 test files for 72 source files (≈2.8 % coverage).  

Additional observations from the static scan:  
- Deep nesting (max indent 8) in three Rust files makes control flow hard to follow.  
- Repeated 6‑line blocks across 19 hydrator files indicate duplicated logic.

## The Bottom Line  
The repo delivers a functional, modular For‑You feed pipeline with clear separation between ingestion (Thunder), retrieval (Phoenix) and ranking (home‑mixer). However, the codebase suffers from insufficient automated testing, missing CI/CD, and maintainability concerns (deep nesting and duplicated code). Teams that need a proven baseline for a recommendation stack can adopt it, but should invest early in CI, test expansion, and refactoring of the high‑complexity modules.

forks.name: xai-sdk-python
forks.description: The official Python SDK for the xAI API
forks.summary:
## The Problem

Applications that talk to xAI's models (Grok chat, image generation, embeddings, document collections) need a typed client that handles gRPC transport, auth, streaming, and message history. Without an SDK, each consumer re-implements that layer against raw protobuf stubs. This repo is the official Python SDK for that API surface.

## What This Does

The SDK is a gRPC-based Python library (Python 3.10+) exposing both synchronous (`xai_sdk.Client`) and asynchronous (`xai_sdk.AsyncClient`) clients. The `src/xai_sdk/` tree covers chat, image generation/understanding, files, collections, search, tokenizer, and telemetry. It ships generated protobuf code for two API versions under `src/xai_sdk/proto/v5/` and `v6/`.

The `examples/` folder has 36 runnable scripts mirroring every feature in both sync and async variants (e.g. `examples/sync/function_calling.py`, `examples/aio/stored_chat.py`). Tests live in `tests/`, including a mock gRPC server in `tests/server.py`.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts at `main` in `examples/aio/auth.py`, which reaches 179 functions. The hot path is short: `main` instantiates `Client` (called from 18 places) and makes a network call via `session.get` in two hops. The `create` function is the highest-blast-radius symbol, called from 117 places; `user` follows at 82. `src/xai_sdk/chat.py` is the core module: 68 functions, 6 classes, imported by 21 files. It owns `_make_chat`, `sample`, and message append logic.

The module graph shows `src/xai_sdk/proto/__init__.py` as a hub with 24 importers — churn there ripples widely. `tests/server.py` (52 functions, 13 classes) is the mock server that the test suite routes through. There are no circular dependencies across the 153 analyzed modules.

## How To Use It

**Setup** — install from PyPI:
```bash
pip install xai-sdk
# or
uv add xai-sdk
```

**Configuration** — the client reads the `XAI_API_KEY` environment variable by default; you can pass it explicitly via `Client(api_key=...)`.

**Running it** — instantiate the client and hold a chat session:
```python
from xai_sdk import Client
from xai_sdk.chat import system, user

client = Client()
chat = client.chat.create(model="grok-3", messages=[system("You are a pirate assistant.")])
chat.append(user("Hello"))
response = chat.sample()
print(response.content)
```

Full runnable examples are in `examples/sync/` and `examples/aio/`.

## Real-World Use

A support bot that persists conversation context: the `append`/`sample` loop manages history client-side while the API stays stateless. For long-running services, use the async client (`examples/aio/chat.py`) to avoid blocking on gRPC calls, and `chat.sample_batch` for offline processing.

## Code Health & Issues

Static analysis (not opinion) found 27 issues: 5 high, 22 medium, across 4 kinds.

- **High** – Oversized files: `src/xai_sdk/chat.py` (971 lines), `tests/server.py`, `tests/aio/chat_test.py`. High cognitive load; changes ripple widely.
- **High** – Duplicated code blocks: 3261 repeated 6-line blocks across 102 files, concentrated in the mirrored sync/async examples. Extract shared helpers.
- **High** – Deep nesting: max indentation depth 9 in `src/xai_sdk/chat.py`, `tests/server.py`, `examples/aio/function_calling.py`. Flatten with early returns.
- **Medium** – Hub modules: `src/xai_sdk/proto/__init__.py` (24 importers), `tests/__init__.py` (14), `src/xai_sdk/telemetry/__init__.py` (12). Keep stable and small.

SDLC gaps: no dependency lockfile (non-reproducible builds), no Dependabot/Renovate, no dependency vulnerability scan in CI, and workflow jobs lack `timeout-minutes`.

## The Bottom Line

A solid, well-tested official SDK with real coverage of the xAI API surface and both sync/async paths. The main costs are maintainability: duplicated example code and oversized core modules. Use it if you need Grok chat or xAI image/collection features from Python; just be prepared for slow merges on `chat.py`.

forks.name: rzweb
forks.description: A complete browser-based reverse engineering platform built on Rizin, running entirely client-side via WebAssembly.
forks.summary:
## The Problem

rzweb solves the accessibility problem of Rizin, the powerful reverse engineering framework, by bringing it to the browser via WebAssembly. Engineers can analyze binaries locally without installing Rizin or uploading files to remote servers, but the client-side architecture introduces maintainability concerns around code quality and deployment pipelines.

## What This Does

rzweb is a browser-based reverse engineering platform built on Rizin that runs entirely client-side via WebAssembly. The React + Tailwind frontend (53 source files in `src/`) provides views for terminal access, disassembly, control flow graphs, hex dumps, and string extraction. State management uses Zustand, the terminal is powered by xterm.js, and Rizin binaries are loaded from the companion `rzwasi` repository. Files are processed locally—binaries never leave the user's device—with supported formats including ELF, PE/PE+, Mach-O, and Raw. The project structure organizes code into `src/components` (UI and views), `src/lib/rizin` (Rizin integration), `src/lib/utils` (helpers), `src/stores` (state), `src/pages`, and `src/providers`. Entry points include `index.html`, `src/main.tsx`, and component index files that wire the UI together.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts at `src/providers/ThemeProvider.tsx:46` with the `handler` function, which reaches one function and is called by nothing else in the repo. The internal call graph contains 76 resolved call edges between repository functions, with `cn` called from 33 places and `executeCommand` from 8 places. The most connected modules are `src/components/ui/index` (Ce 13), `src/components/views/index` (Ce 5), and `src/stores/index` (Ce 5). Effects outside the repo are limited to 3 functions that read or write files: `src/lib/rizin/RizinInstance.ts`, `src/pages/AnalysisPage.tsx`, and `src/components/file/FileDropZone.tsx`. File routing flows through stores (`src/stores/fileStore.ts`, `src/stores/rizinStore.ts`, `src/stores/uiStore.ts`) and providers (`src/providers/ThemeProvider.tsx`), with `src/lib/rizin/RizinInstance.ts` and `src/lib/rizin/RizinLoader.ts` handling the Rizin WASM module lifecycle. The module dependency graph has 58 internal modules with 38 import edges and no circular dependencies, but the high branching density in `src/lib/utils/version.ts` (15 branch points over 45 lines) and deep nesting in three view files (max indentation depth 8) indicates control flow that is hard to follow.

## How To Use It

**Setup**: Clone the repository verbatim:
```bash
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/rzweb
cd rzweb
npm install
```

**Configuration**: No environment variables or keys are required. The project uses Vite (`vite.config.ts`), Tailwind (`tailwind.config.ts`), and ESLint (`tsconfig.json`, `.eslintrc.json`) as defined in the root config files.

**Running it**: Start the development server:
```bash
npm run dev
```
Then open the browser to the local URL. Drop a binary file onto the page or select one via the file zone. Click **Analyze** to load the binary into the WebAssembly Rizin instance. The terminal accepts Rizin commands (e.g., `pdf`, `afl`, `px`), and views update accordingly. For production builds, `npm run build` generates static assets.

## Real-World Use

A security analyst needs to quickly inspect a suspicious binary received via email. Instead of installing Rizin locally or running it in a sandbox, they open rzweb in a browser, drop the binary onto the page, and immediately have access to a fully functional terminal and analysis views. The analyst runs `aa` to perform full analysis, `afl` to list functions, and `pdf` to disassemble functions of interest. Strings extracted via the Strings view reveal hardcoded API keys and embedded URLs. Because all processing occurs client-side, no binary data leaves the analyst's machine, satisfying air-gapped environment constraints. The control flow graph view helps identify obfuscated jump targets, and the hex dump view allows byte-level inspection of suspicious sections.

## Code Health & Issues

- **HIGH** - Add a test suite; this repository has none (58 source files, no test files). Any change ships with no signal that existing behaviour still holds, so a regression reaches production undetected.
- **HIGH** - Add a workflow that builds and tests this repository (57 source files, no CI configuration). Every change merges with nobody having run the build once.
- **MEDIUM** - Enable Dependabot or Renovate (1 manifest, no update bot configured). Without a bot a published advisory sits unpatched until someone audits by hand.
- **MEDIUM** - Review the install lifecycle script and disable scripts in CI - `package.json` contains `postinstall` which is the execution vector for every npm compromise.
- **LOW** - Add the repository convention files this project lacks (missing `.editorconfig`, `.gitattributes`, a formatter config).

## The Bottom Line

This is a functional, privacy-respecting browser-based Rizin frontend that lowers the barrier to entry for binary analysis. The client-side-only architecture is its strongest feature, but the absence of tests, CI, and dependency automation represents a genuine risk for any production use. Engineers who need a quick, local analysis surface will find it immediately useful; teams requiring reliable long-term maintenance should prioritize the test and CI gaps before depending on it for critical work.

forks.name: document-to-podcast
forks.description: Blueprint by Mozilla.ai for generating podcasts from documents using local AI
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Enterprises that need to turn policy documents, research papers, or internal reports into audio for broader consumption often rely on cloud APIs that expose proprietary models and data. The cost, latency, and privacy concerns of sending raw text to external services become blockers for regulated environments.

## What This Does  
`document-to-podcast` is a self‑contained Python Blueprint that runs entirely on‑premise. It parses PDFs, DOCX, HTML or plain‑text, cleans the content, feeds it to a local LLM (via `llama.cpp`) to generate a script, and then uses a locally‑hosted TTS model to synthesize two speaker tracks that are stitched together into a podcast episode.

Key implementation pieces:  

* **CLI entry point** – `src/document_to_podcast/cli.py` defines `document_to_podcast()` (called from the `document-to-podcast` console script) and `main()`.  
* **Demo UI** – `demo/app.py` builds a Streamlit interface; the heavy lifting lives in the same functions used by the CLI.  
* **Model loading** – `src/document_to_podcast/inference/model_loaders.py` implements `load_llama_cpp_model`, `_load_kokoro_tts`, `load_tts_model`, and the `TTSModel` class.  
* **Pre‑processing** – `src/document_to_podcast/preprocessing/data_loaders.py` reads files (`load_pdf`, `load_txt`, `load_docx`, `load_url`) and `src/document_to_podcast/preprocessing/data_cleaners.py` normalises HTML/Markdown via `clean_html`, `clean_markdown`, and `clean_with_regex`.  
* **Inference** – `src/document_to_podcast/inference/text_to_text.py` runs the LLM (`chat_completion`, `text_to_text_stream`) and `src/document_to_podcast/inference/text_to_speech.py` produces audio (`text_to_speech`).  
* **Utility** – `src/document_to_podcast/utils.py` concatenates audio chunks with `stack_audio_segments`.

The internal call graph shows a shallow flow: the CLI → `document_to_podcast` → config validation → model loaders → preprocessing → inference → audio stacking. The most widely used functions (`load_txt`, `text_to_text_stream`, `load_llama_cpp_model`, `load_tts_model`, `clean_with_regex`) each have ≤6 callers, limiting blast radius for changes.

## How It Is Wired  
Execution starts at the console script defined in `pyproject.toml` (`document-to-podcast`). This invokes `src/document_to_podcast/cli.py:document_to_podcast`, which:

1. Reads the user‑supplied `config.yaml` (filesystem read via `Path.read_text`).  
2. Validates input files and model paths (`src/document_to_podcast/config.py`).  
3. Calls `load_llama_cpp_model` (model loader) and `load_tts_model` (TTS loader).  
4. Loads the source document through `load_pdf`/`load_txt`/`load_docx`/`load_url`.  
5. Cleans the raw text with `clean_html`/`clean_markdown` → `clean_with_regex`.  
6. Generates a script by streaming LLM responses (`text_to_text_stream` → `chat_completion`).  
7. Converts each segment to audio (`text_to_speech` → `_text_to_speech_kokoro`).  
8. Stacks the resulting WAV chunks (`stack_audio_segments`) and writes the final podcast file.

The demo Streamlit app (`demo/app.py`) follows the same pipeline but adds UI callbacks (`gen_button_clicked`). The file suffers from deep nesting (max indentation depth 7), making the control flow harder to follow; refactoring into guard clauses would improve readability.

External interactions are limited to:

* **Filesystem** – reading the input document and config, writing the podcast output.  
* **Network** – optional URL loading (`load_url`) and any model files fetched by the user; no built‑in remote API calls.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/document-to-podcast
cd document-to-podcast

# Install the package (uses pyproject.toml)
pip install .
# or, for an isolated build:
docker build -t doc2pod -f demo/Dockerfile .
```

Run the CLI (example from README):

```bash
document-to-podcast \
  --input_file "example_data/Mozilla-Trustworthy_AI.pdf" \
  --output_folder "example_data" \
  --text_to_text_model "Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct-GGUF/qwen2.5-1.5b-instruct-q8_0.gguf"
```

Or start the UI:

```bash
python demo/app.py
```

Configuration lives in `example_data/config.yaml`; adjust model paths and speaker parameters there.

## Real‑World Use  
A compliance team can integrate the CLI into an internal CI pipeline that watches a `policies/` folder. On each push, a GitHub Action runs `document-to-podcast` to generate an MP3 that is then uploaded to the company’s internal media server. Because all models are loaded from local disks, no confidential text leaves the network.

## Code Health & Issues  

* **High – Pin GitHub Actions** – `.github/workflows/*` uses tags like `pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish@release/v1`. Replace with a 40‑char SHA to avoid supply‑chain drift.  
* **High – Missing lockfile** – `pyproject.toml` declares dependencies but no `poetry.lock`/`uv.lock`. Generate and commit a lockfile to guarantee reproducible builds.  
* **Medium – Least‑privilege `GITHUB_TOKEN`** – `.github/workflows/lint.yaml` lacks explicit permissions; add `permissions: contents: read`.  
* **Medium – Pin Docker base image** – `demo/Dockerfile` uses `nvidia/cuda:12.2.2-cudnn8-devel-ubuntu22.04` without a digest. Use `@sha256:<digest>`.  
* **Medium – No dependency vulnerability scan** – Add `dependency-review-action` or `osv-scanner` to CI.  
* **Medium – Notebook outputs** – `demo/notebook.ipynb` stores >22 MiB of outputs; install `nbstripout` and clear them.  
* **Medium – Large binaries** – The same notebook exceeds 5 MiB; track with Git LFS or external storage.  
* **Medium – Checkout persist‑credentials** – `.github/workflows/docs.yaml` should set `persist-credentials: false`.  
* **Low – Job timeouts** – `.github/workflows/docs.yaml` lacks `timeout-minutes`; add sensible limits.  
* **Medium – Deep nesting** – `demo/app.py` has indentation depth 7; refactor for maintainability.

No critical or low‑severity functional bugs were detected by static analysis.

## The Bottom Line  
`document-to-podcast` provides a clear, fully local path from document to audio and is organized around a modest, well‑tested codebase. To move to production, address the high‑severity CI and lockfile gaps, pin mutable dependencies, and simplify the demo UI’s nesting. It is suitable for teams that need on‑premise podcast generation without exposing content to cloud services.

forks.description: Build a full-stack Uber Clone Application with Expo’s latest features and lightning-fast edge-ready Postgres database in React Native.
forks.summary:
## The Problem

A rideshare product touches mobile UI, live maps, auth, payments, and a database. Wiring those together by hand is a multi-week effort. This repository is the companion code to a JavaScript Mastery YouTube tutorial that demonstrates the full stack — React Native, Expo, PostgreSQL, Stripe, Google Maps, Clerk, and zustand — in one runnable app.

## What This Does

It is an Expo React Native app using file-based routing. The `app/` directory splits into three route groups: `app/(auth)/` for sign-in/sign-up/welcome, `app/(root)/` for the authenticated tabs (`home`, `rides`, `chat`, `profile`) plus the ride-booking flow (`find-ride`, `book-ride`, `confirm-ride`), and `app/(api)/` for serverless API routes named with the Expo `+api.ts` convention. Those routes (`user+api.ts`, `ride/create+api.ts`, `ride/[id]+api.ts`, `driver+api.ts`, `(stripe)/create+api.ts`, `(stripe)/pay+api.ts`) handle backend work against serverless Postgres and Stripe.

`components/` holds the reusable UI (`Map`, `RideCard`, `DriverCard`, `Payment`, `OAuth`, `InputField`, `CustomButton`). `lib/` contains `auth.ts`, `fetch.ts`, `map.ts`, and `utils.ts`; `store/index.ts` is the zustand store; `constants/index.ts` defines shared values. Styling is Tailwind via `tailwind.config.js`.

## How It Is Wired

The static import analysis resolved 45 internal modules but traced 0 import edges, so a precise call graph has not been mapped for this repository — the wiring below comes from the file structure, not a traced path.

Execution starts at `app/index.tsx`, which routes to the auth group. `app/(auth)/welcome.tsx` leads to `sign-in.tsx` / `sign-up.tsx`, which use `components/OAuth.tsx` and `lib/auth.ts` (Clerk) for authentication. Authenticated users land in `app/(root)/(tabs)/home.tsx`, which renders `components/Map.tsx` with live location and recent rides.

The booking flow is the core path: `find-ride.tsx` → `book-ride.tsx` → `confirm-ride.tsx`, ending in a Stripe payment through `app/(api)/(stripe)/create+api.ts` and `pay+api.ts`. On successful payment, `app/(api)/ride/create+api.ts` persists the ride. These API routes are the only files that touch external services (database, Stripe), so they carry the widest blast radius — a change to `pay+api.ts` affects every paid booking.

## How To Use It

Setup requires `npm install` (a `package-lock.json` is present). Environment configuration is the missing piece: the README's Quick Start section is not included in the excerpt, so the exact env var names are not documented here — expect Expo public keys for Clerk, Google Maps, Stripe, and a Postgres connection string. Run with `npx expo start` from the repository root.

## Code Health & Issues

Static analysis found 1 high-severity issue: duplicated code blocks — 30 repeated 6-line blocks across 6 files including `app/(auth)/sign-in.tsx`, `app/(auth)/sign-up.tsx`, `app/(root)/(tabs)/home.tsx`, and `app/(root)/(tabs)/rides.tsx`. The fix is extracting shared helpers.

SDLC gaps evident from the structure:

- **High** — no test suite; 45 source files, zero test files.
- **High** — no CI configuration; nothing builds or tests on push.
- **High** — no LICENSE file; default all-rights-reserved applies.
- **Medium** — no Dependabot/Renovate config for dependency updates.
- **Low** — missing `.editorconfig`, `.gitattributes`, and formatter config.

## The Bottom Line

This is a well-organized tutorial scaffold that demonstrates a realistic full-stack mobile architecture. It is reference material, not a production base — no tests, CI, or license means you should not ship it as-is. Use it to learn the Expo + serverless Postgres + Stripe pattern, then build your own on top.

forks.displayName: system prompts and models of ai tools
forks.description: FULL Augment Code, Claude Code, Cluely, CodeBuddy, Comet, Cursor, Devin AI, Junie, Kiro, Leap.new, Lovable, Manus, NotionAI, Orchids.app, Perplexity, Poke, Qoder, Replit, Same.dev, Trae, Traycer AI, VSCode Agent, Warp.dev, Windsurf, Xcode, Z.ai Code, Dia & v0. (And other Open Sourced) System Prompts, Internal Tools & AI Models
forks.summary:
## The Problem
This repository functions as a curated catalog of system prompts extracted from commercial AI coding tools. Teams or individuals seeking to understand, reverse-engineer, or benchmark the underlying instructions governing AI assistant behavior will find organized collections here. There is no software product, runtime, or deliverable produced by this repo - it is purely a reference collection.

## What This Does
The repository groups system prompts and companion tool definitions by vendor (e.g., `Anthropic/`, `Cursor/`, `Windsurf/`, `VSCode Agent/`). Each vendor directory typically contains a `Prompt.txt` file (the core system instruction) and a `Tools.json` file (defining available functions or capabilities). File types are homogeneous within categories: prompts are `.txt` or `.yaml`, tool definitions are `.json`. Notable examples include `Anthropic/Claude Code/Prompt.txt`, `Cursor Prompts/Agent Prompt 2.0.txt`, and `VSCode Agent/gpt-5.txt`. The collection spans 30+ vendors and includes both closed‑source tool prompts and genuinely open‑sourced equivalents under `Open Source prompts/`. No source code that executes; the artifacts are static instruction files.

## How It Is Wired
There is no execution graph, entry point, or runtime wiring in this repository. The contents are entirely static documentation—prompt text and JSON schemas intended to be consumed by external systems (LLM clients, agent frameworks, integrated development environments). The repository itself is a flat collection of files organized by vendor name; no module, function, or script ties them together. Any "call graph" would be defined by the consumer of these prompts, not by code within this repo. The only cross‑file dependency is the informal grouping under vendor directories, which the README does not formalize beyond listing.

## How To Use It
There are no build, install, or runtime commands associated with this collection. The files are ready to be copied or referenced by whatever system consumes system prompts. If you are integrating a prompt into a framework, the typical pattern is to point the framework's configuration at the `Prompt.txt` and `Tools.json` for the desired vendor. No environment variables, keys, or secret material are required to read the files— the repo contains no committed secrets. Example layout:

```text
# To reference the Cursor Agent Prompt 2.0:
Cursor Prompts/Agent Prompt 2.0.txt

# To reference the Claude Code tools definition:
Anthropic/Claude Code/Tools.json
```

No `package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `Dockerfile`, or `Makefile` exists in the repo, so there is no formal setup process, dependency resolution, or container build pipeline.

## Real-World Use
A practitioner benchmarking LLMs against vendor‑specific instructions can pull the relevant `Prompt.txt` to establish a baseline prompt for their model. For example, comparing model behavior under `Anthropic/Claude Code/Prompt.txt` versus `Cursor Prompts/Agent Prompt 2.0.txt` isolates differences in how each tool frames reasoning, tool use, and code generation expectations. The companion `Tools.json` files expose which functions each system declares as available, which can inform tool‑calling schema design or evaluation suites. This repo is useful as a reference dataset, not as a functional component.

## Code Health & Issues
The static analysis produced the following measured findings:

- **tests present: yes** - 1 test file exists
- **CI: no** - no `.github/` workflow or CI configuration detected
- **Dockerfile: no** - no container build definition
- **lockfile: no** - no `package-lock.json`, `yarn.lock`, or similar
- **licence: yes** - `LICENSE.md` is present
- **committed secrets: none found**

Beyond the measured block, the structure itself reveals the repo's nature: it is a static prompt collection with no source code, no testable units, and no automation. The single test file and absent CI pipeline are consistent with a reference/curated repo rather than a deliverable project.

## The Bottom Line
This is a well‑organized catalog of system prompts from major AI coding tools, useful as a reference or benchmarking dataset. It ships with a license, no secrets, and a single test file, but offers no runtime code, no CI/CD, and no installation pathway. Teams looking to study prompt patterns, compare vendor instructions, or build evaluation suites will find immediate value; anyone seeking a functional agent framework, deployable tooling, or automated quality gates will need to look elsewhere.

forks.name: OpenGlasses
forks.description: 3D-printable wearable that fuses AI, design, and human expression — turning ordinary glasses into extraordinary minds.
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Makers who want an AI‑enhanced wearable must source disparate hardware schematics, 3‑D models, and software snippets, then stitch them together manually. The lack of a single, version‑controlled repository forces designers to hunt for scattered assets, increasing setup time and the risk of missing critical safety guidance (e.g., lithium‑battery handling).

## What This Does  
`README.md` provides the full product narrative, safety warnings, and a high‑level parts list. The printable frame lives in `3d printables/latest_iteration_v1.stl`. The only executable code is `scripts/init.py`, which is intended to bootstrap the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W (install OS, configure Wi‑Fi, set up the ElevenLabs API, etc.). Asset graphics such as `assets/featured_image.png` are used by the README banner but are not part of the runtime.

## How It Is Wired  
The repository contains a single Python module:

* **Entry point** – `scripts/init.py` is the only script. The static import graph shows **0 import edges**, meaning the file does not import any internal or third‑party modules.
* **Call flow** – Because no functions or classes are referenced elsewhere, the only possible execution path is the top‑level code that runs when the file is invoked (`python scripts/init.py`). The analysis reports `Ca 0, Ce 0, instability 0`, confirming that `init.py` neither depends on nor is depended upon by other modules.
* **External effects** – The source does not contain any I/O, network, or hardware‑control calls, so the current codebase does not interact with the Pi, the microphone/speaker HAT, or any cloud LLM endpoint. In practice, the intended behavior must be added manually or resides in unpublished scripts.
* **Wiring gaps** – No mapping exists for hardware‑to‑software integration; the repository stops at the printable model and a placeholder init script. Any change that adds real device control will introduce the first external dependency and become the primary hub of the call graph.

## How To Use It  
```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/OpenGlasses
cd OpenGlasses

# (Optional) Inspect the printable frame
# Use your slicer of choice on 3d printables/latest_iteration_v1.stl

# Run the placeholder init script (no effect yet)
python scripts/init.py
```

*No configuration files, environment variables, or package managers are present, so the repository cannot be built or run beyond the no‑op script.* To make the wearable functional, you will need to supply your own OS image, install required Python packages, and implement the hardware‑control logic referenced in the README’s “Getting Started” steps.

## Real‑World Use  
A maker could clone the repo, 3‑D print the frame, and then replace `scripts/init.py` with a script that:

```python
import subprocess

# Flash Raspberry Pi OS
subprocess.run(["dd", "if=raspbian.img", "of=/dev/sdx"])

# Configure Wi‑Fi
with open("/boot/wpa_supplicant.conf", "w") as f:
    f.write("network={...}")
```

The surrounding documentation already warns about battery safety, so the user can follow those guidelines while adding the missing provisioning steps.

## Code Health & Issues  

- **Medium – Large binary in repo** – `assets/featured_image.png` (19.8 MB). Large files increase clone time and storage cost. Fix: store via Git LFS or external object storage.  
- **Medium – No CI/CD pipeline** – No `.github/` or other CI config. Automated testing or linting is absent.  
- **Medium – No LICENSE** – Repository lacks a license file, leaving usage and redistribution rights ambiguous.  
- **Low – Tests present but not linked** – A single test file exists without a test runner configuration, so tests are not automatically executed.

## The Bottom Line  
OpenGlasses offers a clear hardware bill of materials and a printable frame, but the software side is essentially a stub (`scripts/init.py`) with no functional code, CI, or licensing. It is suitable as a starting point for hobbyists who are prepared to write the device‑control layer themselves; enterprises or developers needing a ready‑to‑run AI‑wearable stack will find the repository incomplete.

forks.name: deepseek_ocr_app
forks.description: A quick vibe coded app for deepseek OCR
forks.summary:
## The Problem

Extracting usable text from images and scanned PDFs is a common but fiddly task: OCR models return raw text, and getting it into a shareable format (Markdown, Word, HTML) usually means manual cleanup. This app wraps DeepSeek-OCR with a web UI and format conversion so a non-technical user can upload a document and download a clean, structured result.

## What This Does

A React frontend (`frontend/src/App.jsx`) talks to a FastAPI backend (`backend/main.py`) that runs DeepSeek-OCR. It supports single-image OCR with four modes (plain, describe, find, freeform) and multi-page PDF processing with progress tracking. Results export to Markdown, HTML, DOCX, or JSON via `backend/format_converter.py`.

The whole thing deploys with `docker compose up --build`. The backend image is based on `nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:25.09-py3` and downloads the model (~5–10GB) on first run.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts in `frontend/src/main.jsx`, which mounts `App.jsx`. `App` is the clear hub: it has 5 outgoing imports and 0 incoming, giving it instability 0.83 — every feature routes through it. The five components (`ImageUpload`, `PDFProcessor`, `ModeSelector`, `ResultPanel`, `AdvancedSettings`) are all leaves (Ca 1, Ce 0): nothing imports them except `App`, so they are cheap to replace but `App` itself is the single point of change.

On the backend, `backend/main.py` is the API entry point. It handles uploads, calls the OCR model, and delegates file handling to `pdf_utils.py` (PDF extraction) and `format_converter.py` (export formats). The import graph shows 14 internal modules, 6 edges, and no cycles — the structure is simple and acyclic. `App.jsx` is the file with the widest blast radius because all UI state and API calls pass through it.

## How To Use It

```bash
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/deepseek_ocr_app
cd deepseek_ocr_app
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up --build
```

Then open `http://localhost:3000` (frontend) and `http://localhost:8000/docs` (API docs). The `.env` file configures ports and upload limits. The first run downloads the model, which takes time.

## Real-World Use

A document digitization workflow: a user uploads a scanned 50-page PDF in `PDFProcessor`, the backend runs OCR page-by-page with progress tracking, and the result converts to `.docx` for editing in Word. The same pipeline handles academic papers, preserving LaTeX formulas and table structure.

## Code Health & Issues

Static analysis found 6 issues (2 high, 4 medium). High: deep nesting in `backend/format_converter.py`, `backend/main.py`, and `frontend/src/App.jsx` (max indentation depth 8) — control flow is hard to follow; fix with early returns and extraction. Medium: `backend/pdf_utils.py` opens files without a context manager (handle leak risk), and `backend/main.py` uses broad exception handling that swallows errors.

The broader audit flags: no test suite across 17 source files, no CI configuration, no lockfile beside `frontend/package.json` (non-reproducible builds), a wildcard CORS origin paired with credentials in `backend/main.py`, an unpinned base image, and no non-root `USER` in the backend Dockerfile. No committed secrets were detected.

## The Bottom Line

A working, demo-grade OCR app with a clean client-server split and genuinely useful PDF/format-conversion features. It is not production-ready: no tests, no CI, and a wildcard CORS config that browsers will reject with credentials anyway. Fine for a self-hosted tool or a starting point; add tests and a lockfile before putting it behind real traffic.
