forks.name: noteGPT
forks.description: Record voice notes & transcribe, summarize, and get tasks
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Users need a quick way to capture spoken ideas, turn them into searchable text, and extract actionable items without leaving a single interface. Manual transcription and note‑taking are slow and error‑prone, especially when the user is on the move.

## What This Does  
`noteGPT` is a Next.js app that records voice notes in the browser, uploads the audio to Convex file storage, and triggers a Whisper model (via Replicate) to produce a transcript. The transcript is summarized with a Mixtral LLM (via Together.ai) and parsed into a list of action items that are stored in Convex’s vector search for later retrieval.  

Key files:  

* `app/record/page.tsx` – UI for starting/stopping a recording and submitting it.  
* `convex/whisper.ts` – calls Replicate’s Whisper API, writes the transcript to Convex.  
* `convex/together.ts` – sends the transcript to Together’s LLM, stores the summary and extracted tasks.  
* `convex/notes.ts` – CRUD helpers that the frontend consumes through the generated API (`convex/_generated/api.d.ts`).  

The frontend wraps the Convex client in `app/ConvexClientProvider.tsx`, exposing hooks used by components such as `components/pages/dashboard/RecordedfileItemCard.tsx` and `components/pages/recording/RecordingDesktop.tsx`.

## How It Is Wired  
Execution begins when a developer runs `npm run dev`. Next.js launches the server and loads `app/layout.tsx`, which mounts `ConvexClientProvider`. When a user clicks “record”, `components/pages/recording/RecordingDesktop.tsx` (or the mobile counterpart) invokes the browser MediaRecorder API, then calls `convex/notes.ts` via the generated client (`api.recordNote`).  

`convex/notes.ts` stores the raw audio file in Convex file storage. A Convex mutation defined in `convex/whisper.ts` is automatically queued; it fetches the file, posts it to Replicate, and writes the returned transcript back to the same note record. After the transcript is saved, `convex/together.ts` reads it, calls the Together Mixtral endpoint, and writes both the summary and the derived action items to the note document and to Convex vector search (`convex/utils.ts` assists with embedding generation).  

The internal import graph shows three hubs:  

* `convex/_generated/api` – imported by 3 files, no outgoing imports (instability 0).  
* `convex/utils` – imported by 3 files, imports only one module (instability 0.25).  
* `components/ui/UserNav` – imports 3 modules, is imported once (instability 0.75).  

No circular dependencies were detected, so changes to a hub affect at most three downstream modules.

## How To Use It  
```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/noteGPT.git
cd noteGPT

# Install dependencies
npm install

# Create a .env.local (copy .example.env) and add:
#   CLERK_ISSUER_URL – from your Clerk dashboard
#   REPLICATE_API_KEY – from Replicate
#   TOGETHER_API_KEY – from Together.ai

# Run the dev server
npm run dev
```
The dev server starts the Next.js frontend and, on first run, prompts you to log into Convex and create a project. After the environment variables are set in Convex’s dashboard, the UI is usable; recordings will be stored, transcribed, summarized, and displayed on the dashboard.

## Real‑World Use  
A sales professional could open the web app on a laptop, dictate a meeting recap, and instantly receive a bullet‑point list of follow‑up tasks. The tasks are searchable via Convex vector search, and can be exported to a Notion page once the planned integration is added.

## Code Health & Issues  
* **High – Missing LICENSE** – no licence file at repository root; legal reuse is blocked.  
* **High – No test suite** – 41 source files, zero test files; regressions are undetectable.  
* **High – No CI pipeline** – no `.github/workflows` or other CI config; builds and tests are never automatically verified.  
* **Medium – No Dependabot** – only `package-lock.json` present; dependencies are not auto‑updated.  
* **Medium – Duplicated code blocks** – identical 6‑line snippets appear in `app/dashboard/action-items/ais.tsx`, `components/pages/recording/RecordingDesktop.tsx`, `components/pages/recording/RecordingMobile.tsx`, and generated API typings. Refactor into shared helpers.  
* **Medium – Deep nesting** – max indentation depth of 6 in the same three files makes the control flow hard to follow; early returns or extracted sub‑functions would improve readability.

## The Bottom Line  
`noteGPT` delivers a functional end‑to‑end voice‑note pipeline with modern cloud services, but it lacks the engineering hygiene (tests, CI, licence) required for production confidence. It is suitable for proof‑of‑concept work or as a foundation for a custom internal tool, provided the team adds testing, CI, and proper licensing before scaling.

forks.name: rpsync
forks.description: Gather your online presence stats in a small local database.
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
People who want a personal analytics dashboard for social‑media accounts must either trust third‑party SaaS platforms with their data or build a custom stack from scratch. Maintaining a local database, handling OAuth flows, and exporting to CSV/Notion are repetitive, error‑prone tasks that most hobbyists cannot afford to implement securely.

## What This Does  
`rpsync` is a self‑hosted Go service that pulls post‑level statistics from Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Bluesky, and other networks, stores them in a SQLite/PostgreSQL DB, and serves a React‑based UI. Core logic lives under `internal/`; the HTTP server is started from `main.go` (line 43) and renders templates such as `templates/index.html`. Docker support is provided by `Dockerfile` and `docker-compose.yml`, while the one‑shot installer lives in `install.sh`.

Key modules:  

* `internal/fetcher/*` – API clients for each network (e.g. `telegram.go`, `tiktok.go`).  
* `internal/database/*.sql.go` – autogenerated query wrappers (e.g. `sources.sql.go`, `analytics.sql.go`).  
* `internal/api/handlers/*.go` – Gin HTTP handlers (e.g. `auth_login.go`, `redirects.go`).  
* `internal/worker/worker.go` – background sync orchestration (`SyncAll`, `SyncSource`).  

## How It Is Wired  
Execution begins in **`main.go:43`** → `main` creates a DB (`LoadDatabase` → `sql.Open`), loads configuration (`LoadConfig`), and registers routes via `internal/api/handlers/handlers.go`. The root router calls `CommonData` (used by 32 handlers) to assemble user‑specific context, making it the widest‑impact function.

A typical sync cycle follows the internal call graph:

1. `main` → `LoadDatabase` (filesystem) → `internal/database/db.go.New`.  
2. `Start` (worker) → `Check` (network `http.Get`).  
3. `SyncAll` → `RunSync` → `DeleteOldStats` (DB `q.db.ExecContext`).  

The most invoked symbols are `New`, `Redirect`, and `CommonData`, each referenced from >30 distinct callers, indicating high blast radius for any change. Database‑write hot spots reside in `internal/database/sources.sql.go` (8 functions, 4 types, called from 17 files) and `internal/database/db.go` (core DB wrapper). Network outbound calls appear in 15 functions (e.g., fetcher clients) and file I/O in 6 functions (e.g., token encryption).

The import graph shows a single internal module with no circular dependencies, but deep nesting (max depth 8) and duplicated 6‑line blocks across many handlers inflate cognitive load. `internal/database/analytics.sql.go` is 645 lines, and `internal/pusher/common/helpers.go` contains 18 branch points in 53 lines, both flagged as maintenance hotspots.

## How To Use It  
```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/rpsync.git
cd rpsync

# Build the container (Dockerfile uses golang:1.25.5 + debian:bookworm)
docker compose build

# Create a .env file (see README for required keys)
cp .env.example .env   # if the repo provided one; otherwise create manually

# Start services
docker compose up -d
```
The installer script (`install.sh`) automates the above steps and generates TLS certificates when run on a Linux host. Once the containers are healthy, the UI is reachable at the address printed by the script (default `https://<IP>:8443`).

## Real‑World Use  
A user runs the Docker stack on a home server, adds their Instagram and TikTok accounts via the web UI, and schedules a nightly sync. The worker (`internal/worker/worker.go`) polls each network, stores per‑post metrics in `internal/database/posts.sql.go`, and the dashboard (`templates/*.html`) visualises trends without any external data collection.

## Code Health & Issues  

- **Critical** – `golang.org/x/crypto@0.47.0` (CVE‑2026‑42508) and `google.golang.org/grpc@1.78.0` (CVE‑2026‑33186) are pinned; upgrade required.  
- **High** – `github.com/gotd/td@0.137.0` (CVE‑2026‑54638) and `go.opentelemetry.io/otel@1.39.0` (CVE‑2026‑29181) need updating.  
- **High** – No test suite (79 source files, 0 test files). Add unit/integration tests and CI gate.  
- **High** – No GitHub Actions workflow; add a build‑and‑test pipeline.  
- **High** – Dockerfile lacks a build‑gate; introduce a CI step that builds the image and validates manifests.  
- **Medium** – Enable Dependabot/Renovate for automated dependency updates.  
- **Medium** – Pin base images by digest to avoid mutable tag drift.  

Additional SDLC observations: repository contains a LICENSE and lockfile (`go.sum`), but no CI configuration, and documentation is limited to two Markdown files.

## The Bottom Line  
`rpsync` delivers a functional, locally hosted analytics hub with a clear separation between fetchers, DB wrappers, and HTTP handlers. However, deep nesting, duplicated handler logic, and an oversized analytics file make future changes risky. The most pressing actions are upgrading critical dependencies, introducing automated testing/CI, and refactoring the high‑complexity modules. Suitable for developers comfortable with Go and Docker who need a privacy‑first analytics stack and are willing to invest in improving test coverage and maintainability.

forks.name: transformer-explainer
forks.description: Transformer Explained Visually: Learn How LLM Transformer Models Work with Interactive Visualization
forks.summary:
## The Problem

Understanding how transformer LLMs like GPT work internally is genuinely hard—the math (attention, embeddings, layer norm) is abstract and buried behind framework APIs. This tool makes it concrete by running a live GPT-2 model in the browser and letting you watch each internal operation as it predicts the next token.

## What This Does

An interactive visualization tool that runs a real GPT-2 model in-browser via ONNX. You type text, and it shows, step by step, how embeddings, attention, MLP layers, and softmax produce the next-token probability distribution.

The UI is SvelteKit with Tailwind. Each transformer stage has its own component in `src/components/`: `Attention.svelte`, `Embedding.svelte`, `QKV.svelte`, `Mlp.svelte`, `LinearSoftmax.svelte`, `Sampling.svelte`, `Temperature.svelte`. Popover components in `src/components/Popovers/` explain each operation, and `src/components/textbook/` holds guided tutorial pages. It also ships a research paper (arXiv 2408.04619, IEEE VIS 2024).

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts in `src/routes/+page.svelte`. All state flows through `src/store/index.ts`, the central Svelte store that coordinates the model, inputs, and UI. The model itself is a chunked ONNX GPT-2 in `static/model-v2/gpt2.onnx.part0` through `.part62`, fetched by `src/utils/fetchChunks.js`. The Python scripts in `src/utils/model/` (`model.py`, `export_to_onnx.py`, `quantize.py`, `chunk.py`) generated and split that model.

The module graph is small and clean: 25 internal modules, 6 import edges, zero circular dependencies. The most-connected modules are `tailwind.config` (imported by 3 files) and `src/utils/animation.ts` (imported by 2, itself imports 1)—animation is the shared utility most components depend on for transitions. No module carries a wide blast radius; the risk is concentrated in the two oversized components instead.

## How To Use It

Per the README, prerequisites are Node.js 20+ and NPM 10+. No environment variables or config files are required.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/transformer-explainer
cd transformer-explainer
npm install
npm run dev
```

Then open http://localhost:5173.

## Real-World Use

This fits in teaching and onboarding: ML courses, conference demos, or a team getting familiar with transformer internals. A lecturer can fork it, add custom example inputs in `src/constants/examples/`, and demonstrate attention patterns live. It is also a reference implementation for anyone building similar model-visualization tools.

## Code Health & Issues

Measured static analysis (not opinion) found 32 findings: 12 high, 20 medium. The high findings are deep nesting (max indentation depth 9 across `Attention.svelte`, `Embedding.svelte`, `InputForm.svelte`) and 243 duplicated 6-line code blocks across 23 files. The medium findings are two oversized files—`Sankey.svelte` and `article/Article.svelte` at 645 lines each.

SDLC gaps from the structure: no test files anywhere, no CI configuration, and no dependency-update bot. The repository also carries 63 blobs over 5MB—the ONNX model parts are 10MB each—which bloats every clone and CI checkout. 19 of 39 declared dependencies are behind their current major version, with `@sveltejs/adapter-auto` and `@sveltejs/vite-plugin-svelte` four majors behind.

## The Bottom Line

A solid, well-documented educational tool that works as described and is easy to run. It is not production code: add tests, a CI build step, and move the ONNX model files to Git LFS before treating it as anything but a demo or teaching aid.

## The Problem  
Tesla dashcam footage is stored as a series of one‑minute MP4 clips with embedded SEI telemetry. Users must manually stitch clips, extract telemetry, and overlay data—a time‑consuming, error‑prone process that usually requires third‑party tools.

## What This Does  
`exportdash.cam` is a client‑side viewer and exporter. The UI lives under `src/app/` with `page.tsx` as the Next.js entry point. Dropping a `TeslaCam` folder onto `src/components/DropZone.tsx` triggers `src/hooks/useSeiData.ts`, which reads each clip, parses SEI packets via `src/lib/dashcam-mp4.ts` (protobufjs‑driven) and builds a time‑aligned telemetry stream.  

Key UI pieces:  
* `VideoPlayer.tsx` – multi‑camera playback with controls.  
* `TelemetryCard.tsx` – live speed/G‑force overlay.  
* `TelemetryTimeline.tsx` – event bar (brake, gas, turn signals).  
* `MapView.tsx` – Leaflet map synced to GPS data.  
* `VideoExporter.tsx` – WebCodecs‑based export that burns telemetry into a new MP4.

All processing stays in the browser; no server‑side storage or upload is required.

## How It Is Wired  
1. **Entry point** – `src/app/page.tsx` renders `<DropZone />`.  
2. **File ingestion** – `DropZone.tsx` calls `useSeiData` with the dropped folder path.  
3. **SEI extraction** – `useSeiData.ts` iterates files, invoking `dashcam-mp4.ts` → `parseMp4` → `extractSei` (protobuf schema in `public/dashcam.proto`). The resulting telemetry objects are stored in React state.  
4. **Sequence detection** – `src/lib/sequence-detector.ts` groups consecutive clips into a single playback sequence; the detector is called from `useSeiData`.  
5. **Rendering** – `VideoPlayer.tsx` receives the ordered clip list and telemetry; it composes `TelemetryCard`, `TelemetryTimeline`, `MapView`, and optional `VideoExporter`. Each component imports only the data it needs, keeping the import graph shallow (18 internal modules, 6 edges, no cycles).  
6. **Export** – When the user clicks “Export”, `VideoExporter.tsx` pulls the current playback buffer, uses WebCodecs to re‑encode, and writes telemetry frames into the output MP4.  

The most connected module is `src/components/VideoPlayer.tsx` (imports 4 others, depth 8), making it the primary impact zone for any UI change.

## How To Use It  
```bash
# Clone the upstream repository
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/exportdash.cam.git
cd exportdash.cam

# Install dependencies (npm is declared in package.json)
npm install

# Development server
npm run dev        # starts Next.js on http://localhost:3000
```
For containerised deployment:  

```bash
docker build -t exportdash .
docker run -p 8080:80 exportdash   # UI reachable at http://localhost:8080
```
Or with Compose: `docker compose up`.

No environment variables or external services are required; all assets are under `public/`.

## Real‑World Use  
A fleet‑maintenance tool can embed this repo in an internal portal. Technicians drop a vehicle’s `TeslaCam` folder, review telemetry‑enhanced playback, and export a single video for incident reports—all without leaving the browser or exposing raw footage to a backend.

## Code Health & Issues  
* **HIGH – Dependency advisory** – `next@16.1.4` has CVE‑2026‑44575. Upgrade to the patched version.  
* **HIGH – No test suite** – 18 source files, zero test files. Add unit/integration tests and a CI step.  
* **HIGH – No CI pipeline** – No GitHub Actions or other workflow. Create a build‑and‑test workflow.  
* **HIGH – No Docker build gate** – Dockerfile exists but is never validated automatically. Add a CI job that builds the image.  
* **MEDIUM – Dependabot missing** – No automated dependency updates. Add `.github/dependabot.yml`.  
* **MEDIUM – Base images not pinned** – `node:20-alpine` and `nginx:alpine` are mutable tags. Pin by digest.  
* **MEDIUM – Container runs as root** – No `USER` directive. Create a non‑root user and switch before `CMD`.  
* **MEDIUM – Oversized files** – `VideoPlayer.tsx` (743 lines), `TelemetryTimeline.tsx`, `VideoExporter.tsx`. Split by responsibility.  
* **MEDIUM – Deep nesting** – `VideoPlayer.tsx` has indentation depth 8; refactor with early returns/guards.  
* **LOW – Missing repo conventions** – No `.editorconfig`, `.gitattributes`, or formatter config. Add them to standardise contributions.  

No tests, CI, or build validation currently exist, which raises regression risk for UI‑heavy components.

## The Bottom Line  
`exportdash.cam` delivers a fully client‑side Tesla dashcam viewer with telemetry overlay and export, built on Next.js, Tailwind, and WebCodecs. The code works but suffers from large, deeply nested components, an outdated Next.js version with a known CVE, and a missing testing/CI infrastructure. It is suitable for teams that need a quick, self‑hosted viewer and are prepared to invest in refactoring and adding automated quality gates.

forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Rendering every road in a city requires pulling large OSM datasets, converting them to a compact format, and drawing millions of line segments in the browser. Developers need a ready‑made visual pipeline that handles data fetching, caching, and WebGL rendering without reinventing the wheel.

## What This Does  
The repo delivers a single‑page app that queries Overpass or a pre‑built protobuf cache, builds a Three.js‑style scene, and draws all road segments with WebGL. Core logic lives under `src/` – for example `src/lib/createScene.js` creates the renderer, while `src/lib/request.js` handles network fetches and progress reporting. UI components such as `src/components/FindPlace.vue` and the color picker live in `src/components/`. The entry HTML is `index.html`, and the JavaScript bootstrap is `src/main.js`.

## How It Is Wired  
Execution starts at `src/main.js`, which imports the Vue app (`src/App.vue`) and calls the scene factory in `src/lib/createScene.js`. `createScene` (24 functions, called from three other files) builds the WebGL renderer, registers event handlers from `src/createOverlayManager.js` and exposes `render`, `clear`, `getRenderer`, and `getWGL`.  

User interaction (e.g., clicking a road) triggers overlay callbacks defined in `src/createOverlayManager.js`. Those callbacks delegate to the drawing helpers in `src/lib/createScene.js` (`addRect → addPoint` is invoked four times).  

Data flow begins with `src/lib/request.js` (7 functions, called from three places). It issues HTTP GETs to the Overpass API or the protobuf cache, updates progress via `src/lib/Progress.js`, and writes temporary files (the only file‑system interaction in the repo). The response is decoded by `src/proto/decode.js` and `src/proto/encode.js`, then transformed into geometry by `src/lib/createScene.js`.  

Search queries are orchestrated by `src/lib/Query.js`. Its `run` method (reached via a single call at line 45) constructs a `LoadOptions` object (`src/lib/LoadOptions.js`) and triggers the request pipeline.  

The most widely used functions are `_colorChange`, `removeOverlay`, and `request`, each called from three distinct locations, giving them the largest blast radius. No circular import cycles were detected, but `src/lib/createScene.js` imports six other internal modules, making it a hub that must be changed carefully.

## How To Use It  
```bash
# clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/city-roads.git
cd city-roads

# install dependencies (npm is declared in package.json)
npm install

# start the development server (hot‑reload on localhost:8080)
npm run dev

# build a production bundle
npm run build
```
The app runs entirely in the browser; no server‑side configuration or API keys are required beyond the public Overpass endpoint.

## Real‑World Use  
A municipal data portal could embed the built `dist/` bundle as a visual explorer. The portal would pass a city name to the Vue component `FindPlace.vue`, which internally invokes `src/lib/Query.js` to fetch and render the road network without any additional backend code.

## Code Health & Issues  
- **High – No test suite** – 40 source files, no test files.  
- **High – No CI workflow** – repository lacks any GitHub Actions or other CI config.  
- **Medium – Dependabot missing** – only `package.json`/`package-lock.json` present; no `.github/dependabot.yml`.  
- **Medium – High branching density** – files `src/proto/place.js`, `src/components/vue3-color/mixin/color.js`, `src/lib/canvas2BlobPolyfill.js` each contain >20 branch points in <45 lines; refactor into smaller, table‑driven units.  
- **Medium – Duplicated UI logic** – similar 6‑line blocks appear in `Alpha.vue`, `Hue.vue`, and `Saturation.vue`; extract shared helpers to reduce duplication.

## The Bottom Line  
The project provides a functional, browser‑based road visualizer with a clear separation between data fetching, scene creation, and UI components. However, the lack of tests, CI, and outdated dependencies make it risky for production use without additional engineering effort. It is suitable for prototyping or as a visual demo; teams planning to extend or embed it should first add testing, update the build stack, and address the identified code‑clarity hotspots.

forks.name: tensortrade
forks.description: An open source reinforcement learning framework for training, evaluating, and deploying robust trading agents.
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Trading‑strategy research often stalls because data pipelines, environment simulation, and RL agent wiring are each built from scratch. The result is duplicated code, fragile imports, and a high cost to prototype or move from notebook to production.

## What This Does  
`tensortrade` supplies a modular RL‑driven trading stack. Core pieces live under `tensortrade/` – e.g. `environments/trading_environment.py` builds a `TradingEnvironment` that glues together an **exchange** (`exchanges/*_exchange.py`), an **action strategy** (`actions/*_strategy.py`), a **reward strategy** (`rewards/*_strategy.py`), and a **feature pipeline** (`features/feature_pipeline.py`).  

The library is deliberately thin on runtime scaffolding; the entry point for most users is the `TradingEnvironment` class and the strategy classes in `strategies/` (e.g. `tensorforce_trading_strategy.py`). Example notebooks in `examples/` show end‑to‑end usage without needing a separate CLI.

## How It Is Wired  
Execution begins when a client instantiates `tensortrade.environments.trading_environment.TradingEnvironment`. Its `__init__` (17 functions total) stores references to:

1. **Exchange** – concrete classes such as `exchanges/simulated/simulated_exchange.py` (20 functions) or `exchanges/live/ccxt_exchange.py`. They expose `reset`, `step`, and market‑data accessors.  
2. **ActionStrategy** – abstract base in `actions/action_strategy.py` (9 functions) with concrete `ContinuousActionStrategy`, `DiscreteActionStrategy`, etc. These expose `action_space` and `action_type`.  
3. **RewardStrategy** – defined in `rewards/reward_strategy.py` and specialized in `simple_profit_strategy.py` or `risk_adjusted_return_strategy.py`.  
4. **FeaturePipeline** – `features/feature_pipeline.py` (9 functions) orchestrates a list of `FeatureTransformer` objects from `features/feature_transformer.py`.  

During a training episode, `TradingEnvironment.step()` calls the exchange’s `step()`, passes the observation through the `FeaturePipeline`, asks the **strategy** for an action, and finally computes a reward via the **reward strategy**. The resulting `Trade` objects are created by `trades/trade.py` (13 functions) and aggregated by the hub module `trades/__init__.py`, which is imported by 17 other modules – the largest blast radius in the import graph.

The import graph contains **12 circular dependencies** (e.g. `actions/__init__.py`, `rewards/__init__.py`, `slippage/__init__.py`). These cycles increase cognitive load and make refactoring risky because a change in any cycle member can trigger import‑time side effects across the stack.

Deep nesting (max depth 16) appears in several exchange and action‑strategy files, making the control flow hard to follow. Duplicated 6‑line blocks are scattered across `setup.py` and the three action‑strategy implementations, suggesting a missed utility layer.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/tensortrade
cd tensortrade

# Install Python deps (exact versions are pinned in requirements.txt)
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

Optional: build the provided Docker image for an isolated environment.

```bash
docker build -t tensortrade .
docker run -it --rm tensortrade /bin/bash
```

Run an example notebook, e.g. `examples/TensorTrade_Tutorial.ipynb`, which creates a `TradingEnvironment`, attaches a `TensorForceTradingStrategy`, and calls `environment.run()` inside a training loop.

No additional config files are required; the examples construct all components programmatically. If you need a live broker, import the classes under `exchanges/live/` and supply API keys directly to the constructor (the code does not read environment variables).

## Real‑World Use  
A quant team can replace a bespoke back‑test harness with:

```python
from tensortrade.environments import TradingEnvironment
from tensortrade.exchanges import SimulatedExchange
from tensortrade.actions import DiscreteActionStrategy
from tensortrade.rewards import SimpleProfitStrategy
from tensortrade.features import FeaturePipeline
from tensortrade.strategies import TensorForceTradingStrategy

exchange = SimulatedExchange(data_frame=my_prices)
pipeline = FeaturePipeline([MyIndicator()])
env = TradingEnvironment(exchange=exchange,
                         action_strategy=DiscreteActionStrategy(),
                         reward_strategy=SimpleProfitStrategy(),
                         feature_pipeline=pipeline)

agent = TensorForceTradingStrategy(environment=env)
agent.train(episodes=500)
```

The agent can then be exported and deployed in a production service that streams live market data to the same `SimulatedExchange` subclass adapted for a real broker.

## Code Health & Issues  

- **High – Import cycles** – `actions/__init__.py`, `rewards/__init__.py`, `slippage/__init__.py` (12 circular edges).  
- **High – Duplicated code** – repeated 6‑line blocks across `setup.py` and three action‑strategy files.  
- **High – Deep nesting** – max indentation depth 16 in `exchanges/simulated/simulated_exchange.py` and related files.  
- **Medium – Hub module** – `trades/__init__.py` is imported by 17 modules; changes here have wide impact.  
- **Medium – Broad exception handling** – `exchanges/simulated/fbm_exchange.py` uses bare `except`.  
- **Low – Stale TODO/FIXME** – 14 markers in live‑exchange modules.  
- **Dependency drift** – `pandas==0.25.0` (current 3.x) and `numpy==1.16.4` (current 2.x) are pinned far behind upstream releases, risking incompatibility with modern tooling.  
- No lockfile; reproducible builds rely on `requirements.txt` alone.  

CI runs on Travis (`.travis.yml`) and a Dockerfile are present; tests exist (`tests/`), but coverage is modest (8 test files).

## The Bottom Line  
`tensortrade` offers a well‑documented, component‑driven RL trading framework that can accelerate prototyping and provide a clear path to production. However, the import cycles, deep nesting, and outdated pinned dependencies make the codebase fragile to change and potentially hard to maintain. It is suited for teams comfortable with Python refactoring and willing to modernize the dependency stack before extending the library.

forks.name: deepseek-ocr-client-macos
forks.description: A real-time Electron-based desktop GUI for DeepSeek-OCR
forks.summary:
## The Problem

Running DeepSeek-OCR from the command line is slow and unfriendly: you manage a Python environment, download a multi-gigabyte model, and get output as raw text. This repo wraps the model in a desktop GUI with drag-and-drop image upload, real-time OCR, click-to-copy regions, and ZIP export—so a non-technical user can run OCR without touching a terminal.

## What This Does

`start.py` is the orchestrator: it checks prerequisites, installs Node and Python dependencies, and launches the Electron app. `main.js` is the Electron main process; `renderer.js` is the frontend logic (755 lines) handling drag-and-drop, progress display, and export. `backend/ocr_server.py` is the Python side: it loads the model, runs inference via `perform_ocr`, streams progress through `update_progress`, and serves results.

The app targets Windows (via `start-client.bat`); Linux/macOS support is untested per the README.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts at `main` in `start.py:254`, which reaches 9 functions. It calls `setup_python_environment`, which leaves the process via `subprocess.run` and touches the filesystem (`temp_req.unlink`). So a run first provisions the environment, then boots Electron.

The hub of the system is `update_progress`, called from 5 places—`load_model_background` calls it 9 times, `monitor_download` 3 times, `perform_ocr` 2 times. Change its signature and you break the model loader, the download monitor, the OCR path, and the streaming writer. Second is `get_preferred_device` (4 callers), which gates CUDA selection for `load_model_background`, `health_check`, and `perform_ocr`.

File-by-file map: `backend/ocr_server.py` owns model loading, inference, and progress (16 functions, 1 class). `start.py` owns environment setup and process launching (10 functions, runs external commands). `renderer.js` owns the UI state. The import graph shows 5 modules with zero edges between them—each file is effectively isolated, so there is no hub-and-spoke coupling to unwind, but also no shared contract.

## How To Use It

```bash
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/deepseek-ocr-client-macos
cd deepseek-ocr-client-macos
# Windows: double-click start-client.bat
# Linux/macOS: ./start-client.sh
```

First run installs dependencies automatically. Then click "Load Model" in the GUI, drop an image, and run OCR. A CUDA-capable NVIDIA GPU, Node 18+, and Python 3.12+ are required. No environment variables or config files are documented.

## Real-World Use

A document-processing workflow: a user drags a scanned invoice onto the window, the model runs locally (no data leaves the machine), OCR text appears in real time, and the user clicks a region to copy the value, then exports the full result as a ZIP with markdown images. For a small office handling sensitive documents, that local inference is the selling point.

## Code Health & Issues

From static analysis (measured, not opinion):

- **High – deep nesting** – `backend/ocr_server.py` and `renderer.js` reach indentation depth 8; control flow is hard to follow. Fix with early returns and extracted inner blocks.
- **Medium – broad exception handling** – `backend/ocr_server.py` swallows errors with bare/`Exception`-wide `except` clauses. Catch specific exceptions and re-raise the rest.
- **Medium – oversized file** – `renderer.js` at 755 lines concentrates UI state and logic; splitting it by responsibility reduces ripple.
- **High – vulnerable pinned dependency** – `torch@2.9.1` (CVE-2026-24747, high, plus 3 more) and `transformers@4.46.3` (CVE-2026-4372, high, plus 41 more). The pinned version is what installs. Upgrade to the fixed versions and commit the lockfile.
- **Medium – no update bot** – no Dependabot/Renovate config, so advisories sit unpatched. Add `.github/dependabot.yml`.

SDLC gaps: no test files, no CI pipeline. Six dependencies are behind major versions, including `electron` (^28 vs 43).

## The Bottom Line

A functional single-purpose OCR GUI that works, but it is a quickly-assembled prototype (the README admits this): deep nesting, broad exception handling, and a 755-line renderer will hurt whoever maintains it. The pinned vulnerable torch/transformers versions should be addressed before production use. Fine for a local, offline OCR tool; not ready for anything with a release pipeline.

forks.name: airllm
forks.description: AirLLM 70B inference with single 4GB GPU
forks.summary:
## The Problem

Running large language models (70B+ parameters) typically requires multiple high-end GPUs with 80GB+ of VRAM each. AirLLM addresses this by enabling inference of 70B models on a single 4GB GPU card without quantization, distillation, or pruning, and even claims support for Llama3.1 405B on 8GB VRAM. This makes large-model inference accessible to developers without expensive hardware.

## What This Does

The core package in `air_llm/` implements memory-efficient inference by loading model layers to GPU one at a time and keeping the rest on CPU/disk. The `air_llm/airllm/airllm_base.py` file defines the `AirLLMBaseModel` class with methods like `load_layer_to_cpu`, `move_layer_to_device`, and `set_layers_from_layer_names` that orchestrate this layer-by-layer execution. Model-specific subclasses (`airllm_llama_mlx.py`, `airllm_baichuan.py`, `airllm_qwen.py`, etc.) handle architecture variations.

The repo also contains several independent projects: `anima_100k/` (long-context training), `rlhf/` (DPO fine-tuning), `training/` (QLoRA), and `eval/` (evaluation notebooks). These are separate efforts sharing the AirLLM ecosystem rather than one integrated codebase.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts at `air_llm/airllm/__init__.py` (imports 12 modules). The entry point for users is typically `AutoModel` in `auto_model.py`, which routes to the correct model class. The central hub is `airllm_base.py` — 9 modules import it, making it the highest-fan-in module. It defines `init_model` and `set_layers_from_layer_names`, which most model implementations call.

The `persist/` directory contains `model_persister.py` and its subclasses (`mlx_model_persister.py`, `safetensor_model_persister.py`), which handle model serialization. These three files participate in a circular import cycle, complicating refactoring.

Key control flow: `AirLLMBaseModel.__init__` → `init_model` → loads config → `set_layer_names_dict` → generation loop calls `load_layer_to_cpu`/`move_layer_to_device` per layer, with `utils.py` handling `clean_memory` and `load_layer` between steps. The `utils.py` module has high branching density (98 branch points over 286 lines).

## How To Use It

```bash
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/airllm
cd airllm
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install -e air_llm/
```

The README documents usage via the `airllm` pip package:

```python
from airllm import AutoModel
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("meta-llama/Llama-2-70b-hf")
output = model.generate(input_ids)
```

Configuration is minimal — model paths and generation parameters are passed directly. No environment variables or config files are required. Example notebooks exist in `air_llm/examples/`.

## Real-World Use

A developer with a single consumer GPU (4–8GB VRAM) wants to run Llama-3-70B for prototyping. AirLLM loads the model from HuggingFace, keeps embedding layers in GPU memory, and streams transformer layers through GPU memory during generation. The trade-off is speed: each layer must be loaded from disk/CPU for every forward pass, making inference significantly slower than with full GPU residency.

## Code Health & Issues

Static analysis (20 findings: 8 high, 12 medium) identified:

- **High - Deep nesting** - `airllm_base.py`, `utils.py`, `airllm_llama_mlx.py` have max indentation depth of 22, making control flow hard to follow.
- **High - Import cycle** - `persist/model_persister.py`, `mlx_model_persister.py`, `safetensor_model_persister.py` are mutually reachable.
- **High - Duplicated code** - 683 repeated 6-line blocks across 10 files.
- **Medium - Broad exception handling** - `rlhf/qlora_dpo.py`, `training/qlora.py` use bare `except`.
- **Medium - Oversized files** - `anima_100k/modeling_flash_llama.py` (761 lines), `longer_training.py`, `rlhf/qlora_dpo.py`.

No CI pipeline, no lockfile, and no Dockerfile. Tests exist (10 files) but aren't automated.

## The Bottom Line

AirLLM is a practical solution for running large models on constrained hardware, with a proven track record (3k+ stars upstream). The code works but has maintainability issues — deep nesting, import cycles, and duplication. Use it for inference workloads where hardware constraints matter more than speed; expect to invest effort if you need to modify core logic.

forks.name: TradingAgents
forks.description: TradingAgents: Multi-Agents LLM Financial Trading Framework
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Financial research teams need a coordinated workflow where multiple specialist LLM agents (fundamental, sentiment, technical) exchange analyses and reach a unified trading decision. Building that orchestration from scratch requires handling data ingestion, agent state, inter‑agent communication, and result persistence – all of which are error‑prone and hard to reproduce.

## What This Does  
`TradingAgents` provides a ready‑made multi‑agent framework that mirrors a trading desk. Core agent classes live under `tradingagents/agents/` (e.g., `fundamentals_analyst.py`, `market_analyst.py`, `news_analyst.py`). Shared utilities such as `agent_utils.py` and `memory.py` manage LLM prompts, embeddings, and situation memories.  

Data ingestion is implemented in `tradingagents/dataflows/` – modules like `alpha_vantage.py`, `googlenews_utils.py`, and `y_finance.py` fetch market data, news, and fundamentals via external APIs.  

The graph engine in `tradingagents/graph/` (especially `trading_graph.py` and `setup.py`) builds a directed workflow where each agent is a node; the graph drives the sequence of calls and propagates state between agents.

The CLI (`cli/main.py`) ties everything together, offering an interactive console that steps through the analysis, displays intermediate messages, and writes final reports to `results_dir`.

## How It Is Wired  
Execution starts at the `analyze` function in `cli/main.py` (line 1104). It creates the results directory, then calls `run_analysis` (line 738).  

* `run_analysis` orchestrates the core loop, invoking the graph via `setup_graph` (from `tradingagents/graph/setup.py`).  
* `setup_graph` builds a `TradingAgentsGraph` instance (defined in `tradingagents/graph/trading_graph.py`) and registers tool nodes for each agent.  
* The graph’s `propagate` method walks the node list, calling each agent’s primary method (`run` or similar) which lives in the analyst and manager modules.  

Key downstream calls:  

* Data fetches – e.g., `get_indicator` → `_make_api_request` (in `tradingagents/dataflows/alpha_vantage_common.py`) reach out to external services (Alpha Vantage, Google News, Yahoo Finance).  
* Memory handling – `add_situations` and `get_memories` (in `tradingagents/agents/utils/memory.py`) store and retrieve embeddings, invoking an LLM model via `openai.py` or `google.py`.  
* Reporting – `update_report_section` (in `cli/main.py`) writes markdown files under the results folder.  

The most connected modules are `tradingagents/agents/__init__.py` (imports 15 others, part of a circular dependency with `agent_states.py`) and `tradingagents/graph/trading_graph.py` (imports 11 modules). These hubs have the largest blast radius: a change to their import list or public API can cascade across >10 files.

Two import cycles are present (`agents/__init__.py` ↔ `agents/utils/agent_states.py`). They increase cognitive load and risk of runtime import errors; breaking them by moving shared constants to a dedicated module would reduce instability.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/TradingAgents
cd TradingAgents

# Install dependencies (pip is the implied manager)
pip install -r requirements.txt   # or: pip install -e .  (uses setup.py/pyproject.toml)

# Provide required API keys in a .env file based on .env.example
# Example (Alpha Vantage, OpenAI, Google):
#   ALPHAVANTAGE_API_KEY=your_key
#   OPENAI_API_KEY=your_key
#   GOOGLE_API_KEY=your_key

# Run the interactive CLI
python -m cli.main
```

The CLI walks the user through ticker selection, date range, and displays each agent’s contribution. Results are written to `results_dir` (created under the current working directory).

## Real‑World Use  
A quant research team can embed the framework in an automated overnight pipeline: a cron job runs `python -m cli.main --ticker=AAPL --start=2024-01-01 --end=2024-01-31`. The pipeline captures the generated markdown report, archives it, and feeds the final trading signal into an execution engine. Because agents are modular, a team can replace the `risk_manager` node with a proprietary model without touching the rest of the graph.

## Code Health & Issues  

- **High – No test suite** – 53 source files, 0 test files. Add at least one test per public entry point and a CI step to run them.  
- **High – No CI pipeline** – No `.github/workflows/` or other CI config. Add a GitHub Actions workflow that runs `pip install -e . && pytest` on push/PR.  
- **Medium – No dependency lockfile** – `pyproject.toml` and `requirements.txt` are present but no `uv.lock` or `requirements-lock.txt`. Enable Dependabot (`.github/dependabot.yml`) to keep packages up‑to‑date.  
- **High – Import cycle** – `tradingagents/agents/__init__.py` ↔ `tradingagents/agents/utils/agent_states.py`. Break the cycle by extracting shared enums/types to a new module.  
- **High – Duplicated analyst code** – Repeated 6‑line blocks across the four analyst files. Consolidate common logic into a helper (e.g., `agent_utils.py`).  
- **Medium – File opened without context manager** – `tradingagents/dataflows/local.py` uses raw `open()`. Switch to `with open(...) as f:` to guarantee closure.  
- **High – Deep nesting** – Functions in `cli/main.py` and several dataflow modules exceed 8 indentation levels, hampering readability. Refactor with early returns or helper functions.  

## The Bottom Line  
`TradingAgents` delivers a functional multi‑agent LLM trading sandbox with clear module boundaries and a usable CLI, but the codebase suffers from high coupling, duplicated logic, and a lack of automated testing or CI. It is suitable for research prototypes or teams willing to invest in refactoring and test coverage before production use.

forks.name: PythonRobotics
forks.description: Python sample codes and textbook for robotics algorithms.
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Students and researchers need ready‑to‑run Python implementations of core robotics algorithms (localization, mapping, SLAM, path planning, control). Existing textbooks often omit runnable code or provide fragmented snippets, forcing users to re‑implement the logic and waste time on debugging.

## What This Does  
The repository supplies self‑contained Python scripts that demonstrate a full spectrum of classic algorithms. The `PathPlanning/` folder (92 files) hosts A*, D*, RRT*, Hybrid A*, and Frenet‑optimal planners; `SLAM/` and `Localization/` implement EKF, FastSLAM, particle filters, and ICP. 3‑D drone trajectory following lives in `AerialNavigation/drone_3d_trajectory_following/` and arm‑navigation examples under `ArmNavigation/`.  

Key entry points are:  

* `PathPlanning/DStar/dstar.py` – defines `run()` (line 159) that builds a grid map, invokes the D* planner, and visualises the result.  
* `AerialNavigation/drone_3d_trajectory_following/drone_3d_trajectory_following.py` – `main()` (line 192) creates a `Quadrotor` instance, runs a simulation loop, and calls the generic `plot()` helper (77 callers).  

All algorithms share utility modules `utils/angle.py` (26 importers) and `utils/plot.py` (8 importers), which centralise geometry calculations and Matplotlib visualisation.

## How It Is Wired  
Execution starts in a concrete script, e.g. `PathPlanning/DStar/dstar.py` → `run()`. `run()` constructs a map, calls `DStar` class methods (`cost`, `set_state`) and then invokes `plot()` from `utils/plot.py`. The call graph shows `plot` is the most frequently called internal function (77 distinct callers), giving it the widest blast radius; any change here ripples through most planners and visualisations.  

`main` in the drone example follows a similar pattern:  

1. Instantiate `Quadrotor` (`AerialNavigation/.../Quadrotor.py`).  
2. Loop over time steps, calling `calculate_position`, `calculate_velocity`, and `calculate_acceleration`.  
3. Each step ends with `plot` to render the trajectory.  

The internal call graph records 1 607 intra‑repo call edges; notable hot spots are `flatten` (16 callers) and `Node` (24 callers) used by the Time‑Based Path Planning submodule. No circular import cycles were detected, but `utils/angle.py` is a hub (26 importers), so stability there is critical. Deep nesting (max indentation depth 6) appears in `PathPlanning/TimeBasedPathPlanning/GridWithDynamicObstacles.py`, `utils/plot.py`, and `MissionPlanning/StateMachine/state_machine.py`, making those files harder to modify safely.  

External interaction is limited to five functions that launch shell commands; the code otherwise stays in‑process and writes only image files for visualisation (e.g., `PathPlanning/SpiralSpanningTreeCPP/map/*.png`).

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the exact upstream repository
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/PythonRobotics.git
cd PythonRobotics

# Install the declared Python deps (no lockfile, so versions may vary)
pip install -r requirements/requirements.txt
```

*To run a planner*:  

```bash
python PathPlanning/DStar/dstar.py        # executes run() → visualises D* path
```

*To simulate the drone demo*:  

```bash
python AerialNavigation/drone_3d_trajectory_following/drone_3d_trajectory_following.py
```

The `docs/Makefile` can build the Sphinx documentation (`make -C docs html`) if you need the textbook‑style narrative.

## Real‑World Use  
A robotics research team can import a planner directly, e.g.:

```python
from PathPlanning.RRTStar.rrt_star import RRTStar
planner = RRTStar(start, goal, obstacle_map)
path = planner.plan()
```

The returned `path` can feed a ROS node’s trajectory controller without further modification, because the data structures are plain Python lists of (x, y) tuples.

## Code Health & Issues  

*Measured findings* (static analysis)  
- **HIGH – Hub module**: `utils/angle.py` (26 importers). Keep API stable; extract volatile logic.  
- **HIGH – Deep nesting**: observed in `PathPlanning/TimeBasedPathPlanning/GridWithDynamicObstacles.py`, `utils/plot.py`, `MissionPlanning/StateMachine/state_machine.py`. Refactor to early returns.  
- **HIGH – Duplicated code**: similar 6‑line blocks across multiple `ArmNavigation/` files. Consolidate into shared helpers.  

*Code‑health audit* (GitHub Actions)  
- **HIGH** – Pin third‑party actions to commit SHA (`.github/workflows/*`).  
- **HIGH** – CI does not run the test suite; add a `pytest` step.  
- **MEDIUM** – Declare least‑privilege `permissions` for `GITHUB_TOKEN` (`.github/workflows/Linux_CI.yml`).  
- **MEDIUM** – Add a dependency‑vulnerability scan (e.g., `dependency-review-action`).  
- **MEDIUM** – Set `persist-credentials: false` on checkout to avoid credential leakage.  
- **LOW** – Set `timeout-minutes` on workflow jobs to prevent hangs.  

No Dockerfile, no lockfile, and the repository relies on a single `requirements.txt`, which limits reproducibility.

## The Bottom Line  
The repo delivers a breadth of well‑organised, runnable robotics algorithms useful for education and rapid prototyping. Its primary limitation is operational hygiene: CI does not execute tests, and dependency management lacks lockfiles and pinned actions, which raises reproducibility and security concerns. Teams comfortable managing their own CI pipeline will find the code valuable; others should first address the health issues before adopting it in production.

forks.summary:
## The Problem

AI agents need persistent memory that survives across sessions, with semantic search, knowledge graph visualization, and cloud synchronization capabilities. The repository provides this as an MCP server, but the codebase shows significant structural debt that increases the risk and cost of modifications.

## What This Does

Memora is a lightweight MCP server for semantic memory storage, knowledge graphs, and cross-session context. The Python core (`memora/`) handles storage backends, memory operations, and cloud sync via Cloudflare D1, S3, and R2. The TypeScript frontend (`memora-graph/`) provides a React-based visualization server with graph routes and Cloudflare Workers integration. The claude-plugin hooks (`claude-plugin/`) integrate memory operations into Claude Code workflows. Execution starts at `memora/server.py:1704` (`main`), which routes through 134 functions; `memora/graph/server.py:120` (`api_graph`) reaches 87 functions for graph data; and `memora/graph/server.py:130` (`api_memory`) reaches 41 functions for memory operations. The import graph contains 2 modules in circular dependencies (`memora/backends.py` ↔ `memora/storage.py`), and `memora/storage.py` (87 functions) is the most connected data hub, called from 5 other files and performing database reads/writes, file operations, and model inference.

## How It Is Wired

Control flows from entry points through the call graph. `main` in `memora/server.py` reaches `compute_content_hash` (crypto via hashlib.md5) and ultimately performs database writes via `add_memory` → `conn.execute`. `api_graph` routes to `connect` (sqlite3.connect) and `get_graph_data`. `memory_create` flows through `_create_memory` → `add_memory`. An outbound request in `memora/graph/server.py` has no timeout, so a slow peer can hold workers indefinitely. The circular import between `memora/backends.py` (62 functions, 9 classes) and `memora/storage.py` (87 functions) means either module cannot load without the other, increasing blast radius for changes. `memora/graph/data.py` and `memora/graph/server.py` both define `_get_memora_version`, indicating duplicated version-detection logic. Six functions make outbound network calls (R2, D1, CloudSQLiteBackend), and three call models for inference (embedding operations).

## How To Use It

**Setup:**
```bash
pip install git+https://github.com/agentic-mcp-tools/memora.git
# Or for local embeddings:
pip install "memora[local]" @ git+https://github.com/agentic-mcp-tools/memora.git
```

**Configuration:** Required environment variables belong in `.mcp.json` project root:
- `MEMORA_DB_PATH` for local SQLite
- `MEMORA_STORAGE_URI` (d1://<account-id>/<database-id>) for Cloud Cloudflare D1
- `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` for cloud auth
- `MEMORA_ALLOW_ANY_TAG` to permit unrestricted tagging

**Running it:**
```bash
# Stdio mode (default MCP)
memora-server

# Graph visualization server
memora-server --graph-port 8765

# HTTP transport
memora-server --transport streamable-http --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080
```

## Real-World Use

In a multi-session Claude Code workflow, a user extracts research notes in one session and later resumes context in another. The server stores memories with vector embeddings (TF-IDF or OpenAI), auto-links cross-references based on similarity, and preserves tag hierarchies. When the graph visualization is enabled (`--graph-port`), an interactive Mermaid render appears at the configured port, showing clusters and edges. Cloud sync via D1 allows the same memories to be shared across deployed workers without manual DB migration.

## Code Health & Issues

- **[HIGH] Commit a lockfile beside the manifest** - `pyproject.toml` has no generated lockfile, so tested and shipped artifacts can differ.
- **[HIGH] Add a workflow that builds and tests this repository** - 24 source files, no CI configuration; every merge runs untested.
- **[HIGH] Replace the wildcard CORS origin** - `memora-graph/worker/src/index.ts` has `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: "*`; paired with credentials this allows any site to perform authenticated requests.
- **[MEDIUM] Enable Dependabot or Renovate** - 2 manifest(s), no update bot configured; published advisories remain unpatched indefinitely.
- **[MEDIUM] Give the outbound request a timeout** - `memora/graph/server.py` has 1 outbound call with no timeout; `requests` has no default, so a slow peer hangs workers.
- **[LOW] Add repository convention files** - missing `.editorconfig`, `.gitattributes`, and formatter config.

## The Bottom Line

The repository delivers a functional MCP server with semantic memory, graph visualization, and cloud sync out of the box, making it immediately useful for agents needing persistent cross-session context. However, the circular import between backends and storage, absent CI/CD, wildcard CORS, and missing lockfile represent real risks for production use and long-term maintenance. Teams that can tolerate the current code health gaps and add their own CI/tooling will find value quickly; others should budget refactoring time for the import cycle and cognitive-load hotspots before relying on this in critical paths.

forks.summary:
**Technical Briefing – unbound‑dashboard**  
Repository: `https://github.com/moses-y/unbound-dashboard` (clone with `git clone https://github.com/moses-y/unbound-dashboard`)  

---  

### The Problem  
Operators of the recursive DNS resolver **Unbound** need a ready‑made Grafana view that surfaces resolver health, query statistics, and log streams without building a custom exporter or dashboard from scratch.  

### What This Does  
The repo supplies only artefacts that let you **assemble** the monitoring stack:

* **`info.md`** – detailed description of each Grafana panel, metric source, and Loki log query.  
* **`release.md`** – change log for each dashboard version; the latest release bundles a trimmed `grafana.ini` and a pre‑filled `prometheus.yml`.  
* **`README.md`** – step‑by‑step install guide for Grafana OSS, Prometheus, the Go‑based Unbound exporter (external to this repo), and Loki.  
* **`screenshots/`** – PNG of the final dashboard (e.g., `dashboard-2.3.png`) and a short markdown index.

No source code for the exporter or container definitions lives here; the repository is a **documentation‑only** package that references the exporter code hosted elsewhere.  

### How It Is Wired  
Because the repository contains no executable files, the internal call graph cannot be derived. The only wiring that can be described is the **deployment flow** documented in `README.md`:

1. **Grafana** is installed (deb package) and started as `grafana-server`.  
2. **Prometheus** reads the bundled `prometheus.yml`, which scrapes the HTTP endpoint exposed by the external Unbound exporter (default `http://<host>:9167/metrics`).  
3. **Loki** is configured separately (outside this repo) to ingest Unbound log files; Grafana panels query Loki directly.  
4. The user imports the JSON dashboard (included in the release assets) into Grafana, which then visualises metrics from Prometheus and logs from Loki.

No code in this repository touches the network, filesystem, or external services; all runtime behaviour resides in the external exporter and the standard Grafana/Prometheus/Loki binaries.  

### How To Use It  

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/unbound-dashboard
cd unbound-dashboard

# 2. Follow the README steps (example for Raspberry Pi OS)
wget https://dl.grafana.com/oss/release/grafana_11.1.0_arm64.deb
sudo apt install musl               # required for Grafana ≥10.2.3
sudo dpkg -i grafana_11.1.0_arm64.deb
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now grafana-server

sudo apt install prometheus
# replace /etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml with the file from the release assets
sudo cp releases/vX.Y.Z/prometheus.yml /etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
sudo systemctl restart prometheus

# 3. Deploy the external Unbound exporter (see https://github.com/ar51an/unbound-redis)
#    Ensure it listens on port 9167 and is reachable from Prometheus.

# 4. In Grafana UI (http://<RP‑IP>:3000) import the dashboard JSON
#    (provided in the GitHub release assets).
```

*Configuration files*: `prometheus.yml` (in the release assets) and the optional `grafana.ini` are the only config artefacts shipped. No environment‑variable list is present in the repo.  

### Real‑World Use  
A typical Raspberry Pi 4 DNS resolver runs Unbound, the Go exporter, Prometheus, Loki, and Grafana on the same host. Grafana dashboards give ops staff a single pane showing query rates, cache hit ratios, and error logs, enabling rapid identification of mis‑configurations or upstream failures.  

### Code Health & Issues  

* **Medium – No test files** – repository-wide (static analysis).  
* **Medium – No CI/CD pipeline** – no `.github/` workflows or other CI config.  
* **Low – No Dockerfile** – container builds must be authored externally.  
* **Info – License present** – `LICENSE` file included.  
* **Info – No lockfile** – dependency versions are not pinned in this repo.  
* **Info – No committed secrets** – static scan found none.  

The repo’s scope is strictly documentation; therefore the usual software‑quality metrics (unit tests, CI) are not applicable but should be added if future code (e.g., exporter updates) is stored here.  

### The Bottom Line  
`unbound-dashboard` delivers a ready‑made Grafana view and the minimal Prometheus/Loki configuration needed to monitor Unbound, but it contains **no executable code**. It is suitable for teams that already run the external exporter and want a quick, documented way to import the dashboard. Lack of tests, CI, and container support means the repo is low‑maintenance documentation rather than a production‑ready codebase. Engineers should treat it as a reference bundle and manage the actual exporter and deployment tooling separately.

forks.name: FlyingCarpet
forks.description: Cross-platform AirDrop. File transfer between Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, and Windows over ad hoc WiFi. No network infrastructure required, just two devices with WiFi chips (and optionally Bluetooth) in close range.
forks.summary:
## The Problem

Moving files between devices without shared infrastructure is still painful. USB drives fail across filesystems, cloud services need accounts and bandwidth, and AirDrop is Apple-only. FlyingCarpet solves this by creating an ad hoc WiFi link between any two devices with wireless chips—no router, no internet, no account.

## What This Does

FlyingCarpet is a cross-platform file transfer tool covering Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, and Windows. The repository contains a Rust core library (`core/`) that handles the transfer logic, a Tauri-based desktop app (`Flying Carpet/src-tauri/`) with a web frontend (`Flying Carpet/src/index.html`, `main.js`), and a Kotlin Android app (`Android/`). The core is split per-OS: `core/src/linux/` and `core/src/windows/` each have `network.rs`, `bluetooth.rs`, `central.rs`, and `peripheral.rs` modules.

Version 9 added Bluetooth for transfer negotiation—the WiFi hotspot handles bulk data, while Bluetooth exchanges keys and device info first. The `core/src/sending.rs` and `core/src/receiving.rs` modules handle chunked, encrypted file transfer.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts at `start_async` in `Flying Carpet/src-tauri/src/main.rs:118`, which reaches 55 functions—the widest blast radius in the repo. The path to real work is short: `start_async -> start_transfer -> send_file`, where `send_file` in `core/src/sending.rs` leaves the process via `File::open` to read the file off disk. No database, no network service—the filesystem is the only external effect.

The call graph resolves 113 internal edges. `fc_error` is called from 19 places and `output` from 12, making both load-bearing: change their signatures and the most code breaks. `negotiate_bluetooth` is the busiest hub, calling `process_bluetooth_message` 13 times, `unpair` 7 times, and `generate_password` 3 times—it orchestrates the Bluetooth handshake before WiFi transfer begins.

File-by-file map:

- `Flying Carpet/src-tauri/src/main.rs` — Tauri commands: `output`, `show_progress_bar`, `show_pin`, `cancel_transfer`. Called from 8 files.
- `core/src/utils.rs` — `run_command`, `get_key_and_ssid`, `hash_file`. Called from 6 files.
- `core/src/linux/network.rs` — `start_hotspot`, `stop_hotspot`, `join_hotspot`, `connect_to_peer`. Called from 4 files.
- `core/src/error.rs` — error types. Called from 7 files.
- `core/src/windows/network.rs` — the only module running external commands (`run_shell_execute`), via `stop_hotspot` and `connect_to_peer`.

The module graph is clean: 2 internal modules, 1 import edge, no circular dependencies.

## How To Use It

```bash
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/FlyingCarpet
cd FlyingCarpet
cargo install tauri-cli
cargo tauri dev        # development
cargo tauri build      # release artifacts
```

Linux requires system dependencies listed in the README (`libsoup2.4*`, `libwebkit2gtk*`, etc.). The Android app builds via Gradle in `Android/FlyingCarpet/`. No environment variables or config files are required—the app handles everything at runtime.

## Real-World Use

A consultant needs to move a 4GB database dump from a client's Windows laptop to a Linux server in a room with no network. Both machines run FlyingCarpet, one hosts a hotspot, the other joins it, and the transfer completes over direct WiFi. No flash drive, no cloud, no filesystem format issues.

## Code Health & Issues

Measured findings from static analysis (19 total: 2 high, 15 medium, 2 low):

- **High — Deep nesting** — max indentation depth of 9 in `core/src/windows/central.rs`, `Android/.../Bluetooth.kt`, and `Android/.../MainActivity.kt`. Flatten with early returns and guard clauses.
- **High — Duplicated code** — 19 repeated 6-line blocks across `core/src/linux/bluetooth.rs`, `core/src/windows/bluetooth.rs`, `core/src/linux/network.rs`, and `core/src/windows/network.rs`. Extract shared helpers.
- **Medium — High branching density** — 56 branch points over 181 lines in `core/src/linux/central.rs` and the Windows modules.
- **Low — TODO/FIXME markers** — 8 unresolved markers in `core/src/windows/network.rs` and `core/src/windows/peripheral.rs`.

SDLC observations: no CI/CD pipeline exists—26 source files merge without an automated build gate. No Dependabot or Renovate is configured despite 3 manifest files. Tests exist (2 test files) but are minimal.

## The Bottom Line

Solid, practical codebase for a genuinely useful tool. The core logic is well-factored per-OS, but the Windows and Linux modules carry duplicated logic and deep nesting that will slow future changes. The lack of CI is the biggest risk—any change can break the build silently. Worth using for the transfer capability; worth adding CI before contributing.

forks.name: videosos
forks.description: Enable AI models for video production in the browser
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Web‑based video editors normally rely on server‑side rendering or proprietary SaaS APIs, exposing user media and API keys to third‑party services. Teams that need full privacy, offline capability, or fine‑grained cost tracking lack an open‑source, client‑only alternative that can still tap modern text‑to‑video, image‑to‑image and audio models.

## What This Does  
`videosos` delivers a full‑featured video editor that runs completely in the browser. The UI lives under `src/app/` and `src/components/`, while model‑selection, pricing, and cost aggregation are implemented in `src/lib/` (e.g., `src/lib/fal.ts`). Model metadata lives in `data/fal_models_schemas.json`. The project bundles FFmpeg‑wasm and Remotion for client‑side rendering, and stores everything in IndexedDB (`src/app/api/uploadthing/` utilities).  

Key files:  

* `src/app/[locale]/page.tsx` – entry page rendered by Next.js.  
* `src/components/right-panel.tsx` – UI hub that pulls pricing (`src/lib/pricing.ts`) and model lists.  
* `src/lib/fal.ts` – central façade for the fal.ai API; the largest source file (≈2 k lines).  

## How It Is Wired  
1. **Startup** – `npm run dev` (or `docker compose up`) launches the Next.js server defined by `next.config.mjs`. The first request hits `src/app/layout.tsx`, which injects global CSS (`src/app/globals.css`) and loads locale data from `messages/*.json`.  
2. **Model Loading** – `src/components/right-panel.tsx` imports `src/lib/fal.ts`. That module reads `data/fal_models_schemas.json` and exposes `fetchModels()` which calls the fal.ai endpoint (API key read from `process.env.FAL_API_KEY`).  
3. **Cost Calculation** – UI components (`src/components/ui/*`) pull pricing via `src/lib/pricing.ts`. This module is imported by only a handful of components (instability 0.9) but performs HTTP calls to the provider’s pricing API, then caches results in IndexedDB.  
4. **Media Generation** – When a user triggers generation, `src/components/media-panel.tsx` invokes `src/lib/fal.ts`’s `generateMedia()` which returns a streaming URL. The response is stored via the `uploadthing` helpers (`src/app/api/uploadthing/core.ts`) and displayed in the timeline (`src/components/video-frame-selector.tsx`).  
5. **Export** – The “Export” button calls `src/components/export-dialog.tsx`, which uses Remotion (`remotion` dependency) to compose the final video. Rendering happens in the browser via FFmpeg.wasm; the only external effect is a Blob download.  

The import graph shows **no circular dependencies** and 95 internal modules with 82 edges. The most‑connected node is `src/components/ui/button` (10 inbound imports, 0 outbound), indicating a stable, low‑risk UI primitive. Conversely, `src/components/right-panel` imports 16 modules but is not imported elsewhere, giving it an instability of 1 – changes here have the widest blast radius.

## How To Use It  
```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/videosos
cd videosos

# Install Node dependencies
npm ci           # uses package-lock.json

# Copy example env and add your API keys
cp .env.example .env
# edit .env → set FAL_API_KEY, RUNWARE_API_KEY, etc.

# Run locally (Docker optional)
npm run dev      # starts Next.js on http://localhost:3000

# Or containerised build
docker compose up --build   # builds docker/node/Dockerfile
```
The `Makefile` provides shortcuts (`make lint`, `make test`) that run the GitHub Actions lint workflow locally.

## Real‑World Use  
A marketing team can spin up the app on an internal workstation, load their private fal.ai key, and produce short promotional videos without any data leaving the device. The UI lets them select a model, preview cost (`src/lib/pricing.ts`), generate assets, arrange them on the timeline, and export a final MP4—all client‑side.

## Code Health & Issues  
* **HIGH – Oversized files** – `src/lib/fal.ts`, `src/components/media-panel.tsx`, `src/components/right-panel.tsx` each exceed 2 k lines; refactor into focused modules.  
* **HIGH – Duplicated code** – Repeated 6‑line blocks across 22 script files (`scripts/*.ts`); extract shared helpers.  
* **HIGH – Deep nesting** – Max indentation depth 11 in `src/components/right-panel.tsx`, `tools/docs-scraper/scrape_models.py`, `src/components/left-panel.tsx`; flatten with guard clauses.  
* **MEDIUM – Broad exception handling** – `scripts/parse_fal_models.py` uses bare `except`; replace with specific catches.  
* **MEDIUM – High branching density** – `src/lib/pricing.ts` and related scripts contain >70 branches; consider strategy tables.  

Additional observations: CI is defined in `.github/workflows/lint.yml`, but only linting runs; no test suite execution despite a single test file present. The repository contains committed secrets (`docs/fal/pages/real-time/secrets.md`). License (MIT) and lockfiles are present.

## The Bottom Line  
`videosos` offers a functional, privacy‑first browser editor with a rich model catalog, but the codebase suffers from large monolithic files and duplicated script logic that will increase maintenance cost. It is suitable for teams comfortable with Next.js and willing to invest in refactoring for long‑term stability.

## The Problem

Building Three.js Shading Language (TSL) materials by hand means juggling GLSL-style code fragments, texture loading, and WebGPU quirks with no visual feedback. This repo is a node-graph editor that lets you assemble TSL materials visually, preview them live in WebGPU, and export the result as code — aimed at developers who want a Material Editor-style workflow for Three.js.

## What This Does

`src/App.tsx` drives the React-based node graph UI. `src/viewer.ts` owns the WebGPU preview pipeline and texture handling, including `ensureKtx2Support`, `isKtx2Entry`, and `textureFromNode`. `src/tslGltfExporter.ts` handles serialization: `cleanArgs`, `assignLink`, and `createDefaultNodeSerializer` convert the node graph into TSL, material, or app output (JS/TS). `public/basis/` ships the Basis transcoder WASM for KTX2 texture support.

The fork adds GLTF geometry/material/texture nodes and export paths beyond the upstream. The README is candid: experimental, "vibe-coding" approach, pull requests not accepted, issues welcome.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts at `src/main.tsx` mounting `App.tsx`; `index.html` and `viewer.html` are the two HTML entry points. The static analysis resolved 6 internal modules with 0 import edges between them — the module graph shows no hub and no cycles, so there is no central coupling point to worry about. Within files, 7 internal call edges exist; the densest path is `textureFromNode` calling `isKtx2Entry` and `ensureKtx2Support` in `src/viewer.ts`, which is where KTX2 texture loading routes through. `src/tslGltfExporter.ts` is the serialization owner with 4 functions and 3 types; it carries the highest cognitive load at 52 branch points over 177 lines. Cross-module wiring beyond this is not mapped by the analysis.

## How To Use It

**Setup**: `npm install` (lockfile present, Node.js 18+ required).
**Running**: `npm run dev` starts the Vite dev server; open in a WebGPU-capable browser (Chrome/Edge 113+). The live demo is at https://takahirox.github.io/tsl-node-editor/. No environment variables are required.

## Real-World Use

A team prototyping a WebGPU product page can assemble a PBR material from GLTF geometry and KTX2 textures in the node graph, verify it live in the preview pane, then export the resulting TSL/JS and drop it into their Three.js app. The export path (`createDefaultNodeSerializer`) is the integration seam — generated code is plain Three.js TSL, so it ports into an existing renderer without this editor at runtime.

## Code Health & Issues

Static analysis found 1 medium finding: high branching density in `src/tslGltfExporter.ts` (52 branch points over 177 lines); the suggested fix is decomposing decision-heavy logic into table/strategy dispatch.

Additional findings from the audit:
- **Med** – No dependency update bot configured; add `.github/dependabot.yml`.
- **Med** – No dependency vulnerability scan in CI; add `dependency-review-action` or `osv-scanner`.
- **Med** – `deploy.yml` checkout keeps the GitHub token (`persist-credentials` not disabled); a malicious postinstall script could read a pushable credential.
- **Low** – No `timeout-minutes` on workflow jobs; a wedged job runs to the platform default.
- **Low** – Missing `.editorconfig`, `.gitattributes`, and formatter config.
- **Med/SDLC** – No test files detected anywhere in the repo.

Seven of 17 declared dependencies are behind major versions, including `typescript` (2 majors behind) and `vite` (1 major behind).

## The Bottom Line

A functional, focused node editor for Three.js TSL with working WebGPU preview and GLTF export — genuinely useful for prototyping. The lack of tests, the high branching in the exporter, and 7 stale dependencies make it risky as a production dependency, but it is fine as a reference implementation or a single-user tool. The upstream README's "no PRs accepted" stance means you should fork it if you need changes.

forks.name: tgterm
forks.description: Control your MacOS terminals via Telegram, for fun coding agents interaction and profit
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Developers who rely on remote agents need a quick way to type into a macOS terminal without setting up SSH tunnels, VPNs, or multiplexers. Existing solutions require extra networking layers and cannot capture on‑screen graphics, which hampers workflows that need visual feedback (e.g., debugging GUI output).

## What This Does  
`tgterm` builds a native macOS binary that bridges a Telegram bot to local terminal windows.  
* The source files `bot.c` (contains `main`) and `botlib.c/h` implement the Telegram API calls, message parsing, and keystroke injection.  
* `cJSON.c/h` and `json_wrap.c` handle JSON payloads from Telegram.  
* `qrcodegen.c/h` renders the QR code shown on first run for TOTP provisioning.  
* `sqlite_wrap.c/h` stores the Telegram user ID and OTP secret in a local SQLite DB.  
* Utility libraries `sds*` provide dynamic strings, while `sha1.c/h` supplies the HMAC‑SHA1 needed for TOTP generation.

The program runs as a single user‑space process, reads the API key from the command line (`./tgterm --apikey <key>`), and then waits for Telegram messages. Commands such as `.list` and `.2` let the owner select a terminal window; subsequent messages are translated into keystrokes via macOS Accessibility services, and screenshots are sent back using the Screen Recording permission.

## How It Is Wired  

**Entry point** – `bot.c:main` parses `--apikey`, initializes the bot (`bot_init()` in `botlib.c`), loads the SQLite DB (`sqlite_open()` in `sqlite_wrap.c`), and registers the Telegram update callback `bot_handle_update()`.

**Message flow**  
1. Telegram delivers an HTTP update → `botlib.c` uses libcurl to POST to the Telegram API.  
2. `bot_handle_update()` extracts the text, checks the sender against the stored owner ID (SQLite).  
3. If the user is not yet authenticated, `totp_verify()` (uses `sha1.c` + `sds` helpers) validates the 6‑digit code generated from the secret shown in the QR code (`qrcodegen.c`).  
4. Authenticated commands are dispatched:  
   * `.list` → `list_terminals()` (macOS window enumeration, defined in `bot.c`).  
   * `.N` → `select_terminal(N)` (stores the target window handle).  
   * any other text → `inject_keystrokes()` (Accessibility API calls, also in `bot.c`).  
5. After each command, `capture_screenshot()` (macOS screen‑recording API) writes a PNG buffer that `bot_send_photo()` (in `botlib.c`) uploads back to Telegram.

**Data stores** – `sqlite_wrap.c` is the sole persistence layer; it holds the owner’s Telegram ID and the encrypted TOTP secret. No other external files are touched.

**Dependency graph** – `bot.c` depends on `botlib.c/h`, `sqlite_wrap.c/h`, `json_wrap.c`, `cJSON.c`, `qrcodegen.c/h`, `sds*.c/h`, and `sha1.c`. The call graph is a star centered on `bot.c`; no circular imports were detected.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/tgterm
cd tgterm

# Build the binary (requires libcurl and libsqlite3 development headers)
make

# Run, supplying the Telegram Bot API key
./tgterm --apikey <YOUR_API_KEY>
```

* First execution prints a QR code and a base‑32 secret. Scan it with any TOTP app.  
* Open the bot in Telegram, send any message to become the owner, then reply with the 6‑digit code.  
* Use `.list` to see open terminal windows, `.2` (or similar) to select one, and type any further text to have it injected into that window.  

The README lists the same commands; no additional configuration files are required.

## Real‑World Use  
A developer working on a macOS‑only GUI tool can start `tgterm` on their laptop, then, while away, open Telegram on their phone, authenticate with the TOTP, and issue `.list` → `.3` → `make test`. The bot will type `make test` into the chosen terminal, capture the resulting output screenshot, and send it back—all without an SSH tunnel or a VPN.

## Code Health & Issues  

- **High – Add CI workflow** – 8 source files, no CI configuration. Without automated builds, any change can break the compile or runtime behavior.  
- **High – Deep nesting** – `botlib.h`, `sds.c`, `sqlite_wrap.c` contain blocks nested up to 10 levels, making reasoning difficult.  
- **High – Duplicated code** – Repeated 6‑line blocks across `botlib.c`, `sds.c/h`, `sdsalloc.h`. Consolidate into shared helpers.  
- **High – Oversized files** – `cJSON.c`, `bot.c`, `botlib.c` each exceed 2 500 lines; splitting by logical responsibility would reduce blast radius.  
- **Medium – High branching density** – `bot.c`, `json_wrap.c`, `qrcodegen.c` have >200 branch points in ~750 lines; refactor into smaller decision tables or strategy objects.  
- **Low – TODO/FIXME markers** – 3 markers remain in `cJSON.c`; resolve or file as issues.

Additional observations: the repository includes a LICENSE but no test suite, Dockerfile, or lockfile. No secrets were found in the commit history.

## The Bottom Line  
`tgterm` delivers a functional, macOS‑only bridge between Telegram and local terminals with minimal setup, but the codebase suffers from large, deeply nested files and a lack of automated testing or CI. It is suitable for personal or experimental use; teams planning production deployment should first refactor the core modules and introduce a CI pipeline.
