forks.summary:
## The Problem
Engineers evaluating large-scale system patterns confront scattered references and inconsistent organization. This repository centralizes proven scalability, reliability, and performance patterns from battle-tested systems, delivering a structured reading list without executable code or automated quality gates.

## What This Does
The repo contains 10 files: a curated `README.md` organizing patterns across Principle, Scalability, Availability, Stability, Performance, Intelligence, Architecture, Interview, Organization, Talk, Book, and Book sections; `.github/FUNDING.yml` and `_config.yml` as the two YAML files handling metadata and site configuration; issue templates `bug_report.md` and `feature_request.md`; and supporting docs `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `LICENSE`, and `SECURITY.md`. Six markdown files host the pattern listings; two YAML files manage repository metadata. No source code, functions, or runtime components exist.

## How It Is Wired
This is a static documentation repository. No entry points, function calls, database queries, or network requests are present. Execution begins and ends with reading markdown via any viewer. The "call graph" is human-navigated: `README.md` links to external articles through URLs. No automated wiring, builds, or tests touch the filesystem beyond rendering. The widest blast radius is the completeness of the curated link set, which depends on external site availability. The wiring has not been mapped for executable paths.

## How To Use It
Clone the repository:
```bash
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/awesome-scalability
```
Open `README.md` to browse pattern categories. No installation, build, or run commands are defined. Configuration is limited to `_config.yml` if using a static site generator, but the repo provides no build pipeline, environment variables, or runtime entry point.

## Real-World Use
A system designer preparing for an interview can browse the Architecture and Interview sections to reference real-world diagrams and anti-patterns. An engineering manager can compare team-structuring approaches across tech companies using the Organization section. The value lies in the curated links for knowledge grounding, not executable workflows.

## Code Health & Issues
- Medium (SDLC) - No test files detected - repository-wide
- Medium (SDLC) - No CI/CD pipeline detected - .github/ or CI config absent
- Repository hygiene: tests present: no | CI: no | Dockerfile: no | licence: yes | lockfile: no | committed secrets: none found

## The Bottom Line
This is a well-organized, credible reading list for scalability patterns, maintained with community contributions. It excels as a reference for interview prep, architecture reviews, and learning proven strategies from large-scale systems. However, it provides no executable code, automated quality gates, or runtime components, so it cannot be integrated into a CI/CD pipeline or used as a functional system component. Use it for knowledge grounding, not as a code dependency.

forks.name: claude-code-remote
forks.description: Claude Code Remote - Access Claude Code sessions from any device 📱💻
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Developers who work with Claude Code locally need a way to reach a running terminal session from a phone or any remote device. Without a dedicated tunnel they must expose ports manually (ngrok, port‑forwarding) or keep a laptop attached to the same network, which adds friction and security risk.

## What This Does  
The repository implements a small self‑hosted service that starts a local PTY, creates a Cloudflare (or Tailscale) tunnel, and serves a single‑page web UI that can be opened on a mobile device.  

* `server/index.ts` hosts the WebSocket control channel, broadcasts messages, and persists session data.  
* `server/pty-session.ts` wraps the PTY process, exposing `getInfo`, `isExecutable`, and other helpers.  
* `web/app.js` (1797 lines) renders the UI, handles QR‑code display and forwards user input to the WebSocket.  
* Tunnel providers live under `server/tunnel/` (`cloudflare.ts`, `tailscale.ts`) and are selected via `server/config.ts`.

All runtime code is TypeScript except the monolithic UI bundle (`web/app.js`).

## How It Is Wired  
Execution begins when the CLI (`npx claude-code-remote`) runs the `start` script defined in `package.json`, which imports `server/index.ts`. The primary entry point is the **WebSocket handler**:

* **`handleControlMessage`** (`server/index.ts:247`) receives commands from the browser, reaches **44 functions** across the codebase and is the only place that calls `ws.send` (network outbound).  
* It frequently invokes **`sendControl`** (called 31 times) which builds a control packet and writes it to the WebSocket.  
* `handleControlMessage` also calls **`cleanupSessionHandlers`**, **`getInfo`** (`server/pty-session.ts`), **`broadcastToAll`**, and **`getSession`**.  

Session lifecycle is managed by **`server/session-manager.ts`**, whose `createSession`, `getSession`, and `destroySession` are referenced by 1–3 callers each. The scheduler (`server/scheduler.ts`) reads/writes schedule files and performs a cryptographic operation when generating tokens.

Tunnel startup follows a short chain: **`startTunnel`** (`server/tunnel/index.ts:19`) → **`isAvailable`** (`server/tunnel/cloudflare.ts` or `tailscale.ts`) → **`start`** (creates the remote URL). This path touches only three functions.

File‑level responsibilities (ordered by blast radius):

| File | Core duties | External effect |
|------|-------------|-----------------|
| `server/index.ts` | WebSocket routing, client broadcast | Network (ws.send), file I/O |
| `server/scheduler.ts` | Load/create cron schedules, token crypto | File I/O, crypto |
| `server/pty-session.ts` | PTY process control, info queries | File I/O |
| `server/tunnel/*` | Tunnel provider abstraction, remote URL creation | Network |
| `server/auth.ts` | Token validation middleware | Network |
| `web/app.js` | UI rendering, QR code, input forwarding (1797 LOC) | Browser ↔ WebSocket |

The import graph shows **no circular dependencies**; the most “unstable” module is `server/index` (instability = 1) because it imports nine others but is not imported itself, so changes there have the widest impact.

## How To Use It  
```bash
# Clone the exact repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/claude-code-remote
cd claude-code-remote

# Install dependencies (Node 18+ required)
npm ci

# Run the service (creates a local server and a Cloudflare tunnel)
npx claude-code-remote
```
The CLI prints a local URL (e.g., `http://localhost:3456`) and a remote Cloudflare URL with a QR code. Scanning the code with a phone opens the UI from `web/index.html` served by the Express server in `server/index.ts`. No additional configuration files are required; optional `cloudflared` must be installed separately if remote access is desired (see README).

## Real‑World Use  
A developer starts the tool on a workstation, scans the QR code on a phone, and runs `git status` inside the PTY from the mobile UI. Because the tunnel is managed automatically, the session persists across Wi‑Fi changes and can be revisited hours later without re‑authenticating.

## Code Health & Issues  
- **High – Oversized file**: `web/app.js` (1797 LOC) makes the UI hard to maintain.  
- **Medium – Deep nesting**: Same file reaches indentation depth 6.  
- **Medium – High branching density**: `server/activity-detector.ts` and `server/process-detector.ts` each contain >44 branch points in <150 LOC.  
- **Medium – Missing tests**: No test files detected across the repo.  
- **Medium – No LICENSE**: Repository lacks a license file despite the README claiming MIT; legal reuse is ambiguous.  

CI is present (`.github/workflows/publish.yml`), lockfile exists, and no secrets are committed.

## The Bottom Line  
The project delivers a functional, zero‑config remote terminal for Claude Code with a clear separation between server logic and tunnel providers. However, the monolithic UI bundle, lack of automated tests, and missing license hinder long‑term maintainability. Suitable for teams needing rapid remote access and willing to refactor the front‑end and add tests before scaling.

forks.name: deepops
forks.description: Observe any stack, any service and any data,  using any UI components you prefer, never missing any X factors and resolve them before they become real problems.
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Businesses need a single pane that can ingest metrics, logs, and traces from any source, surface them in real‑time dashboards, and alert before an issue escalates. Existing tools often require multiple products or heavyweight agents, creating operational overhead and blind spots.

## What This Does  
`deepops` is a portfolio of four loosely coupled projects that together form “XO”, an observability platform aimed at developers:

* **datav** – the UI and API server (≈ 1 072 files). It renders dashboards, panels, and large‑screen views. Core entry points are `datav/frontend/src/index.tsx` and `datav/frontend/src/App.tsx`. The UI is built with React/TypeScript, bundled by Vite (`datav/frontend/vite.config.js`).  
* **otel-collector** – a Go‑based OpenTelemetry collector (≈ 187 files) that receives spans, metrics and logs, then forwards them to the datav backend.  
* **examples** – sample Go applications (e.g., `examples/hotrod`) that emit OTLP data for quick validation.  
* **deploy** – minimal Helm‑style manifests and scripts for deploying the stack in Kubernetes.

Common techniques across the suite are Go modules (`go.mod`), Docker multi‑stage builds (`datav/Dockerfile`, `datav/frontend/Dockerfile`), and a shared TypeScript type layer for dashboard definitions.

## How It Is Wired  
Execution starts with the **frontend** Docker image built from `datav/frontend/Dockerfile`. The image runs Vite’s production build (`npm run build`) and serves `index.html` via an Nginx template (`datav/frontend/nginx.template`). The compiled bundle calls `src/index.tsx`, which mounts the React app onto the DOM and registers routes such as `/dashboard/:id` (handled in `src/pages/dashboard/index.tsx`).

When a dashboard loads, the UI contacts the **backend API** (served by the same Go binary in `datav/Dockerfile`). The API reads configuration from `datav/.env` (currently committed) and opens a gRPC server that the **otel‑collector** talks to. The collector (`otel-collector/main.go`) subscribes to OTLP over gRPC, normalizes data, and writes it into the internal time‑series store used by the UI.

Key wiring points:

| Module | Responsibility | Blast‑radius |
|--------|----------------|--------------|
| `datav/frontend/src/views/dashboard/plugins/built-in/plugins` | Registers all built‑in panel plugins (imports 27 other modules) | High – any change ripples through most dashboards |
| `datav/frontend/src/components/largescreen/autoResize` | Provides responsive layout utilities (imported by 24 modules) | Low – stable helper |
| `datav/frontend/src/views/dashboard/edit-panel/EditPanel` | Handles panel edit UI (imports 15 modules, only 1 inbound) | Very high instability (0.94) – prone to breakage |

The static import graph shows **27 import cycles** (e.g., `plugins.ts ↔ query_runner.ts ↔ PanelGrid.tsx`). These cycles inflate compile time and hinder refactoring because a change forces recompilation of many unrelated modules.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/deepops
cd deepops

# Build the UI container
docker build -t datav-frontend -f datav/frontend/Dockerfile .

# Build the backend/API container
docker build -t datav-backend -f datav/Dockerfile .

# (Optional) Run the OpenTelemetry collector
docker build -t otel-collector -f otel-collector/Dockerfile .
docker run -p 4317:4317 otel-collector
```

The UI expects environment variables defined in `datav/frontend/.env` (e.g., `VITE_API_URL`). Remove this file from the repository, replace it with a template (`.env.example`), and supply the variables at container start:

```bash
docker run -e VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:8080 -p 80:80 datav-frontend
```

The backend API runs on port 8080 by default; start it with:

```bash
docker run -p 8080:8080 datav-backend
```

The example applications can be built with Go modules:

```bash
cd examples/hotrod
go build -o hotrod .
./hotrod
```

## Real‑World Use  
A SaaS provider can deploy the three containers (frontend, backend, collector) into a Kubernetes namespace using the manifests in `deploy/`. The collector receives OTLP data from microservices, the backend stores it, and the UI lets operators assemble custom dashboards without leaving the platform.

## Code Health & Issues  

* **High – No CI/CD** – 1069 source files lack any GitHub Actions or other pipeline.  
* **High – No build gate for `datav/Dockerfile`** – Docker image is never validated automatically.  
* **High – Committed `.env`** – Secrets are tracked in source history; must be removed and rotated.  
* **Medium – Dependabot missing** – No automated dependency updates for `package.json`, `go.mod`, or Docker images.  
* **Medium – Base images not pinned** – `golang:1.21.4-alpine3.18`, `node:16`, `alpine:3.18` are mutable tags.  
* **Medium – No pre‑commit secret scan** – Increases risk of future leaks.  
* **Medium – Container runs as root** – `datav/Dockerfile` lacks a non‑root `USER`.  
* **Low – Missing repo conventions** – No `.editorconfig`, `.gitattributes`, or shared formatter config.

Additional static findings (192 total) include 27 import cycles, several hub modules with > 20 inbound imports, deep nesting (up to 8 levels), and a 611‑line `PanelGrid.tsx` file that should be split.

## The Bottom Line  
`deepops` offers a functional, UI‑rich observability stack that can be containerised and deployed with minimal effort, but the codebase suffers from architectural debt (import cycles, oversized modules) and a lack of production‑grade hygiene (no CI, secret leakage, root containers). It is suitable for teams that need a quick, customizable dashboard layer and are prepared to invest in refactoring and adding CI/security gates.

forks.name: Home-Assistant-core
forks.description: :house_with_garden: Open source home automation that puts local control and privacy first.
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Home‑Assistant‑core is a 24 k‑file Python‑centric home‑automation platform, but two reproducible‑build and CI‑security gaps let a malicious patch or a wedged CI step slip past the project’s own quality gates. The static analysis flagged **no lockfile beside `pyproject.toml`** and **GitHub Actions pinned only to branch tags**, meaning the exact dependency set and action versions that passed tests can differ from what ships to users.

## What This Does  
Home Assistant provides local‑first home automation, exposing a modular component model under `homeassistant/components/`. Core runtime lives in `homeassistant/__main__.py` (entry point *main*) and orchestrates services, config flows, and integrations through a central `Hass` instance. The framework is exercised by 11 350 test files and 12976 source files, predominantly Python (16 516) with JSON configs (5 450) and YAML manifests (794).  

Key structural facts:  

* **Internal call graph** – 1 850 resolved self‑call edges; the most‑called functions are `response` (43 callers), `_is_feature_available` (16), `add_context_property` (15), and `_async_schedule_save` (14).  
* **Entry points** – `main` in `homeassistant/__main__.py:168` reaches 14 functions; `execute` in `homeassistant/components/assist_pipeline/pipeline.py:1684` reaches 32 functions and is invoked by nothing else in the repo.  
* **What the code touches outside itself** – 15 functions read/write files, 7 perform crypto/secrets ops, 14 make outbound network calls, 7 call a model for inference, 1 reads/writes a database. Traced paths: `main → restore_backup [filesystem via backup_file_path.unlink]` and `ensure_config_path [filesystem via os.mkdir]`.  
* **Files with most route traffic** – `homeassistant/components/alexa/capabilities.py` (153 functions, 30 types, called from 3 files); `homeassistant/auth/__init__.py` (45 functions, 4 classes, performs crypto, reads/writes files, makes network calls); `homeassistant/components/assist_pipeline/pipeline.py` (69 functions, 21 classes, reads/writes files).  

## How It Is Wired  
Execution starts at `homeassistant/__main__.py:168` (`main`). From there the flow reaches `ensure_config_path` (mkdirs config dir), then proceeds to component set‑up via `async_setup_entry` across many integrations. The assist pipeline (`pipeline.py`) executes `execute` (line 1684) which resolves language models and runs intent pipelines, touching the filesystem for language data and making outbound calls to speech‑to‑text services.  

A concrete leak path: `main → restore_backup [filesystem via backup_file_path.unlink]` demonstrates that a backup‑restore routine can delete arbitrary files if the backup path is controllable. Another path: `ensure_config_path [filesystem via os.mkdir]` shows that missing config directories are auto‑created, which can be abused to plant files under the Home Assistant user’s home.  

The call graph reveals cycles through `interfaces → Alexa → AlexaEndpointHealth` and `capability_resources → serialize_capability_resources`, meaning changes to the Alexa capability definition ripple across 23 downstream edges, inflating the blast radius of any breaking change.

## How To Use It  

**Setup**  
```bash
# Clone the exact repo the brief references
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/Home-Assistant-core.git

# Install into a virtualenv (pip is the declared package manager)
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e .[all]   # installs with optional extras
```

**Configuration**  
The single config file is `configuration.yaml` (created under `$HOME/.homeassistant/` on first run). Secrets are stored in `secrets.yaml` – the code‑health audit flagged `tests/components/elmax/fixtures/direct/cert.pem` and `tests/util/yaml/test_secrets.py` as secret‑shaped paths; ensure any real keys live there and are **not** committed to version control.

**Running it**  
```bash
# Start the Home Assistant server (Docker alternative also available)
ha core start
# or, via the entry point
python -m homeassistant --config $HOME/.homeassistant
```

The CLI entry point is `homeassistant/__main__.py:168` (`main`). Docker users can build from `Dockerfile`; the image tags are not pinned to a commit SHA (see Code Health below).

## Real‑World Use  
A developer adding a new Z‑Wave lock creates a component under `homeassistant/components/zwave/`. The component’s `async_setup_entry` registers a `Lock` entity, which the assist pipeline can expose via Alexa through `homeassistant/components/alexa/capabilities.py`. The pipeline’s `execute` function resolves the lock state, calls the model for natural‑language intent, and writes the resulting state to the Home Assistant state store (SQLite by default). If the lock’s firmware update API is reachable, the same flow makes an outbound network call – the analyst should verify TLS certs and restrict outbound hosts in `configuration.yaml`.

## Code Health & Issues  
The static analysis produced three findings (0 critical, 2 high, 0 medium, 1 low):

* **HIGH – Pin third‑party GitHub Actions to a commit SHA**  
  Evidence: `.github/workflows/*` reference `home-assistant/actions/helpers/info@master`, `…/version@master`, `…/verify-version@master`, `…/git-init@master`. A tag can move, so the action running with repository secrets may change without a code change.  
  Fix: Replace each `@vN` with the 40‑character commit SHA (keep the version comment) and let Dependabot bump the SHAs.

* **HIGH – Commit a lockfile beside the manifest**  
  Evidence: `pyproject.toml` has no lockfile in scope. Without a locked set of transitive dependencies, the artifact tested can differ from the artifact shipped.  
  Fix: Run `pip lock` (or `uv lock`) once and commit the generated `requirements.txt` / `uv.lock` alongside `pyproject.toml`.

* **LOW – Set timeout‑minutes on the workflow jobs**  
  Evidence: 3 workflows in `.github/workflows/` declare no `timeout-minutes`. A wedged step can run six hours (platform default), causing overlapping runs on a two‑hourly schedule.  
  Fix: Add a realistic `timeout-minutes` to each job (e.g., 120 for build, 60 for test).

No lockfile, unpinned Actions, and missing job timeouts are the only SDLC gaps the structure supports; otherwise the repo has CI (GitHub Actions), Dockerfiles, and a licence file.

## The Bottom Line  
Home‑Assistant‑core is a large, modular home‑automation codebase with solid test coverage and a clear component model. Its main weaknesses are reproducibility (missing lockfile) and CI security (Actions pinned only to branch tags). Teams that need deterministic builds and supply‑chain safety should lock dependencies and pin Actions to SHAs immediately. For operators who value local control and can tolerate manual dependency management, the platform remains a capable, well‑documented foundation.

forks.name: terraink
forks.description: TerraInk: The Cartographic Poster Engine that creates unique and customizable map posters
forks.summary:
## The Problem
This repository lacks automated quality gates: no test suite, no CI/CD pipeline, and no dependency lockfile means changes ship without signal that existing behavior is preserved, and builds are non-reproducible across environments.

## What This Does
TerraInk is a cartographic poster engine that generates custom city map posters from OpenStreetMap data. Users search locations via geocoding, select or build themes through a color palette system, and export high-resolution PNG posters at defined dimensions. The source lives primarily in `src/` (130 files), with 117 TypeScript and 42 TSX files handling theming (`src/features/theme/`), map rendering (`src/features/map/`), markers (`src/features/markers/`), and export pipelines (`src/features/export/`). Poster generation flows through `src/core/http/index.ts` for API calls and `src/core/cache/` for local storage. Two functions make outbound network calls (`nominatimAdapter.searchLocations`, `nominatimAdapter.geocodeLocation`) and one writes files (`pdfExporter` pipeline). The project uses Bun as its runtime, Vite for dev/build, and MapLibre GL for vector tile rendering.

## How It Is Wired
Execution starts at `src/App.tsx:65` (`AppShell`), which is called from nothing else in the repo, and `src/App.tsx:27` (`SettingsDrawer`), also uncall ed from internal callers. The primary export path is `compositeExport` at `src/features/poster/infrastructure/renderer/index.ts:15`, which reaches 8 functions and is itself called from 1 place. The internal call graph shows 314 resolved call edges; `clamp` is called from 20 places, `normalizeHexColor` from 13, and `usePosterContext` from 11. The most connected hub is `src/shared/utils/color.ts` (14 functions, 2 classes, called from 9 files) defining `normalizeHexColor`, `toUniqueHexColors`, `parseHex`. Deep nesting of 3 levels appears in `src/features/map/ui/MapDimensionFields.tsx`, `src/features/markers/ui/MarkersSection.tsx`, and `src/features/poster/ui/PreviewPanel.tsx`, with max indentation depth of 6. Oversized files include `src/features/map/infrastructure/maplibreStyle.ts` and `src/features/markers/ui/MarkersSection.tsx` at 631 lines each, making changes hard to hold and reason about. No circular dependencies exist across 120 analyzed modules, but 109 repeated 6-line blocks across 25 files indicate duplicated logic that should be extracted.

## How To Use It
**Setup:** `bun install` (bun.lock present; project uses Bun as runtime).  
**Configuration:** No environment variables are required for basic operation; `src/core/config.ts` centralizes project config.  
**Running it:** `bun run dev` (via vite.config.js) starts the development server; `bun run build` produces a production build. The app runs at `http://localhost:5173`.  
**Exporting:** Use the export UI (`src/features/export/ui/`) or invoke `compositeExport` programmatically from `src/features/poster/infrastructure/renderer/index.ts`.

*Note: The README documents these commands verbatim.*

## Real-World Use
A user opens the app, searches “Austin, TX” via the geocoder (`src/features/location/infrastructure/nominatimAdapter.ts`), selects a curated theme or defines a custom palette using the `src/features/theme/ui/ColorPicker.tsx`, adjusts map layer visibility and typography controls, then clicks “Export Poster.” The system geocodes the location, renders the MapLibre vector map with selected styles, overlays text with chosen Google Fonts, and writes a PNG file via the `pdfExporter`/`pngExporter` pipeline. The result is a print-ready city map poster at the specified dimensions.

## Code Health & Issues
- **[HIGH] Add a test suite** — 120 source files, no test files; any change reaches production without signal that behavior is preserved.
- **[HIGH] Add a CI/CD workflow** — no automated build/test gate; across this estate this pattern appears in 499 repositories.
- **[HIGH] Add a build gate for Docker artifacts** — deployment artifacts exist with no workflow validating the image or manifests.
- **[MEDIUM] Enable Dependabot or Renovate** — one manifest, no update bot; across 1,322 repositories this means advisories sit unpatched.
- **[MEDIUM] Pin container base image by digest** — `oven/bun:1-alpine` and `nginx:1.29-alpine` are mutable; today’s build and last month’s contain different libc and CVE sets with no record.
- **[LOW] Add convention files** — missing `.editorconfig`, `.gitattributes`, formatter config.

These findings come from static analysis of the repository structure and source code.

## The Bottom Line
The codebase is functional and well-structured for a solo developer project, with a clear feature set and a working map-rendering pipeline. However, the absence of tests, CI, and a lockfile makes it unsuitable for team or production use without significant investment in quality gates. It’s appropriate for individual exploration or forking with the intention to add those gates; teams should expect to implement a test suite, CI workflow, and pinned Docker bases before shipping changes confidently.

forks.name: CodeGraphContext
forks.description: An MCP server plus a CLI tool that indexes local code into a graph database to provide context to AI assistants.
forks.summary:
# Technical Briefing: CodeGraphContext

## The Problem

AI assistants need structured code context to provide meaningful assistance, but indexing local repositories into queryable graphs requires significant engineering effort. CodeGraphContext addresses this by building an MCP server and CLI toolkit that parses codebases and stores them in a graph database for AI consumption. The project supports 10+ languages via tree-sitter parsers and produces a navigable import/dependency graph.

## What This Does

CodeGraphContext indexes local code into Neo4j (via kuzu/falkordb backends) to provide context to AI assistants. The core pipeline runs from `src/codegraphcontext/server.py` and `src/codegraphcontext/cli/main.py`, parsing source files through language-specific tree-sitter parsers (Python, JavaScript/TSX, TypeScript, PHP, Shell, C, Dart) and persisting entities (functions, classes, imports) into a graph database. The website (`website/`) and VS Code extension (`extensions/vscode/`) consume the MCP interface.

Key files:
- `src/codegraphcontext/server.py` — MCP server entry point, defines `add_code_to_graph_tool` (reaches 381 functions) and `add_package_to_graph_tool` (reaches 381 functions)
- `src/codegraphcontext/cli/main.py` — CLI entry point, defines `add_package` (reaches 400 functions)
- `src/codegraphcontext/tools/tree_sitter_parser/` — Parsers for multiple languages; `src/codegraphcontext/tools/tree_sitter_parser` is the most connected module (Ca=1, Ce=24, instability=0.96)
- `src/codegraphcontext/core/database.py` — Database layer (19 functions, 3 classes); `src/codegraphcontext/core/database_kuzu.py` (46 functions, 5 classes) implements kuzu-specific operations
- `src/codegraphcontext/tools/indexing/persistence/writer.py` — Persistence writer (67 functions); large file with deep nesting (max indent 7)

The import graph contains 335 internal modules and 289 edges, with 4 modules in circular dependencies (`src/codegraphcontext/cli/cli_helpers`, `src/codegraphcontext/tools/graph_builder`).

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts at the CLI (`src/codegraphcontext/cli/main.py:2808`, `main` reaches 24 functions) or the MCP server (`src/codegraphcontext/server.py:606`, `run` reaches 112 functions). The most frequently called functions are `resolve` (168 call sites), `parse` (96), and `session` (92). `_get_node_text` is the deepest dependency, called from 75 places and central to parsing across all language modules.

Traced paths from entry points:
- `run` → `debug_log` [filesystem via `Path(debug_file).parent.mkdir`]
- `main` → `load_json` [filesystem via `path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore").strip`]
- `add_package` → `_load_credentials` → `ensure_config_dir` [filesystem via `path.mkdir`]

The module hub is `src/codegraphcontext/utils/debug_log.py` (24 dependents, 0 outgoing calls, instability 0). High branching density and deep nesting across `config_manager.py`, `code_finder.py`, and `writer.py` make changes ripple widely—`config_manager.py` has 948 lines with max indentation depth 7.

## How To Use It

**Setup**: Install with `pip install codegraphcontext` or build from source via the `Dockerfile` (base image `python:3.12-slim`). The VS Code extension (`extensions/vscode/package.json`) provides the local MCP client.

**Configuration**: Required env vars are managed through `src/codegraphcontext/cli/config_manager.py` (`ensure_config_dir`, `load_config`). The `.cgcignore` file controls which paths are excluded from indexing. Database credentials and connection strings are loaded from config in `src/codegraphcontext/core/database.py`.

**Running it**:
- CLI: `python -m codegraphcontext.cli add-package <path>` (invokes `main.py:1480`)
- Server: Start the MCP server via `src/codegraphcontext/server.py`; the `add_code_to_graph_tool` endpoint indexes a codebase into the graph.

Environment setup requires populating config dirs and ensuring the database driver is available. The Dockerfile and `docker-compose.template.yml` provide containerized deployment.

## Real-World Use

An AI IDE integrated via MCP can call `add_code_to_graph_tool` to index a user's repository on-demand. The server parses the code, builds the import graph, and stores function/class signatures in Neo4j/kuzu. When the assistant needs to answer a question about code structure, it queries the graph for related functions, call chains, and dependencies—avoiding full-text search and leveraging the structured graph for precise answers. The VS Code extension (`extensions/vscode/src/extension.ts`) surfaces this graph in the editor sidebar.

## Code Health & Issues

**Measured findings (181 total): 52 high, 128 medium, 1 low**

- [HIGH/cognitive_load] Deep nesting x40 — `src/codegraphcontext/cli/config_manager.py`, `src/codegraphcontext/tools/code_finder.py`, `src/codegraphcontext/tools/indexing/persistence/writer.py`. Max indentation depth 7; control flow hard to follow. Fix: flatten with early returns/guard clauses.
- [HIGH/cognitive_load] Oversized files x4 — Same three files. 948 code lines in `config_manager.py`; hard to hold in one head. Fix: split into cohesive units by responsibility.
- [HIGH/cognitive_load] Broad exception handling x12 — `src/codegraphcontext/utils/debug_log.py`, `src/codegraphcontext/cli/config_manager.py`, `src/codegraphcontext/core/database.py`. Bare `except` swallows errors indiscriminately. Fix: catch specific exceptions; re-raise or log the rest.
- [HIGH/soundness] Import cycle member — `src/codegraphcontext/cli/cli_helpers.py`. Participates in circular import dependency. Fix: break the cycle by extracting shared types or inverting a dependency.
- [MEDIUM/resource_safety] File opened without context manager — `src/codegraphcontext/cli/cli_helpers.py`. `open(...)` not wrapped in `with`; handle may leak on error. Fix: use `with open(...) as f:`.
- [MEDIUM/clarity] Hub module — `src/codegraphcontext/utils/debug_log.py`. 24 modules depend on it; churn is high-blast-radius. Fix: keep stable and small; move volatile logic out.

**SDLC observations**: Committed secrets detected in `tests/fixtures/sample_projects/sample_project/edge_cases/hardcoded_secrets.py`. License present. CI: GitHub Actions (16 workflows). Dockerfile yes. Lockfile absent for `pyproject.toml` (no committed lockfile). 3 blobs over 5MB in `images/` (install&cli.gif 9.2MB, Usecase.gif 7.3MB).

## The Bottom Line

CodeGraphContext is a functional MCP server + CLI that successfully indexes local code into a queryable graph database, supporting multiple languages and producing usable context for AI assistants. The engineering is substantial—338 of 338 code files analyzed, 2362 functions and 286 classes parsed via tree-sitter. However, the codebase carries significant technical debt: 4 circular import dependencies, 4 oversized files exceeding 900 lines, and 12 high-severity code health findings including unpinning GitHub Actions, missing lockfile, wildcard CORS with credentials, and absent Dependabot. Teams should plan to address the lockfile and action pinning immediately; the nesting and exception-handling issues require refactoring effort proportional to the file sizes. This is best suited for teams needing custom code-graph integration with AI and who have capacity to manage the identified health debt.

forks.name: city2graph
forks.description: Transform geospatial relations into graphs for Graph Neural Networks and network analysis
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Urban analysts often have to convert raw geospatial layers (buildings, streets, GTFS feeds, OD matrices) into network structures before they can apply graph‑based algorithms or GNNs. Manual stitching of `geopandas`, `networkx` and `torch‑geometric` pipelines is error‑prone and hard to reproduce across projects.

## What This Does  
`city2graph` provides a library that bridges those ecosystems. Core converters live in `city2graph/graph.py` (`gdf_to_nx`, `gdf_to_pyg`), while domain‑specific helpers sit in `city2graph/morphology.py`, `city2graph/proximity.py`, `city2graph/transportation.py` and `city2graph/mobility.py`. The public API is exposed through `city2graph/__init__.py`, which re‑exports the most‑used functions. Documentation (the 48 files under `docs/`) describes each module and includes Jupyter notebooks that demonstrate typical workflows (e.g., `docs/examples/generating_graphs_by_proximity.ipynb`).

## How It Is Wired  
Execution starts in the test suite; the only explicit entry point is the `execute` function in `tests/test_transportation.py:339`. Real‑world usage would call the same converters directly.  

* **Control flow hot‑spots** – The internal call graph shows that `gdf_to_nx` (in `city2graph/utils.py`) is invoked from **44** locations, `create_isochrone` (in `city2graph/morphology.py`) from **43**, and `dict_to_con` (in `city2graph/transportation.py`) from **39**. These functions are therefore the highest‑blast‑radius nodes; any change ripples through many modules and tests.  

* **Module responsibilities** –  
  * `city2graph/utils.py` (111 functions, 2 classes) handles generic conversions and validation; it is called from 10 other files.  
  * `city2graph/graph.py` (38 functions, 3 classes) implements the `Graph` class and the `gdf_to_pyg` / `pyg_to_gdf` pipelines.  
  * `city2graph/proximity.py` (39 functions, 3 classes) computes spatial‑weight matrices and validates proximity inputs.  
  * `city2graph/morphology.py`, `city2graph/transportation.py`, `city2graph/mobility.py` each provide domain‑specific builders that ultimately call the generic utils.  

* **External interactions** – Only two functions perform I/O: one reads GeoJSON files (`tests/data/*.geojson`) and another writes temporary files during test fixtures. A single function launches an external command via `subprocess` (used in the GTFS loader). No database connections are present.  

* **Circularity** – The import graph contains 25 internal modules with **zero** circular dependencies, so the dependency chain is acyclic and relatively safe to refactor.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/city2graph
cd city2graph

# Install with uv (lockfile present) or pip
uv pip install -e .      # editable install, respects pyproject.toml
# or
pip install -e .
```

The library can also be run inside the provided Docker image:

```bash
docker build -t city2graph .
docker run --rm -v $(pwd):/app city2graph python -c \
  "import city2graph as c2g; g = c2g.graph_from_geojson('tests/data/sample_segments.geojson')"
```

No environment variables are required; the only configuration is the optional `pyproject.toml` extras (`cpu`, `cu126`, etc.) for PyTorch support.

## Real‑World Use  
A data‑science team can load a city’s building footprint, convert it to a NetworkX graph, enrich it with a proximity matrix, then feed the result to a GNN:

```python
import city2graph as c2g
buildings = c2g.read_geojson("city_buildings.geojson")
nx_graph = c2g.gdf_to_nx(buildings)
prox_matrix = c2g.proximity_matrix(nx_graph, radius=200)
pyg_data = c2g.gdf_to_pyg(buildings, edge_weight=prox_matrix)
# pass `pyg_data` to a torch_geometric model
```

## Code Health & Issues  

- **HIGH** – Pin GitHub Actions to commit SHA (`.github/workflows/*.yaml`).  
- **HIGH** – Oversized files (`city2graph/utils.py`, `graph.py`, `proximity.py` – >4 k lines each).  
- **HIGH** – Deep nesting (max indent depth = 6) in `utils.py`, `morphology.py`, `transportation.py`.  
- **HIGH** – Duplicated code blocks across `base.py`, `utils.py`, `data.py`, tests.  
- **MEDIUM** – Base Docker image uses mutable tag `jupyter/datascience-notebook:latest`.  
- **MEDIUM** – No dependency‑vulnerability scan in CI.  
- **MEDIUM** – Large binary assets (`docs/assets/logos/city2graph.psd`, several `.ipynb` and `.mp4` files) inflate the repo; should be moved to LFS or external storage.  
- **LOW** – Workflow jobs lack `timeout-minutes` limits.

No missing license, CI is present, and a lockfile (`uv.lock`) mitigates reproducibility for Python packages.

## The Bottom Line  
`city2graph` delivers a functional bridge between geospatial data frames and graph‑oriented ML tools, with a well‑documented public API. However, the core utility modules are large and deeply nested, making maintenance risky; refactoring into smaller, single‑responsibility files would lower cognitive load. It is suitable for teams that need a ready‑made conversion layer but should allocate effort to improve code modularity and tighten CI security.

forks.name: nvitop
forks.description: An interactive NVIDIA-GPU process viewer and beyond, the one-stop solution for GPU process management.
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
GPU‑process oversight in heterogeneous clusters is usually split between ad‑hoc `nvidia-smi` calls, fragmented Python wrappers, and dashboards that require separate exporters. Teams end up maintaining custom scripts just to see *who* is using a GPU, *why* utilization spikes, and how to export metrics for monitoring stacks.  

## What This Does  
`nvitop` is an interactive TUI that visualises NVIDIA‑GPU processes, resource usage, and device topology in real time. It also ships `nvitop‑exporter`, a Prometheus‑compatible endpoint that translates the same data into metrics for Grafana/Prometheus.  

Key components (from the responsibility map):  

- **`nvitop/api/device.py`** – 148 functions, 12 types; defines `transmit`, `receive`, `__repr__`, `is_available`, `driver_version`. Called from 13 other files; runs an external command (`_parse_cuda_visible_devices` via `subprocess.check_output`).  
- **`nvitop/api/process.py`** – 66 functions, 2 classes; provides `add_quotes`, `command_join`, `auto_garbage_clean`.  
- **`nvitop/api/collector.py`** – 26 functions, 4 classes; snapshot collection (`take_snapshots`, `collect_in_background`).  
- **`nvitop/tui/tui.py`** – the TUI entry; max indentation depth 6, control flow hard to follow.  
- **`nvitop/api/__init__.py`** – hub module; 17 other modules import it, making it a high‑blast‑radius point.  

The exporter lives in **`nvitop-exporter/nvitop_exporter/`** (`cli.py`, `exporter.py`, `utils.py`) and exposes Prometheus metrics via a simple HTTP server.  

## How It Is Wired  
Execution starts at **`nvitop/cli.py:272`** (`main`). From there the call graph fans out:  

- `main` → `parse_arguments` → `parse_cuda_visible_devices` → `_parse_cuda_visible_devices` (subprocess).  
- `main` → `cprint` → eventually reaches **204** functions.  

The most‑connected symbols (call‑edge counts) are `nvmlQuery` (35 callers), `max` (27), `nvmlCheckReturn` (25), `bytes2human` (23).  

**Circular import cycle** involves `nvitop/api/__init__.py`, `nvitop/tui/library/__init__.py`, and `nvitop/tui/tui.py` – 26 modules are inside cycles, creating instability (instability 0.44 for `nvitop/tui/library/__init__`).  

**Hub modules** (`nvitop/api/__init__.py`, `nvitop/tui/library/__init__.py`, `nvitop/tui/tui.py`) have 17+ dependents; changes ripple widely.  

**Duplicated code** appears as 292 repeated 6‑line blocks across 43 files (e.g., `install-nvidia-driver.sh`, `nvitop/__init__.py`, `nvitop/api/__init__.py`, `nvitop/api/caching.py`).  

**Broad exception handling** in `nvitop/tui/library/host.py` and `nvitop-exporter/nvitop_exporter/utils.py` swallows errors indiscriminately.  

## How To Use It  

| Step | Command / File | Note |
|------|----------------|------|
| **Install** | `pip install nvitop` (or `pip install -e .` from repo root) | `pyproject.toml` and `setup.py` define the package. |
| **Docker (TUI)** | `docker build -t nvitop . && docker run --rm -it --net=host --gpus all nvitop` | Dockerfile uses `ubuntu:latest` (mutable tag – see hygiene). |
| **Exporter** | `pip install -e nvitop-exporter && nvitop-exporter/cli.py --port 9090` | Entry point `nvitop-exporter/nvitop_exporter/cli.py:34` reaches 113 functions. |
| **Grafana dashboard** | Point Prometheus to `http://<host>:9090/metrics`; dashboard JSON in `nvitop-exporter/grafana/dashboard.json`. |  

Environment variable `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` is respected; the tool auto‑detects devices via `subprocess.check_output(['nvidia-smi', '-L'])`.  

## Real‑World Use  
A ML ops team runs a cluster of 8 A100 nodes. They start `nvitop` via SSH (`ssh user@node nvitop`) to instantly see which PID owns each GPU, memory‑copy rates, and kernel launch queues. When a job stalls, they switch to the exporter (`nvitop-exporter/cli.py`) and feed the Prometheus metrics into Grafana, where they correlate GPU utilisation with training loss. The same metrics also trigger alerts if a process exceeds a configurable memory‑threshold, all without writing custom polling scripts.  

## Code Health & Issues  

**Measured static‑analysis findings (65 total)**  

- **[HIGH/soundness]** Import‑cycle member x26 – files `nvitop/api/__init__.py`, `nvitop/tui/library/__init__.py`, `nvitop/tui/tui.py` participate in circular dependencies.  
- **[HIGH/cognitive_load]** Deep nesting x21 – max indentation depth 6 in `nvitop/tui/tui.py`, `nvitop/api/device.py`, `nvitop/tui/library/keybinding.py`.  
- **[HIGH/cognitive_load]** Oversized file x7 – `nvitop/api/device.py` 2688 lines, `nvitop/api/utils.py`, `nvitop/api/process.py`.  
- **[HIGH/clarity]** Duplicated code blocks – 292 repeated 6‑line fragments across 43 files (e.g., `install-nvidia-driver.sh`, `nvitop/__init__.py`, `nvitop/api/__init__.py`, `nvitop/api/caching.py`).  
- **[MEDIUM/clarity]** Hub module x3 – `nvitop/api/__init__.py`, `nvitop/tui/library/__init__.py`, `nvitop/tui/tui.py` are depended on by 17+ modules each.  
- **[MEDIUM/resilience]** Broad exception handling x2 – bare `except` in `nvitop/tui/library/host.py` and `nvitop-exporter/nvitop_exporter/utils.py`.  

**SDLC hygiene observations**  

- **[HIGH]** Pin third‑party GitHub Actions to commit SHAs – current workflows use `@release/v1`, `@v4` tags (`.github/workflows/*`).  
- **[HIGH]** Add a test suite – repository has no test files (57 source files, zero tests).  
- **[HIGH]** Commit a lockfile – `nvitop-exporter/pyproject.toml` lacks a generated lockfile.  
- **[MEDIUM]** Pin container base image by digest – Dockerfile uses `ubuntu:latest`.  
- **[MEDIUM]** Gate pull requests on a dependency vulnerability scan – no `dependency-review-action` in CI.  
- **[MEDIUM]** Set `persist-credentials: false` on checkout – `build.yaml` checkout retains the token.  
- **[MEDIUM]** Add a non‑root USER to the Docker image – no `USER` directive in any Dockerfile.  

## The Bottom Line  
`nvitop` delivers a capable, single‑pane TUI and exporter for GPU‑process visibility, with solid API surface and Prometheus integration. However, the codebase suffers from import cycles, oversized files, duplicated logic, and missing reproducibility guards (no lockfile, mutable Docker base, unpinned Actions). Teams that need rapid GPU utilisation insights will find immediate value, but anyone planning to extend or ship the tooling should budget time to break the import cycles, split the large API files, and add a lockfile + CI dependency scanning before production use.

**Technical Briefing – editor (Pascal Editor)**  
*Clone: `https://github.com/moses-y/editor`*  

### Overview  
This Turborepo monorepo (664 files) provides a browser‑based 3D building editor. The core stack is **React Three Fiber** + **Next.js** (apps/editor) with three packages: `@pascal-app/core` (schemas, Zustand scene store, spatial queries), `@pascal-app/viewer` (3D rendering), and `apps/editor` (UI, tools, behaviours). State is managed via three Zustand stores (`useScene`, `useViewer`, `useEditor`). Nodes are flat dictionary entries with `parentId` links; a scene‑registry map (`Map<id, Object3D>`) lets renderers pull refs without graph traversal.

### The Problem  
The codebase suffers from **high‑radius instability** and **circular import chains** that make safe modifications risky. The hub module `packages/editor/src/store/use-editor` is imported by 44 other modules (instability 0), and 31 files participate in circular dependencies (e.g., `tree-node.tsx`, `use-scene.ts`, `node-renderer.tsx`). Adding or refactoring a node type can ripple through these edges without compile‑time protection, and there are **no test files** to verify behaviour after change.

### What This Does  
- **Schema & state** – `packages/core/src/schema/index.ts` defines node types (Wall, Item, Zone, etc.) that extend `BaseNode`; `packages/core/src/store/use-scene.ts` provides CRUD middleware (persist, undo/redo).  
- **Rendering** – `packages/viewer/src/components/renderers/node-renderer.tsx` registers refs via `useRegistry`; renderers for walls, slabs, roofs etc. live under `packages/viewer/src/components/renderers/`.  
- **Editor UI** – `packages/editor/src/components/editor/index.tsx` composes the main toolbar; `packages/editor/src/components/ui/action-menu/index.tsx` and `command-palette/index.tsx` provide tool selection. The oversized `site-panel/index.tsx` (1413 loc) and `item-catalog/catalog-items.tsx` house bulk of the UI logic.  
- **Import graph** – 237 internal modules, 596 edges; 31 modules in cycles; hub `use-editor` (Ca 44, Ce 0) and utility `lib/utils.ts` (Ca 43, Ce 0) are the most connected points.

### How It Is Wired  
1. **Entry point** – `apps/editor/app/page.tsx` renders the `<Editor />` component.  
2. **State bootstrap** – `useEditor` (packages/editor/src/store/use-editor.tsx) is initialized; UI components read `activeTool`, panel visibility, etc.  
3. **Node creation** – Calling `useEditor.getState().createNode(...)` flows into `packages/core/src/store/use-scene.ts` which updates the flat node dictionary and triggers the persist middleware.  
4. **Render sync** – The scene registry (`packages/core/src/scene-registry.ts`) maps node IDs to Three.js `Mesh` refs; when a node is updated, the registry is refreshed and the corresponding renderer re‑renders.  
5. **Cycle cost** – Any change that touches a circular‑import member can silently break another branch; the 31‑member cycle includes `tree-node.tsx`, `use-scene.ts`, and `node-renderer.tsx`.

### How To Use It  
| Step | Command / File |
|------|----------------|
| **Clone** | `git clone https://github.com/moses-y/editor` |

### The Bottom Line  
The editor is a well‑structured React‑Three‑Fiber monorepo with a clear separation of core schemas, viewer rendering, and editor UI. Teams comfortable with React Three Fiber who are prepared to invest in test infrastructure and cycle‑breaking refactors can benefit from the platform; others may find the initial ramp‑up costly.

forks.name: collab-public
forks.description: Collaborator is a place to create with agents.
forks.summary:
## The Problem

Developer tooling is fragmented across terminals, editors, and file managers. Agents need context files, running code, and persistent sessions, but coordinating these across separate apps creates constant context switching. Collaborator consolidates agentic development onto a single infinite canvas where terminals, files, and code live side by side.

## What This Does

Collaborator is a native macOS desktop app (Electron 40, React 19) that provides an end-to-end environment for agentic development. The main application lives in `collab-electron/` with a multi-webview architecture: a navigator sidebar for file management, an infinite canvas for arranging tiles, and a viewer for file content. Terminals run through `xterm.js` backed by persistent `tmux` sessions, and code editing uses Monaco Editor.

The app is organized as an npm monorepo with packages for `components` (UI), `shared` (types and utilities), and `theme`. All state persists locally as JSON in `~/.collaborator/`. The README states it's early-stage, macOS-only (Apple Silicon), and in active development.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts in `collab-electron/src/main/index.ts` (Electron main process), which imports 12 modules. The central hub is `collab-electron/src/main/ipc.ts` — it has 14 incoming imports and 14 outgoing ones (instability 0.93), making it the highest-traffic module. It routes renderer requests to filesystem operations in `src/main/files.ts` (5 modules import it) and filtering logic in `src/main/file-filter.ts` (6 importers, zero dependencies — a pure utility leaf).

The renderer side splits into multiple windows: `src/windows/shell/src/renderer.js` (1,234 lines) handles canvas rendering, `src/windows/nav/src/App.tsx` manages the navigator, and `src/windows/viewer/src/App.tsx` displays file content. The `packages/components/src/TreeView/` directory owns file tree logic across 11 files, with `useFileTree.ts` and `SearchSortControls.tsx` carrying the deepest nesting. The `WorkspaceGraph/` module (8 files) renders a D3 force-directed graph of workspace connections.

The import graph shows 117 internal modules with 120 edges and zero circular dependencies — a clean structure. The risk is concentration: `ipc.ts` and `renderer.js` are change hotspots where modifications ripple widely.

## How To Use It

```sh
# Clone and install
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/collab-public
cd collab-public/collab-electron
npm install

# Build and run
npm run dev
```

The README documents a curl installer (`install.sh` at repo root) and prebuilt macOS releases. Configuration is minimal — the app works on local folders without accounts. Note: no lockfile is committed, so `npm install` won't be reproducible across environments. The `bunfig.toml` suggests Bun is also supported, but package.json lacks a `bun.lockb`.

## Real-World Use

A developer working with an AI coding agent opens Collaborator, adds a workspace via `Cmd+Shift+O`, and drags a terminal tile onto the canvas. The agent runs in the terminal (backed by tmux for persistence), while the developer drags context files from the navigator onto the canvas as tiles. Monaco Editor tiles handle code review, and the viewer shows markdown notes with KaTeX math rendering. All sessions survive app restarts via tmux.

## Code Health & Issues

Static analysis (23 findings: 13 high, 10 medium) identified four issue kinds:

- **High** — Deep nesting (13 instances): `TreeView/useFileTree.ts` and `SearchSortControls.tsx` hit indentation depth 10; control flow is hard to follow. Fix: early returns and extraction.
- **High** — Duplicated code (43 repeated 6-line blocks across 15 files): `SourcesFeed.tsx`, `TreeView.tsx`, `shared/src/types.ts`. Fix: extract shared helpers.
- **High** — Oversized files (8): `WorkspaceGraph/forceGraph.ts`, `main/workspace-graph.ts`, and `shell/src/renderer.js` exceed 1,200 lines each. Fix: split by responsibility.
- **Medium** — High branching density: `shared/src/extract-cover-image.ts` has 24 branch points over 54 lines.

SDLC gaps: no CI/CD pipeline (no `.github/`), no lockfile for reproducible builds. Tests exist (11 files), and no secrets were committed. A license is present.

## The Bottom Line

A well-structured Electron app with a clean module graph and no circular dependencies, but the codebase shows signs of rapid growth — deep nesting, duplication, and oversized files will make maintenance harder. Suitable for developers who want a local-first agentic workspace and are comfortable with early-stage software; not ready for production teams needing reproducibility guarantees.

forks.description: Real-time ASL sign language detector using MediaPipe hand landmarks + XGBoost — 98.43% accuracy, skin-tone agnostic, no CNN
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Deploying a hand‑gesture classifier that works reliably across skin tones and lighting conditions usually requires a large CNN and GPU resources. Teams that need a lightweight, CPU‑only solution for real‑time ASL alphabet detection lack a ready‑made pipeline.

## What This Does  
The repository delivers a proof‑of‑concept that extracts 21 MediaPipe hand landmarks (63 × float features), normalises them to the wrist, and classifies the resulting vector with a pre‑trained XGBoost model (`asl_model_xgb.pkl`).  

* `Retrained_with_XGBOOST.ipynb` defines the core preprocessing routine `normalize_landmarks`.  
* `sign_detection.ipynb` loads `asl_model_xgb.pkl` and `label_encoder.pkl`, opens a webcam with OpenCV, runs MediaPipe’s `HandLandmarker`, applies `normalize_landmarks`, and calls the XGBoost model for inference.  
* The notebook visualises predictions on‑screen and includes a static confusion matrix (`confusion_matrix.png`) for reference.

## How It Is Wired  
1. **Entry point** – execution starts in `sign_detection.ipynb`. The notebook imports the helper function `normalize_landmarks` (originating in `Retrained_with_XGBOOST.ipynb`).  
2. **External touchpoints** – MediaPipe’s hand‑landmark solution performs a one‑time download of its binary model (outbound network call). The XGBoost classifier (`predict`) is the sole inference call to a local model file.  
3. **Data flow**  
   * `cv2.VideoCapture` → frame image.  
   * MediaPipe `HandLandmarker.process(frame)` → raw landmarks.  
   * `normalize_landmarks(raw_landmarks)` → wrist‑centred, scale‑invariant vector (63 floats).  
   * `xgb_model.predict(normalized_vector)` → class index → `label_encoder.inverse_transform` → printable letter.  
4. **Effect ownership** – all side‑effects (camera I/O, model loading, network download) are confined to `sign_detection.ipynb`. No other modules import or reuse the function, so the blast radius is limited to this notebook. Because the code lives in notebooks, there is no explicit package graph; any refactor must first extract `normalize_landmarks` and the inference loop into reusable modules.

## How To Use It  
```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/asl-sign-detection-mediapipe-rf
cd asl-sign-detection-mediapipe-rf

# Install Python dependencies
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

# Launch the demo notebook
jupyter notebook sign_detection.ipynb
```
Inside the notebook run the cells sequentially. No additional configuration files, environment variables, or API keys are required. The webcam will open, and the predicted ASL letter will be overlaid on each frame.

## Real‑World Use  
A tele‑health platform could embed the inference loop in a lightweight Flask route:

```python
from flask import Response, stream_with_context
import cv2, mediapipe as mp
from xgboost import XGBClassifier
from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder

model = XGBClassifier()
model.load_model('asl_model_xgb.pkl')
le = LabelEncoder()
le.classes_ = joblib.load('label_encoder.pkl')

def gen_frames():
    cap = cv2.VideoCapture(0)
    while True:
        ret, frame = cap.read()
        lm = mp.solutions.hands.HandLandmarker().process(frame).landmarks
        norm = normalize_landmarks(lm)
        pred = le.inverse_transform(model.predict([norm]))[0]
        # draw pred on frame …
        yield (b'--frame\r\n'
               b'Content-Type: image/jpeg\r\n\r\n' + jpeg_bytes + b'\r\n')
```
The route streams annotated video to a browser, providing on‑device ASL transcription without a GPU.

## Code Health & Issues  
* **Medium – Enable Dependabot** – one manifest (`requirements.txt`) present, no automated update bot configured.  
* No test suite (`tests` folder missing).  
* No CI/CD pipeline (`.github/` workflows absent).  
* No LICENSE file – redistribution rights unclear.  
* No lockfile (`requirements.txt` only) – builds are not reproducible.  

All items stem from the static analysis results; no additional concerns were detected.

## The Bottom Line  
The repo showcases a high‑accuracy, CPU‑friendly ASL alphabet recogniser that runs from a notebook with minimal setup. It is suitable for prototyping or educational demos but lacks production‑grade safeguards (tests, CI, licensing, reproducible builds). Teams that need a maintainable, deployable service should extract the notebook logic into a package, add tests, and address the listed SDLC gaps.

forks.name: error-monitoring-agent
forks.description: Intelligent error monitoring agent that uses Airweave to find context from your code, tickets, and Slack. Clusters similar errors, enriches with relevant context, and creates actionable alerts.
forks.summary:
**The Problem**  
Production systems generate a flood of raw error events that alert‑ing tools surface without context. Engineers spend time hunting the related code, existing tickets, or Slack discussions to decide whether an alert is new, a regression, or already being handled. The lack of semantic linkage drives noise and slows incident response.

**What This Does**  
The repository implements an end‑to‑end agent that ingests raw errors, clusters them by root cause, enriches each cluster with code snippets, Linear tickets, and Slack threads via **Airweave**, and emits a single actionable alert per cluster. The pipeline lives in `backend/` (Python) while a minimal React/Tailwind UI in `frontend/` visualises the flow (e.g., `frontend/src/App.tsx`, `frontend/src/components/pipeline-visualizer.tsx`). Core data models live in `backend/schemas.py` (e.g., `RawError`, `ErrorCluster`). Configuration defaults are provided in `.env.example` and `backend/config.py`.

**How It Is Wired**  

1. **Entry point** – `backend/main.py` runs a FastAPI server. The two public routes are:  
   * `run_demo` (line 544) – triggers the demo pipeline, traversing 33 functions.  
   * `websocket_endpoint` (line 555) – streams live pipeline state, touching 34 functions.  

2. **Pipeline kickoff** – `run_demo` calls `run_pipeline` (line 100). `run_pipeline` constructs a `PipelineStep` chain and invokes `run_pipeline -> broadcast` (18 calls) and `run_pipeline -> PipelineStep` (5 calls).  

3. **Core processing** – Within `backend/pipeline/` the steps are:  
   * **Clustering** (`backend/pipeline/clustering.py::cluster_errors`) → creates clusters via `_create_cluster` (called from 6 places).  
   * **Enrichment** (`backend/pipeline/enrichment.py::enrich`) → builds Airweave queries (`_search_code`) and calls the LLM (`_init_llm`).  
   * **Analysis** (`backend/pipeline/analysis.py::analyze_errors`) → runs LLM‑based severity logic (`_llm_analyze`).  

4. **External touches** –  
   * Filesystem I/O: `_read_json` / `_write_json` (both invoked from 7 places) read/write state under `backend/state.py`.  
   * Network calls: `backend/clients/airweave_client.py::search` (Airweave API), `backend/clients/linear_client.py::create_issue`, and `backend/clients/slack_client.py::post_alert`.  

5. **State handling** – `backend/state.py` owns 22 functions, is referenced by 5 other modules, and performs the only persistent reads/writes.  

6. **Module hot‑spots** – The most connected module is `backend/pipeline/__init__` (imports 6 others, instability 1). Its high import count means any change ripples through the entire pipeline. No circular dependencies were detected.

**How To Use It**  

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/error-monitoring-agent
cd error-monitoring-agent

# Backend setup
cp .env.example .env
python -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r backend/requirements.txt
uvicorn backend/main:app --reload --port 8000   # starts FastAPI (run_demo available at /demo)

# Frontend setup
cd frontend
npm install
npm run dev   # Vite serves UI at http://localhost:3000
```

*Configuration* – Populate `.env` with Airweave keys (`AIRWEAVE_API_KEY`) and, for production, one of the data‑source blocks (e.g., `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN`, `AZURE_CLIENT_ID`). The `backend/config.py` module validates required variables.

*Running the demo* – Open the UI, click **Run Demo**; the backend executes `run_demo`, which walks the pipeline, stores interim state in JSON files, and returns a visual summary.

**Real‑World Use**  
A SaaS platform can replace the sample source (`backend/sources/sample_source.py`) with `backend/sources/sentry_source.py` by setting `DATA_SOURCE=sentry`. Errors streamed from Sentry feed into `run_pipeline`, which clusters them, pulls matching code and tickets via Airweave, and posts a single Slack message (via `backend/clients/slack_client.py::post_alert`) and Linear issue (via `backend/clients/linear_client.py::create_issue`). This reduces alert volume from hundreds to a handful of actionable items per hour.

**Code Health & Issues**  

- **High – No LICENSE** (`root/`): add MIT or Apache‑2.0.  
- **High – No test suite** (35 source files): introduce unit tests for public entry points, gate with CI.  
- **High – No CI/CD** (`.github/` absent): add a GitHub Actions workflow that installs `requirements.txt`, runs `pytest`, and builds the frontend.  
- **High – Wildcard CORS** (`backend/main.py`): replace `allow_origins=["*"]` with an explicit whitelist.  
- **Medium – Dependabot missing**: add `.github/dependabot.yml`.  
- **Medium – Large binary** (`docs/error-monitoring-agent-demo.mp4` 8 MB): move to LFS or external storage.  
- **Low – Missing repo conventions**: add `.editorconfig`, `.gitattributes`, formatter config.

**The Bottom Line**  
The agent delivers a functional, end‑to‑end error‑context pipeline with clear separation between data ingestion, clustering, enrichment, and alerting. It is usable out‑of‑the‑box for demos, but production adoption requires adding licensing, tests, CI, and tightening security (CORS). Engineers modifying the pipeline should start at `backend/main.py` → `run_pipeline` and be aware that `backend/pipeline/__init__` is the primary import hub.

forks.name: OpenClaw-bot-review
forks.description: A lightweight web dashboard for viewing all your OpenClaw Bots/Agents/Models/Sessions status at a glance.
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Managing dozens of OpenClaw agents across platforms (Feishu, Discord, etc.) forces operators to open multiple terminals, hunt through JSON files, and manually verify gateway health. There is no single view that shows which bot uses which model, its token consumption, or whether the underlying gateway is reachable.

## What This Does  
The repository ships a **Next.js** web UI that reads the local OpenClaw configuration (`~/.openclaw/openclaw.json`) and session files, then renders a dashboard with:

* **Bot cards** – `app/components/agent‑card.tsx` shows name, emoji, model, platform, and health status.  
* **Model list**, **session explorer**, **statistics charts**, and an **Alert Center** – pages live under `app/models/page.tsx`, `app/sessions/page.tsx`, `app/stats/page.tsx`, and `app/alerts/page.tsx`.  
* **Pixel Office** – an animated office view built on the **pixel‑office** engine in `lib/pixel-office/`. Core types live in `lib/pixel-office/types.ts`; the renderer (`lib/pixel-office/engine/renderer.ts`) drives the canvas, while `lib/pixel-office/engine/officeState.ts` maintains the world state.

All data is fetched from the filesystem; no external database is required.

## How It Is Wired  
1. **Entry point** – `npm run dev` starts Next.js, which loads `app/layout.tsx` and the route handlers under `app/api/`.  
2. **API layer** – each endpoint (e.g., `app/api/agent-status/route.ts`, `app/api/pixel-office/layout/route.ts`) imports helper functions from `lib/`. The most common helper is `lib/openclaw-cli.ts`, which invokes the OpenClaw CLI to read `openclaw.json` and session files.  
3. **Data flow** – an API request ultimately calls `lib/config-cache.ts` (caches the parsed JSON) → `lib/openclaw-paths.ts` (resolves file locations) → returns a plain JavaScript object to the route handler, which responds with JSON.  
4. **UI consumption** – client components (`app/page.tsx`, `app/sidebar.tsx`) use Next.js `fetch` to call `/api/*`. The data populates React state and drives the UI.  
5. **Pixel Office rendering** – the browser loads `app/pixel-office/page.tsx`, which instantiates `new OfficeState()` from `lib/pixel-office/engine/officeState.ts`. The state imports the hub module `lib/pixel-office/types.ts` (19 inbound imports) and passes sprite data from `lib/pixel-office/sprites/spriteData.ts` (1124 lines) to `renderer.render()`. The renderer imports 11 other engine modules, giving it the highest *instability* (1.0) in the import graph.  
6. **Blast radius** – changes to `lib/pixel-office/types.ts` affect 19 modules; modifications in the oversized `officeState.ts` ripple through the entire pixel‑office subsystem. The duplicated 6‑line blocks across 27 API routes (`app/api/alerts/check/route.ts`, `app/api/pixel-office/idle-rank/route.ts`, etc.) mean a bug fix in one place must be replicated manually.

No circular dependencies were detected, but the hub module and the oversized engine files are clear hotspots for future maintenance effort.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the exact repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/OpenClaw-bot-review.git
cd OpenClaw-bot-review

# Install Node dependencies (npm is defined in package.json)
npm install

# Development server
npm run dev          # starts Next.js on http://localhost:3000

# Optional: point at a custom OpenClaw config
export OPENCLAW_HOME=/opt/openclaw   # defaults to ~/.openclaw
npm run dev
```

### Docker deployment  

```bash
docker build -t openclaw-dashboard .
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 \
  -e OPENCLAW_HOME=/opt/openclaw \
  -v /path/to/openclaw:/opt/openclaw \
  openclaw-dashboard
```

The container image ships the same Next.js server; the only required runtime variable is `OPENCLAW_HOME`.

## Real‑World Use  
A DevOps team runs the dashboard inside their monitoring namespace. When a new Discord bot is added, they drop the updated `openclaw.json` into `~/.openclaw/`. The dashboard instantly shows the new agent card, updates the pixel‑office animation, and triggers an alert if the gateway health endpoint (`app/api/gateway-health/route.ts`) reports a failure. No database migrations or additional configuration are needed.

## Code Health & Issues  

- **High – Cognitive load** – `lib/pixel-office/sprites/spriteData.ts`, `lib/pixel-office/engine/officeState.ts`, `lib/pixel-office/bugs/bugSystem.ts` each exceed 1 000 lines. Split by responsibility.  
- **Medium – Hub module** – `lib/pixel-office/types.ts` is imported by 19 modules; keep its API stable, move volatile logic elsewhere.  
- **High – Deep nesting** – `app/sidebar.tsx`, `app/components/agent-card.tsx`, `app/alerts/page.tsx` reach 8 levels of indentation; refactor with early returns or helper functions.  
- **High – Duplicated code** – identical 6‑line blocks appear in 27 API route files; extract to a shared utility (e.g., `lib/api/helpers.ts`).  
- **Medium – Branch density** – `lib/pixel-office/layout/*` files contain 77 branch points over 269 lines; consider strategy tables.  
- **Low – TODO/FIXME** – nine markers remain in `lib/pixel-office/engine/officeState.ts`; resolve or file issues.  
- **SDLC gap** – No CI/CD configuration (`.github/` or similar) is present; add a GitHub Actions workflow to run `npm test` and build the Docker image on push.  
- **Tests** – Nine test files exist, but coverage is unclear; consider expanding to cover the duplicated API logic and the pixel‑office engine.  

## The Bottom Line  
The repo delivers a functional, zero‑database dashboard that visualizes OpenClaw agents and includes a novel pixel‑office animation. However, key modules are oversized, duplicated logic is widespread, and the project lacks automated CI. It is suitable for teams that need quick visibility and are comfortable refactoring the identified hotspots before scaling.

Here's a concise, professional technical briefing for `insanely-fast-whisper`, written to consultant standards.

---

## The Problem

This repository provides a CLI for on-device Whisper transcription using 🤗 Transformers, Optimum, and flash-attn. It targets users who need fast, local transcription without relying on cloud APIs. The pain point it addresses is the latency gap between cloud Whisper services and local execution—particularly for long-form audio—while maintaining model quality. The project differentiates itself through Flash Attention 2 and batching optimizations, claiming 150 minutes of audio in under 2 seconds on A100 hardware.

## What This Does

The codebase is small: 8 Python files, 3 notebooks, and a CLI entry point. Execution flows through `src/insanely_fast_whisper/cli.py:main`, which orchestrates the transcription pipeline. The core work is distributed across the `utils/` subpackage: `diarize.py` handles audio preprocessing, diarization, and an outbound network call via `requests.get` (no timeout configured); `result.py` defines `JsonTranscriptionResult` and `build_result`; `diarization_pipeline.py` exposes a single `diarize` function; and `convert_output.py` defines formatters (`SrtFormatter`, `VttFormatter`, `TxtFormatter`) and chunk-processing utilities (`format_chunk`, `format_seconds`, `preamble`). The entry point `main` reaches 9 functions total, with the longest call chain being `main -> diarize -> preprocess_inputs` [network via requests.get].

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts at `src/insanely_fast_whisper/cli.py:111` (`main`). From there, the call graph resolves as follows:

- `main -> convert` — handles model loading and the primary inference path.
- `main -> convert -> preamble` / `format_chunk` / `format_seconds` — output formatting.
- `main -> diarize` — triggers the diarization pipeline.
- `diarize -> preprocess_inputs` — makes an outbound network call to fetch diarization data via `requests.get` (no timeout).
- `diarize -> diarize_audio` / `post_process_segments_and_transcripts` — internal audio processing.
- `main -> build_result` / `convert` — final result assembly.

The outbound network call in `src/insanely_fast_whisper/utils/diarize.py` is the only edge leaving the process. No CI/CD pipeline is configured, and there is no dependency lockfile, meaning builds are not reproducible across environments.

## What Each File Is Responsible For

| File | Functions | Classes/Types | Outbound Effects |
|------|-----------|---------------|------------------|
| `convert_output.py` | 10 | 3 (TxtFormatter, SrtFormatter, VttFormatter) | Calls into 2 internal modules; defines formatting primitives used by the CLI. |
| `src/insanely_fast_whisper/utils/diarize.py` | 3 | – | Makes an outbound network call via `requests.get`; no timeout configured. Defines `preprocess_inputs`, `diarize_audio`, `post_process_segments_and_transcripts`. |
| `src/insanely_fast_whisper/utils/result.py` | 1 | 1 (JsonTranscriptionResult) | Called from 1 other file; defines `build_result`. |
| `src/insanely_fast_whisper/utils/diarization_pipeline.py` | 1 | – | Called from 1 other file; defines `diarize`. |
| `src/insanely_fast_whisper/cli.py` | 1 (`main`) | – | Entry point; reaches 9 function(s); itself called from 1 place. |

## How To Use It

**Setup**  
The project uses `pyproject.toml` for dependencies and tooling. No lockfile is committed, so installs should be pinned explicitly. Install via `pipx`:

```bash
pipx install insanely-fast-whisper==0.0.15 --force
```

Or with `pip` if you need to override Python version constraints:

```bash
pip install insanely-fast-whisper --ignore-requires-python
```

**Configuration**  
No environment variables or config files are required for basic transcription. The only external dependency is network access for the diarization endpoint, which is invoked from `src/insanely_fast_whisper/utils/diarize.py` via `requests.get`.

**Running it**  
The CLI entry point is `insanely-fast-whisper`. From any path:

```bash
insanely-fast-whisper --file-name <filename or URL>
```

On macOS, add `--device-id mps`. To enable Flash Attention 2:

```bash
insanely-fast-whisper --file-name <filename or URL> --flash True
```

To use distil-whisper:

```bash
insanely-fast-whisper --model-name distil-whisper/large-v2 --file-name <filename or URL>
```

## Real-World Use

A developer transcribing a 30-minute meeting recording on a workstation with an NVIDIA GPU can run:

```bash
insanely-fast-whisper --file-name meeting.wav --flash True
```

This loads the Whisper Large v3 model with Flash Attention 2 and batching, producing a timed transcript in under 2 minutes. The output can be formatted as SRT or VTT via the CLI flags. If the meeting requires speaker diarization, the built-in pipeline will make an outbound request to a diarization service—ensure network access is available and consider adding a timeout, as the request has none configured.

## Code Health & Issues

- **[MEDIUM/cognitive_load]** `src/insanely_fast_whisper/utils/diarize.py` — Max indentation depth 6; control flow is hard to follow. Fix: flatten with early returns/guard clauses; extract inner blocks.
- **[HIGH] No CI/CD pipeline** — 8 source files, no automated build/test gate. Every change merges without having been built. Fix: add a workflow running the project build and test command on push and pull_request.
- **[MEDIUM] No dependency lockfile** — `pyproject.toml` declares dependencies without a lockfile, meaning builds are not reproducible. Fix: commit `pdm.lock` or add a `requirements.txt` pinned at the desired version.
- **[MEDIUM] Outbound request has no timeout** — `src/insanely_fast_whisper/utils/diarize.py` makes an unbounded `requests.get` call. Fix: pass `timeout=` on every call, or use a session with one configured.

## The Bottom Line

The repository delivers on its promise: a lightweight, opinionated CLI that transcribes hours of audio in minutes using Flash Attention 2 and batching. The codebase is focused and the performance claims are credible given the optimization stack (Transformers + Optimum + flash-attn). However, the absence of CI, a lockfile, and a timeout on the diarization network call are production-grade gaps. Use this for local, GPU-accelerated transcription workflows where network access is available and the diarization endpoint is acceptable. Teams requiring reproducible builds, automated testing, or hardened network calls should add the recommended CI and timeout fixes before depending on this in a service context.
