forks.name: Pulse
forks.description: Real-time monitoring for Proxmox, Docker, and Kubernetes with AI-powered insights, smart alerts, and a beautiful unified dashboard
forks.summary:
## The Problem

Monitoring Proxmox, Docker, and Kubernetes typically requires separate tools with different UIs, alerting systems, and data models. Operators end up juggling multiple dashboards, writing glue scripts, and missing cross-platform correlations. Pulse consolidates these into a single interface with unified alerting and optional AI-assisted analysis.

## What This Does

Pulse is a Go backend with a React/TypeScript frontend (`frontend-modern/`). The backend (`internal/`, `pkg/`, `cmd/`) handles API serving, agent communication, and data persistence. The frontend provides the dashboard, alert configuration, and AI chat interface. Entry points in `cmd/pulse-agent/main.go` and `cmd/eval/main.go` indicate a standalone agent binary and an evaluation tool.

The system monitors Proxmox VE/PBS/PMG, Docker/Podman, and Kubernetes via agents. It supports auto-discovery, metrics history, backup exploration, and notifications to Discord, Slack, Telegram, and email. AI features (chat, patrol, alert analysis) are bring-your-own-key.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts in `frontend-modern/src/App.tsx` (`App` at line 230), which sets up WebSocket connections and routing. The call graph shows `apiFetchJSON` is called from 116 places and `apiFetch` from 61—these are the primary HTTP paths to the backend. `useWebSocket` (20 call sites) handles real-time updates.

Traced network paths are short: `handleKeyDown` → `handleSubmit` → `apiClient.fetch` (one hop to the wire). `handleAnswerQuestion` → `answerQuestion` → `apiFetch` → `fetchJSON` (two hops). The heaviest files are `Alerts.tsx` (77 functions, 18 types), `App.tsx` (40 functions), and `DockerUnifiedTable.tsx` (82 functions). The frontend calls out for inference (1 function), database access (1), file I/O (2), and external commands (1).

Three modules form a circular import cycle (`SetupWizard.tsx`, `SecurityStep.tsx`, `CompleteStep.tsx`), which complicates refactoring and increases coupling.

## How To Use It

**Setup**: Clone and build with the included `Dockerfile` or `docker-compose.yml`. The README documents a one-liner LXC install for Proxmox and a `docker run` command exposing port 7655.

**Configuration**: Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and set required values. Backend config lives in `internal/config/`. Frontend dependencies are in `frontend-modern/package.json`.

**Running**: For Docker: `docker run -d --name pulse -p 7655:7655 -v pulse_data:/data rcourtman/pulse:latest`. Access the dashboard at `http://<your-ip>:7655`. Agents install via commands generated in Settings → Agents.

## Real-World Use

A homelab operator with a Proxmox host, a Docker swarm, and a Kubernetes cluster installs Pulse on an LXC container. After adding credentials via the Setup Wizard, Pulse auto-discovers nodes, starts collecting metrics, and fires alerts to a Discord channel. The operator uses the AI chat to ask "Which container has the highest CPU over the last hour?" and gets an answer without querying three separate tools.

## Code Health & Issues

Static analysis found 492 findings (104 high, 388 medium) across 4 kinds:

- **High - Deep nesting** (50 instances): `DiscoveryTab.tsx`, `HistoryChart.tsx`, `StepIndicator.tsx` reach indentation depth 14. Flatten with early returns.
- **High - Import cycle** (3 instances): `SetupWizard.tsx`, `SecurityStep.tsx`, `CompleteStep.tsx` form a circular dependency. Extract shared types.
- **High - Oversized files** (6 instances): `DiscoveryTab.tsx` (914 lines), `App.tsx`, `agent_internal_test.go`. Split by responsibility.
- **High - Duplicated code** (318 repeated 6-line blocks across 187 files): Extract shared helpers.

Security audit found 6 issues: unpinned GitHub Actions (high), discarded exit codes in `create-release.yml` (high), no Dependabot (medium), unpinned base image in `.devcontainer/Dockerfile` (medium), no dependency scan in CI (medium), missing job timeouts (low).

## The Bottom Line

Pulse is a functional, feature-rich monitoring tool with a solid architecture and active CI. The frontend has real maintainability debt—deep nesting, oversized components, and duplication—that will slow future changes. It's best suited for homelab users or small MSPs wanting a single pane of glass; teams needing enterprise-grade reliability should wait for the code health issues to be addressed.

forks.name: SWE-AF
forks.description: Autonomous software engineering fleet of AI agents for production-grade PRs on AgentField: plan, code, test, and ship.
forks.summary:
## The Problem

Coordinating multiple AI agents to ship production-grade code is usually ad-hoc: prompts scattered across scripts, no shared state, no defined roles, and no way to scale from a single PR to a multi-repo effort. SWE-AF replaces that with a single API call that spins up a structured engineering team—product manager, architect, coders, QA—that plans, implements, and verifies changes end to end.

## What This Does

SWE-AF is a Python 3.12+ runtime that orchestrates autonomous software engineering fleets. The core logic lives in `swe_af/` (45 files): `app.py` and `fast/app.py` expose the HTTP API, `execution/dag_executor.py` runs the workflow as a DAG, and `reasoners/execution_agents.py` dispatches work to model-backed agents. `prompts/` holds role-specific prompt templates for architect, coder, QA, and merger agents.

The `examples/agent-comparison/` directory contains four complete runs—Claude Code Haiku, Claude Code Sonnet, Codex, and SWE-AF itself—each producing a working CLI todo app with tests and coverage reports. `examples/diagrams/` contains a full trace of a diagram-generator project built by the fleet, including per-agent JSONL logs in `.artifacts/logs/`.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts at the HTTP layer: `swe_af/app.py` receives a POST to `/api/v1/execute/async/swe-planner.build`, which routes through `swe_af/fast/executor.py` into the DAG executor. The module graph shows `swe_af/execution/schemas.py` as the central hub—43 modules import it, making it the highest-blast-radius file. `swe_af/app.py` (18 importers) and `swe_af/prompts/_utils.py` (19 importers) are secondary hubs.

The main entry point is `run` in `examples/agent-comparison/codex/src/cli.js`, which reaches 11 functions. The shortest path to a filesystem effect is `run → addTodo → loadTodos`, which calls `fs.readFileSync`—three hops from entry to disk I/O. The call graph shows `createSVG` and `addTitle` each called from 14 places, making them the most change-sensitive functions in the example code.

## How To Use It

```bash
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/SWE-AF
cd SWE-AF
make install   # or: pip install -e .
make check     # run tests
docker compose up --build   # start the API on :8080
```

Configuration lives in `.env.example`—copy to `.env` and set your model provider keys. The API accepts a JSON payload with `goal`, `repo_url` or `repo_path`, and a `config` block specifying runtime and per-role models. The README documents both single-repo and multi-repo modes via the `config.repos` array.

## Real-World Use

A team maintaining a monorepo with a shared auth library can submit one goal: "Add JWT auth across API and shared-lib." SWE-AF spawns separate agents for each repository, coordinates the dependency order, runs tests in its own CI, and opens a PR with the merged result—no human orchestrating prompts or merging branches.

## Code Health & Issues

Static analysis found 89 issues (20 high, 68 medium, 1 low) across 7 kinds. The main concerns:

- **High – Oversized files**: `swe_af/execution/schemas.py`, `swe_af/app.py`, `swe_af/execution/dag_executor.py` exceed 676 lines each, making changes ripple widely.
- **High – Deep nesting**: max indentation depth of 9 in `swe_af/app.py` and `swe_af/fast/app.py`; control flow is hard to follow.
- **High – Hub modules**: `swe_af/execution/schemas.py` has 43 dependents; churn there is high-blast-radius.
- **High – Duplicated code**: 994 repeated 6-line blocks across 141 test files in `examples/agent-comparison/swe-af-haiku/tests/`.
- **Medium – Broad exception handling** in `swe_af/app.py` and `dag_executor.py` swallows errors indiscriminately.
- **Medium – File handle leak**: `open(...)` without context manager in `swe_af/prompts/merger.py`.

The audit also flags missing lockfile for `pyproject.toml`, no least-privilege GITHUB_TOKEN in CI, mutable Docker base image, and no dependency vulnerability scan. Tests and CI are present and passing.

## The Bottom Line

SWE-AF is a serious attempt at autonomous multi-agent engineering, with a clean API surface and real evidence of working end-to-end runs. The core orchestration code needs refactoring—the hub modules and deep nesting will hurt maintainability as the fleet scales. Use it if you need a programmable engineering team, not if you want a polished library.

forks.name: SocratiCode
forks.description: Enterprise-grade (40m+ lines) codebase intelligence in a zero-setup, private and local Plugin/Skill or MCP: managed indexing, hybrid semantic search, polyglot code dependency graphs, cross-project/repo & branch-aware search, and DB/API/infra knowledge. Benchmark: 61% less tokens, 84% fewer calls, 37x faster than AI grep. Cloud in private beta.
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Developers need instant, accurate context about huge codebases (tens of millions of lines) without manually curating docs or running heavyweight indexing pipelines. Existing “AI‑grep” tools require large token budgets, many API calls, and fragile setup, which slows down debugging, onboarding, and AI‑assisted development.

## What This Does  
SocratiCode installs a local indexing service that watches a repository, builds polyglot dependency graphs, and serves a hybrid semantic‑plus‑structural search API. The core runtime lives under `src/` – e.g. `src/services/qdrant.ts` (vector store wrapper), `src/services/indexer.ts` (checkpointed indexing), and `src/services/docker.ts` (Docker orchestration). Configuration lives in `src/config.ts` and `src/constants.ts`. The plugin wrappers (`.claude-plugin/`, `.cursor-plugin/`, etc.) expose the same engine to different IDE/agent hosts.

## How It Is Wired  
Execution starts at `src/index.ts` → `main` (line 375). `main` creates the `SocraticodeConfig`, then calls `autoResumeIndexedProjects`, which eventually invokes `getLockHolderPid` (filesystem read). From there the flow follows the internal call graph:

* `main` → `autoResumeIndexedProjects` → `ensureInfrastructure` (`src/tools/index-tools.ts`) → `startQdrant` (`src/services/qdrant.ts`) → `withRetry` → `getClient` (calls the Qdrant client library).  
* Indexing is driven by `src/services/indexer.ts`: `indexProject` calls `onProgress` (used by many progress‑reporting spots) and `ensureCollection` in `qdrant.ts`.  
* File‑system writes are funneled through `src/services/lock.ts` (`acquireProjectLock`, `releaseProjectLock`).  
* Semantic search queries travel `src/tools/query-tools.ts` → `handleQueryTool` → `isIndexingInProgress` (`indexer.ts`) → `ensureReady` (`provider-*.ts`) → the embedding provider (`provider-openai.ts`, `provider-ollama.ts`, or `provider-google.ts`).  

The most widely referenced functions are:

| Function | Callers |
|----------|---------|
| `getClient` | 31 places |
| `projectIdFromPath` | 22 places |
| `getEmbeddingConfig` | 16 places |
| `onProgress` | 13 places |
| `ensureMetadataCollection` | 13 places |

These constitute the “blast radius” – changes here ripple through dozens of modules. Hub modules identified by the import graph are `src/services/logger.ts`, `src/constants.ts`, and `src/services/docker.ts`, each imported by >10 other files. No circular dependencies were found, but the hub nature makes them high‑impact change points.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repo (use the exact URL)
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/SocratiCode
cd SocratiCode

# Install Node dependencies
npm ci

# Start supporting services (Qdrant vector store, optional Ollama)
docker-compose up -d   # pulls qdrant & ollama images defined in docker-compose.yml

# Launch the indexing server (CLI entry)
node -r ts-node/register src/index.ts   # runs main()
```

*Configuration* – edit `src/config.ts` or provide a JSON file referenced by `src/config.ts` (e.g. `config.json`) for Git branch detection, collection names, and Docker image tags. The repository includes a sample `.socraticodeignore.example` for path exclusions.

*Running a query* – once the server is up, send a POST to `http://localhost:8000/query` (the exact endpoint is defined in `src/services/startup.ts`). The request body matches the `QueryRequest` type in `src/types.ts`.

## Real‑World Use  
A CI pipeline can invoke `node src/index.ts --mode=resume` to ensure the index is always up‑to‑date before a test run. An LLM‑powered assistant (Claude, Cursor, etc.) then calls the local HTTP API to retrieve relevant symbols, file snippets, or dependency graphs, allowing a developer to ask “show me all functions that touch the `User` table” without scanning the repo manually.

## Code Health & Issues  

* **MEDIUM – Enable Dependabot or Renovate** – `package.json` is the only manifest; no bot configured.  
* **MEDIUM – Add a dependency‑vulnerability scan to CI** – `.github/workflows/ci.yml` lacks a scan step.  
* **MEDIUM – Checkout should use `persist-credentials: false`** – current workflow leaves the token in `.git/config`.  
* **LOW – Set `timeout-minutes` on CI jobs** – prevents runaway builds.  

Static analysis also flagged:

* **HIGH – Duplicated code blocks** across `constants.ts`, `code-graph.ts`, `docker.ts`, and tests – 81 identical 6‑line fragments. Consolidate into shared helpers.  
* **MEDIUM – Oversized files** (`qdrant.ts`, `indexer.ts`, `graph-imports.test.ts` each > 750 lines). Split by responsibility.  
* **MEDIUM – High branching density** in `embedding-config.ts`, `config.ts`, `context-tools.ts`. Refactor to strategy tables or smaller functions.  
* **MEDIUM – Hub modules** (`logger.ts`, `constants.ts`, `docker.ts`) are imported by > 20 modules; keep their API stable.

No critical or low‑severity structural red flags were found; tests, CI, Dockerfile, and license are present.

## The Bottom Line  
SocratiCode delivers a self‑contained, zero‑setup indexing engine that can handle enterprise‑scale repositories and expose a fast, local search API. The codebase is well‑tested but contains a few large, highly‑connected modules and duplicated snippets that increase maintenance risk. Teams needing private, on‑prem AI code‑understanding—especially those already using Docker and Node—will find it ready to adopt, provided they address the modest health items (dependency updates, CI hardening, and refactoring of hub files).

forks.name: claude-prism
forks.description: An offline-first scientific writing workspace powered by Claude. LaTeX + Python + 100+ scientific skills all running locally.
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Scientists and engineers need a desktop authoring environment that keeps source files, LaTeX builds, and Python packages on‑disk while still offering AI‑assisted writing. Cloud‑only tools force every document to leave the local machine, creating privacy and latency concerns.

## What This Does  
`ClaudePrism` bundles a **Tauri 2** native shell (Rust) with a **React/TypeScript** UI to deliver an offline‑first LaTeX workspace. The UI lives under `apps/desktop/src/` – entry point `src/main.tsx` renders `<App/>` from `src/App.tsx`. `App` stitches together core panels (workspace, Claude chat, template gallery) that live in `src/components/`.  

The Rust side under `apps/desktop/src-tauri/` implements the heavy‑lifting back‑ends:

* `src-tauri/src/claude.rs` – wraps Anthropic’s Claude API and exposes Tauri commands used by `src/components/claude-chat/*`.
* `src-tauri/src/latex.rs` – invokes the embedded **Tectonic** compiler for offline PDF generation.
* `src-tauri/src/uv.rs` – drives **uv** to create per‑project Python virtual environments.

All UI‑to‑backend calls go through Tauri’s `invoke` bridge, so a single JavaScript/TS call (e.g., `invoke('compile_latex', {src})`) ends up in the matching Rust function, which writes files under `apps/desktop/public/examples/` or the user’s project folder.

## How It Is Wired  

1. **Process start** – `apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/main.rs` builds the Tauri application and serves `apps/desktop/index.html`.  
2. **Frontend bootstrap** – `src/main.tsx` (React entry) mounts `<App/>`.  
3. **Core UI flow** – `App.tsx` renders the workspace layout (`src/components/workspace/workspace-layout.tsx`) and the Claude chat drawer (`src/components/claude-chat/claude-chat-drawer.tsx`).  
4. **AI interaction** – UI components call `window.__TAURI__.invoke('prompt_claude', …)`. The call is handled by `src-tauri/src/claude.rs`, which formats the request, sends it to Anthropic, and returns the response.  
5. **LaTeX compilation** – When the user clicks “Build PDF”, `src/components/workspace/editor/latex-editor.tsx` invokes `compile_latex`. The Rust handler in `src-tauri/src/latex.rs` runs Tectonic, writes the PDF to `public/examples/...`, and notifies the UI via an event channel.  
6. **Python env** – The “UV Setup” button triggers `invoke('setup_uv')` → `src-tauri/src/uv.rs`, which downloads and configures `uv`, then creates a `.venv` for the project.  

**Import‑graph hot spots** – `latex-editor` imports six other modules (instability 0.86) and is the biggest blast‑radius front‑end file. The Rust `claude.rs` module also has deep call chains (no circular deps). These hubs are where most change impact propagates.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/claude-prism
cd claude-prism

# Install JS dependencies (pnpm is declared in root package.json)
pnpm install

# Install Rust toolchain (required by Tauri)
rustup target add x86_64-apple-darwin   # macOS example
rustup target add x86_64-pc-windows-msvc # Windows example

# Copy example env and add your Anthropic API key
cp apps/desktop/src-tauri/.env.example apps/desktop/src-tauri/.env
# Edit apps/desktop/src-tauri/.env → set CLAUDE_API_KEY=<your key>

# Run the desktop app in development mode
pnpm tauri dev   # script defined in apps/desktop/package.json
```

The build pipeline is defined in `.github/workflows/build-desktop.yml` (GitHub Actions) and the lockfile `pnpm-lock.yaml` guarantees reproducible JS installs.

## Real‑World Use  
A bioinformatics team can open a local LaTeX project, click “Create Python env”, and let Claude suggest code snippets for data analysis. The team compiles PDFs offline, stores all results in Git, and only the prompt/response payloads travel to Anthropic’s servers. No source or compiled PDFs leave the workstation.

## Code Health & Issues  

* **HIGH cognitive_load** – deep nesting (max depth 8) in `template-preview.tsx`, `src-tauri/src/claude.rs`, `src-tauri/src/history.rs`.  
* **HIGH clarity** – duplicated 6‑line blocks across >30 files (e.g., test helpers in `stores/*`).  
* **HIGH cognitive_load** – oversized files: `latex-editor.tsx` (1,642 LOC), `sidebar.tsx` (1,582 LOC), `src-tauri/src/claude.rs` (1,489 LOC).  
* **MEDIUM cognitive_load** – high branching density in `lang-bibtex.ts`, `use-claude-events.ts`, `use-keyboard-shortcuts.ts`.  

All findings come from the static import‑graph analysis (110 internal modules, 40 import edges, no cycles). Tests (`apps/desktop/src/__tests__/*.test.ts`) and CI (`.github/workflows/*.yml`) are present, licence (`MIT`) is included, and no secrets are committed.

## The Bottom Line  
`ClaudePrism` delivers a functional offline LaTeX/Python workspace with AI assistance, backed by a clear Tauri/React split. The codebase works but contains several large, deeply nested modules and duplicated test logic that will increase maintenance cost. Teams comfortable with Rust‑JS interop can adopt it for privacy‑sensitive scientific writing; developers should plan refactoring of the highlighted hot spots before extending core functionality.

forks.name: n8n-as-code
forks.description: Give your AI agent n8n superpowers. 537 nodes with full schemas, 7,700+ templates, Git-like sync, and TypeScript workflows.
forks.summary:
## The Problem

n8n workflows are typically managed through a click-driven UI, which makes version control, review, and automation difficult. Teams end up exporting JSON, losing history, and re-creating workflows by hand. The real pain is that AI agents lack the structured knowledge to work with n8n accurately — they guess at node schemas, produce broken workflows, and can't integrate with a live instance.

## What This Does

`n8n-as-code` gives AI agents and developers a typed, scriptable interface to n8n. It bundles 537 node schemas, 7,700+ templates, and TypeScript workflow definitions into a local, searchable knowledge base. The core is a CLI (`packages/cli`) that syncs workflows between a local directory and a live n8n instance — think `git pull`/`push` for workflows. It also ships integrations for VS Code (`packages/vscode-extension`), Claude Code (`.claude-plugin`), and MCP (`packages/mcp`).

The transformer (`packages/transformer`) converts n8n JSON workflows to TypeScript and back, so you can write workflows as code. The skills package (`packages/skills`) provides the AI context — node schemas, docs, and workflow examples — to ground agent responses.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts at `run` in `packages/cli/src/commands/convert.ts`, which reaches 193 functions. The main flow: the CLI parses commands, loads config via `config-service.ts`, and calls the n8n API through `n8n-api-client.ts`. The `sync-manager.ts` orchestrates the git-like pull/push, using `workflow-state-tracker.ts` to map local files to remote workflow IDs.

The most critical modules are the **hub** — `packages/cli/src/core/types.ts` (17 modules depend on it) and `packages/cli/src/core/index.ts` (12 depend on it). Changes here have wide blast radius. The `parse` function is called from 34 places; `getApiKey` from 16. These are the load-bearing functions.

The system makes outbound network calls (n8n API), reads/writes files (workflow JSON), and runs external commands (npx). A typical sync: `run -> getHealth` (network) then `main -> generate -> injectOrUpdate` (filesystem). The wiring to the live instance is direct — few hops from CLI to API.

## How To Use It

**Setup**: Clone and install dependencies. The repo uses pnpm (implied by `pnpm/action-setup` in CI). There is no lockfile committed, so builds are not reproducible — run `pnpm install` once and commit the lockfile.

**Configuration**: Copy `.env-example` to `.env` and set your n8n instance URL and API key. The `config-service.ts` reads local config; the CLI expects a workspace with workflow files.

**Running it**: Use the CLI directly — `npx @n8n-as-code/cli sync pull` or `push`. For AI agents, install the Claude plugin via `/plugin marketplace add https://github.com/EtienneLescot/n8n-as-code`. The VS Code extension activates from the command palette (`n8n: Configure`).

## Real-World Use

A team maintains workflows in a Git repo. A developer writes a workflow in TypeScript, commits it, and CI runs `n8n-as-code sync push` to deploy to a staging instance. An AI agent, grounded by the bundled schemas, proposes a new workflow — the developer reviews the diff, merges, and the same sync pushes it to production. No manual JSON editing, no drift between environments.

## Code Health & Issues

Static analysis found 89 issues (14 high, 75 medium). Key findings:

- **High - Deep nesting** in `n8n-api-client.ts`, `workflow-state-tracker.ts` (max indentation depth 8). Control flow is hard to follow.
- **High - Duplicated code** — 180 repeated 6-line blocks across 61 files. Extract shared helpers.
- **Medium - Empty catch blocks** in `proxy-service.ts`, `webview-html.ts`, `create-test-workflows.mjs` — errors silently swallowed.
- **Medium - Hub modules** — `types.ts` and `index.ts` are chokepoints; keep them stable.

SDLC observations: no lockfile (non-reproducible builds), GitHub Actions pinned to mutable tags (supply-chain risk), and large JSON assets (29MB+) in the repo bloat every clone. CI exists with tests (87 test files), which is good.

## The Bottom Line

This is a well-architected tool for teams that want GitOps for n8n and AI-assisted workflow development. The TypeScript transformer and bundled schemas are genuinely useful. The main risks are supply-chain (unpinned actions, no lockfile) and the complexity of the core sync logic. Teams already invested in n8n and AI agents will get the most value; casual users may find the setup overhead not worth it.

forks.name: code-review-graph
forks.description: Local knowledge graph for Claude Code. Builds a persistent map of your codebase so Claude reads only what matters — 6.8× fewer tokens on reviews and up to 49× on daily coding tasks.
forks.summary:
# code-review-graph Technical Briefing

## The Problem

AI coding tools re-read entire codebases on every task, burning tokens unnecessarily. This repo addresses that by building a persistent structural map so assistants read only what matters. The README states 6.8× fewer tokens on reviews and up to 49× on daily coding tasks.

## What This Does

`code-review-graph` uses tree-sitter to parse code structure and tracks changes incrementally. The core graph lives in `code_review_graph/graph.py` (63 functions, 5 classes, called from 52 other files), while `code_review_graph/parser.py` (80 functions, 4 classes) handles language-specific parsing. Incremental updates are managed by `code_review_graph/incremental.py` (35 functions, 2 classes). The system exposes MCP-compatible tools via `code_review_graph/main.py` — `get_minimal_context_tool` (line 158, reaches 42 functions) and `get_review_context_tool` (line 240, reaches 30 functions) are the primary entry points for AI assistant integration. The VS Code extension in `code-review-graph-vscode/` provides the UI layer, with `src/backend/cli.ts` as its entry point.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts at the CLI: `code_review_graph/cli.py:315` (`main`) reaches 280 functions and is called from 4 places. The import graph has 121 modules and 277 edges with zero circular dependencies. The most connected module is `code_review_graph/graph` (54 importers, 3 imports, instability 0.05), while `code_review_graph/tools/__init__` has high instability at 0.72 (5 importers, 13 imports). 

Traced paths to external effects: `main -> get_db_path` triggers filesystem deletion via `side.unlink`; `get_minimal_context_tool -> get_minimal_context -> _has_git_changes` runs `subprocess.run`; `get_review_context_tool -> get_review_context` reads files via `full_path.read_text`. The call graph contains 2,585 resolved edges — `commit` is called from 78 places, `NodeInfo` from 60, `parse_file` from 55.

## How To Use It

**Setup**: `pip install code-review-graph` (or `pipx`). Then `code-review-graph install` auto-detects platforms and writes MCP configuration. Supported via `--platform cursor`, `--platform claude-code`, or `--platform kiro`. Requires Python 3.10+; `uv` is recommended for `uvx` integration.

**Build**: `code-review-graph parse` constructs the graph. Initial build takes ~10 seconds for a 500-file project; subsequent updates happen automatically on file edits and git commits.

## Real-World Use

After `code-review-graph install`, open your project and invoke: `Build the code review graph for this project`. The assistant then uses `get_minimal_context_tool` to retrieve only relevant code — the graph ensures it reads ~6.8× fewer tokens during reviews. On daily coding tasks, context is further reduced, keeping the AI focused on the modified area.

## Code Health & Issues

Static analysis of 122 code files identified these findings:

- **[MEDIUM] Broad exception handling x7** — `code_review_graph/graph.py`, `code_review_graph/communities.py`, `code_review_graph/embeddings.py`: Bare `except` clauses swallow errors indiscriminately.
- **[HIGH/cognitive_load] Deep nesting x35** — `code_review_graph/graph.py`, `code_review_graph/parser.py`, `code_review_graph/incremental.py`: Max indentation depth 7; control flow is hard to follow. Fix: flatten with guard clauses.
- **[HIGH/cognitive_load] Oversized file x12** — Same files: 1,156-line files ripple changes widely. Fix: split into cohesive units.
- **[HIGH/clarity] Hub module x5** — `code_review_graph/graph.py` is depended on by 54 modules; churn here has high-blast-radius. Fix: keep stable and small; move volatile logic out.
- **[HIGH/clarity] Duplicated code blocks** — 2,027 repeated 6-line blocks across 60 files in `code-review-graph-vscode/`. Extract shared helpers.

Repository hygiene findings: no Dependabot/Renovate configured, no dependency vulnerability scan in CI, checkout retains token (`persist-credentials` not disabled), two workflow jobs lack timeouts, and convention files (.editorconfig, .gitattributes) are absent.

## The Bottom Line

The graph construction and incremental update logic work well — the token reduction claim is credible given the module mapping and call-graph analysis. However, the codebase shows significant maintainability risk: three files carry most import and call traffic, deep nesting is prevalent, and exception handling is broad. The hygiene gaps (no update bot, no dependency scanning) are easy to remediate. This is worth adopting if you control the AI assistant pipeline and want to reduce token consumption, but plan to allocate engineering time to restructure the high-traffic modules.

*Word count: ~480*

forks.name: awesome-vehicle-security
forks.description: 🚗  A curated list of resources for learning about vehicle security and car hacking.
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Security researchers and automotive engineers need a single, vetted source of references for vehicle‑security concepts, tools, and community contacts. Scattered across blogs, conference talks, and vendor docs, the information is hard to discover and keep current.

## What This Does  
The repository is an *awesome‑list* – a curated Markdown collection of links, brief annotations, and related media. The root contains the primary documentation files:

* `README.md` – the public facing list, organized into logical sections (Learn, Projects, Hardware, Software, etc.).  
* `_config.yml` – Jekyll configuration used by GitHub Pages to render the list.  
* `contributing.md` – guidelines for community additions.  
* `LICENSE` – an MIT‑style permissive license.

The `assets/` folder holds two GIFs referenced by the README (`car_hacking.gif`, `car_hacking_jeep.gif`). No source code, scripts, or binaries are present; the repo’s purpose is purely informational.

## How It Is Wired  
There is no executable code or runtime graph. The only “entry point” is the Markdown renderer that GitHub Pages (or a local Jekyll build) uses:

1. **GitHub Pages / Jekyll** reads `_config.yml` to apply the default theme and layout.  
2. The `README.md` is served as the main HTML page; all hyperlinks are static and point to external resources.  
3. No internal functions, data stores, or network calls exist within the repo itself. Consequently, there are no call graphs, dependency trees, or side‑effects to map.

Because the repository is purely documentation, any modification (e.g., adding a new link) is a direct edit to `README.md` or `contributing.md` and does not propagate through code paths.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/awesome-vehicle-security
cd awesome-vehicle-security

# View the list locally (optional)
# If you have Jekyll installed, you can serve it:
gem install jekyll
jekyll serve   # renders README.md via the _config.yml theme
```

*No additional build steps, environment variables, or runtime commands are required.* Users typically browse `README.md` directly on GitHub or via the rendered GitHub‑Pages site.

## Real‑World Use  
A penetration‑testing team preparing for an automotive audit can open `README.md`, locate the “Learn → Articles” or “Software → Libraries and Tools → Python” sections, and click the curated links to obtain up‑to‑date tutorials, tool repositories, and research papers. The list can be forked and extended with internal tooling references to keep a private knowledge base aligned with the public effort.

## Code Health & Issues  

- **Medium – No tests** – repository contains no test files (`tests present: no`).  
- **Medium – No CI/CD** – no `.github/` workflows, Dockerfile, or other pipeline definitions (`CI: no`).  
- **Low – No lockfile** – dependency lockfiles (e.g., `package-lock.json`, `requirements.txt`) are absent (`lockfile: no`).  
- **Info – License present** – `LICENSE` file grants permissive reuse.  
- **Info – No committed secrets** – static scan reported none.

These findings are deterministic from the repository’s static analysis; there are no hidden build scripts or hidden configuration files.

## The Bottom Line  
The repo delivers a well‑structured, community‑driven catalogue of vehicle‑security resources, useful as a reference point for researchers and engineers. Its limitation is the lack of any testable code, CI, or automation, which is expected for an “awesome list” but means the repository offers no executable functionality or verification of its content. Ideal for teams that need a starting bibliography rather than a software toolkit.

forks.name: pigeon-pod
forks.description: Listen to YouTube & Bilibili. Anywhere.
forks.summary:
## The Problem

Self-hosting a podcast aggregator for YouTube and Bilibili means juggling yt-dlp, RSS generation, download queues, proxy routing, and auth—each a separate moving part. PigeonPod packages those into one deployable app with a web UI for managing subscriptions, downloads, and feeds.

## What This Does

PigeonPod turns YouTube and Bilibili channels, playlists, or single videos into RSS feeds and downloadable audio/video files. The backend (`backend/src/main/java/top/asimov/pigeon/`) is a Spring Boot app handling subscriptions, sync, downloads, and feed generation. The frontend (`frontend/src/`) is a React app with pages for the dashboard, feed management, and settings.

The README documents features like cookie-based access for restricted content, proxy support for network isolation, per-feed filters, and OPML export. Eight UI languages are supported via locale files in the backend.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts in `frontend/index.html`, which loads `frontend/src/App.jsx`. That component sets up routing and pulls in `GlobalPlayer` for playback. The frontend calls the Spring backend through REST endpoints; the backend uses MyBatis Plus against SQLite (default) or another configured datasource.

The frontend import graph shows `frontend/src/helpers/index` as a hub — 8 modules import it. `UserContext` (6 importers) and `useDateFormat` (5 importers) are the next most connected. `App` imports 12 modules but is imported by only 1, so it is a leaf that wires everything together. No circular dependencies exist.

The backend's `PlaylistService` (1574 lines) carries the widest blast radius — it owns playlist and subscription logic, so most sync and feed operations route through it. `BilibiliPlaylistHelper` has deep nesting (indentation depth 9), making its control flow hard to follow. The database migration `V38__Backfill_episode_duration_seconds.java` and `EpisodeDurationHelper.java` duplicate the same 6-line blocks.

The wiring for download execution, proxy routing, and feed generation is not fully mapped in this analysis — the static import graph covers module dependencies but not the runtime call paths through `yt-dlp` or the S3 client.

## How To Use It

**Setup**: The Dockerfile builds the full stack. Use Docker Compose as documented in the README:

```yaml
version: '3.9'
services:
  pigeon-pod:
    image: 'ghcr.io/aizhimou/pigeon-pod:latest'
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - '8834:8080'
    environment:
      - SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:sqlite:/data/pigeon-pod.db
    volumes:
      - data:/data
volumes:
  data:
```

**Configuration**: Environment variables in `docker-compose.yml` — `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` for the database path, `PIGEON_AUTH_ENABLED` (defaults to `true`) to disable built-in auth behind a trusted proxy. The backend reads these via `AuthProperties.java` and `StorageProperties.java`.

**Running it**: `docker compose up -d`, then open `http://localhost:8834`. For development, `backend/pom.xml` is a Maven project (`mvn spring-boot:run`) and `frontend/package.json` is a Vite app (`npm run dev`).

## Real-World Use

A team running a private podcast service for internal training videos: they subscribe to a YouTube playlist, enable cookie auth for restricted content, set a proxy for network isolation, and configure a retention filter to keep only videos under 30 minutes. The app syncs daily, downloads new episodes as audio, and exposes a protected RSS feed that their podcast client polls. Failed downloads trigger a webhook digest so an operator can retry or cancel in bulk from the dashboard.

## Code Health & Issues

Static analysis found 26 findings (10 high, 16 medium) across 4 kinds:

- **High - Deep nesting** (11 instances): `frontend/src/pages/DashboardEpisodes/index.jsx`, `frontend/src/pages/Feed/index.jsx`, `backend/src/main/java/top/asimov/pigeon/helper/BilibiliPlaylistHelper.java` — max indentation depth 9 makes control flow hard to follow. Fix: early returns, extract inner blocks.
- **High - Duplicated code blocks** (145 repeated 6-line blocks across 62 files): `V38__Backfill_episode_duration_seconds.java`, `EpisodeDurationHelper.java`, `AuthProperties.java` — extract shared helpers.
- **High - Oversized files** (11 instances): `frontend/src/pages/Feed/index.jsx`, `Setting/index.jsx`, `PlaylistService.java` (1574 lines) — split by responsibility.
- **Medium - High branching density** (3 instances): `OutboundProxyHolder.java`, `FeedService.java`, `FeedEpisodeVisibilityHelper.java` — 30 branch points over 104 lines; decompose with strategy dispatch.

SDLC observations from the file structure:

- **High - CI doesn't run tests**: 8 test files exist, but `.github/workflows/build-and-publish.yml` has no test command. The green check is meaningless.
- **High - Unpinned GitHub Actions**: `docker/login-action@v3`, `docker/setup-qemu-action@v3`, `docker/setup-buildx-action@v3`, `docker/build-push-action@v5` use mutable tags — pin to commit SHAs.
- **Medium - No dependency update bot**: no Dependabot or Renovate config.
- **Medium - Mutable base images**: `node:22`, `maven:3.9.6-eclipse-temurin-17`, `cgr.dev/chainguard/wolfi-base:latest` in the Dockerfile — pin by digest.
- **Medium - No dependency scan in CI**: no `dependency-review-action` or `osv-scanner`.
- **Medium - Container runs as root**: no `USER` directive in the Dockerfile.
- **Medium - Test coverage is thin**: 8 test files against 220 source files (ratio 0.036).
- **Low - No job timeouts** in the workflow; **Low - missing** `.editorconfig`, `.gitattributes`, formatter config.

## The Bottom Line

PigeonPod is a functional, feature-complete podcast aggregator with a polished UI and solid deployment story. The backend has real complexity in `PlaylistService` and the feed helpers that will need refactoring before significant feature work. The CI gaps — no tests run, unpinned actions, no dependency scanning — are the first things to fix. Use it if you need a self-hosted YouTube/Bilibili-to-RSS pipeline; budget time for test coverage and build hardening before trusting it in production.

forks.name: ForgeCAD
forks.description: Multi-backend code-first parametric CAD in JavaScript/TypeScript with live params, constraints, assemblies, and exact STEP/BREP export.
forks.summary:
## The Problem

Most CAD systems force a choice between a visual editor and a code API. Visual editors are hard to version-control and automate; pure code APIs lack live feedback. ForgeCAD treats TypeScript as the file format, so models are plain code that runs in the browser with live parameter sliders and exact STEP/BREP export through CadQuery/OpenCascade.

## What This Does

ForgeCAD is a multi-backend parametric CAD system. The public API (`param()`, `roundedRect()`, `extrude()`, `subtract()`) is kernel-agnostic; interactive geometry runs on Manifold, while exact export goes through CadQuery/OpenCascade. The `examples/` directory holds 238 files: 217 code examples, benchmarks, and a compiler corpus.

The repo is the community home—active development is private. It contains the API examples (`examples/api/`), constraint demonstrations (`examples/constraints/`), and LLM benchmark harnesses (`examples/bench/`, `examples/bench-v2/`) that grade model-generated CAD scripts.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts in a `.forge.js` script, which runs in the browser or CLI (`forgecad studio`). The API is globally available—no imports required. The measured call graph shows 142 internal edges; the most-connected functions are `pieceBase` (6 callers), `S` (4), `axle` (4), `rad` (4), and `ring` (4)—change these and the most examples break.

The `examples/` directory is a flat collection of standalone scripts. `examples/robot_hand_2.forge.js` defines 19 functions including `rad`, `clamp`, `add3`, and `explodeShape`. `examples/chess-set.forge.js` defines `ring`, `pieceBase`, and piece shapes. The benchmark harnesses (`examples/bench/*/harness.forge.js`) each define `gate`, `test`, `bboxCenter`, and `bboxSize` to evaluate model outputs. The module graph shows no circular dependencies; the 5 import edges are all in `examples/api/` where `.forge.js` files import helper modules like `js-module-pillars.js`.

The repo writes nothing to a database or network at runtime—scripts produce geometry and exports. CI (`GitHub Actions`) builds and publishes.

## How To Use It

**Setup**: `npm install -g forgecad`

**Running**: `forgecad studio /path/to/your/project` or `forgecad studio --blank` for a scratch file. A minimal script:

```javascript
const width = param("Width", 120, { min: 60, max: 220, unit: "mm" });
const base = roundedRect(width, 80, 10).extrude(12).color("#5f87c6");
return base;
```

**Configuration**: No environment variables or config files are required. The `.agents/` and `.kiro/` directories contain agent settings, not runtime configuration.

## Real-World Use

A mechanical engineer can define a parameterized bracket, share the `.forge.js` file, and let a colleague adjust the `Width` slider in the browser. The same script exports an exact STEP file for manufacturing. For AI-assisted design, the repo includes agent skills (`forgecad skill install`) and a benchmark suite that grades how well models like GPT-5.4-mini and Claude Sonnet 4 generate valid CAD scripts.

## Code Health & Issues

Static analysis found 11 findings (1 high, 10 medium). The high-severity issue is duplicated code blocks: 234 repeated 6-line blocks across 26 files in `examples/api/` and `examples/constraints/`. The medium findings are high branching density in three benchmark harnesses (e.g., 29 branch points over 95 lines in `examples/bench/door-hinge/harness.forge.js`).

The CI audit found 4 issues. High: third-party GitHub Actions are pinned to tags (`dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable`, `softprops/action-gh-release@v2`)—pin to commit SHAs. Medium: no `permissions:` declaration in `ci.yml` and `persist-credentials: false` is not set on checkout. Low: no `timeout-minutes` on workflow jobs.

Tests exist (13 files), CI is present, and no secrets were committed. The duplicated example code is a maintenance cost, not a functional risk.

## The Bottom Line

ForgeCAD is a serious code-first CAD system with a clean API and a strong example corpus. The duplicated examples and unpinned CI actions are hygiene issues, not architectural problems. Use it if you want version-controlled, AI-friendly parametric modeling with exact STEP export; the private development model means the public repo is a showcase, not the full source.

forks.name: graph-memory
forks.description: Openclaw记忆插件Knowledge Graph + Memory；Knowledge Graph Context Engine for OpenClaw — extracts structured triples from conversations, compresses context 75%, enables cross-session experience reuse
forks.summary:
## The Problem

Long agent conversations consume context windows linearly — 174 messages can eat 95K tokens, forcing truncation and lost state. New sessions start with amnesia; yesterday's solved problems are gone. The repo addresses both by extracting a typed knowledge graph from conversation history and recalling relevant subgraphs on demand.

## What This Does

`graph-memory` is a plugin for OpenClaw that converts conversation transcripts into a SQLite-backed property graph. It extracts triples (subject-predicate-object) from user/assistant turns via `src/extractor/extract.ts`, stores nodes and edges in `src/store/db.ts`, and compresses context by replacing raw history with graph nodes. The README claims 75% token reduction (95K → 24K over 7 rounds).

The recall path (`src/recaller/recall.ts`) runs two parallel searches: precise vector/FTS5 matching with graph traversal, and generalized community-summary matching. Top-ranked nodes pull original conversation snippets back into context. The graph runs community detection (`src/graph/community.ts`) and PageRank (`src/graph/pagerank.ts`) for ranking.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts at `index.ts`, which exposes the plugin entry points: `register`, `ingest`, `assemble`, `compact`, `afterTurn`, and `execute`. The main path is `execute` (index.ts:601), which reaches 42 functions and calls `upsertNode`, writing to SQLite via `db.prepare("UPDATE gm_nodes SET content=?, description=?, va...")`. Only 3 hops from entry to database write.

The hub is `src/types.ts` — 13 modules depend on it, so changes there have high blast radius. `src/store/store.ts` is the operational core: 42 functions, called from 6 files, owning `uid`, `toNode`, `normalizeName`, and `findByName`. The most-called functions are `normalizeName` (7 call sites) and `findByName` (5 sites) — changing either ripples widely. `index.ts` is the entry-point file (22 functions) but also calls into 11 modules and reads/writes the database directly.

The module graph has no circular dependencies (21 modules, 57 edges). The database is SQLite with FTS5; the model calls go through `src/engine/embed.ts` (raw `fetch` to any OpenAI-compatible endpoint) and `src/engine/llm.ts` for extraction.

## How To Use It

```bash
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/graph-memory
cd graph-memory
npm install
npm test
```

Configuration lives in `openclaw.plugin.json` and `index.ts`. The embedding endpoint is set via `cfg.baseURL` (defaults to `https://api.openai.com/v1`). The plugin registers as `plugins.slots.contextEngine` in OpenClaw. The repo ships a Windows installer per the README, but no Dockerfile or CI pipeline exists.

## Real-World Use

A 7-round session installing `bilibili-mcp` and logging in: without the plugin, tokens grow linearly to 95K; with it, they stabilize around 24K. Cross-session, the graph links "installed libgl1" to "ImportError: libGL.so.1" via a `SOLVED_BY` edge, so a new session recalls the fix without re-diagnosing.

## Code Health & Issues

Static analysis found 8 issues (1 high, 7 medium). The high finding is **duplicated code blocks**: 53 repeated 6-line blocks across 7 files, including `src/engine/embed.ts`, `src/engine/llm.ts`, and `src/extractor/extract.ts` — extract shared helpers. Medium findings: high branching density (168 branch points over 516 lines in `src/store/store.ts`, `src/engine/embed.ts`, `src/engine/llm.ts`), the `src/types.ts` hub module, and `index.ts` at 718 lines (split by responsibility).

SDLC gaps: no CI pipeline, no lockfile (declared ranges reach `vitest@1.4.0` with a published CVE), no dependency update bot. Tests exist (7 files) but nothing runs them automatically. Five of seven dependencies are behind current major versions.

## The Bottom Line

The architecture is sound: a clean module graph, no cycles, and a clear separation between extraction, storage, and recall. The main risks are maintainability — the duplicated logic and oversized `index.ts` — and the missing lockfile, which makes builds non-reproducible. Suitable for teams running OpenClaw who need persistent memory; not yet production-hardened for broader use.

forks.name: ART
forks.description: Agent Reinforcement Trainer: train multi-step agents for real-world tasks using GRPO. Give your agents on-the-job training. Reinforcement learning for Qwen3.5, GPT-OSS, Llama, and more!
forks.summary:
## The Problem

ART addresses the pain of training multi-step LLM agents for real-world tasks. Without a structured RL harness, practitioners face manual reward engineering, fragile episode loops, and infrastructure overhead that separates code from experimentation. The framework promises GRPO integration "out of the box" but the collected-project structure means integration effort varies significantly across the four sub-projects.

## What This Does

ART is a collection of 4 self-contained projects rather than a single monorepo: `src` (162 files, the core framework), `examples` (79 files with notebooks and code demos), `dev` (26 files with prototypes and benchmarks), and `scripts` (9 utility scripts). The `src` layer provides the RL harness—`src/art/model.py` defines `TrainableModel` and is called from 54 other files, while `src/art/trajectories.py` manages `TrajectoryGroup` and `Trajectory` objects called from 48 files. GRPO training hooks live in the backend services; `src/art/local/backend.py` handles GPU cost resolution and automatic training steps, and `src/art/megatron/service.py` manages rollout weight modes and vLLM base URL configuration. The framework supports Qwen3.5, GPT-OSS, Llama, and unsloth variants through model-specific service files under `src/art/*/service.py`.

Serverless RL is the standout capability: `examples/just-the-facts/main.py` is the primary entry point, reaching 399 functions and itself called from 1 place. A typical workflow instantiates `art.TrainableModel`, registers a `ServerlessBackend` with a W&B API key, then iterates edits via the backend. The `examples/mcp-rl` directory adds tool-use servers (Alpha Vantage, Google Maps, Balldontlie) that agents learn to call, extending the task horizon beyond text completion.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts at `main` in `examples/just-the-facts/main.py` (1 call site). From there, control flows to `register` (27 calls), `train` (21 calls), and `rollout` (20 calls). The `rollout` function triggers `Trajectory` (25 calls) and `create` (22 calls). The internal call graph contains 3250 resolved edges; `list` is called from 95 places, `TrajectoryGroup` from 57, and `Model` from 56. 

Two significant structural patterns affect maintainability. First, 25 modules live in circular dependencies—`src/art/__init__` (instability 0.41, in cycle), `src/art/trajectories` (instability 0.11, in cycle), and `src/art/model` (instability 0.5, in cycle) are the primary members. Second, `src/art/types` has 13 dependents and 0 outgoing imports, making it a high-blast-radius hub: any change ripples across 17 dependent modules. The call graph shows `main -> get_step -> gather_trajectory_groups -> register` as a representative path, and `chat_completions -> build_generation_prompt -> render_message -> image_to_chunk` as a path that leaves the process via network (urllib.request.urlopen) and filesystem (Image.open).

## How To Use It

**Setup**: No root-level `Dockerfile` or `Makefile`. The package uses `pnpm` as package manager (evidenced by `docs/package.json` and `pyproject.toml` files across examples). Install with `pip install -e .` from the repo root, or `pnpm install` if working in the `docs` or an example directory.

**Configuration**: Required environment variables are not explicitly documented in the root, but the README snippet shows a `ServerlessBackend` instantiation accepting `api_key="your_wandb_api_key"`. The `.env.example` at root level likely contains additional vars (WANDB_PROJECT, base model names). The `examples/just-the-facts/pyproject.toml` and `examples/mcp-rl/pyproject.toml` define per-example dependencies.

**Running it**: Invoke the primary entry point with `python examples/just-the-facts/main.py`. For the MCP-RL tool-use demos, start individual server scripts under `examples/mcp-rl/servers/python/`. The Colab notebooks (linked from the README) provide the lowest-friction on-ramp.

## Real-World Use

A practical scenario: your team needs an agent that can retrieve current stock prices. You instantiate `art.TrainableModel(project="finance", name="price-agent", base_model="OpenPipe/Qwen3-14B-Instruct")`, register a `ServerlessBackend` with your W&B key, and define a reward function that checks whether the agent's tool call to Alpha Vantage returned the correct price. The agent runs GRPO across multiple episodes, learning when and how to call `mcp_alphavantage` versus when to respond from cached knowledge. Each checkpoint becomes instantly available via W&B Inference for downstream product use.

## Code Health & Issues

The static analysis produced 172 findings across 55 high, 116 medium, and 1 low severity issues. The 7 SDLC health findings are:

- **HIGH** - Pin third-party GitHub Actions to a commit SHA: `.github/workflows` references `pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish@release/v1`; a tag move changes which code runs with your secrets.
- **HIGH** - Open a pull request instead of pushing to the default branch: `create-draft-release.yml` pushes with `git push origin release/v${{ steps.bump.outputs.NEW_VERSION }}`; automated commits deploy without test validation.
- **MEDIUM** - Enable Dependabot or Renovate: 2 manifest(s) exist but no update bot is configured.
- **MEDIUM** - Gate pull requests on a dependency vulnerability scan: no dependency scan is in CI.
- **MEDIUM** - Move large binaries to Git LFS or out of the repository: `examples/data/temporal-clue/puzzles.json` is 13.7MB, `dictionary.json` 7.8MB.
- **MEDIUM** - Set `persist-credentials: false` on checkout: the default checkout step keeps the token available to all later steps.
- **LOW** - Set `timeout-minutes` on workflow jobs: 4 jobs declare no timeout, risking overlap on a two-hourly schedule.

Beyond the measured block: the repo contains no `Dockerfile`, but `LICENSE` and `lockfile` are present. No committed secrets were detected. The four-project collection means "getting started" depends on which sub-project you target—`src` for framework extension, `examples` for immediate demos.

## The Bottom Line

ART delivers a functional GRPO harness with serverless RL infrastructure that dramatically reduces the DevOps overhead of agent training. The four-project layout gives breadth (email agents, 2048, MCP tool use, just-the-facts) but requires mapping the right sub-project to your use case. Health is decent—license and lockfile are present, CI runs—but the GitHub Actions pinning and PR gating issues should be fixed before any production deployment. Use the Colab notebooks for quick experimentation; commit to `src/` modifications only if you need to extend the framework itself.

forks.name: ministack
forks.description: Ministack: Free, open-source local AWS emulator - 40+ services, Terraform compatible, real databases. Free forever. MIT   licensed.
forks.summary:
## The Problem

LocalStack moved core services behind a paid plan, breaking teams that relied on it for local development and CI/CD. MiniStack is a free, MIT-licensed alternative that emulates 40+ AWS services on a single port (4566) with real databases and Terraform compatibility.

## What This Does

MiniStack is a Python-based AWS emulator (130 Python files) with a Flask-style HTTP server in `ministack/app.py`. It implements service handlers across `ministack/services/` — S3, EC2, Lambda, Cognito, RDS, CloudFormation, and others. The `core/` directory holds shared infrastructure: `responses.py`, `persistence.py`, and `router.py`.

Real infrastructure support is notable: RDS spins up actual Postgres/MySQL containers, ElastiCache runs Redis, Athena uses DuckDB, and ECS/Lambda execute real Docker containers. Testcontainers bindings exist for Go, Java, and Python in the `Testcontainers/` directory. The README claims ~270MB image and ~21MB RAM idle, versus LocalStack's ~1GB image.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts in `ministack/app.py` — `app` (line 1026) reaches 426 functions, `_handler` (line 126) reaches 402. The shortest paths to effects: `_handler -> handle_request` reaches crypto via `os.urandom`; `main -> _cleanup` touches the filesystem. Network calls leave via `client.get` from `handle_oauth2_authorize` in Cognito.

The critical hub is `ministack/core/responses.py` — 65 modules import it, and its `json_response` is called from 520 places, `error_response_json` from 409. Change that file and you change the entire system. `persistence.py` (46 importers) and `services/__init__.py` (21 importers) are similar blast radii.

The `lambda_svc.py` file (124 functions, 3,559 lines) is the most complex — it makes outbound network calls, runs external commands, and participates in an import cycle with `core/lambda_runtime.py` and `cloudformation/__init__.py`. The cycle means changes ripple unpredictably.

## How To Use It

```bash
# Option 1: PyPI
pip install ministack
ministack

# Option 2: Docker
docker run -p 4566:4566 ministackorg/ministack

# Option 3: Clone and build
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/ministack
cd ministack
docker compose up -d

# Verify
curl http://localhost:4566/_ministack/health
```

Configuration is runtime-based via `POST /_ministack/config` (e.g., `{"lambda_svc.LAMBDA_EXECUTOR": "docker"}`). State resets via `POST /_ministack/reset`. The `Makefile` and `pyproject.toml` suggest standard Python tooling.

## Real-World Use

For CI pipelines that need AWS integration tests without cloud costs: run MiniStack in a Docker container, point `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:4566` at it, and execute Terraform plans or boto3 tests against it. The internal reset endpoint lets you wipe state between test runs — something real AWS can't do.

## Code Health & Issues

Static analysis found 187 findings (63 high, 124 medium). Key issues:

- **Critical** — `golang.org/x/crypto@0.45.0` carries CVE-2026-42508 (critical); the pinned version is exactly what installs. Upgrade and commit the lockfile.
- **Critical** — `.github/workflows/docker-publish-on-pr.yml` checks out PR code in a privileged workflow with `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` exposed. This is the most reliably exploited Actions pattern.
- **Critical** — Same workflow exposes publish-scoped Docker Hub credentials to fork-triggered jobs.
- **High** — Third-party Actions pinned to tags (`@v4`, `@v6`) instead of commit SHAs; tags can be moved (the tj-actions pattern).
- **High** — `docker-compose.yml` mounts the Docker socket with privileged mode and host networking.
- **High** — `ministack/app.py` sets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: "*"`, enabling cross-site authenticated requests.
- **High** — No lockfile for `pyproject.toml`; transitive dependencies can drift.
- **High** — `containerd@1.7.29` and `docker/docker@27.1.1` carry published advisories.
- **Medium** — No Dependabot/Renovate configured; no `permissions:` declarations in CI workflows.

Deep nesting (depth 6) and oversized files (3,559 lines in `lambda_svc.py`) make the code hard to follow. The import cycle compounds this.

## The Bottom Line

A genuinely useful LocalStack alternative with real infrastructure support and a small footprint. The architecture is sound but the security posture needs immediate attention — fix the workflow privileges and pinned dependencies before adopting it in production CI. Best suited for teams that want free local AWS emulation and can tolerate the maintenance overhead of a young project.

forks.name: warp
forks.description: Warp is an agentic development environment, born out of the terminal.
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Warp positions itself as an “agentic development environment born out of the terminal,” yet the repository is a mosaic of six independent projects glued together under one monorepo.  Teams that want a seamless terminal‑centric AI assistant must stitch together UI, agent, and infrastructure crates while contending with loose dependency pinning, uncommitted secrets, and CI jobs that can mask test failures.  The result is a setup that works for quick demos but demands disciplined maintenance to be production‑ready.

## What This Does  
Warp bundles a terminal UI (`app/` – 2734 files, 1940 code files), a Rust‑based AI crate (`crates/ai/` – 1703 files, 1461 code files) that forwards prompts to OpenAI‑compatible models, an asset‑cache layer (`crates/asset_cache/`) for binary blobs, and a collection of skill‑scripts (`/.agents/skills/`) that teach the system how to create PRs, resolve conflicts, and run unit tests.  The `command-signatures-v2/js/build/main.js` file encodes CLI command signatures that the terminal parses to dispatch commands.  Resources such as `specs/` and `resources/` hold Markdown specs and static assets, while `script/` contains bootstrap and run helpers.  Secret‑shaped paths are present in `app/src/env_vars/view/secrets.rs`, `app/src/server/server_api/managed_secrets.rs`, and `app/src/terminal/model/grid/secrets.rs`, flagged by the code‑health audit as low‑risk but worth reviewing.

## How It Is Wired  

**INTERNAL CALL GRAPH**  
- User input → `app/src/lib.rs` (Rust entry) → terminal event loop → `command-signatures-v2/js/build/main.js` dispatches the command.  
- Coding‑agent requests flow through `crates/ai/src/lib.rs`, which calls the `openai` provider wrapper, then returns generated code to the UI.  
- Asset‑cache operations (`crates/asset_cache/src/lib.rs`) read/write large binaries from the filesystem or Git LFS, feeding the UI’s preview pane.  

**ENTRY POINTS**  
| File | Role |
|------|------|
| `app/src/lib.rs` | Top‑level Rust binary; starts the Warp UI and orchestrates crates. |
| `command-signatures-v2/js/build/main.js` | JSON‑encoded command signatures; parsed by the terminal to map CLI verbs to Rust handlers. |
| `crates/ai/src/lib.rs` | Starts the AI provider client; loads model config, sends chat completions. |
| `crates/app-installation-detection/src/lib.rs` | Detects whether Warp is running from a built binary or a dev environment. |
| `crates/asset_cache/src/lib.rs` | Handles caching of large assets; decides between local file, HTTP fetch, or LFS pointer. |

**WHAT THIS CODE TOUCHES OUTSIDE ITSELF**  
- `crates/ai` makes outbound HTTP calls to the configured LLM endpoint (default OpenAI).  
- `app/src` writes runtime state to `~/.warp/` and interacts with the system terminal via pty allocation.  
- `crates/asset_cache` may download or upload blobs to cloud storage when LFS is not configured.  

**WHAT EACH FILE IS RESPONSIBLE FOR** (summary)  
- `app/src/lib.rs` – process lifecycle, config loading, crate composition.  
- `app/src/env_vars/view/secrets.rs` – UI view for displaying/exposing env‑var secrets (audit flag).  
- `crates/ai/src/lib.rs` – model selection, prompt templating, streaming responses.  
- `crates/app-installation-detection/src/lib.rs` – feature‑flag gating for build vs. install modes.  
- `crates/asset_cache/src/lib.rs` – blob storage abstraction, LFS integration.  

A hub‑like cycle exists between `app/src/lib.rs` and `crates/ai/src/lib.rs`; any change to the AI provider config ripples through config loading, UI theming, and the skill‑script dispatcher.

## How To Use It  

**Setup**  
```bash
# Clone the repo (use the exact URL)
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/warp

# Platform‑specific bootstrap (script/bootstrap chooses the right path)
./script/bootstrap   # installs Rust toolchain, node, Docker if missing
```

**Configuration**  
- Required env vars are defined in `app/src/env_vars/view/secrets.rs`; copy `warp/.env.example` to `~/.warp/.env` and set `OPENAI_API_KEY` (or another provider).  
- For LFS‑tracked binaries, add entries to `.warp/lfs.yml` (not in the repo but referenced in `crates/asset_cache/src/lib.rs`).  

**Running it**  
```bash
# Build and start the Warp terminal
./script/run   # equivalent to `cargo run --release -p warp` inside app/
```

The `./script/presubmit` target runs `fmt`, `clippy`, and the test suite (1117 test files) before any push.

## Real‑World Use  
A developer opens Warp’s terminal and types `/code “implement a binary search in Rust”`.  The terminal forwards the request to `crates/ai/src/lib.rs`, which calls the OpenAI chat completion API, returns a snippet, and the UI inserts it into the active buffer.  Simultaneously, the asset‑cache ensures any referenced binary dependencies (e.g., `dxcompiler.dll`) are available without cluttering the clone size.  The skill‑script `/.agents/skills/create-pr/SKILL.md` can then be invoked to open a PR with the change, thanks to the command‑signature mapping in `command-signatures-v2/js/build/main.js`.

## Code Health & Issues  

The static analysis produced the following measured findings (8 total, 0 critical, 3 high, 4 medium, 1 low):

- **HIGH** – Pin third‑party GitHub Actions to a commit SHA: `.github/workflows` contains `warpdotdev/repo-sync/actions/validate-markers@main` and `warpdotdev/generate-changelog@main`.  Replace `@vN` with 40‑character SHAs.  
- **HIGH** – Upgrade a pinned dependency with a published advisory: `diesel@2.3.4` (GHSA‑h5x4‑m2qf‑r4f2) and `futures-util@0.3` (CVE‑2020‑35908).  Upgrade to the fixed version and commit the lockfile.  
- **HIGH** – Remove `continue-on-error` from correctness‑gate steps in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (line 269).  
- **MEDIUM** – Declare least‑privilege permissions for `GITHUB_TOKEN` in `.github/workflows/check_approvals.yml` (add `permissions: contents: read`).  
- **MEDIUM** – Pin the container base image by digest in `.github/actions/bundle_arch_package/Dockerfile` (use `archlinux:base-devel@sha256<digest>`).  
- **MEDIUM** – Gate pull requests on a dependency vulnerability scan; currently no scan in CI.  Add `dependency-review-action` on `pull_request`.  
- **MEDIUM** – Move large binaries (>5 MB) out of the repo: `crates/command-signatures-v2/js/.yarn/cache/typescript-patch-…zip` (38.8 MB) and similar blobs.  Enable Git LFS or fetch in a setup step.  
- **LOW** – Set `timeout-minutes` on workflow jobs in `.github/workflows/check_approvals.yml` (two jobs lack a timeout).  

Beyond these, the repository hygiene check confirms: tests present, CI (GitHub Actions) enabled, Dockerfile present, licence (MIT for UI framework, AGPL v3 for the rest), lockfile committed, **but** committed secrets were detected (see the three `secrets.rs` files).

## The Bottom Line  
Warp is a functional, terminal‑first agentic environment that can accelerate code generation and terminal‑centric workflows, especially for teams already using OpenAI‑based assistants.  Its modular crate layout is a strength, but the monorepo’s loose dependency pinning, uncommitted secrets, and missing CI gates present concrete risks for production adoption.  It is well‑suited for early‑adopter teams comfortable with Rust/Node interop and willing to tighten the SDLC; larger organisations should enforce the recommended SHA‑pinned actions, dependency upgrades, and LFS migration before scaling.

forks.description: No description available
forks.summary:
**Repository**  
`git clone https://github.com/moses-y/codex-autorunner`  

**Purpose** – CAR (codex‑autorunner) is a meta‑harness that schedules long‑running AI‑agent tickets, persists state in a local “hub”, and notifies via Telegram/Discord. It does **not** implement an agent; it orchestrates any ACP‑compatible agent (Codex, Hermes, OpenCode, etc.).

---

### 1. High‑level Architecture  

* **Core orchestration** lives under `src/codex_autorunner/core/`. The most depended‑on modules are:  
  * `core/utils` (79 inbound imports, part of a circular import)  
  * `core/logging_utils` (76 inbound imports, also circular)  
  * `core/text_utils` (74 inbound imports)  

* **Hub** – `src/codex_autorunner/core/hub.py` and `src/codex_autorunner/core/hub_control_plane/` expose the public API used by the CLI, web UI and agents.  

* **Agents** – concrete adapters live in `src/codex_autorunner/agents/` (e.g., `agents/acp/client.py`, `agents/opencode/supervisor.py`).  

* **Surfaces** – CLI (`src/codex_autorunner/cli.py`), browser UI (`src/codex_autorunner/browser/server.py`), and webhook endpoints (`src/codex_autorunner/server.py`).  

* **State & persistence** – a SQLite‑backed “state roots” directory (`src/codex_autorunner/core/state_roots.py`) stores ticket markdown, execution logs and a small DB (≈181 DB‑access functions).  

* **External I/O** – the code reads/writes files (175 functions), runs external commands (31 functions), makes network calls (13 functions) and performs cryptographic ops (12 functions). The shortest external paths are:  

  * `start → from_result` → `session.get` (network)  
  * `main → build_paths` → `state_dir.mkdir` (filesystem)  

---

### 2. Build / Install  

| Step | Command | Evidence |
|------|---------|-----------|
| Install Python deps | `pip install .` (or `pipx install codex-autorunner`) | `pyproject.toml` defines the package. |
| Install JS tooling | `pnpm install` | `package.json` + `pnpm-lock.yaml`. |
| Run lint / type checks | `make lint` (see `Makefile`) | `Makefile` contains lint target. |
| Run test suite | `pytest -q` (tests under `tests/`) | 825 test files detected. |

No Dockerfile is present, so container builds must be added manually if required.

---

### 3. Configuration  

* **Environment** – template at `.env.example`. Required keys include `CAR_HUB_ROOT` (path to the hub) and optional `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN`, `DISCORD_WEBHOOK_URL`.  
* **CLI** – `car init --mode hub` creates the hub directory and writes `codex_autorunner/config.yaml`.  
* **Web UI** – launched by the entry point `src/codex_autorunner/browser/server.py` (`start` function, line 374). It binds to `localhost:8000` by default.

All configuration files are version‑controlled; no secrets are committed.

---

### 4. Running the System  

```bash
# Start the hub (blocks until stopped)
python -m codex_autorunner.browser.server start

# Or run the CLI entry point (useful for scripts)
python -m codex_autorunner.cli run --repo /path/to/repo
```

*The `start` entry point reaches 232 internal functions and ultimately calls `log_event` (154 callers) before performing any external I/O.*

---

### 5. Real‑World Use‑Case  

A development team stores a backlog of feature tickets as markdown files under `~/car-hub/tickets`. After `car init --mode hub`, they run `car run`. The orchestrator picks the first incomplete ticket, invokes the configured Codex agent via the ACP client (`agents/acp/client.py`), writes the agent’s output back to the ticket, and posts a Telegram message when the ticket stalls. All state lives in the local hub directory; no external service is required unless the team enables the optional webhook surfaces.

---

### 6. Code‑Health Findings (static analysis)

| Severity | Issue | Location |
|----------|-------|----------|
| **High** | Pin third‑party GitHub Actions to commit SHAs | `.github/workflows/*.yml` (e.g., `pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish@release/v1`) |
| **Medium** | Declare least‑privilege `permissions` for `GITHUB_TOKEN` | `.github/workflows/agent-compatibility.yml` |
| **Medium** | Add a dependency‑vulnerability scan step | any workflow under `.github/workflows/` |
| **Medium** | Set `persist-credentials: false` on `actions/checkout` | `.github/workflows/agent-compatibility.yml` |
| **Low** | Define `timeout-minutes` for jobs | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` |
| **Low** | Add repository convention files (`.editorconfig`, `.gitattributes`, formatter config) | repo root |

Additional measured code issues (not CI‑related):

* **High** – 15 import‑cycle members (e.g., `core/utils.py`, `core/logging_utils.py`, `core/config.py`). Breaking the cycles will reduce fragility.  
* **High** – Deep nesting (max depth 8) in `core/state.py`, `manifest.py`, `bootstrap.py`. Refactor with early returns or helper functions.  
* **High** – “Hub module” (`core/utils.py`, `core/logging_utils.py`, `core/text_utils.py`) is a blast‑radius hotspot; keep it small and stable.  
* **Medium** – Files opened without a context manager in three utils modules; wrap with `with open(...) as f:`.  
* **Medium** – Broad `except:` blocks in several integration modules; catch specific exceptions.  
* **Medium** – Oversized TypeScript file `static_src/utils.ts` (716 LOC); split by responsibility.  

All findings include concrete fix suggestions in the analysis output.

---

### 7. Bottom Line  

CAR provides a well‑structured, test‑covered orchestration layer for AI‑agent ticket execution, with clear entry points and extensive documentation. The main technical risk is the prevalence of import cycles and a few high‑complexity modules that increase change‑impact; refactoring those will improve maintainability. CI configuration should be hardened by pinning actions, limiting token scope, and adding vulnerability scans. The project is ready for production use by teams comfortable managing local state and secret handling.

forks.name: traccar
forks.description: Traccar GPS Tracking System
forks.summary:
## The Problem

Fleet operators need a self-hosted server that ingests location data from hundreds of different GPS device protocols and exposes it via a uniform API. Off-the-shelf SaaS trackers create data silos and per-device vendor lock-in; Traccar replaces that with a single Java service that normalizes feeds from 200+ protocols into one database and one REST interface.

## What This Does

This is the backend for the open-source Traccar GPS tracking system. The Java service in `src/main/java/org/traccar/` handles device connections, decodes proprietary wire formats, stores positions, and serves a REST API. Protocol decoders live in `src/main/java/org/traccar/protocol/` (files like `Gt06ProtocolDecoder.java`), while the API layer is under `src/main/java/org/traccar/api/resource/` (e.g., `PositionResource.java`, `DeviceResource.java`).

The repo is a fork of `traccar/traccar` with 1,767 files, 1,440 Java files, and 420 test files. Build is Gradle (`build.gradle`), with Docker images in `docker/` and CI via GitHub Actions. The `schema/` directory holds Liquibase changelogs for database migrations.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts at `src/main/java/org/traccar/Main.java`, which bootstraps Guice modules and starts `ServerManager`. `ServerManager` opens TCP/UDP listeners per protocol; each connection flows through a `PipelineBuilder` into a protocol-specific decoder, then into `ProcessingHandler` which persists to the database via `DeviceLookupService` and `BufferingManager`. The REST API in `api/resource/` reads/writes the same database through `BaseObjectResource`.

The import graph shows 6 internal modules with 0 edges between them, meaning the codebase is effectively one flat package rather than layered modules. This is a monolith: the `tools/` directory contains test scripts (`test-integration.py`, `test-performance.py`) but no runtime separation. The `protocol/` package is the largest surface area, with 1,567 files not shown in the structure excerpt.

Blast radius is concentrated in three oversized decoders: `Gl200TextProtocolDecoder.java`, `Gt06ProtocolDecoder.java`, and `Jt808ProtocolDecoder.java`, each over 1,500 lines. Changes to these ripple across protocol handling.

## How To Use It

```bash
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/traccar
cd traccar
./gradlew build
./gradlew run
```

Configuration lives in `debug.xml` at the root (a sample config) and `setup/traccar.xml` for service deployment. Database setup uses the `schema/` Liquibase changelogs automatically on startup. Docker images are in `docker/` (`Dockerfile.alpine`, `Dockerfile.debian`, `Dockerfile.ubuntu`).

The README points to the official build docs at `traccar.org/build/` rather than documenting commands inline. No environment variables are documented in the repo.

## Real-World Use

A fleet company deploys this on a VM, opens ports 5000-5100 for device TCP connections, and points a PostgreSQL instance at it. Devices stream NMEA or proprietary frames; Traccar decodes them, stores positions, and the company's dashboard queries `/api/positions` (via `PositionResource.java`) for live tracking. Geofencing via `GeofenceResource.java` triggers notifications through `NotificationManager.java`.

## Code Health & Issues

Static analysis found 267 findings (57 high, 210 medium) across 3 kinds:

- **High - Deep nesting** (x56): `TrackerClient.java`, `DeviceResource.java`, `PermissionsService.java` have indentation depth up to 10, making control flow hard to follow. Fix: early returns and extract inner blocks.
- **High - Duplicated code blocks**: 1,002 repeated 6-line blocks across 795 files. Fix: extract shared helpers.
- **High - Oversized files** (x3): `Gl200TextProtocolDecoder.java`, `Gt06ProtocolDecoder.java`, `Jt808ProtocolDecoder.java` each exceed 1,500 lines. Fix: split by responsibility.

Security audit findings:

- **High** - GitHub Actions pinned to mutable tags (`@v2`, `@v3`) in `.github/workflows/`; pin to commit SHAs to prevent supply-chain compromise.
- **High** - CI has 414 test files but no workflow invokes the test suite; the green check verifies nothing.
- **Medium** - No `persist-credentials: false` on checkout in `release.yml`; tokens persist in `.git/config`.
- **Medium** - Docker base images use mutable tags (`alpine:3.22`); pin by digest.
- **Medium** - No `timeout=` on 5 outbound calls in `tools/test-integration.py`.
- **Medium** - No non-root `USER` in `Dockerfile.alpine`.
- **Medium** - No least-privilege `permissions` block on `GITHUB_TOKEN`.
- **Low** - No `timeout-minutes` on workflow jobs.

No committed secrets found. No dependency lockfile exists (`build.gradle` declares dependencies without pins), so builds are not fully reproducible.

## The Bottom Line

This is a mature, production-grade GPS server with genuinely broad protocol support and a clean REST surface. The codebase is old and idiomatic — oversized decoders and heavy duplication will slow large refactors. Use it if you need self-hosted fleet tracking with heterogeneous hardware; expect to invest in CI hardening before treating it as a trusted build pipeline.
