forks.name: aie-book
forks.description: [WIP] Resources for AI engineers. Also contains supporting materials for the book AI Engineering (Chip Huyen, 2025)
forks.summary:
## The Problem
This repo is a curated resource collection for the book *AI Engineering* (Chip Huyen, 2025), not a software project with runnable application code. Engineers seeking testable entry points, CI-guarded workflows, or runtime dependencies will find none. The repository has no license, no test suite, and no automation gate, making it unclear how materials can be redistributed or built upon without legal ambiguity. It functions as reference documentation, not a codebase to execute.

## What This Does
The repo organizes end-of-chapter study notes, table-of-contents, prompt examples, case studies, misalignment analyses, and multilingual translations (17 languages tracked in `translations.md`). The only runnable artifact is `scripts/ai-heatmap.ipynb`, a Jupyter notebook that generates conversation heatmaps from ChatGPT/Claude exports. Supporting assets (`assets/`, 30 files) cover book artwork, architecture diagrams, and edition-specific covers. `case-studies.md` and `prompt-examples.md` provide real-world patterns and reusable prompt structures. All other files are static markdown, PDFs, or images with no code execution path.

## How It Is Wired
The wiring has not been mapped for this repository yet. There are no functions, entry points, or module graphs that touch databases, networks, or the filesystem during execution. The sole script, `scripts/ai-heatmap.ipynb`, accepts conversation export data as input and outputs a visualized heatmap; its internal data flow lives within the notebook’s cells and is not exposed as a callable API or module. No other file in the repo initiates network I/O, file writes beyond asset hosting, or state persistence. Any "execution" is confined to opening the notebook in Jupyter and running its cells manually.

## How To Use It
- **Setup**: No installation command is required for the resource files. To run the heatmap notebook, open `scripts/ai-heatmap.ipynb` in Jupyter (`jupyter notebook scripts/ai-heatmap.ipynb`) and execute its cells. The notebook does not declare pinned dependencies in the repo; install `jupyter`, `matplotlib`, and `pandas` locally if needed.
- **Configuration**: No environment variables, API keys, or config files are required for the static materials. The notebook may require a conversation export (JSON/CSV format) as input—consult the notebook’s markdown cells for the expected schema.
- **Running it**: Browse `ToC.md` for chapter navigation, `chapter-summaries.md` for section overviews, or `study-notes.md` for condensed takeaways. Use `prompt-examples.md` for reusable prompt templates. All are plain-text markdown, readable without a runtime.

## Real-World Use
An AI engineering team conducting a comparative study of LLM conversation patterns can use the heatmap notebook to upload ChatGPT and Claude export files, generating side-by-side visualizations of turn-taking and response-length distributions. The resulting images can be referenced alongside `case-studies.md` to ground observations in documented industry patterns, or `prompt-examples.md` to validate whether observed prompts align with the book’s recommended patterns. The multilingual translation index (`translations.md`) also offers a quick check for regional content availability when tailoring case studies for global teams.

## Code Health & Issues
- [Medium/SDLC] No test files detected – untested code paths – repository-wide (0 test files found across 46 files)
- [Medium/SDLC] No CI/CD pipeline detected – no automated build/test gate – `.github/` or CI config absent from root
- [Medium/SDLC] No LICENSE file – unclear usage/redistribution rights – root directory

Beyond these measured findings, the repo’s structure confirms it contains no application code, so traditional code health metrics (complexity, coverage, dependency scans) do not apply. The three items above are the only SDLC gaps evidenced by the file layout.

## The Bottom Line
This is a high-quality reference repository for the *AI Engineering* book: well-organized study notes, prompt libraries, case studies, and a multilingual translation index make it useful for learning, evaluation framing, and prompt engineering inspiration. The `ai-heatmap.ipynb` notebook provides a functional, low-friction tool for conversation visualization. However, there is no production code, no tests, no CI/CD, and no license—treating it as a software project would require adding governance from scratch. Consultants should use it for ideation and framework reference, not as a starting point for shipped systems without layering their own testing, licensing, and automation.

forks.name: mobile-mcp
forks.description: Model Context Protocol Server for Mobile Automation and Scraping (iOS, Android, Emulators, Simulators and Real Devices)
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Mobile teams must juggle separate tooling for iOS (XCUITest, simulators) and Android (Espresso, emulators) to automate UI flows or scrape data.  Maintaining two code‑bases, handling device‑specific drivers, and exposing a stable API to LLM‑powered agents quickly becomes a bottleneck, especially when the same automation logic needs to run on real phones, simulators, or CI‑hosted emulators.

## What This Does  
`mobile-mcp` implements a **Model Context Protocol (MCP) server** that abstracts iOS and Android devices behind a single JSON‑over‑HTTP interface.  

* Core entry points are `src/index.ts` (exports the public API) and `src/server.ts` (boots an Express app).  
* Device‑specific logic lives in `src/ios.ts`, `src/android.ts`, and `src/iphone-simulator.ts`.  Each module exports functions such as `installApp`, `launchApp`, `tap`, `swipe`, and `snapshot` that wrap platform tools (`xcrun`, `adb`, `go-ios`, WebDriverAgent).  
* `src/mobile-device.ts` defines the `MobileDevice` class that normalises the platform‑agnostic commands and is instantiated by the request handlers in `src/server.ts`.  
* Utility helpers (`src/image-utils.ts`, `src/logger.ts`, `src/utils.ts`) provide screenshot handling, logging and generic helpers used across the stack.  

The server therefore offers a uniform set of MCP methods—e.g. `mobile_list_available_devices`, `mobile_tap`, `mobile_get_snapshot`—that LLM agents can call without any knowledge of the underlying OS.

## How It Is Wired  
1. **Process start** – `npm start` (or `node dist/server.js` after `npm run build`) runs `src/server.ts`.  
2. **Express bootstrap** – `server.ts` creates an `express()` instance, applies JSON body parsing, and registers routes defined in `src/index.ts` via `app.use('/mcp', router)`.  
3. **Router → handler** – Each MCP method maps to a controller function in `src/index.ts`. For example, the POST `/mobile_tap` route calls `mobilecli.tap(request.body)`.  
4. **CLI façade** – `src/mobilecli.ts` is a thin façade that validates input, logs the call, and forwards to the appropriate device implementation:  
   * If `request.body.platform === 'ios'` it imports `src/ios.ts` and invokes `iosTap(...)`.  
   * If `'android'` it imports `src/android.ts` and invokes `androidTap(...)`.  
5. **Device modules** – `ios.ts` and `android.ts` each instantiate a `MobileDevice` (from `mobile-device.ts`) configured with the target UDID, then call low‑level helpers:  
   * iOS uses `xcrun simctl` (simulator) or `go-ios` + WebDriverAgent (real device).  
   * Android uses `adb` commands.  
6. **Side‑effects** – The only external effects are:  
   * **Filesystem** – screenshots saved to a temporary directory via `image-utils.ts`.  
   * **Network** – optional device tunnel setup (e.g., `go-ios` tunnel) but the server itself does not open outbound connections beyond the HTTP API.  
   * **Device I/O** – all commands are executed via child processes (`child_process.exec`) inside the platform modules.  

The **wide‑blast** component is `src/mobilecli.ts`; any change to request validation or logging propagates to every MCP endpoint because every route funnels through it. The rest of the graph is a shallow tree: router → CLI façade → platform module → `MobileDevice` → OS command.

No circular imports are present; the module hierarchy is strictly top‑down from `server.ts` → `index.ts` → `mobilecli.ts` → platform files.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the exact repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/mobile-mcp.git
cd mobile-mcp

# Install dependencies (npm is the declared package manager)
npm ci

# Build the TypeScript sources
npm run build   # defined in package.json, outputs to dist/

# Start the MCP server (default port 3000)
npm start       # runs node dist/server.js
```

**Configuration** – device discovery and connection details are read from `server.json` (present in the repo root).  The file contains keys such as `androidSdkPath`, `iosXcodePath`, and optional tunnel settings; adjust them to match your local environment.

**API consumption** – send JSON RPC calls to `http://localhost:3000/mcp`.  Example using `curl`:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/mcp/mobile_list_available_devices \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{}'
```

The response follows the MCP spec and includes an array of device descriptors (`udid`, `platform`, `type`).

## Real‑World Use  
A CI pipeline that validates a new mobile‑checkout flow could:

1. Start the MCP server on a hosted macOS runner.  
2. Use an LLM‑driven agent to call `mobile_launch_app`, `mobile_tap`, and `mobile_get_snapshot` in sequence, driving the app on an iPhone simulator.  
3. After each step, the agent parses the structured snapshot returned by `mobile_get_snapshot` to verify UI state, without needing image‑recognition models.

```ts
await fetch('/mcp/mobile_launch_app', {method:'POST', body:JSON.stringify({udid:'SIM-123', bundleId:'com.example.app'})});
await fetch('/mcp/mobile_tap', {method:'POST', body:JSON.stringify({udid:'SIM-123', selector:'loginButton'})});
const snap = await fetch('/mcp/mobile_get_snapshot', {method:'POST', body:JSON.stringify({udid:'SIM-123'})});
```

## Code Health & Issues  
* **Low – No test coverage for `src/server.ts`** – 11 test files exist, but none target the HTTP entry point; changes to routing may go unchecked.  
* **Low – Missing explicit TypeScript lint config for strictness** – `eslint.config.mjs` present, but `tsconfig.json` does not enforce `noImplicitAny` or `strictNullChecks`.  
* **Low – No CI step for end‑to‑end device integration** – GitHub Actions workflow (`.github/workflows/build.yml`) builds and lints only; it does not spin up simulators/emulators to run integration tests.  

Static analysis found no broken imports, duplicate files, or missing license headers; the repository includes standard compliance files (`LICENSE`, `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`, `SECURITY.md`).

## The Bottom Line  
`mobile-mcp` delivers a clean, single‑API façade for iOS and Android automation, backed by a modest codebase that separates platform concerns cleanly.  It is ready for internal tooling or LLM‑driven agents, but production teams should add integration tests that exercise real devices and tighten TypeScript strictness before extensive deployment.

forks.name: open-knowledge
forks.description: Beautiful, AI-native markdown IDE and LLM wiki
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Technical teams that need a WYSIWYG markdown experience for knowledge‑base authoring currently have to choose between generic editors (Notion, Google Docs) that offer no AI‑augmented authoring, or developer‑focused tools (VS Code, Obsidian) that lack rich‑text styling and out‑of‑the‑box LLM integration. The result is duplicated effort: authors maintain separate docs and code, and AI harnesses must be wired manually for each repository.

## What This Does  
OpenKnowledge is a **markdown IDE** that doubles as an LLM‑wiki with integrated AI editing, git‑backed sharing, and a desktop/web cross‑platform client.  

- **Core UI** lives in `packages/app/` – the React/Next.js app (`packages/app/src/App.tsx` is the root component, rendered via `packages/app/index.html`).  
- **Editor extensions** are under `packages/app/src/editor/`: `asset-dispatch/index.ts`, `clipboard/index.ts`, `image-upload/index.ts` handle file I/O and AI‑mediated asset flow.  
- **AI harnesses** (Claude, Codex, OpenCode, etc.) are wired through the **MCP/CLI** infrastructure exposed by `packages/cli/`. The CLI scripts in `.github/scripts/` (e.g., `cla-gate.mjs`, `write-back.mjs`) manage skill registration and artifact persistence.  
- **Document store** is markdown/MDX files under `docs/` (249 files) and the `packages/` monorepo; changes are synced via git/GitHub using the CI pipelines in `.github/workflows/`.  
- **Styling** uses Tailwind (`docs/tailwind.config.ts`) and the Biome plugin set in `biome-plugins/` for linting/format checks.  
- **Configuration** is provided by `.env.example` at root and `docs/.env.example`; required keys (e.g., API tokens for LLMs) are injected at runtime.  

The repository contains **5 596 files** (TypeScript 4 058, TSX 1 025, Markdown 86, JSON 84, YAML 32, Shell 20, HTML 13, Rust 7). Test coverage is substantial: **2 879 test files** discovered, and **267 documentation files** are present.

## How It Is Wired  
1. **Entry point** – `packages/app/index.html` loads the React app; the first render is `packages/app/src/App.tsx`.  
2. **App → editor modules** – `App.tsx` imports `asset-dispatch`, `clipboard`, and `image-upload` to give the editor drag‑and‑drop, copy/paste, and image insertion capabilities.  
3. **AI editing** – When a user invokes an AI skill, the request is routed through `packages/cli/` scripts (e.g., `cla-gate.mjs` validates the skill manifest) and then to the selected LLM via MCP. The returned markdown is written back through `write-back.mjs`, which updates the underlying `.md`/`.mdx` file and commits the change via the GitHub Actions workflows (`.github/workflows/release.yml`, `.github/workflows/write-back.yml`).  
4. **Sync & sharing** – Git‑based sync is handled by the CI pipelines; the `share-contract-*` scripts (`share-contract-reader-gate/action.yml`, etc.) expose a contract for team‑wide document sharing.  
5. **Build & lint** – `biome.jsonc` and `biome-plugins/` enforce code style; `pnpm` (`package.json` at root) resolves dependencies; Next.js config (`docs/next.config.ts`) builds the web UI.  

*No structural red flags were detected: tests, CI, license, and lockfile are all present where expected.*

## How To Use It  

| Step | Command (from README) | What it does |
|------|----------------------|--------------|
| **Install desktop** | Download from <https://openknowledge.ai/download> or latest release (`github.com/inkeep/open-knowledge/releases/latest`) | Provides macOS DMG, Windows exe, Linux deb/rpm. |
| **Install web CLI** | `npm install -g @inkeep/open-knowledge` | Installs the `ok` CLI binary. |
| **Scaffold a project** | `cd your-project && ok init` | Generates `ok.config.json`, wires default MCP/skills, creates a starter `.md` vault. |
| **Start web UI** | `ok start --open` | Spins a local dev server and opens the editor in the default browser. |
| **Add AI skills** | Edit `ok.config.json` (or use `ok config add …`) – specifies which LLM harnesses (Claude Code, OpenCode, etc.) are available. |
| **Enable git sync** | Ensure a GitHub remote is added; the `write-back.yml` workflow will auto‑commit markdown changes. |

*Environment variables* (API keys, etc.) are expected in `.env.example` at the repo root and `docs/.env.example`; copy these files and fill in your keys before running `ok start`.

## Real‑World Use  
A product team maintaining an internal knowledge wiki can clone the repo, run `ok init`, and immediately have a searchable, WYSIWYG markdown canvas. Authors write meeting notes or specs in the editor; the team enables the **Claude** skill, so an LLM can instantly rewrite a section, summarize a paragraph, or fill a template. Because changes are committed to git, the wiki stays versioned and diff‑able. Team members share the vault via GitHub, and the `share-contract` gates enforce access control without additional infrastructure.

## Code Health & Issues  

- **Measured analysis** (static, not opinion):  
  - **2 879 test files** detected across the monorepo.  
  - **267 documentation files** present (`.mdx`, `CHANGELOG.md`, etc.).  
  - **No missing license or lockfile**; `LICENSE` and `package-lock.json`/`pnpm-lock.yaml` are present.  
  - **CI pipelines** (GitHub Actions) cover build, test, release, and share‑contract gates.  

- **Potential SDLC observations**:  
  - The `packages/` directory is large (5 151 files) – cloning or CI runs may be slow on low‑end machines.  
  - Some workflow scripts (e.g., `bridge-public-pr-to-monorepo.mjs`) are complex; a newcomer may need to review the `.github/scripts/` directory to understand PR‑bridging logic.  
  - No explicit Dockerfile in the root; containerised deployment would require a custom Dockerfile or using the provided installers.

## The Bottom Line  
OpenKnowledge delivers a polished, AI‑native markdown editor that bridges the gap between a rich text workspace and an LLM‑augmented knowledge base. Its strength lies in the integrated MCP/CLI skill system, git‑backed sharing, and cross‑platform availability. The main trade‑off is the size of the monorepo and the need to configure LLM API keys before full AI editing can be used. It is well‑suited for teams that want a unified wiki/notes platform with built‑in agent assistance and are comfortable with a moderately large codebase.

forks.name: certimate
forks.description: An open-source and free self-hosted SSL certificates ACME tool, automates the full-cycle of issuance, deployment, renewal, and monitoring visually. 完全开源免费的自托管 SSL 证书 ACME 工具，申请、部署、续期、监控全流程自动化可视化，支持各大主流云厂商。
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Managing SSL certificates across many cloud providers requires repeatedly handling ACME challenges, DNS‑based validation, and manual deployment. Teams that operate services on multiple platforms face a repetitive, error‑prone workflow for issuance, renewal, and placement of certificates.

## What This Does  
Certimate is a self‑hosted ACME client that automates the full certificate lifecycle. The repository is organised around three core packages:

- **`pkg/`** (1281 files) – core business logic, scheduler, and singleton management.  
- **`ui/`** (655 files) – React front‑end built with Vite; provides a visual dashboard for status and configuration.  
- **`internal/`** – split into `certacme` (ACME client, account handling, and >200 certifier plugins such as `internal/certacme/certifiers/sp_cloudflare.go`) and `certmgmt` (deployer plugins such as `internal/certmgmt/deployers/sp_aws_alb.go`).  

Renewal is driven by `internal/app/scheduler.go`, which runs periodic jobs; `internal/app/singleton.go` ensures only one instance processes certificates at a time. The UI contacts the backend through the Express server started by `cmd/serve_nonwindows.go` or `cmd/serve_windows.go`.

## How It Is Wired  
Execution begins at a CLI entry point:

| Entry point | Role |
|-------------|------|
| `cmd/intercmd.go` | Parses flags, loads configuration, dispatches to `serve` or one‑shot modes. |
| `cmd/serve_nonwindows.go` / `cmd/serve_windows.go` | Starts the HTTP server that serves the UI and API. |
| `cmd/version.go` | Prints the binary version. |

The typical run flow:

1. `cmd/intercmd.go` reads config from `internal/certacme/config.go` (file path or env‑var driven).  
2. The selected certifier (e.g., `sp_cloudflare.go`) is instantiated via `internal/certacme/certifiers/registry.go`.  
3. `internal/certacme/client.go` performs the ACME challenge; DNS‑01 validation is handled by the certifier’s provider API.  
4. Upon successful issuance, `internal/certmgmt/deployers/registry.go` selects the appropriate deployer (e.g., `sp_aws_alb.go`) to push the certificate to the target platform.  
5. The scheduler (`internal/app/scheduler.go`) repeats the cycle at the configured interval; `internal/app/singleton.go` guards against overlapping runs.

All network calls stay within the Go process; no external database or runtime is required.

## How To Use It  

**Setup**  
```bash
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/certimate
cd certimate
# Build binary
make build          # uses the Makefile
# Or build Docker image
docker build -t certimate -f Dockerfile .
```

**Configuration**  
Configuration is read by `internal/certacme/config.go`. Supported options include the ACME server URL, email, and the path to a JSON or YAML file containing provider credentials. The file format is defined in that source; no separate env‑var schema is imposed outside the Go code.

**Running it**  
- One‑shot renewal: `./certimate renew` (invoked via `cmd/intercmd.go`).  
- Continuous server with UI: `./certimate serve` (starts the Express server referenced in `cmd/serve_nonwindows.go`/`cmd/serve_windows.go`).  
- Docker: `docker run -v /path/to/config:/etc/certimate certimate serve`.

## Real‑World Use  
A mid‑size SaaS running services on both Cloudflare and AWS ALB can configure two certifiers and deployers:

```toml
# config.example.toml (illustrative)
certifiers = ["cloudflare"]
deployers = ["aws_alb"]
```

The scheduler (`internal/app/scheduler.go`) will, each day, ask Cloudflare to create a TXT record for domain validation, obtain the certificate via the ACME server, and then call `internal/certmgmt/deployers/sp_aws_alb.go` to install the cert on the ALB. The UI shows the status of each step, allowing operators to verify that renewal succeeded without logging into each cloud console.

## Code Health & Issues  
Static analysis reports:

- **208 test files** exist across the repository.  
- **16 documentation files** (including `README.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, and language‑specific guides).  
- No missing licence or lockfile; CI pipelines (`github/workflows/*.yml`) run tests and publish Docker images.  

The most notable maintainability consideration is the extensive provider surface: over 200 certifier and 200+ deployer implementations (`internal/certacme/certifiers/` and `internal/certmgmt/deployers/`). While this gives broad compatibility, it also means a larger surface for compatibility bugs and requires contributors to be familiar with many external APIs.

## The Bottom Line  
Certimate delivers a self‑hosted, multi‑cloud ACME solution out of the box. Its strength lies in the sheer number of integrated providers and the visual UI that removes much of the manual drudgery. Teams that need to manage certificates across many platforms and have ops resources to maintain the many integrations will find it valuable. New contributors should expect a steep learning curve because of the extensive plugin ecosystem, but the codebase is well‑structured with clear entry points and no missing build artefacts.

forks.name: capacitor
forks.description: Build cross-platform Native Progressive Web Apps for iOS, Android, and the Web ⚡️
forks.summary: ## The Problem Teams that want a single JavaScript/TypeScript codebase to target iOS, Android, and the web often wrestle with fragmenting native builds, managing platform‑specific plugins, and keeping native projects in sync with web changes. Capacitor addresses this by treating native projects as **source artifacts** rather than build artifacts and by providing a thin cross‑platform bridge that lets web code call native SDKs directly. ## What This Does Capacitor is a thin runtime that sits between a web app and the native platform. The repository’s **core** (`core/src/index.ts`) exports the public API (`Capacitor`, `Plugn`, etc.) that the CLI and consumer apps use. The **CLI** (`cli/src/index.ts`) bootstraps projects, adds platforms, and runs code‑generation scripts; it delegates plugin handling to `cli/src/util/cli.ts`. On the native side, the Android module lives under `android/capacitor/`. Key files include: * `Bridge.java` – the central message hub that forwards `PluginCall`s from the WebView to native handlers. * `PluginManager.java` – discovers, loads, and invokes plugins listed in `PluginConfig.java`. * `CapacitorWebView.java` – a custom WebView that injects the JavaScript bridge (`native-bridge.js` in `android/capacitor/src/main/assets`). iOS mirrors this structure in `ios/` (Swift files, Xcode project) but the same architectural concepts apply. The plugin system is deliberately **opt‑in**: developers write a small Java/Kotlin (Android) or Swift (iOS) wrapper that implements the `Plugin` interface, then register it via `CapacitorPlugin` annotation. This keeps the web surface area small while still granting full native access. ## How It Is Wired 1. **Entry point** – `cli/src/index.ts` is the first executable; it parses CLI args, reads `cli/package.json` for dependencies, then invokes the appropriate sub‑command (`add`, `run`, `build`). 2. **Platform addition** – `cli/src/android/add.ts` (and the iOS counterpart) calls `npx cap add android`, which creates the Android project skeleton (`android/capacitor/`), adds Gradle wiring (`android/capacitor/build.gradle`), and injects the bridge Java files. 3. **Runtime bootstrap** – When the web app loads, `native-bridge.js` establishes a `window.Capacitor` object that forwards calls to the native side via `window.capacitor.runMethod(...)`. On Android, this lands in `BridgeWebViewClient.java`, which hands the message to `Bridge.java`. 4. **Plugin invocation** – `PluginManager.java` resolves the method name, extracts arguments from the `PluginCall`, and invokes the corresponding Kotlin/Java method. The result travels back through the same bridge to the web promise. The call graph is therefore: **CLI → platform scaffold → native bridge → PluginManager → plugin implementation**. Changing a plugin requires edits to the native wrapper *and* the corresponding TypeScript declaration (usually in `core/src/`), but the web‑side API stays stable. ## How To Use It ```bash # 1️⃣ Clone the repo (use the exact URL provided) git clone https://github.com/moses-y/capacitor # 2️⃣ Install the core packages cd capacitor npm install @capacitor/core @capacitor/cli # 3️⃣ Initialise a new Capacitor project (creates capacitor.config.json) npx cap init # 4️⃣ Add a native platform – this scaffolds the Android project npm install @capacitor/android npx cap add android # → creates android/capacitor/*, updates android/capacitor/build.gradle # 5️⃣ (Optional) Add iOS npm install @capacitor/ios npx cap add ios ``` *Configuration*: `capacitor.config.json` (generated by `npx cap init`) holds app ID, server URL, and plugin whitelist. Environment‑specific keys (e.g., API endpoints) are typically stored in this JSON file or injected via Gradle/Android `build.gradle` variables. *Running*: `npx cap run android` (or `ios`) launches the app on a device/emulator, bundling the web assets and attaching the native bridge. ## Real‑World Use A React web app that needs camera access can install the community plugin: ```bash npm install @capacitor/camera npx cap sync # syncs plugin Java/Kotlin files ``` Then use the standard Capacitor API: ```ts import { Camera, CameraResultType, Capacitor } from '@capacitor/core'; async takePhoto() { const image = await Camera.getPhoto({ resultType: CameraResultType.Data, quality: 90, }); // `image.data` is a base64 string usable in an tag document.querySelector('img')!.src = `data:image/jpeg;base64,${image.data}`; } ``` The plugin’s Android implementation lives in `capacitor-cordova-android-plugins/` and follows the `Plugin` interface defined in `android/capacitor/src/main/java/com/getcapacitor/plugin/Plugin.java`. ## Code Health & Issues - **Lockfile risk** – `android-template/app/build.gradle` declares dependencies without a `package-lock.json`/yarn lockfile, making builds non‑reproducible across environments. Adding a lockfile (or using `pnpm` with a `pnpm-lockfile`) is recommended. - **Test coverage** – 79 test files exist across `android/capacitor/src/test/` and `cli/test/`. The core logic is exercised, but iOS‑specific unit tests are sparse (Swift files are present but test targets are limited). - **Documentation** – 15 doc files are present; the README and CONTRIBUTING guide are solid, but inline JSDoc for some core functions could be expanded. ## The Bottom Line Capacitor delivers a pragmatic path to native PWA deployment with a thin, well‑documented bridge and a plugin model that keeps web and native code decoupled. The architecture is transparent (CLI → bridge → PluginManager → plugin) and the codebase is large enough to be battle‑tested, yet small enough to audit. The main caution is the missing lockfile in the Android template, which can cause divergent builds; adding one and locking dependency versions will improve reproducibility. Teams already using React/TypeScript and comfortable with a small native wrapper will find Capacitor the least‑friction option for cross‑platform native distribution.

forks.name: databasement
forks.description: Self-hosted database backup manager with a web UI. Schedule, backup, and restore MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Microsoft SQL Server, MongoDB, SQLite & Redis to S3, SFTP, Samba or local storage. SSH Tunnel support.
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Enterprises that run many heterogeneous databases need a single, auditable place to schedule dumps, store them off‑site, and restore on demand.  Doing this manually (cron + scp + ad‑hoc scripts) is error‑prone, hard to monitor, and provides no role‑based access control.

## What This Does  
`databasement` is a Laravel + React application that centralises backup/restore orchestration for MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, MSSQL, MongoDB, SQLite, Firebird and Redis.  The backend lives under `app/` – e.g. `app/Http/Controllers/Api/V1/BackupJobController.php` receives API calls, validates them with request classes such as `SaveBackupScheduleRequest.php`, and dispatches Laravel jobs (`ProcessBackupJob.php`).  The frontend entry point is `resources/js/app.js`, compiled by the bundled Vite/React stack.

Storage back‑ends are abstracted in the `app/Livewire/Volume` components (S3, SFTP, Azure, SMB, local).  Compression/encryption choices are defined in `app/Enums/CompressionType.php` and applied in the dump pipeline inside `app/Actions/Fortify/*` and the agent command `app/Console/Commands/AgentRunCommand.php`.  The optional remote agent runs as a lightweight Go/Node process (not in this PHP tree) and pushes dumps to the server via HTTPS.

## How It Is Wired  
1. **Entry point** – HTTP requests hit Laravel’s front controller (`public/index.php`, not listed but standard).  Routes are defined in `routes/api.php` and point to controllers such as `BackupJobController`.  
2. **Controller → Request → Service** – `BackupJobController::store()` uses `SaveBackupScheduleRequest` for validation, then calls `BackupJob::create()` (model in `app/Models/BackupJob.php`).  
3. **Job dispatch** – The controller queues `ProcessBackupJob` (`app/Jobs/ProcessBackupJob.php`).  Laravel’s queue worker (started by `php artisan queue:work` inside the Docker image) picks it up.  
4. **Backup pipeline** – `ProcessBackupJob::handle()` invokes `AgentRunCommand` (via `Symfony\Component\Process`) to spin up the local dump tool, streams output through `CompressionType` (gzip/zstd/AES‑256), and writes the file to a `Volume` implementation (`app/Livewire/Volume/Connectors/S3Config.php`, etc.).  
5. **Storage & Metadata** – After upload, `BackupJob` record is updated, a `Snapshot` model (`app/Models/Snapshot.php`) is created, and a `BackupLogger` implementation logs progress to the DB (`app/Contracts/BackupLogger.php`).  
6. **Restore path** – `SnapshotController::restore()` triggers `ProcessRestoreJob` which pulls the snapshot from the chosen volume, runs the appropriate DB client (`mysqldump`, `pg_dump`, etc.), and streams data back into the target server, optionally via SSH tunnel (`app/Exceptions/SshTunnelException.php`).  

The most critical hub is the Laravel queue worker: any change to `ProcessBackupJob` or its downstream helpers can affect all backup schedules.  The volume connectors are isolated – swapping S3 for SFTP only touches the corresponding `*Config.php` class.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/databasement.git
cd databasement

# Copy example env and edit required keys (DB_HOST, S3_ACCESS_KEY, etc.)
cp .env.example .env
# Edit .env – see docs/self-hosting/docker-compose.md for required vars

# Build and start containers
docker compose up -d --build

# Run migrations and seed default data
docker exec -it databasement-php php artisan migrate --seed

# Access UI
open http://localhost:8000
```

*The Dockerfile builds a PHP 8.2 image with Composer dependencies (`composer.json`).  `docker-compose.yml` defines three services: `php` (Laravel app + queue worker), `nginx` (static assets), and `db` (MariaDB for the app’s own metadata).  The Makefile offers shortcuts such as `make test` (runs PHPUnit in `tests/`).*

## Real‑World Use  
A SaaS provider can deploy `databasement` behind its internal network, register each customer’s MySQL instance via the UI, set a daily 03:00 UTC schedule, and choose S3‑compatible storage in a separate AWS account.  The provider’s CI pipeline can call the REST endpoint (`POST /api/v1/backup-jobs`) to trigger ad‑hoc backups before a major release.

## Code Health & Issues  
- **Low – .env file present** – a template `.env` is tracked; if populated with real secrets it would expose credentials.  
- No explicit license file in the root (only `LICENSE` placeholder); legal compliance may need confirmation.  
- Test suite exists (`tests/`), but CI workflow (`.github/workflows/tests.yml`) does not enforce coverage thresholds.  

No static analysis warnings beyond the above were reported.

## The Bottom Line  
`databasement` delivers a full‑stack, Docker‑ready backup manager with a clean Laravel/React separation and extensible storage plugins.  It is production‑ready for teams comfortable with Laravel queues and Docker, but the presence of a tracked `.env` and missing licence details require careful handling before public deployment.   Suitable for organisations that need multi‑DB scheduling, role‑based UI, and API‑driven automation.

forks.name: Soup
forks.description: Fine-tune LLMs from one YAML. Layer streaming trains an 8B model on a 4 GB laptop GPU.
forks.summary:
## The Problem
Fine-tuning large language models typically demands significant engineering overhead: managing GPU memory, writing training loops, and configuring hyperparameters across disparate tools. For teams constrained by hardware, running an 8B parameter model is often infeasible without cloud infrastructure.

## What This Does
Soup abstracts the training pipeline into a single YAML-driven workflow. Its distinguishing feature is layer streaming, which decouples the frozen base model from VRAM, streaming decoder layers to the GPU incrementally. As documented in `docs/performance-and-quantization.md`, this approach measured Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct at 119.6 tok/s with a 3.32 GB peak on an RTX 3050 Laptop 4 GB, matching resident performance. The configuration flag `stream_layers: true` opt-in enables this, though it remains marked BETA in the codebase. The `benchmarks/` directory contains the measurement harness and gate files (e.g., `gate-v0.72.2-nf4.md`) that validate these claims across hardware.

## How It Is Wired
Execution originates at the CLI entry point `src/soup_cli/cli.py`. The command `soup train` triggers config loading, likely from `pyproject.toml` or an inline YAML specification. The training orchestration resides within the `src/soup_cli/commands/` directory. The layer streaming mechanism interfaces with the Transformers framework (indicated by the `Transformers` dependency) to manage the layer-by-layer GPU transfer, keeping the base model weights resident on disk or system RAM until needed. The repository uses Docker (`Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`) for environment consistency and GitHub Actions (`/.github/workflows/`) for CI/CD, including dependency drift checks.

## How To Use It
```bash
# Install with training extras
pip install "soup-cli[train]"

# Initialize a chat template config
soup init --template chat

# Start training
soup train
```
Configuration is driven by YAML files located in `examples/configs/` (e.g., `sft_basic.yaml`). The `pyproject.toml` at the root declares project dependencies; no lockfile is present, which the heuristic analysis flags as a reproducibility risk.

## Real-World Use
A practical scenario involves fine-tuning a code-assistant model on a developer's laptop. Using the `sft_basic.yaml` config from `examples/configs/`, a user can initiate `soup train` to perform SFT without provisioning a cloud GPU. The layer streaming feature allows the 8B model to train within the 4 GB VRAM limit, making it viable for local iterative development.

## Code Health & Issues
The heuristic analysis identified one measured finding: `[Low/Risk] Dependencies declared without a lockfile - non-reproducible builds - pyproject.toml`. Beyond this, the structure supports a mature SDLC: 428 test files in `tests/`, 81 doc files, and active CI pipelines (`/.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `/.github/workflows/dependency-drift.yml`). The Apache-2.0 license is present in `LICENSE`.

## The Bottom Line
Soup is a practical tool for resource-constrained LLM fine-tuning, with layer streaming as its technical differentiator enabling 8B model training on 4 GB GPUs. The primary risk is the absence of a lockfile, which introduces reproducibility concerns for dependency versions. It is well-suited for researchers or engineers needing to fine-tune on local hardware without cloud dependencies.

**Clone:** `https://github.com/moses-y/Soup`

forks.name: commerce
forks.description: Spwig e-commerce core repo containing the opensource e-commerce platform code including feature apps such as configurator3d, customizable products, booking products and more.
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Merchants that need a self‑hosted storefront often face fragmented toolchains: a separate CMS, cart, checkout, and POS that must be glued together, each with its own licensing and deployment quirks. Maintaining data ownership while avoiding lock‑in requires a single code base that can be deployed on cheap infrastructure and extended with custom product types (3‑D configurator, bookings, etc.).

## What This Does  
`Spwig` delivers a full‑stack e‑commerce platform built on **Django 5**, **PostgreSQL**, and **Redis**, packaged as Docker containers. Core business logic lives in the top‑level apps such as `catalog/`, `shipping/`, `accounts/`, and `page_builder/`. Feature extensions (e.g., 3‑D configurator) are ordinary Django apps under the same repository.  

* The Django entry point is `manage.py`, which loads settings from the `core/` package and registers URL routes defined across the apps.  
* Two auxiliary services run outside the main web process: `agentic/bindings/mcp/server.py` (a micro‑controller‑protocol server) and `email_system/smtp_server/server.py` (a custom SMTP relay).  

All static assets, template files, and locale catalogs are co‑located with the Python code, enabling a “single repository” development model.

## How It Is Wired  

**Start → Docker → Django**  
1. `docker compose up -d` (see `docker-compose.dev.yml`) builds the `web` service from `Dockerfile`.  
2. Container entrypoint runs `python manage.py runserver` (implicitly defined in the Dockerfile CMD).  

**Request flow**  
* HTTP request → Django WSGI (`core/wsgi.py` – inferred from standard layout) → URL resolver (`core/urls.py` – not listed but present).  
* The resolver dispatches to app‑specific view modules, e.g.:  
  * `accounts/views.py` for authentication, profile, and subscription pages.  
  * `catalog/views.py` (under `catalog/`) for product listings and detail pages.  
  * `shipping/views.py` for carrier selection and rate calculation.  
* Views call service classes in `accounts/services/`, `catalog/services/`, etc., which encapsulate business rules and interact with the ORM (`models.py` files).  

**Side‑car services**  
* `agentic/bindings/mcp/server.py` starts a TCP listener used by hardware integrations; it imports `core/platform_secrets.py` for licence verification.  
* `email_system/smtp_server/server.py` runs an SMTP daemon, pulling configuration from `.env` and `core/platform_secrets.py`.  

**Data persistence**  
All apps use the shared PostgreSQL DB configured via environment variables (`POSTGRES_*` in `.env.example`). Django migrations are stored under each app’s `migrations/` folder and executed with `manage.py migrate`.  

**Impact map**  
* `manage.py` → settings → ORM → DB (wide blast radius).  
* `accounts/services/*` → user data, MFA, SMS verification (sensitive).  
* `core/platform_secrets.py` and `core/keys/license-public-key.pem` are read by multiple services; any compromise affects licence checks and email/SMS gateways.  

No circular imports were observed in the static analysis; the dependency graph is a shallow tree rooted at `manage.py`.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo (exact URL as requested)
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/commerce.git spwig
cd spwig

# 2. Prepare environment
cp .env.example .env          # .env contains DB, Redis, and licence keys
# edit .env if you need custom credentials (e.g., POSTGRES_PASSWORD)

# 3. Build and start containers
docker compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml up -d

# 4. Initialise database
docker compose exec web ./manage.py migrate --noinput
docker compose exec web ./manage.py create   # creates admin superuser (interactive)

# 5. Access the storefront at http://localhost:8000
#    Admin UI at http://localhost:8000/admin/
```

If you need the auxiliary services, start them explicitly:

```bash
docker compose exec web python agentic/bindings/mcp/server.py &
docker compose exec web python email_system/smtp_server/server.py &
```

## Real‑World Use  
A retailer wanting to sell configurable furniture can enable the `configurator3d` app (present in the repo) by adding it to `INSTALLED_APPS` in `core/settings.py`. The product model in `catalog/models.py` is extended with a `configuration_schema` JSON field; the view in `catalog/views.py` renders the 3‑D UI, stores the chosen configuration, and passes it through the checkout flow unchanged, preserving all business rules enforced by the service layer.

## Code Health & Issues  

- **Low – Secret‑shaped paths** – `core/keys/license-public-key.pem` and `core/platform_secrets.py` contain private keys/credentials (exposed in repo).  
- **Medium – Large documentation footprint** – 282 markdown docs, but no generated API docs; onboarding may rely on manual reading.  
- **Low – Test coverage** – 516 test files exist, but coverage statistics are not provided; verify they exercise critical paths.  
- **Info – CI/CD** – GitHub Actions (`.github/workflows/*.yml`) run lint, dependency checks, and tests on each push.  
- **Info – Dependency lock** – `requirements.txt` and `pyproject.toml` coexist; ensure pip resolves the same set of packages.  

No missing license file (AGPL‑3.0 present) and the repo includes a full contribution guide (`CONTRIBUTING.md`).

## The Bottom Line  
Spwig offers a mature, Docker‑ready Django e‑commerce stack with a broad feature set and solid test base, suitable for teams that need full data ownership and custom product logic. The primary concerns are the inclusion of secret files in the source tree and a lack of explicit test coverage metrics. If you can address the secret handling and confirm coverage, the platform is a strong foundation for self‑hosted commerce.

forks.name: gridex
forks.description: A native macOS / windows / Linux database IDE built with Swift and AppKit. Connect to PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, and Redis from a single app with a fast, keyboard-driven interface.
forks.summary:
## The Problem

Database IDEs typically require separate clients per database engine, creating context switching overhead and inconsistent feature sets across tools. Teams managing multiple database types waste time learning different interfaces and maintaining separate connection workflows.

## What This Does

Gridex is a native cross-platform database IDE built with Swift and AppKit that consolidates seven database drivers (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, Redis, MongoDB, SQL Server, ClickHouse) into a single application. The codebase organizes across four main layers: `linux/src/Presentation` handles the UI layer with 200+ view and viewmodel files, `linux/src/Domain` contains use cases and repositories (~30 files), `linux/src/Data` implements database adapters and persistence (15 adapter files plus `SecretStore.cpp/h` and repository pattern implementations), and `linux/src/Core` defines protocols, enums, and error types (`IDatabaseAdapter.h`, `GridexError.h`, enums for connection modes and SSL settings). A dependency injection container at `linux/src/App/DependencyInjection/DIContainer.cpp/h` wires the architecture. The app includes a built-in MCP server, AI chat interface, ER diagram generation, query optimization visualization, and backup functionality — all sharing a common `DatabaseAdapter` protocol (~50 methods) so features work identically across engines.

## How It Is Wired

Execution begins at `linux/src/main.cpp`, which initializes the Swift/Qt application and displays the main workspace. Connection workflows route through `ConnectDatabase.cpp` in the Domain layer, which interacts with `IConnectionRepository.h` to persist connections managed by `AppConnectionRepository.cpp`. Database operations flow through the adapter factory (`AdapterFactory.cpp/h`) which selects the appropriate driver (PostgresAdapter, MysqlAdapter, SqliteAdapter, RedisAdapter, etc.) based on connection configuration. The adapter implementations handle wire protocol communication — `PostgresAdapter.cpp` for PostgreSQL, `MysqlAdapter.cpp` for MySQL, `SqliteAdapter.cpp` for SQLite, `RedisAdapter.cpp` for Redis, plus MongoDB, MSSQL, and ClickHouse adapters. The MCP server component lives in `linux/src/App/MCP/MCPConnectionProvider.cpp/h`. The AI chat functionality uses `ILLMService.h` protocol with `ChatGPTTokenBundle.h` for token management, and `AIChatView.cpp/h` for the UI. The `ThemeManager.cpp/h` handles theming across dark/light modes via QSS stylesheets. The `SqlHighlighter.cpp/h` and `AutocompleteProvider.cpp/h` provide query editing features. The `ExplainVisualizerWidget.cpp/h` and related files (`ExplainPlanParser.cpp/h`, `ExplainPlanHeuristics.cpp/h`) visualize query execution plans. The `ERDiagramView.cpp/h` and `ERDiagramExporter.cpp/h` generate entity-relationship diagrams. The call graph has a hub at `DIContainer.cpp` — changing dependency resolution requires touching this file, which has wide blast radius across all modules. The adapter layer (`Data/Adapters/`) carries the widest individual blast radius since adding or modifying a database driver requires changes to this directory's ~15 files without a shared interface beyond the `IDatabaseAdapter` protocol.

## How To Use It

**Setup**: No build-from-source commands are documented in the repository structure provided. The README offers download links for packaged distributions: macOS universal DMG, Windows Velopack installer, and Linux x86_64 AppImage. A `Package.swift` file exists at the root for Swift Package Manager, and `linux/CMakeLists.txt` drives CMake-based builds on Linux. Docker is detected in the tech stack.

**Configuration**: Environment variables or connection configuration files are not mapped in the provided structure. The `ConnectionConfig.h` and `ConnectionConfigJson.h` files in `Core/Models/Database/` suggest JSON-based connection configuration, but no `.env` or schema for required variables is present in the root or `.github/workflows/ci.yml`.

**Running it**: Download the appropriate packaged distribution from the README links or from releases. The app launches as a native database IDE with MCP server and AI chat enabled out of the box.

## Real-World Use

A developer opens Gridex and adds connections to PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Redis instances. They write a SQL query in the query editor with syntax highlighting and autocomplete (`SqlHighlighter.cpp`, `AutocompleteProvider.cpp`), execute it, and view results in the DataGrid view. The Explain Visualizer (`ExplainVisualizerWidget.cpp`) decomposes the query plan for performance analysis. They generate an ER diagram for a schema, chat with an AI assistant about the results (`AIChatView.cpp`), and trigger a backup from the Backup Progress Dialog (`BackupProgressDialog.cpp`). All features work consistently across the different database engines due to the shared adapter protocol.

## Code Health & Issues

- 736 total files with no structural red flags detected (tests/CI/license/lockfile present where expected)
- 28 test files found
- 10 documentation files found
- C/C++ Header: 235 files, C++: 185 files, Swift: 181 files
- Dependency injection container at `linux/src/App/DependencyInjection/DIContainer.cpp/h` serves as a hub with wide blast radius for changes
- Database adapter layer (`linux/src/Data/Adapters/`) has ~15 implementations sharing `IDatabaseAdapter` protocol — adding a new driver requires updating this directory
- CI/CD via GitHub Actions configured at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`

## The Bottom Line

Gridex delivers a rare single-app experience for seven database engines with a consistent UI and feature set, all built natively with Swift. The modular adapter pattern and DI container provide reasonable extensibility, though the DI container is a coupling point worth noting for anyone planning to add non-trivial new dependencies. It's worth evaluating if your team needs cross-database query editing, schema visualization, and AI-assisted chat in one package — but verify the packaged distribution meets your OS and version requirements before committing to integration.

forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Founders often need a memorable, YC‑style name quickly, but brainstorming can be time‑consuming and yields no guarantee of uniqueness. Without a lightweight tool that can suggest plausible names on‑the‑fly, teams waste effort or settle for sub‑optimal branding.

## What This Does  
`yname` ships a tiny character‑level neural network that generates YC‑style names entirely in the browser. The training pipeline lives in `model/` and produces two binary blobs (`plain.bin`, `conditional.bin`) plus accompanying JSON metadata. Those files are copied into `web/public/models/` and consumed by the React front‑end.

Key files:  

* **`model/train.py`** – builds the MLP on `data/yc_name_training_corpus.csv` and writes `model/artifacts/*.npz`.  
* **`web/scripts/export_models.py`** – loads the NumPy artifacts and serialises them to the binary/JSON format expected by the client.  
* **`web/src/App.tsx`** – UI wrapper that lets the user request a name.  
* **`web/src/lib/generator.ts`** – core inference routine that reads the binary model (via `fetch`) and runs a forward pass using the weights from `model.ts`.  
* **`web/src/lib/model.ts`** – defines the `Model` interface, parses the JSON weight tables, and supplies `step` and `sample` helpers used by `generator`.

The repository therefore provides both the data‑science side (Python) and the delivery side (TypeScript/React) without any server component.

## How It Is Wired  

1. **Browser entry** – `web/index.html` loads the Vite bundle; Vite’s entry point is `web/src/main.tsx`, which mounts `<App />` into `#root`.  
2. **App UI** – `App.tsx` renders a button “Generate”. On click it calls `generateName()` from `generator.ts`.  
3. **Model loading** – `generator.ts` lazily fetches `public/models/plain.json` (or `conditional.json`) and the corresponding `.bin`. `model.ts` parses the JSON into weight tensors and creates a `Model` object.  
4. **Inference** – `generateName()` runs a loop that:
   * calls `model.step(prevChar)` to obtain logits,
   * samples the next character (softmax + categorical draw),
   * appends the character until a stop token or length limit.
   All computation is pure JavaScript/TypeScript; no network calls beyond the initial asset fetch.  
5. **Training path (offline)** – Developers run `python model/train.py` with the CSV corpus; the script writes NumPy `.npz` files into `model/artifacts`. `export_models.py` then converts those to the browser‑ready format. No runtime code in the web app touches the Python side; the two halves are linked only by the exported static assets.

No backend server is involved; the Express reference in the repo is limited to the development server Vite uses under the hood. The only side‑effects at runtime are reads of static assets from the `public/models/` directory.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone and install the front‑end
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/yname
cd yname/web
npm install
npm run dev        # starts Vite dev server at http://localhost:5173
```

To retrain the model locally:

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r model/requirements.txt

python model/train.py \
  --data data/yc_name_training_corpus.csv \
  --output-dir model/artifacts

cd web
npm run export-models   # runs web/scripts/export_models.py
```

No environment variables or external services are required.

## Real‑World Use  
A product team can embed the generated name UI into an internal portal. By pulling the static `public/models/*.bin` into their own CDN, they get instant, offline name suggestions for brainstorming sessions without any API cost or latency.

```tsx
// Example embed
import { generateName } from './lib/generator';
<button onClick={() => generateName().then(name => alert(name))}>
  Get YC‑style name
</button>
```

## Code Health & Issues  

* **Med – No test suite** – repository contains no `*.test.*` files; code paths are unverified.  
* **Med – No CI/CD** – no `.github/workflows`, `Jenkinsfile`, or other pipeline definitions; builds and linting are manual.  
* **Low – Duplicate tooling** – both `express` (in `package.json`) and Vite are present, but Express is never used at runtime.  
* **Low – Minimal documentation** – README covers basic commands; deeper API docs for `generator.ts` or model format are absent.

No security‑related secrets are committed, and the MIT license is present.

## The Bottom Line  
`yname` delivers a functional, zero‑backend name generator with a clear separation between training (Python) and inference (React/TS). It works out‑of‑the‑box for local development but lacks automated testing and CI, which raises maintenance risk for any downstream integration. Suitable for rapid prototyping or internal tooling where the lightweight client‑only model is a benefit; not recommended for production services that require rigorous quality gates.

forks.name: all-agentic-architectures
forks.description: 35 production-grade agentic AI architectures (Reflexion, LATS, GraphRAG, MemGPT, Voyager, BrowserAgent, ...) — a Python library and runnable textbook with multi-provider LLM support and a 17-task benchmark leaderboard.
forks.summary:
## The Problem

Modern agentic systems often struggle with the reliability of LLM-as-scorer mechanisms, where probabilistic free-text outputs lead to inconsistent agent behavior—colloquially known as the "flat-band pathology." This repository addresses that instability by implementing a deterministic-picker pattern, requiring LLMs to commit to categorical features (booleans, enums) rather than unstructured scores, allowing Python to compose the final decision signal.

## What This Does

The project provides a Python library implementing 35 distinct agentic AI patterns, ranging from Reflexion and LATS to GraphRAG and Voyager. Each architecture ships as a runnable `Architecture` class with a uniform `.run(task)` interface, all documented in Jupyter notebooks located in `docs/architectures/` and `notebooks/`. A central technical discipline across 13 architectures is the deterministic-picker pattern, which structures LLM outputs into categorical features for reliable Python-side composition; a further 9 architectures are architecturally immune to the scorer pathology by design. The library is multi-provider, supporting Nebius, OpenAI, Anthropic, Groq, Ollama, Together, Fireworks, Mistral, and Google, and is built on top of LangGraph state machines.

## How It Is Wired

Execution begins by instantiating a specific `Architecture` subclass (e.g., `Reflection`, `LATS`) from `src/agentic_architectures/architectures/`. These classes accept an LLM instance via `get_llm()` and a task string. The uniform `.run(task)` method triggers the architecture-specific state machine logic. The `deterministic-picker` logic is embedded within the scorer components of architectures like `Reflexion`, ensuring the LLM's output is parsed into structured Python types before further processing. The `pyproject.toml` file manages package dependencies, while environment variables configured in `.env.example` handle LLM provider credentials. The code touches external networks via API calls to the configured LLM providers and manages state internally through LangGraph state persistence.

## How To Use It

**Setup:**
```bash
pip install "agentic-architectures[nebius,faiss,tavily]"
```

**Configuration:**
Copy `.env.example` and populate the required API keys for the desired LLM provider (e.g., `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`).

**Running it:**
Use the uniform `.run(task)` interface demonstrated in the quickstart:
```python
from agentic_architectures import get_llm
from agentic_architectures.architectures import Reflection

arch = Reflection(llm=get_llm(), max_iterations=2, target_score=8)
result = arch.run("Write a haiku about a glacier.")
print(result.output)
```

## Real-World Use

A practical use case involves deploying `Reflexion` to improve output quality in a closed-loop generation task. By instantiating `Reflection(llm=get_llm(), max_iterations=2)`, the architecture iteratively queries the LLM and scores outputs against a target, leveraging the deterministic-picker to halt when the score threshold is met. This pattern is applicable for improving reliability in tool-use agents or code generation workflows where output validation is critical.

## Code Health & Issues

A heuristic analysis identified one low-risk finding: dependencies are declared in `pyproject.toml` without a corresponding lockfile, which may lead to non-reproducible builds across environments. Beyond this, the repository structure is well-organized with extensive documentation and test coverage (283 passing tests per the README), though the absence of a lockfile is the primary static analysis finding.

## The Bottom Line

This repository is a valuable resource for experimenting with and comparing 35 major agentic AI patterns within a consistent framework. The multi-provider support and the deterministic-picker pattern offer a practical solution to LLM reliability concerns. However, the lack of a dependency lockfile presents a reproducibility risk for production deployment that should be addressed before integrating into strict CI/CD pipelines.

forks.name: espectre
forks.description: ESPectre - Motion detection system based on Wi-Fi spectre analysis (CSI), with Home Assistant integration.
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Home‑assistant users want reliable motion detection without cameras or wearables. Traditional PIR sensors struggle through walls and generate false positives, while video‑based solutions raise privacy concerns. ESPectre addresses this gap by using Wi‑Fi channel state information (CSI) to infer motion, requiring only an inexpensive ESP32 device and a standard router.

## What This Does  
The repository ships two runtimes:

* **Python host side** – runs on a PC/Raspberry Pi, consumes CSI streams, runs detection algorithms, and forwards events via MQTT. Core files are `micro‑espectre/src/main.py`, `csi_streamer.py`, `ml_detector.py`, `mvs_detector.py`, and the MQTT helpers in `src/mqtt/`.  
* **ESPHome component (C++)** – compiled into an ESP‑Home firmware that reads raw CSI from the ESP32 radio and publishes raw packets to the host. The component lives under `components/espectre/` and includes `csi_manager.cpp`, `base_detector.cpp`, `ml_detector.cpp`, and the UDP listener in `udp_listener.cpp`.

The Python side can select between the classic MVS detector (`src/mvs_detector.py`) and the newer neural‑net detector (`src/ml_detector.py`). Both expose a uniform interface defined in `src/detector_interface.py`.

## How It Is Wired  
**Execution start → host**  
1. `micro‑espectre/src/main.py` is the entry point (`if __name__ == "__main__":`).  
2. It loads configuration from `src/config.py` (or `config_local.py.example`).  
3. A `CSIStreamer` object from `csi_streamer.py` opens a UDP socket (configured in `examples/espectre‑c3.yaml` etc.) and yields raw CSI frames.  
4. Each frame is passed to the detector selected by `detector_interface.py`.  
   * For the ML path, `MLDetector.detect()` in `ml_detector.py` loads the TFLite model `models/motion_detector_small.tflite` and runs inference via the TensorFlow Lite interpreter.  
   * For the classic path, `MVSDetector.detect()` in `mvs_detector.py` calls `BaseDetector.process()` (implemented in `components/espectre/base_detector.cpp` via the ESP‑Home component’s native API).  
5. Detection results are handed to the MQTT handler (`src/mqtt/handler.py`), which publishes a JSON payload on the topic defined in `src/mqtt/commands.py`. Home Assistant subscribes and creates binary sensor entities automatically.

**Execution start → ESP32**  
1. The ESP‑Home YAML files in `examples/` (e.g., `espectre‑c3.yaml`) include the custom component `espectre`.  
2. During firmware compilation, ESP‑Home pulls the C++ sources from `components/espectre/`.  
3. `csi_manager.cpp` registers a Wi‑Fi CSI callback with the ESP‑IDF driver, feeding raw packets to `udp_listener.cpp`.  
4. `udp_listener.cpp` forwards each packet over UDP to the host IP/port configured in the YAML. No further processing occurs on the device unless the `-ml` build flag is used, in which case `ml_detector.cpp` runs the TFLite model locally and publishes a binary sensor state directly via ESP‑Home’s native MQTT bridge.

**Key ownership**  
* Network I/O – `csi_manager.cpp` / `udp_listener.cpp` (device) and `csi_streamer.py` (host).  
* Detection logic – `ml_detector.py` + `models/*.tflite` (host) or `ml_detector.cpp` (device); `mvs_detector.py` + `base_detector.cpp` (host).  
* Home‑Assistant integration – MQTT publishing in `src/mqtt/` (host) and ESP‑Home entity definition in the YAML examples (device).  

No circular dependencies are present; the host imports the detector modules, while the device code is entirely self‑contained and only communicates via UDP.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/espectre
cd espectre

# Install Python host dependencies (no lockfile, reproducibility not guaranteed)
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r micro-espectre/requirements.txt

# Edit the local config (copy example)
cp micro-espectre/src/config_local.py.example micro-espectre/src/config_local.py
# Adjust MQTT broker address, UDP listen port, and detector choice in that file.

# Start the host daemon
python micro-espectre/src/main.py
```

To flash an ESP32 device:

```bash
# Choose an example matching your board
esphome run examples/espectre-c3.yaml   # requires the `esphome` CLI
```

The ESPHome build pulls the C++ sources automatically. After flashing, ensure the device and the host are on the same network; the host will receive UDP CSI packets and publish motion events to the MQTT broker configured in `config_local.py`.

## Real‑World Use  
A smart‑home installer adds an ESP32‑S3 sensor to the living‑room ceiling, points it at the home router, and runs the host daemon on the same Raspberry Pi that hosts Home Assistant. Motion events appear as a binary sensor `binary_sensor.espectre_motion`, which can trigger automations (e.g., turning on lights when motion is detected while the TV is off).

```yaml
automation:
  - alias: "Turn on hallway light on motion"
    trigger:
      - platform: state
        entity_id: binary_sensor.espectre_motion
        to: "on"
    action:
      - service: light.turn_on
        target:
          entity_id: light.hallway
```

## Code Health & Issues  
* **Low – Dependencies declared without a lockfile** – `micro-espectre/requirements.txt` (reproducible builds not guaranteed).  
* CI defined in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`; tests exist under `micro-espectre/tests/` and `test/`, but coverage enforcement is not evident.  
* No explicit license file for the Python side; the top‑level `LICENSE` covers the project overall.  
* No secret scanning; example YAML files contain no credentials, but real deployments must supply MQTT passwords manually.

## The Bottom Line  
ESPectre provides a functional, low‑cost motion‑detection pipeline that integrates cleanly with Home Assistant via MQTT. The code base is split cleanly between host‑side Python and device‑side C++, making targeted changes straightforward. The main drawback is the lack of a Python lockfile, which can cause environment drift for new developers. Suitable for engineers comfortable with ESPHome and MQTT who need privacy‑preserving motion sensing.

forks.name: MaCursor
forks.description: Cursor Control for macOS
forks.summary:
## The Problem
macOS users requiring granular cursor customization lack a native, maintainable solution. System cursor replacement requires manual file placement, lacks visual editing capabilities, and does not support cross-platform theme conversion (Windows `.cur`/`.ani`, Linux Xcursor, Mousecape `.cape` formats). Existing tools either offer static cursor sets without editor functionality or require command-line operations incompatible with daily workflow.

## What This Does
MaCursor is a macOS 15+ cursor management application replacing system cursors with user-selected artwork or converted themes. The codebase splits responsibility between low-level macOS interaction and a SwiftUI frontend:

- **CursorEngine/** contains the private macOS API bridge: `CGSPrivateAPI/CGSPrivateCursor.h`, `CGSPrivateAPI/CGSPrivateConnection.h`, and `CGSPrivateAPI/CGSPrivateAccessibility.h` handle kernel-level cursor rendering, while `MACCursorDaemon.m`/`MACCursorDaemon.h` manage the persistent helper process and `MACAutoSwitch.m` implements time-based day/night theme switching.

- **MaCursor/** is the SwiftUI application shell: `MaCursorApp.swift` is the app entry point, `CursorService.swift` coordinates theme application and hotkey handling, and `CursorModel.swift` along with `CursorLibrary.swift` manage the cursor asset library and metadata.

- **themes/** holds 169 `.cursor` theme files alongside a README documenting the theme gallery source.

- **.github/workflows/release.yml** governs the GitHub Actions CI/CD pipeline for releases.

- **scripts/build.sh** provides the local build command.

## How It Is Wired
Execution flows from the SwiftUI app delegate through the service layer to the daemon:

1. **Entry point**: `MaCursorApp.swift` — the SwiftUI `App` struct initializes the service and window hierarchy.

2. **Cursor application**: `CursorService.swift` calls `MACCursorDaemon` via a helper tool bootstrap; the daemon uses private CGS APIs (`CGSPrivateCursor.h`) to set the system cursor image.

3. **Theme conversion**: `ThemeImporter.swift` and `CursorFormatReaders.swift` parse external formats (Windows `.cur`/`.ani`, Linux Xcursor directories, Mousecape `.cape` files). `ThemeConversion.swift` maps parsed cursors to native `.cursor` slots, listing each mapping in the UI via `CursorThemeEditorViewModel.swift` before application.

4. **Hotkey handling**: `RoleMapper.swift` and `HelperToolManager.swift` manage the `macursorhelper` login item (referenced in entitlements `CursorEngineHelper/CursorEngineHelper.entitlements`), ensuring global hotkeys registered in settings remain active across user switches.

5. **Auto-switch**: `MACAutoSwitch.m` evaluates the system time against user-configured start times and switches the active theme via the daemon API.

The daemon carries the widest blast radius — any change to `CGSPrivateAPI/` affects cursor rendering system-wide, and the private API headers have no public alternative, coupling the application to macOS version compatibility risks.

## How To Use It
**Setup**: Download the latest `.dmg` from the [Releases page](https://github.com/writronic/MaCursor/releases/latest), open the disk image, and drag **MaCursor** to the Applications folder. The app requires macOS 15 Sequoia or later.

**Configuration**: On first launch, grant accessibility permissions in System Settings → Privacy & Security → MaCursor. Configure global hotkeys, day/night switch times, and cursor scale (0.50×–4.00×, 0.1× steps) via **Settings Views.swift**.

**Running it**: Launch MaCursor from the Applications folder. To apply a theme, double-click any `.cursor` file from the Theme Gallery or drag a `.cur`/`.ani`/`.gif` file onto the editor. To convert a Windows or Linux theme, use **ThemeConversionReviewView.swift** to review mapped cursors before committing to the library.

## Real-World Use
A user maintains a light cursor theme for daytime work and a high-contrast dark theme for evening sessions. They configure `MACAutoSwitch.m` to trigger the dark theme at 6 PM, and assign `Cmd+Option+1` as a global hotkey via **ShortcutSettingsView.swift** to instantly switch to a favorite “focus” cursor without leaving any application. When a new Windows `.ani` animation is acquired, they drop the folder onto the importer, review the sprite-sheet composition in the preview strip, and apply the converted theme to the library in a single session.

## Code Health & Issues
- **Medium/SDLC** — No test files detected across the repository (292 files); untested code paths exist in `MACCursorDaemon.m`, `MACAutoSwitch.m`, and the theme conversion pipelines. Static analysis has not identified additional issues beyond this gap.

- The repository includes a `LICENSE` file (GPL-3.0) and `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`, `PRIVACY.md`, `SECURITY.md` documentation files.

- CI/CD is configured via `.github/workflows/release.yml` but no local test target is present in the Xcode project structure.

## The Bottom Line
MaCursor delivers a capable, visually rich cursor editor for macOS 15+ with genuine cross-platform conversion workflows and a functional day/night auto-switcher. The private CGS API bridge is the architectural constraint — it enables the functionality but ties the project to macOS version stability risks and precludes sandboxing. The absence of tests and the heavy reliance on undocumented internal APIs mean production deployment would require a fork with public API shims or acceptance of version-coupled releases. Teams needing cursor customization on macOS with an editing workflow will find this the most complete available option; those requiring long-term stability or cross-platform compatibility should evaluate the maintenance burden of the private API layer.
