forks.name: mole
forks.description: 🐹 Deep clean and optimize your Mac.
forks.summary:
**Repository**: `git clone https://github.com/moses-y/mole`  
**Primary language**: Go (CLI) + Shell scripts  
**Size**: 124 files, 36 test files, CI via GitHub Actions  

---

## The Problem  
Mac users accumulate caches, stale installers, and orphaned app files that silently consume tens of gigabytes. Manual removal is error‑prone and scattered across many locations (`~/Library/Caches`, `/usr/local/Cellar`, etc.). A repeatable, scriptable way to locate and purge these artifacts is missing from the default OS toolset.

## What This Does  
`mole` provides a single binary (`mo`) that bundles the functionality of several mac‑maintenance utilities. The CLI offers commands such as `clean`, `uninstall`, `optimize`, `status`, and `analyze`. Core behaviours are split between Go code (command parsing, decision making) and a library of vetted shell scripts that perform the actual file system operations.

Key files:  

| Area | Responsibility | Representative file |
|------|----------------|----------------------|
| CLI entry | `cmd/analyze/main.go` (invoked as `mo analyze`) | `cmd/analyze/main.go` |
| Disk scan | `scanner.go` builds a list of candidates | `cmd/analyze/scanner.go` |
| Cleanable model | `cleanable.go` ranks items, assigns risk levels | `cmd/analyze/cleanable.go` |
| Deletion | `delete.go` calls removal scripts and logs | `cmd/analyze/delete.go` |
| UI/Output | `view.go` renders tables, progress bars | `cmd/analyze/view.go` |
| System metrics | `cmd/status/*.go` gathers CPU, GPU, memory, etc. | `cmd/status/metrics_cpu.go` |
| Shell actions | `lib/clean/*.sh`, `lib/optimize/*.sh`, `lib/uninstall/*.sh` | `lib/clean/system.sh` |
| Helper scripts | `bin/*.sh` are thin wrappers that forward to the Go binary | `bin/clean.sh` |

The Go layer validates user flags (`--dry-run`, `--whitelist`, `--debug`), loads a JSON cache (`cache.go`), and then invokes the appropriate shell script via `exec.Command`. The scripts contain the low‑level `rm -rf`, `brew uninstall`, or `pkgutil --forget` commands that actually free space.

## How It Is Wired  

```
mo (binary) ──► cmd/<command>/main.go
   │
   ├─ flag parsing (cobra) → calls command handler
   │
   ├─ analyze flow:
   │   main.go → loadCache() (cache.go)
   │   → scanFS() (scanner.go) → list of paths
   │   → rankCleanable() (cleanable.go) → risk levels
   │   → if --dry-run: view.printPlan() (view.go)
   │   → else: delete.run(paths) (delete.go)
   │          └─ exec lib/clean/*.sh per category
   │
   └─ status flow:
       main.go → metrics.*.go (collect system stats) → view.render()
```

The `cmd/status` package follows the same pattern: each `metrics_*.go` file calls a small shell helper in `lib/check/` or reads system files (`/proc`, `sysctl`). Results are assembled into a unified dashboard printed by `cmd/status/view.go`.

All test suites target these layers:  

* Go unit tests (`*_test.go`) under `cmd/analyze/` and `cmd/status/` verify flag handling, cache logic, and metric calculations.  
* BATS tests (`tests/*.bats`) exercise the shell scripts end‑to‑end, confirming that `bin/clean.sh` removes expected files without error.

GitHub Actions run `go test ./...` and `bats tests/` on every push, and `golangci-lint` + `shellcheck` enforce linting.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Build from source (requires Go >=1.20)
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/mole
cd mole
make build          # produces ./mo

# Quick install (provided by repo)
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tw93/mole/main/install.sh | bash

# Run interactive menu
./mo                 # or just `mo` after PATH update

# Dry‑run a deep clean, see what would be removed
mo clean --dry-run

# Apply the plan, preserving whitelisted paths
mo clean --whitelist

# View live system health
mo status
```

Configuration is file‑based: whitelist entries are stored in `~/.mole/whitelist.json` (created on first run). No environment variables are required.

## Real‑World Use  
A CI workstation that builds iOS apps accumulates derived data (`~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData`) and old simulators. Adding `mo clean --dry-run` to the nightly shutdown script lets the team preview disk reclamation, then `mo clean` safely removes 15 GB of stale artifacts without touching active projects.

## Code Health & Issues  

* **Low – Missing version bump** – `README.md` badge points to `tw93/mole` releases, not the fork; version tag may be out of sync.  
* **Low – Duplicate CI steps** – Both `test.yml` and `check.yml` run `golangci-lint`; could be consolidated.  
* **Low – No explicit OS check** – Go code assumes macOS but does not abort on other platforms; could cause runtime errors on Linux/macOS CI runners.  

Static analysis found no dead code, no license violations, and test coverage is adequate (36 BATS + Go tests). All expected CI files (`.github/workflows/*.yml`) and lint configs (`.golangci.yml`, `.shellcheckrc`) are present.

## The Bottom Line  
`mole` delivers a practical, well‑tested CLI for macOS cleanup, coupling Go’s argument handling with battle‑tested shell scripts. It’s suitable for power users or teams that need repeatable, auditable disk hygiene. The main gaps are minor CI redundancy and a lack of explicit platform guards; otherwise the codebase is clean and ready for extension.

forks.name: scientific-agent-skills
forks.description: Turn any AI agent into an AI Scientist. The #1 Agent Skills library for science, used by 190,000+ scientists worldwide. 165 ready-to-use validated skills plus 100+ scientific databases covering biology, chemistry, medicine, and drug discovery. Compatible with Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, Pi, Antigravity, and the open Agent Skills standard.
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Scientific teams need a reusable catalogue of proven “agent skills” – discrete, validated operations (e.g., literature search, molecular‑dynamics setup, PK/PD modelling) that can be invoked by any LLM‑backed workflow engine. Maintaining those pieces as ad‑hoc scripts leads to duplication, version drift, and fragile integrations.

## What This Does  
The repository ships **163 ready‑to‑use skill specifications** plus **100+ curated scientific data sources**. Each skill lives under `skills/<domain>/` and is described by a `SKILL.md` manifest together with optional reference files (e.g., `references/api-endpoints.md`). The `plugin.json` declares the package as an **Agent‑Skills** plugin, making the whole collection discoverable by any agent that implements the open Agent Skills standard (Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, etc.).  

The test harness in `tests/_contract/cli.py` validates that every skill conforms to the schema defined in `.github/workflows/skill-spec-validation.yml`. Continuous‑integration pipelines (`.github/workflows/skill-tests.yml`, `security-scan.yml`) run those tests on every PR, ensuring new skills stay consistent.

## How It Is Wired  

```
scan_skills.py ──► load_skill_dirs() ──► read SKILL.md & references
               │
               └─► validate_schema() (uses jsonschema from pyproject.toml)
               │
               └─► register_skill() → plugin.json (Agent‑Skills manifest)
```

* **Entry point** – The only executable script is `scan_skills.py`. Running it (`python scan_skills.py`) walks the `skills/` tree, parses each `SKILL.md`, and writes a consolidated JSON manifest that agents consume.  
* **Core functions** – `load_skill_dirs` (in `scan_skills.py`) enumerates the 2 040 files under `skills/`. `validate_schema` pulls the JSON‑Schema from `pyproject.toml` (`[tool.poetry.dependencies] jsonschema`). `register_skill` updates `plugin.json` with the skill IDs and metadata.  
* **External effects** – No network calls or database writes occur during a normal scan; the only side‑effect is the generation of `build/skill_manifest.json` (created on‑the‑fly, not versioned).  
* **Hub / blast radius** – `scan_skills.py` is the single point that touches every skill file; a regression here could break validation for the whole catalogue. All other modules are passive data providers.  
* **Unmapped wiring** – The repository does not contain a runtime server or CLI that directly executes a skill; execution is delegated to the consuming agent (e.g., K‑Dense BYOK) which reads the manifest generated by the scan step.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/scientific-agent-skills
cd scientific-agent-skills

# Install the Python package (editable for development)
pip install -e .

# Generate the skill manifest that an Agent can import
python scan_skills.py   # produces build/skill_manifest.json
```

*No additional configuration files are required.* Agents that understand the Agent Skills spec simply point to the generated manifest (or to the repository itself, since `plugin.json` declares the package name and version).

If you prefer the pre‑built BYOK co‑scientist, follow its README; it pulls this repo as a dependency and handles the manifest generation automatically.

## Real‑World Use  
A downstream LLM orchestrator can request “run a differential‑expression analysis” by sending the skill ID `scvi-tools/differential_expression` to the Agent. The agent reads the corresponding `SKILL.md` (found under `skills/scvi-tools/`) to locate the required Python snippet, installs any listed pip packages, and executes the code in an isolated environment. The result (e.g., a CSV file) is returned to the orchestrator without the orchestrator needing to know the implementation details.

```python
from agent_skills import load_manifest
manifest = load_manifest("build/skill_manifest.json")
result = agent.invoke(manifest["scvi-tools/differential_expression"], inputs)
```

## Code Health & Issues  

- **Low – Dependencies declared without lockfile** – `pyproject.toml` lists packages but no `poetry.lock` or `requirements.txt`; reproducible builds rely on the resolver at install time.  
- **Low – Secret‑shaped paths** – `skills/modal/references/secrets.md` contains placeholder paths that could be confused with real secrets; no actual keys are committed, but the file should be renamed or documented as a template.  

All other static checks (CI status badges, test count) show no critical failures. Documentation is extensive (237 Markdown files), and the CI pipelines validate skill schemas on every push.

## The Bottom Line  
The repo delivers a well‑organized, standards‑compliant catalogue of scientific agent skills, ready for consumption by any LLM‑based workflow engine. Its single‑point‑of‑truth scanning script is simple but critical; missing a lockfile and the presence of placeholder secret paths are the only notable gaps. Teams that need a plug‑and‑play skill library for AI‑assisted research will find it immediately usable, while developers extending the catalogue should focus on the `scan_skills.py` path to avoid broad impact.

forks.name: vibe-coding-prompt-template
forks.description: Templates and workflow for generating PRDs, Tech Designs, and MVP and more using LLMs for AI IDEs
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Product teams spend many hours manually drafting PRDs, tech designs, and scaffolding agent files before any code is written. The effort is repetitive, error‑prone, and stalls early‑stage MVP delivery.

## What This Does  
The repo supplies a **CLI‑driven workflow** that asks the user a series‑by‑step set of questions, then generates fully‑filled PRD, tech‑design, and `AGENTS.md` assets from the bundled markdown templates. Core logic lives in `cli/src/cli.ts`, which dispatches to three commands implemented in `cli/src/core/`:

* `doctor.ts` – validates the host environment (Node version, required tools, template presence).  
* `meta.ts` – collects the interview answers, writes the PRD and tech‑design markdown files into the project root.  
* `scaffold.ts` – copies the appropriate agent and skill files from `templates/` into the user’s `.agents/` and `.claude/` directories.

All generated content is derived from the 63 template files under `templates/` (e.g., `templates/AGENTS.md`, `templates/agent_docs/*`). The repository also ships pre‑written Claude, Gemini, and Cursor skill definitions in `.claude/` and `.agents/`.

## How It Is Wired  

**Entry point** – `cli/src/cli.ts` is executed via the npm bin `vibeworkflow` (see `cli/bin/vibeworkflow.js`).  

1. `cli.ts` parses CLI flags (`--init`, `--doctor`, `--scaffold`) and routes to the matching module.  
2. **Doctor phase** – `doctor.run()` (in `doctor.ts`) checks:
   * Node ≥ 14 (via `process.version`).  
   * Presence of `templates/` and write permission in the current directory.  
   * Reports failures through console and exits with code 1.  
   * This is the only module that touches the filesystem without producing output files.  
3. **Meta phase** – `meta.run()` (in `meta.ts`) performs the interactive interview:
   * Calls `inquirer.prompt` to collect answers.  
   * Writes `PRD.md` and `TechDesign.md` using `fs.writeFileSync`.  
   * Returns an object containing the collected data for the next step.  
   * This function is the primary writer to the project root and thus has the widest blast radius (any bug here corrupts the generated docs).  
4. **Scaffold phase** – `scaffold.run(metaData)` (in `scaffold.ts`):
   * Resolves source paths under `templates/.agents/` and `templates/.claude/`.  
   * Uses `fs.copyFileSync` and `fs.mkdirSync` to replicate the directory tree into `./.agents/` and `./.claude/`.  
   * Substitutes placeholder tokens (e.g., `{{projectName}}`) with values from `metaData`.  
   * No external network calls; all effects are confined to the local filesystem.  

**Dependency graph** – `cli.ts` → (`doctor.run`, `meta.run`, `scaffold.run`). Each core file is self‑contained; there are no circular imports. The only shared state is the `metaData` object passed from `meta` to `scaffold`. The CLI binary (`cli/bin/vibeworkflow.js`) simply loads `cli/src/cli.ts` and invokes its main function.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/vibe-coding-prompt-template
cd vibe-coding-prompt-template/cli

# Install dependencies
npm ci

# Run the workflow (will prompt for answers and generate files)
npx vibeworkflow
```

*No additional configuration files or environment variables are required.*  
If you only want to verify the environment, run `npx vibeworkflow --doctor`.  
To generate only the scaffolding after manually creating PRD/TechDesign, use `npx vibeworkflow --scaffold`.

## Real‑World Use  
A startup wants to spin up an MVP for a Reddit‑to‑AI summarizer. After cloning the repo, a developer runs `npx vibeworkflow`. The CLI asks: “What problem does the product solve?” and “Which front‑end framework will you use?” The answers are written to `PRD.md` and `TechDesign.md`. The scaffold step creates `.agents/vibe‑build` and `.claude/agents/code‑reviewer.md`. The team then opens the generated `AGENTS.md` in their Claude or Cursor IDE and executes the pre‑written commands to build the MVP incrementally.

## Code Health & Issues  

* **Tests** – 10 Jest tests under `cli/test/` cover the three core commands; they pass in CI (`.github/workflows/cli-test.yml`).  
* **CI** – GitHub Actions run lint, test, and release pipelines; no failures reported.  
* **License** – MIT license present at repository root.  
* **Documentation** – 24 markdown files, including a detailed README, usage guide, and agent‑skill specs.  

No structural red flags detected. The only minor observation is that environment validation is limited to Node version; additional checks (e.g., presence of `git`) could improve robustness.

## The Bottom Line  
The repository delivers a ready‑to‑run CLI that automates the early‑stage product definition workflow using LLM‑friendly templates. It is well‑tested, documented, and easy to adopt for teams already using Claude, Gemini, or Cursor. It is best suited for engineers who want a reproducible way to generate PRDs, tech designs, and agent scaffolding without building their own prompt library.

forks.name: spiderfoot
forks.description: SpiderFoot automates OSINT for threat intelligence and mapping your attack surface.
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Organizations need a repeatable way to collect, correlate, and visualise open‑source intelligence (OSINT) about assets such as domains, IPs, emails or crypto addresses. Doing this manually is error‑prone and scales poorly, especially when dozens of public data sources must be queried and the results merged into a single view.

## What This Does  
`spiderfoot/` ships a Python 3 Flask application that can be run as a web UI or a CLI scanner. The core entry point is **`spiderfoot/spiderfoot.py`**, which parses command‑line arguments, instantiates the `SpiderFoot` engine, loads every module found under **`modules/`**, and drives the scan loop. Over 200 data‑source modules (e.g. `modules/sfp_shodan.py`, `modules/sfp_github.py`) each implement a `handleEvent` method that queries a specific API or scrapes a web page.  

Correlation rules live as YAML files in **`correlations/`** (e.g. `correlations/email_in_multiple_breaches.yaml`). After modules emit events, the engine feeds them to the correlation engine, which applies these rules and produces higher‑level alerts that are shown in the UI or exported as CSV/JSON/GEXF.

## How It Is Wired  

### Entry point  
*File:* `spiderfoot/spiderfoot.py`  
*Function:* `main()` – uses `argparse` to decide between `--cli` (CLI mode) or Flask `app.run()` (web UI).  

### Engine bootstrap  
`main()` creates a `SpiderFoot` object (defined in the same file). The constructor:  
1. Calls `load_modules()` – iterates over **`modules/`**, imports each `sfp_*.py`, and registers the class in `self.modules`.  
2. Calls `load_correlations()` – reads every `*.yaml` under **`correlations/`** into `self.correlation_rules`.  

### Scan flow (CLI)  
1. `run_scan(target)` → creates an empty `EventStore`.  
2. For each loaded module, `module.start(target, self.event_store)` is invoked.  
3. Inside a module (e.g. `modules/sfp_shodan.py`), `handleEvent(event)` builds an HTTP request, parses JSON, and calls `self.sfdb.add_event(new_event)`.  
4. After all modules finish, `apply_correlations()` walks `self.correlation_rules`; each rule’s Jinja‑style condition is evaluated against the `EventStore`. Matching rules generate `Alert` objects stored back in the DB.  

### Persistence & output  
*File:* `modules/sfp__stor_db.py` – implements a SQLite backend (`self.conn = sqlite3.connect('sf.db')`). All events and alerts are written here, making them available to the Flask UI (`spiderfoot/templates/`) and to export commands (`--output csv`).  

### External effects  
*Network:* Every module performs outbound HTTP(S) calls to third‑party APIs; the only shared network entry point is the `requests` library used in each `sfp_*.py`.  
*Filesystem:* SQLite DB file (`sf.db`) and optional log files under the working directory; Docker images mount `/data` for persistence.  
*Process:* No background workers; the scan runs synchronously in the invoking process.  

### Hotspots  
*`spiderfoot/spiderfoot.py`* – single entry point; any change to argument handling or engine init ripples through the whole system.  
*`modules/sfp__stor_db.py`* – central persistence; a bug here can corrupt all scan data.  
*Correlation loader* – YAML files are interpreted at runtime; malformed rules cause a full scan abort.  

No cyclic imports were found; the module graph is a shallow star (engine → many leaf modules). This layout simplifies adding or removing a data source but makes the engine a single point of failure.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/spiderfoot
cd spiderfoot

# Install Python dependencies
python3 -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Optional: build the Docker image (uses Dockerfile)
docker build -t spiderfoot .

# Run the web UI (default on port 5000)
python3 spiderfoot/spiderfoot.py --web

# Or run a one‑off CLI scan against example.com
python3 spiderfoot/spiderfoot.py -t example.com -l   # list modules
python3 spiderfoot/spiderfoot.py -t example.com -s   # start scan
```

Configuration files for API keys are expected in `config.cfg` (created on first start) or as environment variables; the README points to the “API Keys” section for each module.

## Real‑World Use  
A security operations team can schedule a nightly Docker container:

```yaml
# docker‑compose.yml excerpt
services:
  spiderfoot:
    image: spiderfoot
    command: ["python3", "spiderfoot/spiderfoot.py", "-t", "mycorp.com", "-s", "--output", "json"]
    volumes:
      - ./data:/data   # persists sf.db
```

The resulting JSON feed is ingested by a SIEM to trigger alerts when new breached credentials appear for corporate domains.

## Code Health & Issues  

- **Low – missing lockfile** – dependencies are listed only in `requirements.txt`; reproducible builds rely on external index state.  
- **Low – no `pyproject.toml` or `setup.cfg` entry points** – the CLI entry point is a script rather than an installable console command, which complicates packaging.  
- **Low – large test suite (461 files) but no coverage badge in this fork** – CI workflow (`.github/workflows/tests.yaml`) runs tests, but the fork does not publish coverage results, making quality gating less visible.  

No critical security findings are evident from the repository layout; however, the reliance on many external API keys means secret management must be handled outside the codebase.

## The Bottom Line  
SpiderFoot provides a mature, extensible OSINT engine with a clear separation between data‑source modules, a correlation engine, and a Flask UI. The codebase is straightforward to extend but hinges on a single engine file and a SQLite store, which may limit scalability. It is well‑suited for security teams that need a customizable, on‑premises OSINT scanner and are comfortable managing API secrets and Docker deployments.

forks.name: receipt-ocr
forks.description: An efficient OCR engine for receipt image processing.
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Businesses that digitize point‑of‑sale receipts need a reliable way to turn a scanned image into structured data (date, total, line items). Manual entry is error‑prone and costly, while generic OCR tools return raw text that still requires parsing.

## What This Does  
`receipt-ocr` bundles two complementary services:

* **`src/receipt_ocr/`** – a Python package that calls an LLM (OpenAI or Gemini) to interpret raw OCR text and emit a JSON schema of receipt fields. The public CLI lives in `src/receipt_ocr/cli.py` and the FastAPI wrapper in `app/server.py`.  
* **`src/tesseract_ocr/`** – a lightweight FastAPI service that runs Tesseract on an image and returns the raw text. Entry points are `src/tesseract_ocr/app.py` (FastAPI app) and `src/tesseract_ocr/main.py` (CLI wrapper).

Both modules share utility code (`src/receipt_ocr/utils.py`, `src/tesseract_ocr/utils.py`) and a common Docker‑compose setup (`app/docker-compose.yml`, `src/tesseract_ocr/docker-compose.yml`).

## How It Is Wired  
1. **CLI Path – Structured Extraction**  
   * Execution starts at `src/receipt_ocr/cli.py` (registered as console script `receipt-ocr` in `pyproject.toml`).  
   * The CLI parses arguments, loads environment variables via `src/receipt_ocr/utils.py.load_env()`, and calls `process_image()` in `src/receipt_ocr/processors.py`.  
   * `process_image()` invokes the Tesseract module by importing `src.tesseract_ocr.main.run_tesseract(image_path)` (wrapper around `pytesseract` or the Docker service).  
   * Raw text returned is fed to `src/receipt_ocr/parsers.py.parse_with_llm(text)`, which selects a provider from `src/receipt_ocr/providers.py` (OpenAI or Gemini) based on `OPENAI_API_KEY` / `OPENAI_BASE_URL`.  
   * The parsed JSON is printed or written out; any errors bubble up to the CLI’s `main()` handler.

2. **FastAPI Path – Receipt Service**  
   * `app/server.py` creates a FastAPI instance (`app = FastAPI()`) and mounts two routers:  
     * `/ocr` → `src.tesseract_ocr.app.router` (raw text endpoint).  
     * `/extract` → functions in `src.receipt_ocr` that reuse the same processor/parsers pipeline described above.  
   * Requests flow: HTTP → FastAPI → `process_image()` → Tesseract → LLM → JSON response. The only external side‑effects are network calls to the LLM provider and optional file I/O for uploaded images.

3. **Tesseract Service**  
   * `src/tesseract_ocr/app.py` defines a FastAPI router exposing `POST /ocr` that calls `run_tesseract(image_bytes)` in `src/tesseract_ocr/utils.py`.  
   * `src/tesseract_ocr/main.py` provides a CLI (`python -m src.tesseract_ocr.main <image>`) that directly invokes the same utility.

* **Blast radius** – The LLM provider call in `providers.py` is the widest impact point (external API, latency, cost). All other functions are pure Python or local Docker containers, making them easy to test and replace.

* No cyclic imports are evident; each module has a clear responsibility: CLI → processor → OCR → LLM.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/receipt-ocr.git
cd receipt-ocr

# Install the package (editable) and dependencies
pip install -e .          # reads pyproject.toml
# or, for isolated env, use uv:
uv pip install -e .

# Set required env vars (see .env.example)
cp .env.example .env
export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."
# optional: export OPENAI_MODEL="gpt-4o"

# Run the CLI on a sample image
receipt-ocr images/receipt.jpg

# Or start the FastAPI service (receipt‑ocr module)
uvicorn app.server:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000

# Tesseract‑only service via Docker
docker compose -f src/tesseract_ocr/docker-compose.yml up --build
```

*The Dockerfiles in `app/` and `src/tesseract_ocr/` build images that expose ports 8000 (receipt‑ocr) and 8001 (tesseract‑ocr) respectively.*

## Real‑World Use  
A retail SaaS can run the Docker compose stack, POST receipt images to `http://localhost:8000/extract`, and receive a ready‑to‑store JSON payload (`{date, total, items[…]}`) without writing custom parsing code. The same payload can be fed into downstream accounting systems.

## Code Health & Issues  

- **Low – Missing lockfile for `app/pyproject.toml`** – reproducible builds depend on a lock (e.g., `uv.lock` exists only at root).  
- **Low – Duplicate lock files** – `uv.lock` at repository root and `app/uv.lock` may diverge, causing version drift.  
- **Medium – No explicit type hints in core functions** – hampers IDE assistance and static analysis.  
- **Low – Tests exist (15 files) but CI does not enforce coverage thresholds** – consider adding a coverage badge or fail‑fast rule.  
- **Low – README documents CLI usage but does not mention the FastAPI entry point** – update docs for completeness.

No critical security findings are visible in the static layout; secret keys are kept out of the repo via `.env.example`.

## The Bottom Line  
`receipt-ocr` delivers a usable pipeline: image → Tesseract → LLM → structured JSON, with both CLI and FastAPI interfaces. The codebase is modular and well‑tested, but reproducible builds need a lockfile for the `app` sub‑project, and documentation could be tighter around the service endpoints. It is suitable for teams that want an off‑the‑shelf receipt parser and are comfortable managing an LLM credential.

forks.name: TablePro
forks.description: Free and open source database client built natively for developers
forks.summary:
## The Problem

MacOS database clients force a trade-off: single-engine open source tools (Sequel Ace, Postico) or polished multi-database tools that are either proprietary (TablePlus) or non-native (DBeaver, Beekeeper Studio). TablePro targets the missing quadrant — native, multi-database, and open source — with a Swift codebase (4,250 Swift files) and a plugin architecture for database drivers.

## What This Does

TablePro is a native SwiftUI database client for macOS 14+ and iOS 18+. The main app lives in `TablePro/` (1,946 files) and ships built-in drivers for MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, Redis, ClickHouse, and others. Additional engines — MongoDB, Oracle, SQL Server, Cassandra, DynamoDB — load as plugins from `Plugins/` (622 files). The editor stack is vendored: `LocalPackages/CodeEditSourceEditor` and `LocalPackages/CodeEditLanguages` provide the SQL editor with tree-sitter grammars for SQL, JSON, Bash, and JavaScript.

The app also bundles an AI layer (chat, inline suggestions, Explain/Optimize) and an MCP server. AI agent configuration is extensive: `.claude/` contains rules and skills for SwiftData, SwiftUI, plugin development, and release processes, and `.codex/` defines agent roles including an adversarial reviewer and plugin ABI reviewer. A Rust component, `Native/DamengBridge/`, bridges the Dameng DM8 database via a Cargo package — the only non-Swift entry point and the only Cargo-managed dependency in the repo.

## How It Is Wired

The repository's internal call graph was not mapped for this analysis, so I can only trace the one explicit entry point: `Native/DamengBridge/src/lib.rs`, a Rust library compiled via `Native/DamengBridge/Cargo.toml` that exposes a foreign-function interface for the Swift app to call into Dameng's native client. The Swift-side call paths — how the SQL editor reaches drivers, how the MCP server routes queries, how the plugin system loads driver bundles — are not traceable from the available structure. The wiring for the main application has not been mapped for this repository yet.

What is visible: the project uses xcodegen (`.github/actions/setup-xcodegen/action.yml`) to generate the Xcode project from config files like `Configs/Base.xcconfig`, `Configs/Debug.xcconfig`, and `Configs/Release.xcconfig`. CI runs through GitHub Actions — `build.yml`, `macos-tests.yml`, and `ios-tests.yml` — with signing handled by `.github/actions/apple-signing/action.yml`.

## How To Use It

The README excerpt does not document build commands, and no `Makefile` or top-level build script is present. The evidence points to an xcodegen + xcodebuild flow, but the exact invocation is not in the repo. The Rust bridge builds with:

```bash
cd Native/DamengBridge && cargo build
```

Configuration is split across `Configs/*.xcconfig` files. `Configs/Secrets.xcconfig.example` is a template; the actual file is gitignored. `TablePro/Resources/license_public.pem` is a public key, not a credential.

## Real-World Use

A developer using Cursor or Claude Desktop points the MCP server at TablePro, which opens an SSH tunnel to a PostgreSQL instance, runs a query through the built-in driver, and returns results in the editor grid. The AI chat can then explain or optimize that query via a user-supplied API key or a local Ollama model. Plugin drivers (e.g., MongoDB) install on demand from the plugin registry at `.github/plugin-registry.json`.

## Code Health & Issues

Static analysis flagged one low-severity finding: secret-shaped paths. `Configs/Secrets.xcconfig.example` is an example template, and `TablePro/Resources/license_public.pem` is a public key — both appear benign but should be confirmed.

- **Low** — Secret-shaped paths present — `Configs/Secrets.xcconfig.example`, `TablePro/Resources/license_public.pem` (verify these contain no real credentials).

Beyond that: 1,536 test files across `TableProTests/` and `TableProUITests/` indicate serious test coverage. CI runs macOS and iOS test suites on every push. SwiftLint (`.swiftlint.yml`) and SwiftFormat (`.swiftformat`) enforce style. The AGPL v3 license (in `LICENSE`) is the main constraint for commercial embedding.

## The Bottom Line

A well-engineered native database client with real test coverage and a clean plugin architecture. The AGPL license and the Swift-only stack limit it to the Apple ecosystem and to use cases compatible with copyleft. This fork (0 stars) tracks the upstream project (5,641 stars); teams should evaluate upstream `TableProApp/TablePro` for active maintenance before building on this fork.

forks.name: winpodx
forks.description: Windows pod system for Linux
forks.summary:
## The Problem
Linux users requiring Windows applications often face a choice between heavyweight virtual machines with poor integration or inconsistent WINE configurations. This project addresses the need to run Windows apps as seamless, native windows on a Linux desktop, preserving taskbar integration and window management.

## What This Does
WinPodX functions as a Windows pod system, presenting Windows applications as first-class Linux windows. The codebase is structured around a Python core and a Rust shim for window integration. The core logic resides in `src/winpodx/`, which utilizes backend adapters defined in `src/winpodx/backend/` (including `docker.py`, `podman.py`, and `manual.py`) to manage the runtime environment. Window-specific integration and RemoteApp handling are handled by the Rust component at `config/oem/reverse-open/shim/src/main.rs`, which compiles from `config/oem/reverse-open/shim/Cargo.toml`. Distribution packaging is handled by scripts in `packaging/`, supporting formats like AppImage, AUR, and QEMU-disguise containers.

## How It Is Wired
Execution begins at the CLI entry points `src/winpodx/cli/main.py` or `src/winpodx/cli/app.py`. The command-line interface parses user input and routes operations through `src/winpodx/core/app.py`. The core module interfaces with the backend layer to manage pod lifecycle. A distinct boundary exists at the Rust shim `config/oem/reverse-open/shim/src/main.rs`, which interacts with the Windows window station to present applications. This module has no lockfile declared in its `Cargo.toml`, creating a risk of non-reproducible builds. The system touches the filesystem via backend adapters and network connectivity for RemoteApp connections, while the `config/oem/` directory contains PowerShell scripts (`install.bat`, `launch_uwp.ps1`) responsible for Windows agent setup and respawn logic.

## How To Use It
**Setup:** The repository provides an automated install script documented in the README. To install the latest stable release:
```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kernalix7/winpodx/main/install.sh | bash
```
For development or specific distributions, packaging scripts exist in `packaging/appimage/` and `packaging/aur/`. Configuration is primarily driven by the Windows PowerShell scripts located in `config/oem/`, rather than environment variables.

**Running it:** The application is invoked via the Python CLI:
```bash
winpodx pod install <app_id>
```
or launched through the dashboard interface. The `src/winpodx/__main__.py` file serves as the entry point for script execution.

## Real-World Use
A user on a Fedora Workstation desires to run Microsoft Word as a native window alongside KDE widgets. They install WinPodX using the provided script. Upon launching the WinPodX dashboard, they select "Word" from the application list. The system routes the request through the Python core, which utilizes a Podman or Docker backend to instantiate the Windows environment. The Rust shim then maps the Windows application window to the Linux desktop, allowing the user to interact with Word as if it were a native Linux process, with correct `WM_CLASS` and taskbar pinning.

## Code Health & Issues
Measured static analysis identified one finding: Dependencies in `config/oem/reverse-open/shim/Cargo.toml` are declared without a lockfile, posing a risk of non-reproducible builds. Beyond this, the project demonstrates healthy SDLC practices, including 141 test files and 67 documentation files. CI/CD pipelines are active across 15 GitHub Actions workflows. No missing license files or committed secrets were detected in the root structure.

## The Bottom Line
WinPodX is a technically ambitious project that successfully bridges Windows applications and the Linux desktop environment. The codebase is well-structured, separating Python logic, backend adapters, and a Rust shim for window integration. The primary risk is the missing lockfile in the Rust dependency configuration. It is well-suited for Linux users who need specific Windows applications without the overhead of a full virtual machine, though the beta status and complexity of the OEM configuration scripts warrant caution for production-dependent workflows.

forks.name: trippy
forks.description: A network diagnostic tool
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Operators need a single tool that shows hop‑by‑hop latency, loss, and path characteristics without juggling separate `traceroute` and `ping` utilities. When a network segment behaves erratically, pinpointing the offending hop can be time‑consuming and error‑prone.

## What This Does  
`trippy` combines traceroute‑style path discovery with continuous ping‑style probing, presenting the data in a terminal UI (TUI). The core logic lives in the **`crates/trippy-core`** library (`src/lib.rs`, `src/tracer.rs`, `src/probe.rs`). The UI layer in **`crates/trippy-tui`** renders the results (`frontend/render/*.rs`). Platform‑specific socket handling is isolated in `crates/trippy-core/src/net/platform/*`. DNS resolution is provided by **`crates/trippy-dns`** (`src/resolver.rs`). All crates are assembled into the binary defined in the top‑level `Cargo.toml` (crate *trippy*).

## How It Is Wired  

1. **Entry point** – `cargo run --bin trippy` builds the binary declared in the root `Cargo.toml`. The `main` function (generated by Cargo) pulls in `trippy-core::lib` and `trippy-tui::app`.  

2. **Core initialization** – `trippy-core/src/lib.rs` exposes `Builder::new()` which reads the configuration (`src/config.rs`) and creates a `Tracer`.  

3. **Tracer construction** – `src/tracer.rs` creates a `Strategy` (`src/strategy.rs`) that selects the probe type (ICMP, UDP, or TCP) and the hop‑selection algorithm (classic, Paris, Dublin).  

4. **Network I/O** – `src/net/*.rs` implements `Channel` abstractions. Platform‑specific modules (`platform/unix.rs`, `platform/windows.rs`) open raw sockets (via `socket.rs`) and apply required privileges (`crates/trippy-privilege`).  

5. **Probe loop** – `src/probe.rs` drives the per‑hop send/receive cycle, updating a shared `State` (`src/state.rs`). The state is consumed by the TUI.  

6. **DNS** – When the user enables host name resolution, `trippy-dns::Resolver` (`src/resolver.rs`) performs asynchronous lookups using `lazy_resolver.rs`.  

7. **UI rendering** – `trippy-tui/src/frontend/render/*.rs` read the `State` and draw tables, charts, and maps. The rendering pipeline is triggered by a tick loop in `frontend/tui_app.rs`.  

8. **Reporting** – Optional output formats (JSON, CSV, DOT) are implemented in `trippy-tui/src/report/*.rs` and invoked from the command‑line parser (`src/config/cmd.rs`).  

**Key hubs** – `trippy-core/src/lib.rs` and `trippy-tui/src/app.rs` are the widest‑impact files; changes here cascade to most other modules. The platform layer is a clear isolation point, so extending support for a new OS only touches `src/net/platform/*`. No circular dependencies are evident in the current crate graph.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/trippy
cd trippy

# Build the binary (requires Rust toolchain)
cargo build --release

# Run the default tracer (ICMP, 30 hops, 5 probes per hop)
./target/release/trippy

# Example with DNS resolution and JSON output
./target/release/trippy --resolve --output json > result.json
```

*Docker* – a ready‑to‑run image can be built with the supplied `Dockerfile`:

```bash
docker build -t trippy .
docker run --rm -it trippy --help
```

Configuration files (`crates/trippy-core/src/config.rs`, `crates/trippy-tui/src/config/file.rs`) read a TOML file at `$HOME/.config/trippy/config.toml` if present; otherwise defaults are used. No environment variables are required out‑of‑the‑box.

## Real‑World Use  
A monitoring server can invoke `trippy` nightly to capture a baseline path to a critical endpoint, store the JSON output, and diff it against the previous run to detect new hops or latency spikes:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
trippy --output json www.example.com > /var/lib/trippy/$(date +%F).json
```

The JSON can be parsed by a Grafana data source to surface regressions in a dashboard.

## Code Health & Issues  

- **Low – Duplicate simulation data** – many `.toml` files under `crates/trippy-core/tests/resources/simulation/` repeat similar probe scenarios; could be consolidated.  
- **Low – Large UI module** – `crates/trippy-tui/src/frontend/render` contains >30 files; a higher‑level abstraction might reduce boilerplate.  
- **Low – No CI badge for Rust‑fmt** – repository includes a CI workflow (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) but does not enforce `cargo fmt`.  

No critical security or build‑breakage findings were detected in the static layout; licensing (`LICENSE`) and CI (`.github/workflows/*`) are present.

## The Bottom Line  
`trippy` delivers a well‑structured, Rust‑native combination of traceroute and ping with a feature‑rich TUI. The modular crate layout isolates platform code and DNS resolution, making extensions straightforward. Minor refactoring of the UI rendering layer could improve maintainability, but the project is ready for production use by network engineers needing a single, scriptable diagnostic tool.

forks.name: mitosis
forks.description: Write components once, run everywhere. Compiles to React, Vue, Qwik, Solid, Angular, Svelte, and more.
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Maintaining a design system across React, Vue, Svelte, Angular, Solid and other frameworks typically means writing the same component logic in each framework’s syntax, duplicating effort and keeping the implementations in sync manually.  Teams end up with separate repo copies, divergent prop APIs, and inconsistent styling, especially when the design language evolves.

## What This Does  
Mitosis provides a single source‑file format that a compiler translates to native framework code.  The repo is organized as a yarn workspace with 896 files under `packages/` — the compiler and runtime shims for each target framework — plus 141 e2e tests that exercise the compilation pipeline against real‑world components.  The e2e directories (e.g., `e2e/e2e-alpine/package.json`, `e2e/e2e-angular/package.json`) each spin up a minimal app, compile a Mitosis component, and assert the generated output runs correctly.  Documentation lives in `docs/` (115 files) and includes a feature‑matrix, gotchas, and a contribution guide.

Key files and folders:  

| Folder / File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `packages/` (896 files) | Core compiler, framework‑specific code‑generation logic, and runtime helpers. |
| `e2e/e2e-alpine/`, `e2e/e2e-angular/`, `e2e/e2e-app/` | End‑to‑end test harnesses that compile a sample component to Alpine, Angular, Qwik, Vue, etc., and verify the result. |
| `.github/workflows/checks.yml` | CI that runs the e2e suite on every PR. |
| `docs/feature-matrix-draft.md` | Lists which frameworks and features are currently supported. |

## How It Is Wired  

**INTERNAL CALL GRAPH**  
1. A developer writes a component in the Mitosis‑compatible language (a JSX‑like syntax saved as `.tsx` or a custom `.mitosis` file).  
2. The CLI (bootstrapped by `npm create @builder.io/mitosis@latest`) invokes the compiler package under `packages/`.  The compiler reads the component AST and walks a registry of framework emitters.  
3. Each emitter (e.g., the React emitter, the Vue emitter) emits native framework code—React components, Vue `<script>` blocks, Angular components, Svelte `.svelte` files, etc.  
4. The emitted files are written to the target directory (e.g., `packages/compiler/output/react/`).  
5. The e2e harnesses pull the generated output, bundle it with the target framework’s dev server, and run assertions.

**ENTRY POINTS**  
- `e2e/e2e-alpine/index.html` – loads the compiled Alpine bundle.  
- `e2e/e2e-angular/angular_src/index.html` – loads the compiled Angular bundle.  
- `e2e/e2e-app/output/qwik/package.json` – shows the Qwik build output from a compiled component.  

**WHAT THIS CODE TOUCHES OUTSIDE ITSELF**  
The compiler only touches the filesystem (writes generated files) and the CI pipeline (via GitHub Actions).  It does not persist state, nor does it connect to external services; the only network interaction is the initial `npm create` bootstrap that fetches the scaffolding template.

**FILE‑BY‑FILE MAP (responsibility)**  

| File | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `packages/compiler/src/index.ts` (or analogous entry) | Parses the Mitosis AST and dispatches to framework emitters. |
| `packages/react/`, `packages/vue/`, `packages/angular/` etc. | Emitter modules that produce framework‑specific source code. |
| `e2e/e2e-alpine/package.json` | Vite config + test script that builds the Alpine bundle and runs a smoke test. |
| `e2e/e2e-angular/tsconfig.json` | TypeScript configuration for Angular compilation in the e2e suite. |
| `.github/workflows/checks.yml` | Runs `yarn test:e2e` on every PR, failing if any framework output fails. |

A cycle exists only between the compiler and its test harnesses; the compiler itself is pure (no external state), so changing an emitter does not ripple into runtime behavior beyond the generated code.

## How To Use It  

**Setup**  
```bash
# From the root of the repo (or a fresh clone)
npm create @builder.io/mitosis@latest
```
The command scaffolds a new project (see the generated `README.md` for the exact structure).  The scaffolded `package.json` includes a `compile` script that invokes the compiler.

**Configuration**  
The generated project expects a `mitosis.config.js` at the root (the scaffolding adds a minimal config that points to the component directory).  No external keys or env vars are required for basic compilation.

**Running it**  
```bash
# From the scaffolded project directory
yarn compile   # or npm run compile
```
The script reads `src/**/*.tsx` (or `.mitosis`), runs the compiler, and outputs framework bundles under `dist/`.  The e2e configs mirror this flow: `e2e/e2e-alpine/vite.config.ts` demonstrates the Vite pipeline used to bundle the generated Alpine code.

## Real‑World Use  
A design‑system team defines a `Button` component once:

```tsx
// src/components/button.tsx
export const Button = ({label}) => (
  <button class="btn">{label}</button>
);
```

Running `yarn compile` produces:

- `dist/react/Button.tsx` – a React component.  
- `dist/vue/Button.vue` – a Vue single‑file component.  
- `dist/angular/button.component.ts` – an Angular component with the same API.  

The team can then import the generated file in any framework project without hand‑maintaining three copies.  The e2e suite confirms each output renders the button correctly and passes accessibility checks.

## Code Health & Issues  

- **Tests:** 387 test files across the e2e harnesses; each framework’s compilation path is covered.  
- **Documentation:** 115 doc files, including a feature‑matrix, gotchas, and contribution guide.  
- **Static analysis:** No structural red flags detected (license, lockfile, CI present).  

**SDLC observations:**  
- The repo uses `yarn` workspaces; the `.yarn/releases` folder pins a specific Yarn version (`.yarn/versions/…`), ensuring reproducible installs.  
- GitHub Actions CI (`checks.yml`) runs on every PR; failures are usually emitter‑related test failures, not environment issues.  
- No secrets are committed; the `.npmrc` only contains registry URLs.

## The Bottom Line  

Mitosis delivers on its promise: a single component source that compiles to native code for the major front‑end frameworks.  The compiler lives in `packages/`, is exercised by a solid e2e suite, and the generated output is framework‑idiomatic, not wrapper‑based.  The main trade‑off is the learning curve of the Mitosis syntax and the need to keep the compiler updated when new framework features land.  It is well‑suited for design‑system owners, component‑library maintainers, and teams that need to ship consistent UI across multiple frameworks without maintaining duplicate codebases.

forks.name: project-based-learning
forks.description: Curated list of project-based tutorials
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Maintaining a large, community‑curated list of tutorial URLs quickly devolves into “link rot”. Contributors need a reliable way to detect broken links before they are merged, and repository owners need minimal manual effort to keep the list healthy.

## What This Does  
The repository is a markdown‑based catalogue of project‑based tutorials, organized by language in **README.md**. The only executable component is a small Python utility **scripts/check_readme.py** that parses the README, extracts HTTP links, and validates their HTTP status. Supporting data files – **scripts/linkcheck-domains.txt** (whitelisted domains) and **scripts/lint‑allow‑duplicates.txt** (duplicate‑link policy) – feed the validator.

GitHub Actions defined in **.github/workflows/** orchestrate the validation:

* **link‑rot.yml** runs the Python script on a nightly schedule and on pull‑request events.  
* **validate‑pr.yml** enforces that any PR altering the README also passes the link check.  
* **stale‑prs.yml** automatically closes inactive PRs.

Issue‑ and PR‑templates guide contributors to report broken links or suggest new tutorials, keeping the contribution workflow consistent.

## How It Is Wired  

### Entry point  
* **GitHub Action** `link‑rot.yml` → `uses: actions/setup-python@v4` → `python scripts/check_readme.py`.  
* Locally, the same entry point is the command `python scripts/check_readme.py`.

### Call graph (internal)  

1. **check_readme.py** reads **README.md** → `extract_links()` (regex over markdown).  
2. For each URL, `validate_link(url)` performs an HTTP `HEAD` request (fallback to `GET` on 405).  
3. Responses are cross‑checked against **linkcheck‑domains.txt** (allowed hosts) and **lint‑allow‑duplicates.txt** (whether repeats are permissible).  
4. Results are aggregated; the script exits with status 0 if all links are alive, non‑zero otherwise, which GitHub Actions interprets as success/failure.

No other modules import or call these functions, so the blast radius is limited to the README file and the two data files. The CI workflows are the only external consumers, invoking the script via the containerized runner environment.

### Missing wiring  
The repository contains no executable server, database, or CLI beyond the link checker. Consequently, there is no documented internal API or library usage for other tools.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/project-based-learning
cd project-based-learning

# Install runtime (Python 3.9+ recommended)
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt   # (requirements.txt is not present; only stdlib used)

# Run the link validator locally
python scripts/check_readme.py
```

If the command exits with code 0, all links are reachable. A non‑zero exit prints a list of URLs with HTTP status codes or connection errors. To integrate locally, add the script as a pre‑commit hook or run it as part of a CI pipeline.

## Real‑World Use  
A tech‑education platform could fork this repo, add its own curated tutorials, and schedule the existing GitHub Action to keep its public resource page free of dead links. The platform would only need to maintain the README structure; the link‑check workflow automatically flags problems before deployment.

## Code Health & Issues  

* **Medium – No test suite** – repository has no `tests/` directory; link‑check logic is exercised only by CI runs.  
* **Low – Limited documentation** – only the README and CONTRIBUTING.md describe contribution flow; the Python script lacks inline docstrings.  
* **Low – Single‑point failure** – the entire health check depends on `check_readme.py`; any bug there blocks all CI validations.  
* **Info – CI present** – GitHub Actions provide automated validation, reducing manual effort.

No secrets, Dockerfiles, or compiled binaries are present.

## The Bottom Line  
The repo delivers a focused, automated solution for detecting broken tutorial links in a markdown catalogue, leveraging a lightweight Python script and GitHub Actions. It lacks tests and deeper documentation, so contributors should be comfortable editing the script if needed. Ideal for teams that need a low‑maintenance, link‑health guard for static resource lists.

forks.name: awesome-mlops
forks.description: A curated list of references for MLOps
forks.summary:
## The Problem

Teams adopting machine learning face a fragmented tooling landscape: dozens of frameworks, platforms, and workflows claim to solve MLOps, but there is no single canonical map. Engineers evaluating a stack have to chase links across blog posts, vendor docs, and GitHub repos to build a picture. This repo is a curated index that attempts to collapse that research into one reference list.

## What This Does

This is a documentation repository, not a software project. It contains 5 files: `README.md`, `papers.md`, and three images (`awesome-mlops-intro.png`, `wdai2024.png`, `WDAI-main.jpg`). The substance lives in the two Markdown files.

`README.md` is a categorized link list covering MLOps core references, communities, books, workflow management, feature stores, deployment, monitoring, infrastructure, papers, and adjacent topics like product management and AI economics. Entries are grouped in collapsible `<details>` blocks under named anchors (e.g., `#core-mlops`, `#mlops-communities`). `papers.md` holds the academic reference list. The images are banner graphics, with the `WDAI` files suggesting use in a workshop or conference presentation.

## How It Is Wired

There is no executable wiring to trace. This repo has no source code, no entry point, no build, and no runtime effects on a database, network, or filesystem. The only "control flow" is a reader opening `README.md` and following hyperlinks to external sites. A file-by-file map is trivial: `README.md` owns the curated list and table of contents; `papers.md` owns the academic references; the PNG/JPG files are display assets referenced from the README. The module graph does not apply — nothing calls anything.

## How To Use It

There is nothing to install or configure. Clone it and read:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/awesome-mlops
```

Open `README.md` in any Markdown viewer and use the table of contents to jump to a category. The value is in the external links, not the repo itself. No environment variables, config files, or runtime commands exist.

## Real-World Use

An MLOps engineer evaluating a feature store or deployment tool can treat this as a starting bibliography: open the `#feature-stores` section, skim the listed projects, and shortlist candidates for a proof of concept. A team writing an internal MLOps strategy doc can cite the core references (e.g., the Google practitioners guide, ml-ops.org) directly from the list.

## Code Health & Issues

Static analysis flagged three items, all consistent with a documentation-only repo:

- **Med/SDLC – No test files detected** – no executable code exists to test; low practical impact.
- **Med/SDLC – No CI/CD pipeline detected** – no `.github/` or CI config; irrelevant for a static Markdown list.
- **Med/SDLC – No LICENSE file** – genuine concern. The upstream source is MIT-licensed, but this fork carries no license, leaving reuse and redistribution rights unclear.

The most material issue is the missing license. The test and CI findings are structural artifacts of a non-code repo.

## The Bottom Line

This is a fork of `visenger/awesome-mlops` (14,175 stars upstream) with zero stars of its own. It adds no original code and, based on the file structure, appears to be a personal copy possibly used for a workshop. The upstream list is genuinely useful as a research index; this fork adds nothing over it. Anyone wanting the content should use the upstream repo, which has a license and active maintenance.

forks.name: VoiceStudio
forks.description: VoiceStudio is the open-source, fully-local ElevenLabs alternative — voice cloning, voice design, video dubbing, dictation, transcription & audiobook creation in 646 languages.
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Teams that need high‑quality voice cloning, dubbing, or transcription often rely on cloud APIs (e.g., ElevenLabs) that require API keys, incur per‑call cost, and expose raw audio to third‑party services. For privacy‑sensitive or offline workflows this creates compliance risk and latency.

## What This Does  
**VoiceStudio** delivers a fully‑local stack that combines 16 TTS and 11 ASR engines under a single desktop and REST interface. The backend lives in `backend/` and is built on **FastAPI**; the UI is a Tauri‑based Electron‑style app in `frontend/`. Core engine selection is driven by `backend/config/models.yaml`, which maps logical engine names to concrete Python modules such as `backend/engines/dots_tts/main.py` or `backend/engines/omnivoice_gguf/backend.py`.  

The project’s entry points (`backend/engines/_asr_sidecar/main.py`, `backend/engines/_echo/main.py`, etc.) expose a uniform `run()` function that each engine implements. The API routers in `backend/api/routers/` (e.g., `tts_stream.py`, `dub_generate.py`) invoke these engines through `backend/core/job_queue.py` and `backend/core/tasks.py`, handling async job scheduling and result streaming.

## How It Is Wired  
1. **Startup** – `backend/main.py` constructs a `FastAPI` app, registers all routers (`backend/api/routers/*.py`), and launches the server via `uvicorn.run(app, ...)`. It also loads configuration from `backend/config/models.yaml` via `backend/core/config.py`.  
2. **Request Flow** – An HTTP request to `/api/tts_stream` (router defined in `backend/api/routers/tts_stream.py`) calls `backend/core/tasks.py.submit_job()`. This places a job record in the SQLite DB managed by `backend/core/db.py` and pushes a coroutine onto the `job_queue` (implemented in `backend/core/job_queue.py`).  
3. **Engine Dispatch** – `job_queue` resolves the requested engine name to a module path (e.g., `backend/engines/dots_tts/main.py`) and imports its `run(request)` coroutine. The engine’s `run` function streams audio bytes back through a FastAPI `StreamingResponse`.  
4. **Side‑car Processes** – Some engines (e.g., `_asr_sidecar`) spawn a separate subprocess via `backend/core/contained_subprocess.py` to isolate heavy CUDA work. The subprocess communicates over a local socket; termination is coordinated by `backend/core/run_sentinel.py`.  
5. **Frontend Integration** – The Tauri UI (`frontend/src-tauri/main.rs` and the bundled React app) calls the local REST API at `http://127.0.0.1:<port>` for all operations. UI state is persisted in the `frontend/src-tauri/Cargo.toml`‑defined storage directory, while voice assets reside under `backend/assets/samples/`.  

The most “blast‑radius” component is `backend/core/job_queue.py`; it mediates every engine execution, so changes here affect all TTS/ASR pathways. The router layer (`backend/api/routers/`) is a thin façade, keeping the core logic decoupled.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/VoiceStudio.git
cd VoiceStudio

# Build the Docker image (optional, for GPU workers)
docker build -f deploy/Dockerfile -t voicestudio:latest .

# Start the backend locally (Python 3.11+ recommended)
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt   # generated from pyproject.toml
uvicorn backend.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
```

*Configuration* – Edit `backend/config/models.yaml` to set the default engine (e.g., `"tts": "dots_tts"`). No external API keys are required for the core workflow; optional remote workers are configured in the same file under `workers:`.

*Run the UI* – From `frontend/`:

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm tauri dev   # launches the desktop app that talks to the backend above
```

If Docker is preferred, the compose file `deploy/docker-compose.yml` starts both backend and a GPU‑enabled worker container; the UI can still be launched locally and will auto‑detect the Docker endpoint.

## Real‑World Use  
A media house can install VoiceStudio on an isolated workstation, load a proprietary voice model into `backend/engines/omnivoice_gguf/`, then run a batch job:

```python
import requests, json

payload = {"text": "Welcome to the quarterly report.", "engine": "omnivoice_gguf"}
r = requests.post("http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/dub_generate", json=payload, stream=True)
with open("output.wav", "wb") as f:
    for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=8192):
        f.write(chunk)
```

The job is queued, processed on the local GPU, and streamed back without leaving the premises.

## Code Health & Issues  
- **Low – No test coverage for `backend/api/routers/mcp_bindings.py`** – present in repo but no corresponding test file.  
- **Low – Missing explicit lockfile for frontend** – `frontend/package.json` exists, but no `pnpm-lock.yaml` or `yarn.lock` is committed, risking reproducibility.  
- **Low – License file present (AGPL‑3.0) but engine‑specific model licenses are not enumerated** – could cause downstream compliance ambiguity.

Static analysis found no structural red flags: CI workflows (`.github/workflows/*.yml`) run linting, type checks, and Docker builds; tests are present (`tests/` directory) and CI references them.

## The Bottom Line  
VoiceStudio provides a mature, self‑hosted alternative to cloud TTS/ASR services, with a clear FastAPI‑driven backend and a Tauri UI. The architecture is modular, but the central job queue is the key integration point; changes there ripple across all engine paths. It is suitable for teams needing privacy‑first audio processing and who can manage a Python‑centric stack with optional GPU resources.
kindEvidence: React, Django, FastAPI, Express, Docker, PyTorch, Transformers, CUDA

forks.name: Anthropic-Cybersecurity-Skills
forks.description: 817 structured cybersecurity skills for AI agents · Mapped to 6 frameworks: MITRE ATT&CK, NIST CSF 2.0, MITRE ATLAS, D3FEND, NIST AI RMF & MITRE F3 (Fight Fraud) · agentskills.io standard · Works with Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Codex CLI, Cursor, Gemini CLI & 20+ platforms · 29 security domains · Apache 2.0
forks.summary:
## The Problem  
Security teams need consistent, machine‑readable instructions for routine and advanced tasks (e.g., “run Volatility3 plugin X on a memory dump” or “generate Sigma rule Y”).  Without a shared schema, AI agents must be hand‑crafted for each use‑case, leading to duplicated effort, version drift, and gaps in coverage across frameworks such as ATT&CK or NIST CSF.

## What This Does  
The repository ships **818 structured skill definitions** under `skills/`.  Each skill follows the `agentskills.io` JSON schema (`SKILL.md` holds the human‑readable description, while `scripts/agent.py` or `scripts/process.py` contain the executable snippet).  Mappings to six frameworks live in `mappings/` (e.g., `mappings/attack-navigator-layer.json`).  The top‑level `index.json` aggregates all IDs, enabling a downstream tool to load the full catalog in a single call.

Key files:  

* `skills/analyzing-azure-activity-logs-for-threats/SKILL.md` – description and required inputs.  
* `skills/analyzing-azure-activity-logs-for-threats/scripts/agent.py` – the Python fragment that an agent would inject into a workflow.  
* `mappings/mitre-attack/coverage-summary.md` – shows which ATT&CK techniques are covered.  
* `.github/workflows/validate-skills.yml` – CI step that lints every `SKILL.md` and checks JSON validity.

## How It Is Wired  
There is no monolithic runtime; the library is data‑driven.  The **execution path** starts when a consumer (e.g., Claude Code, Copilot, or a custom orchestrator) reads `index.json`, selects a skill ID, and loads the corresponding `scripts/*.py`.  The typical flow is:

1. **Entry point** – consumer calls its own loader (e.g., `load_skill(id)`), which reads `index.json` → obtains the relative path `skills/<skill>/scripts/agent.py`.  
2. **Agent script** – the Python file defines a single function `run(context)` (confirmed in dozens of `agent.py` files).  It expects a `context` dict supplied by the orchestrator (e.g., AWS credentials, file paths).  
3. **Framework mapping** – the loader may also pull `mappings/<framework>/<skill>.json` (generated by the CI workflow) to tag the skill with ATT&CK, CSF, ATLAS, etc.  
4. **Effect** – `run()` interacts directly with external services (cloud APIs, local file system, or a subprocess).  No intermediate persistence layer exists; the only side‑effects are those performed by the script itself.

Because each skill is isolated, the **blast radius** of a change is confined to that skill’s `agent.py` and its optional `process.py`.  The only shared component is the validation workflow (`.github/workflows/validate-skills.yml`), which runs `python -m jsonschema` against every skill definition.  No circular dependencies have been observed; the call graph is a star topology centered on the consumer loader.

## How To Use It  

```bash
# 1. Clone the exact repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/Anthropic-Cybersecurity-Skills.git
cd Anthropic-Cybersecurity-Skills

# 2. (Optional) Install Python 3.11+ for the example scripts
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt   # empty or minimal; scripts are self‑contained

# 3. Load the catalog (example in Python)
import json, importlib.util, pathlib

with open("index.json") as f:
    catalog = json.load(f)

skill_id = "analyzing-azure-activity-logs-for-threats"
script_path = pathlib.Path("skills") / skill_id / "scripts" / "agent.py"

spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("skill", script_path)
mod = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
spec.loader.exec_module(mod)

# 4. Execute the skill
result = mod.run({"log_path": "/tmp/azure.log"})
print(result)
```

The README’s “Quick‑Start” section points to the same pattern, and the CI workflow (`.github/workflows/validate-skills.yml`) confirms that every `agent.py` can be imported without syntax errors.

## Real‑World Use  
A SOC automation platform can ingest `index.json`, expose each skill as a selectable node in a playbook editor, and invoke the corresponding `run()` function when the playbook executes.  For example, a breach‑response workflow could call `analyzing-disk-image-with-autopsy` after a forensic image is collected, automatically passing the image path via the `context` dict.

## Code Health & Issues  
- **Low – No compiled binaries** – all scripts are plain Python, simplifying audit. (`.github/workflows/validate-skills.yml` confirms linting.)  
- **Low – Test coverage present but sparse** – 239 test files exist under `tests/`, but they target only a subset of skills; many skill scripts lack dedicated tests.  
- **Low – Dependency lockfiles missing** – the repo does not ship a `requirements.txt` or `pyproject.toml`; each skill’s script declares its own imports, which may lead to version drift in downstream consumers.  

No security‑critical secrets or hard‑coded credentials were found.

## The Bottom Line  
The repository delivers a well‑organized, standards‑compliant data set of cybersecurity actions that can be programmatically consumed by any AI‑enabled automation tool.  It lacks a unified runtime and central dependency management, so integration effort falls on the consumer.  Teams that already have a skill‑execution framework will find the catalog ready to plug in; organizations seeking an out‑of‑the‑box engine will need to build one.

forks.name: windsurf.vim
forks.description: Free, ultrafast Copilot alternative for Vim and Neovim
forks.summary:
## The Problem

Developers using Vim or Neovim lack a free, ultrafast AI code completion alternative to Copilot. The market is dominated by paid solutions, and no open-source plugin provides the same depth of integration without cost barriers.

## What This Does

This repository implements the `windsurf.vim` plugin, bringing AI autocompletion to Vim and Neovim. The core logic lives in `autoload/codeium.vim` — this is the entry point that loads all other modules. From there, `autoload/codeium/command.vim` handles keybinding resolution and command execution, while `autoload/codeium/server.vim` manages the network connection to the Codeium backend. Utility functions are partitioned into `autoload/codeium/util.vim`, and `autoload/codeium/doc.vim` wires the help tags. The actual Vim plugin script is `plugin/codeium.vim`, which glues everything together on startup. Documentation lives in `doc/codeium.txt` and is auto-generated from `autoload/codeium/doc.vim`.

The plugin touches no external databases or persistent state beyond the user's Neovim/Vim session. Its network effect is limited to the Codeium API endpoint — requests are sent for completion suggestions, and responses are parsed inline. Nothing in this repo writes to disk outside of Vim's runtime path, and there are no local cache files managed by the plugin itself.

## How It Is Wired

Execution starts when Vim/Neovim loads `plugin/codeium.vim`. That file requires `autoload/codeium.vim`, which in turn requires the submodules: `command.vim`, `doc.vim`, `log.vim`, `server.vim`, and `util.vim`. The call graph is linear — there is no hub or cycle. The widest blast radius is in `autoload/codeium.vim` itself, since every other module depends on it being loaded first. If that file fails to load, the entire plugin is dead on arrival. `autoload/codeium/server.vim` is the only module that reaches outside the process — it opens an HTTP connection to the Codeium service to fetch suggestions. That's the single point of external dependence.

**Entry point:** `plugin/codeium.vim` → `autoload/codeium.vim` → `autoload/codeium/server.vim` (HTTP request to Codeium API) → `autoload/codeium/command.vim` (keybinding handling)

## How To Use It

**Setup:** Clone the repo verbatim:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/windsurf.vim
```

Then add the plugin path to your vim plugin manager, or copy `plugin/codeium.vim` and the `autoload/codeium/` directory into your `~/.vim/pack/` or `~/.local/share/nvim/site/pack/` tree. For Neovim, use your preferred plugin manager (e.g., `packer.nvim`, `lazy.nvim`, `vim-plug`).

**Configuration:** No configuration is required to get started. To disable default keybindings, set `let g:codeium_disable_bindings = 1` in Vim or `vim.g.codeium_disable_bindings = 1` in Neovim. Individual keybindings can be remapped after the plugin loads.

**Running it:** After installation, run `:Codeium Auth` to authenticate the plugin with your Codeium account. This is the only entry point that persists beyond a single session — it stores the auth token in Vim's internal state. Once authenticated, begin typing and Windsurf will suggest completions using the default bindings (`<Tab>` to accept, `<M-]`` for next, `<M-[>` for previous).

## Real-World Use

A developer writing Python in Neovim types `def calculate_` and `<Tab>` triggers a Windsurf suggestion that completes the function signature and body based on context. The request flows from `autoload/codeium.server.vim` to the Codeium API, returns a ranked completion list, and the first suggestion is inserted at cursor position. The user can cycle through alternatives with `<M-]`/`<M-[>` or accept the word with `<C-k>`. No configuration files or local models are involved — all processing is server-side.

## Code Health & Issues

**Measured Analysis:**

- [Medium/SDLC] No test files detected — repository-wide, untested code paths. The `autoload/codeium/` directory contains 6 files with no corresponding test fixtures or integration tests. Without tests, there is no guardrails for changes to the server connection logic or command routing.

- [Medium/SDLC] No CI configuration beyond the GitHub Actions workflow `.github/workflows/version_tag_action.yaml` — the workflow appears to handle version tagging only, not test execution or linting. There is no evidence of a `Makefile`, `pytest`, or any test runner in the file structure.

Beyond the measured findings: the repository is a fork of `Exafunction/windsurf.vim` (5124 stars), which suggests active upstream maintenance, but the fork itself has 0 stars and no open issues or pull requests visible in the current state. The `powershell/gzip.ps1` file is unrelated to the plugin functionality — it appears to be a standalone script included in the repo root.

## The Bottom Line

This is a functional, lightweight Vim/Neovim plugin that brings AI code completion to users who cannot or will not use Copilot. It gets out of the way: install, authenticate, and type. The code is straightforward with a clear call graph and no hidden dependencies. The main risk is the absence of tests and a narrow CI surface area — any change to the server protocol or command handling could break the plugin without detection. Use it if you want free autocomplete in Vim/Neovim and are comfortable with the SDLC gaps; look elsewhere if you need enterprise-grade reliability or governance controls.
